News.title: Anthony Zurcher: Democrats eye sweeping gains and reshaping of political map
News.content:
This is already shaping up to be a very good night for Democrats, with much of the vote counted in the eastern United States and polls closing in key Midwestern battleground states.

Two Senate races that a year ago were thought to be battlegrounds have turned out to be slam dunks for the Democrats - Jon Ossoff's re-election race in Georgia and the open Republican-held seat in North Carolina.

That North Carolina contest, where former Democratic Governor Roy Cooper bested Republican Party insider Michael Whatley, was the first of the four pick-ups Democrats need in order to wrest control of the Senate.

Attention has now turned to Republican-held Senate seats in Texas, Kansas and Ohio, where counting is taking place.

In South Carolina, the BBC's US partner CBS News is rating the Senate race as leaning Democrat, which would be an earth-shaking result.

If you look at key races in House of Representatives, there are other encouraging signs for Democrats.

In Florida, Republicans in the state legislature had redrawn the boundaries of three Democratic-held seats to make it much easier to for them to win.

They lost all three.

Other House races in the state, where Republicans expected to win by comfortable margins, have turned out to be dogfights.

Democrats flipped an open seat in western North Carolina, for instance, and appear in position to make gains in Virginia, Kentucky and Indiana.

In races considered toss-ups across the east, Democrats are poised for the kind of victories that will help secure a House majority for the first time since 2022.

They're doing it on the back of high Democratic turnout, particularly by black voters in the south, and winning back Hispanic voters in Florida who had supported the Republicans just two years ago.

In majority black South Carolina counties, Democratic Senate candidate Annie Andrews is significantly outperforming Kamala Harris's presidential numbers in 2024.

And in Miami-Dade County, which Trump carried that year, Democratic candidates are back on top.

News.title: South Carolina Senate seat flips to Democrats for first time in nearly three decades
News.content:
Republican South Carolina Senate candidate Darline Graham is projected to have lost her race, handing Democrats their first statewide victory in 28 years.

The Democrat, Annie Andrews, a former paediatrician, was on course to pull off a stunning upset in Tuesday's midterm elections, according to the BBC's US partner CBS.

With President Donald Trump's blessing, Graham was appointed to fill the seat in July after the sudden death of her brother, Senator Lindsey Graham.

But the political newcomer conceded during the primary that she was "not that informed on national security".

Trump won the state by 18 points in 2024.

During her primary campaign, Graham acknowledged her lack of political experience, particularly after stumbling during a foreign-policy question during a recent debate.

Asked about the US stance towards Taiwan, Graham had said: "National security is not my thing, not my area of expertise, but I do support the military."

Her brother, Lindsey Graham, was elected to the Senate in 2002 and was one of Washington's most influential voices on foreign policy, often pushing for US military intervention overseas.

News.title: US voters name economy and state of democracy as top issues, poll says
News.content:
The economy and the state of democracy have been named as the top issues for US voters, according to an election day poll.

The survey - officially called the Voter Poll - asks tens of thousands of the American electorate their opinions and motivations, and providing a breakdown by age, gender, education and other demographics.

Polling company SSRS collects data on behalf of a consortium of news companies, and the survey is a representative sample of American voters in the run up to the election, and includes exit polling of both early and on the day voters.

Here are some of the breakdowns from the 2026 voter poll. Like all surveys they are estimates; the numbers are also likely to be updated as more data arrives.

News.title: Democratic rising star Ossoff projected to hold Georgia seat
News.content:
Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff is projected to have won re-election in Georgia, defeating Republican challenger Mike Collins and pushing the crucial swing state deeper into Democratic control, CBS News reports.

Ossoff, a rising star in the Democratic Party, portrayed his opponent as loyal to a "failed president" and made the rising cost of living a central issue in the campaign. Georgia, a key swing state, voted for Donald Trump in 2024.

Collins had blamed rising cost of living on former President Joe Biden and defended his support for Trump's war in Iran.

With polls suggesting Ossoff held a solid lead in the race, Republicans had diverted resources from Georgia to other contests.

News.title: When will we know the results?
News.content:
Congress is made up of two parts - the lower chamber, the House of Representatives and the upper chamber, the Senate.

To win a majority in the House, a party needs 218 seats. In the Senate, a party needs 51 seats for an outright majority. But if the upper chamber is split 50-50, the vice-president has a tie-breaking vote, which gives their party control of it.

The first results to come in won't tell us much about the overall result because these races are in places considered safe bets for Republicans (Kentucky and Indiana) or Democrats (Vermont).

Throughout the night, BBC analysts will focus on the competitive races which will give an indication of how well things are going for Trump.

There are several tight Senate contests in the Eastern Time zone - like Ohio, where polls close at 19:30 EST (00:30 GMT) and Maine, where they shut at 20:00 EST (01:00 GMT). These could provide early indications of the electorate's mood.

Some key contests might start to be "called" by US media outlets. They use models to project which way a state has voted, even before the full vote count has been completed.

This happens when they believe a party or a candidate has gained a lead that cannot be beaten. But in some closely-fought states, outlets could take a long time to make their projections.

The overall timing of the result will depend on how tight the races are and which races end up being decisive.

News.title: Miliband says slavery apology will not bring cost for UK taxpayers
News.content:
Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has insisted the government's willingness to consider formally apologising for the UK's role in the transatlantic slave trade will not lead to higher costs for the British taxpayer.

The prime minister has said the UK will not pay reparations to affected countries, but declined to say whether his new approach could involve additional taxpayer money.

Speaking on the BBC's Newscast podcast, Miliband said previous British governments had a "sweep it under the carpet" attitude to the pain and consequences of slavery, citing what he described as former Prime Minister Sir Tony Blair's "sorry not sorry" remarks on the issue nearly two decades ago.

In 2007, Sir Tony said the UK's involvement in the slave trade was a matter of "deep sorrow and regret".

"Tony Blair did sort of do a kind of sorry not sorry situation. He kind of expressed sorrow, and then said sorry, and then it was walked back by number 10," Miliband said.

Miliband said the former prime minister's approach was still referred to and came up in a recent conversation between Andy Burnham and the Prime Minister of Barbados Mia Mottley.

In addition, Miliband claimed, he and Burnham inherited a more recent mess, which is how the last Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM) played out in Samoa two years ago.

Miliband said: "On the second day as my time as foreign secretary, I was told, 'look, one of your tasks is CHOGM 2024, which happened in Samoa, didn't go well.' To use sort of diplomatic speak, it ended up in a sort of punch up, a sort of verbal punch up about this whole issue."

He added: "This has really been hanging around as an issue for the Commonwealth for sort of 20 years, really. But it's grown and grown."

Given that, Miliband said, "we thought it was right to confront this issue and not to just try and sort of pretend that it didn't exist".

News.title: 'Multi-cancer' blood tests coming to some GP surgeries soon
News.content:
The government-funded trial, led by the University of Birmingham, will assess whether the tests are accurate enough for wider NHS use.

The idea of a blood test that can identify multiple cancers is not new.

A separate NHS trial of a test called Galleri recently failed to meet its main goal of reducing diagnoses of late-stage cancers, although researchers are still assessing its potential benefits.

Prof Peter Johnson, NHS England's national clinical director for cancer, said detecting abdomen cancer early was "notoriously difficult" because symptoms can easily be mistaken for other less serious conditions.

Earlier diagnosis gives patients a much better chance of successful treatment and survival.

Around 71,000 people in England are diagnosed each year with pancreatic, stomach, liver, ovarian or bowel cancer, and nearly 35,000 die from these diseases.

The new STRIDE-RCT trial, external is about detecting bowel, small bowel, stomach, oesophageal, pancreatic, liver, bile duct and gallbladder, ovarian, endometrial, kidney, bladder and prostate cancer.

Patients will provide one or two tubes of blood, taken at their GP practice, alongside routine tests.

Scientists will then analyse the samples for signs of cancer and, if present, may be able to pinpoint where in the body the tumour is located.

A positive result does not automatically mean there is cancer, and a negative result is not a guaranteed all-clear.

Health secretary Yvette Cooper said she hoped simple blood tests such as these would help identify patients needing urgent investigation much sooner.

Michelle Mitchell from Cancer Research UK said: "GPs have long needed better tools to help them navigate that uncertainty by identifying which patients require further testing and this trial in England is an important step towards addressing that need."

News.title: Celebrity loses injunction bid but will stay anonymous pending appeal
News.content:
The case raises highly unusual legal issues concerning whether a court should stop publication when an individual claims that a media investigation would lead to them inflicting harm on themselves.

The celebrity first asked the court in the summer to stop the publication of the investigation after journalists contacted him with allegations about this sexual activities with a large number of young women.

ITN and the Guardian said their investigation had uncovered how the celebrity had allegedly abused his "power and status".

During last week's application for a permanent injunction, Mansoori said making the allegations public would have a "potentially fatal impact".

The barrister told the court that the man had tried to kill himself after he had been contacted by the media organisations and was later detained in hospital for his own protection - but later absconded and tried a second time to end his life.

Those incidents of self-harm had not been because of the allegations themselves but the result of "long-term trauma and the fear of trial by media", she argued.

"The only reason [suicide attempts] would not be fatal is because the claimant would be locked up and prevented from his desire to end his life," she said.

Lawyers for the media groups argued that there was a strong public interest in allowing their investigation to be publicised because of the serious nature of the allegations.

In his judgment, Nicklin wrote: "The proposed publications concern serious allegations about the conduct of a prominent person and the alleged use of status, influence and access in dealings with women and girls.

"The subject matter includes alleged abuse of power, sexual misconduct and inappropriate conduct towards younger or vulnerable persons.

"Those are matters capable of making a significant contribution to public debate."

The celebrity argued that publishing the allegations would breach his protections under the European Convention on Human Rights, including articles that guarantee the right to life and protection from inhuman or degrading treatment.

However, the judge rejected the claim that publication would violate the man's right to life, writing: "No prior case establishes that the Court's knowledge of a suicide risk, together with its power to prohibit the event expected to increase that risk, is by itself enough to require the Court to act."

The judge accepted that publishing would cause the man "acute and potentially prolonged mental suffering" â but said "established law did not impose a positive obligation upon the Court to prevent that suffering by restraining publication".

The man also cited the right to private and family life.

While the judge acknowledged that publication "would interfere exceptionally seriously with the Claimant's private and family life", he also rejected that claim, saying a permanent injunction "would have been an exceptionally serious restriction upon freedom of expression".

The BBC Action Line website has information about organisations that can offer support for the issues raised in this story.

News.title: Poundland supplier 'will lose millions' if retailer collapses
News.content:
One of Poundland's suppliers has said it will lose millions if the firm collapses.

While that supplier will stay afloat, it is feared that some small and medium-sized suppliers could go under.

This is in addition to potentially thousands of job losses among staff.

Politicians have been putting questions to representatives of Poundland owners Gordon Brothers this week seeking "clarity" on plans for the retailer.

Adam Turner, sales director at Highcrest Retail Brands - a family owned Bradford business - told the BBC that Poundland was one of Highcrest's biggest customers, and that the firms have had a relationship for decades.

Highcrest mainly sells confectionary to Poundland, and turns over about Â£50m.

It will "lose a few million" if Poundland becomes insolvent, so it will have a gap in its balance sheet next year, he said.

Highcrest was a "longstanding business that can stomach this", but other medium and small suppliers have told him that "if Poundland goes under, so do they", Mr Turner said.

This echoes a warning from Poundland founder Steve Smith on Monday that two or three thousand suppliers to the firm, which only work for Poundland, would be directly affected by its collapse.

Not only 12,000 Poundland staff would be affected, but also potentially tens of thousands more, he said.

If Poundland's stores are sold to new buyers, some of the employees may get new jobs on the same premises. However, it is understood that buyers are only interested in about half the stores at present - meaning roughly 6,000 employees would not be re-employed.

News.title: UK meat industry hit by cyber-attack which targeted European supermarket freezers
News.content:
Businesses in the UK's food supply chain have been impacted by the cyber-attack which hit supermarket fridges and freezers across Europe on Monday.

The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) says it is aware of "a couple of instances where vulnerable technology had been exploited in the UK."

The NCSC's chief executive Dr Richard Horne told the Today programme, on BBC Radio Four, that it had "worked through the night" to alert potentially affected organisations in the UK.

The British Association of Independent Meat Suppliers (AIMS) told the BBC some of its more than 300 members had unexpectedly become what it called "collateral" as part of the hacks.

Two members saw their fridges begin to defrost, AIMS said, while another saw their cold units rise up to 100C (212F) in temperature.

AIMS spokesman Tony Goodger said the affected devices were empty at the time so no produce was lost - but urged businesses to be vigilant.

The incident "must act as a reminder to all in the food industry at whatever point in the supply chain they are that their businesses may be seen by some as targets," he said.

On Monday, supermarkets in countries including Ireland, Sweden, Estonia, and Belgium reported fridges and freezers being hiked in temperature.

The events followed attacks targeting supermarkets and food suppliers across France in early October.

Hundreds of stores were targeted by the overnight hack, which spoiled fresh and frozen food estimated to be worth millions of euros.

Those attacks exploited vulnerabilities in some systems used to remotely control and manage cold refrigeration units that had been surfaced by cyber-security researchers months prior.

Horne told the BBC on Tuesday that it was still "too early to say" who was behind the hacks.

But he said it pointed to an urgent need for organisations and businesses to ensure the technology underpinning a whole range of applications we use and need daily was secure and up-to-date.

"That technology base we rely on as a society has not been invested on to the extent it needs to be," Horne said, noting many firms had extended systems beyond their end of life, not upgraded them nor kept them in secure compartments disconnected from the internet.

Such actions can create vulnerabilities that many cyber-security experts say amounts to low-hanging fruit for hackers, and can be easily exploited.

But the UK's cyber chief said that they could be found and exploited more quickly and easily via "AI in the hands of our adversaries".

"We do need all organisations to look at what they rely on, to invest in renewal," he said.

"We intervene where we can. But, at the end of the day, it's your business. It's your charity. It's your life. You need to make the choice and choose wisely."

News.title: No more rice grains in Kellogg's Rice Krispies due to changing weather
News.content:
Breakfast cereal giant Kellogg's has stopped using rice grains in Rice Krispies and Coco Pops in the UK due to "changing weather conditions" that have disrupted supplies.

Corn flour and rice flour are being used instead, a Kellogg's spokesperson said on Tuesday, adding that the updated recipes have been "carefully assessed" and the firm has taken customer feedback into consideration.

Those ingredients are replacing rice grains as crops have been hit by dry weather in key producing countries in Asia, reducing harvests and driving up prices.

The new recipes mean cereal packaging will now include a "contains wheat gluten" warning.

Rice Krispies products in the US and Canada will continue to be made with real rice with no changes to their recipes expected, a spokesperson for Kellogg's North American business told the BBC.

The recipe change in the UK will help "maintain consistent quality at a time when changing weather conditions are affecting the quality and availability of some of the rice and grains used in our cereals," a Kellogg's spokesperson told the BBC.

"We appreciate that even small changes to a much-loved product can feel noticeable and that's why we have approached this with a lot of care and consideration."

The company also said that Rice Krispies and Coco Pops will continue to meet UK food standards on levels of fat, salt and sugar in food.

The cereals also contain no artificial colours, flavours or sweeteners and the nutritional benefits in each bowl, such as fibre, Vitamin D and iron are staying the same, the spokesperson added.

News.title: Prince William says UK faces terrifying risk of more wildfires due to climate change
News.content:
There is a "terrifying prospect" of more UK wildfires in future due to climate change and preparation will be "crucial", the Prince of Wales has said.

Visiting Treherbert in Rhondda Cynon Taf, which was threatened by a huge mountain fire in August, Prince William praised a "gargantuan" effort to save homes, land and lives.

"We need to start taking wildfires as seriously as the continent has done," he said, raising issues such as a lack of firefighting aircraft.

He also suggested the community's response to the incident was an example for others to follow, after locals rallied around to support those fighting the flames.

The hillside, just metres away from the community centre where Prince William met fire crews, military personnel and local volunteers is burnt black.

"You looked up [and] the mountain was alight - it was like lava," explained Kath Edwards, managing director of charity Valleys Kids, which runs the building.

"I genuinely thought we were going to lose the centre - but more importantly people were going to lose their homes.

"You never think this is going to come literally to your door and that's what it was - it was just crazy."

News.title: Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor called to give evidence in fraud trial in December
News.content:
Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor has been served with a summons compelling him to give evidence in a fraud trial in the High Court on or around 15 December, the BBC understands

The witness summons will see him giving evidence and taking questions, in a case in which a wealthy woman alleges she was cheated by her former financial adviser.

Mountbatten-Windsor is not accused of wrongdoing, but he could face difficult questions about his financial arrangements as it is said that he was in receipt of some of the disputed payments, including a transfer to him of Â£750,000.

His court appearance will be the first public questioning Mountbatten-Windsor has faced since his BBC Newsnight interview in 2019.

It is also believed that Mountbatten-Windsor is the first royal since the 19th Century to be sent such a witness summons.

Such an unusual royal moment is likely to receive widespread media coverage - not least for the opportunity to hear the former Duke of York's first public comments since being stripped of his titles.

Last month, a judge gave permission for Mountbatten-Windsor to be called as a witness.

The summons was issued this week, with the case set to begin from mid-November and with Mountbatten-Windsor to appear as a witness around the 15 December, which is usually in person, but could be on video.

There have been many questions in recent years about Mountbatten-Windsor's personal finances - and challenges about a lack of transparency - and this case promises to give a rare opportunity to hear his own explanations about his financial dealings.

The case will hear allegations made by Nebahat Isbilen, an elderly Turkish woman, who says her former adviser Selman Turk misled her and used her wealth to his own advantage.

Turk has strongly denied dishonesty.

Mountbatten-Windsor will be asked to give evidence related to disputed questions about the handling of Isbilen's money.

According to court documents, Isbilen claimed she was misled by Turk into paying Â£750,000 to Mountbatten-Windsor, believing it was for help with a passport.

Turk has denied the allegation and says this payment was a gift made on Isbilen's own initiative to create goodwill with the then duke and had nothing to do with a passport.

The case covers payments made at the very end of his time as a working royal.

The transfer of money came the day after Mountbatten-Windsor recorded his BBC Newsnight interview, which was then broadcast the following night, and was soon followed by the then Duke of York stepping down from royal duties.

In 2021, Isbilen's lawyers contacted the then Prince Andrew and the money had been paid back, but the forthcoming court case will consider claims about Turk's behaviour, with Mountbatten-Windsor set to be a significant witness.

Court documents show there will be questions about another significant sum of money paid from Isbilen's account - around Â£768,000 in January 2020.

Turk has claimed it was a loan to Mountbatten-Windsor for the purchase of a chalet in Switzerland - a suggestion which is contested by Isbilen and had been challenged in previous court hearings.

Turk had met Mountbatten-Windsor in autumn 2019 through the Pitch@Palace project, a Dragon's Den-style pitching event run by the former duke.

That had led to social gatherings, bringing together Turk and his family, Isbilen and the then Duke and Duchess of York.

Justice Adam Johnson has said that, given the seriousness of the allegations, Turk should have access to "the evidence he considers relevant and material".

That meant that Turk wanted to use Mountbatten-Windsor's evidence and has been successful in summonsing him for that purpose.

Turk's representatives, Janes Solicitors, said he denies the claims of dishonesty and looks forward to being vindicated in court.

Mountbatten-Windsor has been approached for a response.

The trial at the High Court is expected to begin later this month.

News.title: Chill to grip Bonfire Night as temperatures dip into single digits
News.content:
Dry but chilly weather is forecast this week as millions plan to celebrate Guy Fawkes night on Thursday and the Hindu festival of Diwali on 8 November.

Following the stormy end to October, high pressure has been building in and will dominate for the rest of the week.

For the vast majority of the UK, it will be dry and settled by day with a mixture of cloud and some sunny spells.

By night, temperatures will dip into the single digits with the chance of fog developing in some areas.

News.title: Jury in Russell Brand rape trial begins considering verdicts
News.content:
The jury has begun considering the verdicts in Russell Brand's rape and sexual assault trial.

The media personality, 51, has been on trial at Southwark Crown Court in London for three weeks, facing three counts of rape, three of sexual assault and one of attempted indecent assault.

He has pleaded not guilty to all the charges. Giving evidence, he told the court he had been "obsessed" with sex in the past, but insisted it was always consensual.

The charges relate to allegations from six women spanning a decade between 1999 and 2009. Prosecutors said the complainants described him as someone who "didn't listen" when they said no, and "didn't care".

On Tuesday, judge Mr Justice Bennathan told the jury of eight men and four women he can only accept a verdict they all agree on.

Brand was one of the UK's most high-profile comedians, presenters and actors during the 2000s.

At the trial, he admitted using his fame to "facilitate sexual access", which he now said was wrong, but denied ever doing anything criminal.

His barrister told jurors that Brand "had an immense amount of sex", but that "none of it was unlawful".

He also said none of the women reported the alleged incidents to police at the time, and that allegations in a 2023 TV and newspaper investigation had "poisoned the well of justice" by prompting women to come forward afterwards.

Meanwhile, prosecutors depicted Brand as someone who saw women as a "disposable commodity" who "didn't matter to him" and were simply a "means to an end".

Barrister Riel Karmy-Jones KC, for the prosecution, told the jury that the women said his personality changed "from charming to frightening to nasty" during the alleged attacks.

She said the women, who do not know each other, had been "haunted for years" by their experiences.

One woman accuses Brand of raping her after they had met at the Labour Party conference in Bournemouth in 1999.

She claimed he turned from "camp, friendly and effeminate" to "monster-like" before the alleged assault.

When asked if there was any truth in the allegations that he raped her, he told the court: "No."

Another woman claims that the entertainer grabbed her breasts at a bar in London in 2004 before dragging her into a toilet, where he allegedly orally raped her.

Brand said he remembered going into the toilet with the woman but did not drag or force her there, or force her to perform oral sex.

A third woman had a consensual sexual encounter with Brand and another fan in his dressing room at the Hammersmith Apollo theatre in London in 2009.

She accuses the star of later raping her after he invited her to his house in Hampstead.

She said she had agreed to vaginal sex but did not consent to anal sex. After he texted her six months later, she said she told him he had "treated me like an animal".

Brand told the court they had consensual sex, and denied committing anal rape.

The other allegations come from a woman who says she was pinned against a wall and groped; another who claims he put his head into her lap when she had been forced to give him a massage; and a complainant who says he tried to drag her into a toilet. Brand also denies these charges.

Brand's wife Laura gave evidence in his defence at the trial, describing him as "caring, kind and a wonderful father to our children".

Allegations of sexual misconduct against Brand were first made in a Channel 4 documentary and a Times and Sunday Times investigation in 2023.

He denied those allegations, which related to different women than those involved in the criminal trial.

Brand first rose to fame as a stand-up comedian and became a household name as host of TV shows such as Big Brother's Big Mouth, and with his own radio programmes on stations including BBC Radio 2 and 6 Music.

He went on to establish a Hollywood career, starring in films including Forgetting Sarah Marshall and Get Him To The Greek. He was married to pop star Katy Perry from 2010 to 2012.

In recent years Brand has reinvented himself as an online social, political and religious commentator.

News.title: UK and EU agree draft deal to scrap Brexit red tape over food exports
News.content:
The UK and EU have agreed a draft deal on removing post-Brexit checks from food and agriculture exports, ahead of the UK-EU summit later this month.

The BBC understands the 200-page draft text for this so called "SPS" [sanitary and phytosanitary] agreement has been circulated to EU nations in Brussels for consideration at a meeting on Wednesday.

Similar texts for deals on emissions trading and a youth travel and work scheme have also been circulated alongside a 15-page draft joint statement for UK and EU top leaders.

The food deal is the most significant part of the so-called Brexit reset agreed so far, removing checks and red tape that hit exporters after the UK exited the EU's single market.

As a result of the agreement, the government claims the UK economy will eventually see Â£5.1bn worth of annual benefits.

Speaking during the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (Chogm) in Antigua and Barbuda, the prime minister said a UK-EU deal could add up to 0.4% extra on GDP.

The deal could have the following impact:

Exports to the EU of fresh sausages, burgers, shellfish from domestic waters and seed potatoes would be able to resume

It should remove the need for Â£200 Export Health Certificates, which confirm the product meets the health requirements of the country it is heading to

It should also end the need for Â£25 Phytosanitary certificates, which show that plants or plant products are free from pests and diseases

Inspector fees, organic certificates, some port fees and other checks for exports and imports to and from the EU could be removed

It will bring back passports for British pets being taken into the EU

In return, the UK is expected to commit to observing and adapting to existing EU regulations on plant, animal and food trade standards - a process called "dynamic alignment".

Each of the elements on the table was up for discussion under Sir Keir Starmer, and the summit would have taken place by now had Labour not replaced its leader in July.

Under Andy Burnham, Britain's approach to post-Brexit relations with the EU have shifted significantly. Sir Keir said the UK would not rejoin the bloc in his lifetime, while Burnham has said he would like to see Britain back in the EU in his.

At Chogm on Tuesday, Burnham said: "I think people in Britain would expect me to take that with both hands, given where we've been in recent times, and that's what I'm doing."

Pressed on whether it would be acceptable for the UK to have its rules on food trade made by the EU, he said: "We're not in the EU, therefore we do have to work with them in a different way.

"But if that can get growth, if that can help our farmers, if that can remove red tape from British businesses, I think most people would expect me to go to that summit and negotiate the best deal that I can.

"And that's what I've been doing in recent weeks, leaning in, being positive, having a really constructive relationship with our European partners and hopefully we can land a good deal for Britain in terms of growth but also I hope more collaboration on controlling immigration."

The White House has made it clear who it plans on blaming for Republican Midterm election losses - the candidates.

An Trump administration official claimed the president had done a better job promoting many candidates than they had themselves.

The beginning of the blame game came as CNN projected Democrats are set to regain control of the House, with Hakeem Jeffries on the path to become speaker.

Results are rolling in thick and vast in the Midterm elections, as millions of voters give their verdict on the second Trump presidency.

While not on the ballot, Trump’s agenda for the next two years is at stake if Democrats are able to take back control of both chambers.

So far the Democrats have already managed to pick up a number of big wins, including Jon Ossoff in Georgia and Democrat Roy Cooper in North Carolina.

Overall, Democrats will need to flip four Senate seats and three House seats to gain the majority.

The president, meanwhile, has spent the early part of the evening repeatedly posting about Fox News on social media, about how much he dislikes their coverage.

News.title: From embarrassment to the Man United of old – Michael Carrick saves his job, for now...
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Michael Carrick may still need a greater comeback than this if he is to taste another Champions League night at Old Trafford. But if this proves to be the last, what a way to go. The romantic in Carrick remembers what Manchester United used to be, the days that seemed to be consigned to the past. Suddenly, salvation came from the United of old.

When it seemed Carrick’s job was untenable, there was an extraordinary fightback, a victory plucked from the jaws of defeat, a strange kind of glory from complete ignominy. The crowd who had reacted to the award of a penalty by calling for the Glazer family to go ended up galvanised and roused, cheering a team who had been an absolute embarrassment for 45 minutes to a victory few saw coming, chorusing Carrick’s name.

He has a lifeline. “He needed that win tonight, the club needed that win, the players needed that win,” said the captain Bruno Fernandes. After 54 days without a victory, everyone did. “Big character, big fight,” said Youri Tielemans. “It’s unbelievable, really,” said Kobbie Mainoo.

open image in gallery Man United fans were booing and throwing tennis balls on the pitch in protest during the first half ( Getty )

open image in gallery But they were celebrating the most remarkable of comebacks by the end ( Getty )

United were both unbelievably and believably bad at the start. It defied credibility when they emerged as victors.

Carrick had said he knew it sounded crazy when he said he was looking forward to this game. By half-time, his optimism appeared delusional. But now and again, even when they are at their lowest ebb for decades, United can justify the faith.

Carrick had talked on Monday about a magical night against Roma. That was 20 seasons ago, when United destroyed them 7-1. Fast forward from 2007 to 2026 and, out of nowhere, this version of United stumbled across something wondrous of their own. “This place can do magical things,” said Carrick, attributing it to the power of Old Trafford. It was as good an explanation as any.

open image in gallery Michael Carrick saved his job ( PA )

Roma could be forgiven for wondering what happened, if they are cursed on this ground. Two goals to the good, they almost made it three on the stroke of half-time. Gian Piero Gasperini’s side were showing it was possible to play dynamic attacking football and produce a coherent team in a 3-4-3 formation at Old Trafford, something Ruben Amorim never accomplished despite his best efforts.

Roma’s first win in England in 17 attempts and 25 years appeared a certainty. Instead, they departed defeated, taking regrets for eternity back to the eternal city. Overwhelmed by a Real Madrid fightback in the last 10 minutes two months ago, they suffered again in a strange sequel.

open image in gallery Roma were left stunned by the end of the match ( Getty )

The catalysts for the comeback were Fernandes and Matheus Cunha. The Portuguese scored one goal and made another, showing why Carrick had to restore him to the team after his post-match criticisms of the manager in Italy. The Brazilian had a part in the first goal, scored the equaliser, then the winner and still had time to collect a red card.

Booked for celebrating his goal in the crowd, Cunha was sent off in injury time, sliding recklessly into Leonardo Balerdi. He is out of United’s trip to Lisbon to face Sporting in three weeks’ time.

Victory came at another cost: Carlos Baleba had appeared the first United player to sprint all game when he burst through on goal just after half-time but pulled up holding his hamstring and went off in tears. He presumably will not be seen again until December.

open image in gallery Carlos Baleba pulled up holding his hamstring ( Getty )

So he went off before the game was transformed. If Carrick has been luckless of late, United may have had twin strokes of fortune. They were awarded a penalty, with Gianluca Mancini deemed to have fouled Cunha, and then a retake after Roma’s third-choice goalkeeper Devis Vazquez saved from Fernandes but Bryan Cristante was punished for encroachment. The United captain’s aim was surer the second time around and he ended his own goal drought, which dated back almost two months.

There was almost an instant equaliser. Cunha released Bryan Mbeumo with a wonderful pass and the Cameroonian’s shot hit both posts but did not cross the line. As Old Trafford rediscovered energy and excitement, Diogo Dalot had a header cleared off the line by Cristante.

Then Cunha doubled his tally of goals for the season within the space of four minutes. When Fernandes crossed, Balerdi inexplicably missed his kick and Cunha slotted in. Shortly after, he whipped in a sumptuous shot off the near post to complete a remarkable turnaround.

open image in gallery Matheus Cunha completed the incredible turnaround ( Getty )

“Matheus can do them things,” said Carrick, vaguely. The manager had played his part, too: bringing on Shea Lacey added a threat on the right flank, swapping Cunha and Mbeumo at half-time worked.

And so United’s nine-game run without a win was ended. A second victory in the Champions League this season reduces the chance they will fail to even get a top-24 finish. Yet when the Stretford End threw tennis balls on to the pitch in protest, it was tempting to think that, given United’s problems with football, they were merely seeing if they could fare better with something else.

To begin with, United had surged into a two-goal deficit, conceding twice in the space of eight minutes. It was the earliest any visiting side had ever scored twice at Old Trafford in Europe.

The lack of an alternative left-back has been damaging since Luke Shaw was injured. It was a factor in Roma’s swift double. Preferred to the dropped Lisandro Martinez, Ayden Heaven’s recall swiftly turned hellish. Dalot was dismal, even by his own standards

open image in gallery United were hopeless defensively in the first half ( Getty )

When Rodrigo Mora swept a cross-field ball and a jumping Heaven only succeeded in heading thin air, Dalot was caught upfield, allowing an unmarked Matias Soule to sweep in a low shot. Remarkably, Dalot was out of position again, allowing Soule room behind him, when the Argentinian’s shot hit Heaven’s arm.

Donyell Malen converted the penalty. It was his 12th goal in 13 games. There was almost a 13th, when Senne Lammens made a fine save after the Red Devils’ defence parted like the Red Sea. Forever unmarked, Soule then curled a shot just wide.

Roma could have finished United, and perhaps Carrick, off. Instead, he has a reprieve. “I don’t have a crystal ball to know what happens next,” he said. But whether with a crystal ball, a tennis ball or a football, this was hard to predict.

News.title: Democrat Jon Ossoff rails against 'lame duck' Trump after winning Georgia Senate race
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff of Georgia secured a second term on Tuesday, fending off Republican Rep. Mike Collins to retain a crucial Senate seat in the midterm elections.

The victory has elevated the chamber's youngest member into a prominent figure within his party, as Democrats seek to counter President Donald Trump during the remainder of his term in office.

Entering the campaign as the sole Democratic senator seeking reelection in a state won by Trump in 2024, the 39-year-old was initially viewed as a primary Republican target. However, he launched a sharp campaign focused on criticizing the administration, regularly sharing posts denouncing "a failed president" that circulated widely on social media nationwide.

His campaign generated over $100 million in donations, fueling talk of a prospective 2028 presidential run. Throughout the race, he accused the chief executive of abusing the presidency for personal financial gain while undermining the nation's economic and political foundations.

open image in gallery Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff was reelected Tuesday to a second term, holding a key seat for Democrats ( Getty Images )

Speaking to voters on Tuesday evening, Ossoff reinforced his central message, alleging widespread corruption within the Trump administration and arguing that working families were being left behind.

"Together, we’ve affirmed that our task is not just to contain one president’s wickedness, but to heal the brokenness beneath," Ossoff told the crowd. Pointing to broader Democratic successes across the country, he added: "The American people have rebuked the depravity, corruption and incompetence of the failed lame duck president Donald J. Trump."

Ossoff's opponent struggled to find momentum, raise money

For Trump, Ossoff’s victory is a notably bitter confirmation of his decline toward lame duck status. Trump endorsed Collins for the Republican nomination in a state where the president anchored his false claims that his 2020 defeat was rigged.

But the two-term congressman, first elected echoing Trump’s election lies, never found momentum. He struggled to raise money, navigate his alliance with the president and defend against his ties to white nationalists and an unresolved House ethics investigation.

Collins told supporters Tuesday night that it had been an honor to serve under Trump, who he called the best president of his lifetime. “The results may not be what we wanted tonight, but y’all, that’s OK,” he said.

It had been a blistering campaign with Ossoff hammering Collins repeatedly as a “bigot,” emphasizing the congressman’s past social media posts, his onetime chief of staff’s communications with white supremacists and white nationalist advocacy from Collins’ son-in-law.

“If John Lewis were marching today from Selma to Montgomery, Mike Collins would be grabbing a billy club,” the senator said, referring to the late civil rights icon’s role in Bloody Sunday and the Voting Rights March in 1965.

Collins insisted he had always denounced racism and antisemitism, but the onslaught left him largely unable to land counterattacks that Ossoff was too liberal for Georgia.

“No one has ever asked or held Jon Ossoff accountable for any of his votes,” Collins said, accusing the senator of supporting open borders, allowing transgender athletes to compete in girls’ and women’s sports, and voting “100% of the time with Bernie Sanders,” the democratic socialist senator from Vermont.

Most Georgia voters, about two-thirds, say Ossoff is not “too extreme,” according to The AP Voter Poll. That included most independents and about 3 in 10 Republicans.

Ossoff's aggressive approach against Trump became a model

Ossoff was first elected in 2020, defeating Republican Sen. David Perdue in a runoff held the day before Trump supporters attacked the U.S. Capitol with hopes of stopping Democrat Joe Biden’s certification as president-elect. Ossoff’s fellow Democrat, Sen. Raphael Warnock, won a special election at the same time, both breaking historical barriers: Warnock as Georgia’s first Black senator, Ossoff as its first Jewish senator.

Warnock won reelection in 2022 with a campaign targeted more at Georgia’s moderate swing voters, reflecting the difference for a Democratic senator running for reelection with Biden in the White House as opposed to Trump. Still, Ossoff’s unabashedly aggressive approach initially struck some Democrats as a gamble. It quickly became a model, with Ossoff holding carefully produced rallies where he delivered his withering critiques of the president as young aides quickly cut video clips that were distributed online in real time.

open image in gallery Georgia U.S. Senate candidate Rep. Mike Collins speaks to members of the media during a campaign event on Monday, Nov. 2, 2026, in Atlanta, Georgia ( AP Photo/Ryan Murphy )

Ossoff mocked “Prince Don Jr.,” Eric Trump and Jared Kushner, the president’s sons and son-in-law, for their international business deals. The senator called for ending the Iran war, rolling back many of Trump’s tax cuts, and blasted the president’s tariffs. He highlighted his stalled legislative proposal to bar members of Congress from trading individual stocks and pitched a constitutional amendment to limit corporate money in campaigns.

The senator also carefully navigated the politics of Israel, saying he values Israel’s security and “the lives of innocent Palestinians.” He has voted for some U.S. military aid to Israel and against other munitions grants. Ossoff said the Israeli military has violated international standards of warfare in Gaza but avoided the question of whether Israel is committing genocide — a charge levied by some on the Democrats’ left flank. Ossoff said that’s a matter for the International Criminal Court to decide.

Ossoff also leveraged the work he’s done for constituents in Georgia, earning endorsements from some local Republican officials in the historically conservative state who said he’s been an effective advocate for hurricane relief, infrastructure investments and other federal funding.

“This is what small men like Donald Trump and Mike Collins will never understand,” Ossoff said as he campaigned, “that our national greatness flows not through our blood or our genes, but through our ideas and our aspirations and our care for one another.”

News.title: US midterm election latest predictions: Democrats’ tipped to sweep Congress as first results announced
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Results in the 2026 U.S. Midterm elections are flying in, with the Democrats off to a strong start as the party flips the key seat of North Carolina.

US Senator Jon Ossoff also secured reelection in Georgia in the early stages of the counting in a blow to Republicans who were eyeing the seat.

Other Senate seats to go Democrat include Illinois, Delaware, Rhode Island and Colorado as the party takes eleven to the Republicans’ five so far.

The Democrats would need to flip four seats in total to take control of the Senate, and three to take the House – of which they have already secured two.

This lines up Hakeem Jeffries to be the next Speaker of the House, and the first Black speaker in U.S. history.

Live prediction market data shows that the Democrats’ chances of winning control of both the Senate and House of Representatives for the Democrats continues to grow as voting closes.

If borne out, the predictions would represent a major setback for Donald Trump as he enters the final two years of his presidency.

With the final votes now being cast, Kalshi is predicting a massive 99 percent chance of the Democratic Party taking control of both the U.S. Senate and House. The odds of Democrats winning both chambers of Congress were at 28 percent in January.

A few hours into the voring, Kalshi also predicts that there is just a 0.3 percent chance that Democrats take control of the House while the GOP retains control of the Senate. The chances of a Republican sweep also stands at 0.3 percent, bettors say.

The prediction platform has reported that over $1.6 billion worth of bets on the Midterms have been placed with it this year.

Follow the latest US Midterm results and news on The Independent’s live blog

Polymarket, another online prediction platform, also offered little hope for the GOP. Earlier on Tuesday, its bettors said that the Democrats have a 75 percent chance of taking the Senate while Republicans have a 26 percent chance of retaining it.

open image in gallery A prediction market linked to the president’s son, Donald Trump Jr., has reported the highest odds yet for a Democratic sweep in the midterm elections ( Getty )

The figures represent the Democratic Party’s highest and the GOP’s lowest chances in the market of holding the House since July 2025.

Donald Trump Jr. joined Kalshi as an adviser last year and was given shares in the company worth around $300,000, according to The Financial Times. The president’s eldest son joined Polymarket's advisory board in August 2025 and has an undisclosed investment in the company, via his 1789 Capital venture capital fund, according to a press release.

​Millions of Americans are heading to the polls Tuesday to vote in elections across the country. While President Trump is not on the ballot, he has encouraged supporters to “pretend” like he is.

Numerous polls have predicted grim outcomes for Republican candidates amid public anger over the soaring cost-of-living and the president’s unpopular war in Iran.

In the Senate, the GOP holds a slim majority of 53 seats to 47 held by Democrats and two independents who usually vote with the party.​ There are 35 Senate seats up for grabs in the midterms.

open image in gallery ​Democratic candidates have surged in polls even in deep-red states. In Texas, ​Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico is neck and neck with Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton. ( Getty )

​Democratic candidates have surged in polls, even in deep-red states. In Texas, ​Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico is neck-and-neck with Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton.

Democrats and Republicans are also battling for control of the House of Representatives, where the GOP currently holds a majority. Republicans hold 219 seats compared to the Democrats’ 214. A total of 218 seats is needed for a majority in the House. A number of polls have shown that the Democrats have a strong chance of winning a majority in the House.

​A POLITICO Poll, conducted by PF Global, says that around 9 percent of Trump’s 2024 voters plan to cast their ballot for a Democrat in the midterms.

News.title: Keisha Lance Bottoms makes history as first Black woman elected Georgia governor
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms made history Tuesday as the first Black woman elected governor of Georgia, defeating Republican businessman Rick Jackson and flipping the top office in a critical swing state.

The former Atlanta mayor achieved the win despite being heavily outspent by Jackson, a billionaire who poured over $200 million of his personal wealth into his campaign.

Her election marks the first Democratic victory in a Georgia governor race since 1998.

"What we do in this moment will echo through history," Bottoms said prior to Election Day.

Throughout her campaign, she frequently downplayed the historic nature of her run, choosing instead to focus on addressing economic disparities and acting as a counterweight to President Donald Trump’s administration in Washington.

"Let’s choose hope over fear, progress over division, and come together to build a better Georgia for everyone," she urged.

Bottoms' win defies a historical reluctance among voters to select state leaders from Atlanta, highlighting the political transformation driven by the expansion of the state’s primary metropolitan area.

Supporters react to US Democratic gubernatorial nominee for Georgia Keisha Lance Bottoms's victory ( Reuters )

Her victory follows Georgia reelecting its first Jewish senator, Democrat Jon Ossoff, alongside its first Black senator, Raphael Warnock.

Term limits prevented Republican Gov. Brian Kemp from running for a third term, opening the seat Bottoms will now fill.

This election marked the third consecutive cycle featuring a Black woman at the top of the state's Democratic ticket, following two runs by voting rights advocate Stacey Abrams, who chose not to compete this year.

Bottoms was one of eight Black major-party gubernatorial candidates nationwide on Tuesday's ballot.

Across US history, only three Black governors, all Democratic men, have ever been elected.

Bottoms and Minnesota Republican Lisa Demuth were the two Black women contesting governor races this year.

Although a descendant of enslaved Georgians, Bottoms seldom highlighted the historic implications of her candidacy directly, though she regularly referenced her personal heritage.

"I am at least a fifth-generation Georgian," she explained. "I say ‘at least’ because we can only trace our family back five generations — to a plantation in Crawfordville."

She reflected on how her grandfather had to "walk through these back doors" of downtown buildings that she subsequently entered through the front as mayor, noting that her ancestry "is always present with me."

News.title: Trump staffers order Cheesecake Factory after Obama insult in grim election night fail
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

President Donald Trump’s staffers have ordered dinner from The Cheesecake Factory on a grim election night- meant to be a snide reference to Barack Obama’s insult about White House renovations.

While campaigning for Democratic midterm candidates last month, the former president said Trump “got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory.”

Fox News Senior White House Correspondent Pete Doocy said that some White House officials were gathering in the East Room for a “viewing reception” as votes from Tuesday’s elections came in — and other staffers decided to order dinner from The Cheesecake Factory.

Democrats need to flip four Senate seats and three House seats to win the majority as Trump desperately tries to hang on to control of Congress. While many races have yet to be called, Democrats did see some early wins, including Jon Ossoff keeping his Senate seat in Georgia and Roy Cooper gaining a Senate seat in North Carolina.

open image in gallery President Donald Trump’s staffers have ordered dinner from The Cheesecake Factory on a grim election night in a snide reference to Barack Obama’s insult about White House renovation ( Getty Images )

One White House official told CNN’s Kaitlan Collins, “President Trump did a better job promoting many of the candidates on the ballot than the candidates did themselves."

The president “was not on the ballot, and it’s proven that Trump voters show up when he is on the ballot,” the official added.

MAGA supporters were up in arms over what they saw as an “elitist” dig from Obama about a restaurant chain that many Americans consider an upscale establishment.

Obama has brushed off the uproar, making it clear he has no problem with The Cheesecake Factory and, in fact, it was his “jam for about a decade” while raising his two daughters.

Marin Richardson, CEO of publicity firm Disrupt PR, previously told The Independent that the Trump-Obama feud over the Cheesecake Factory is a win for the chain.

“Both sides are fighting over who loves it more,” Richardson said. “Most brands would pay a fortune for that.”

While Trump’s staff is chowing down on oversized entrees and fancy cheesecake slices, the president is raging on Truth Social at an unlikely target — the conservative Fox News network.

“The Fox News poll, always the worst, is so insulting with the questions they ask. Every question is a hit job, and every answer is ‘BULLS***!’ This has been going on for years,” Trump wrote Tuesday evening.

open image in gallery As staffers chowed down on food from The Cheesecake Factory, Democrats saw some early election wins, including Jon Ossoff keeping his Senate seat in Georgia and Roy Cooper gaining a Senate seat in North Carolina ( Getty Images for The Cheesecake Factory )

Fifty-six percent of voters said that Trump was not a strong leader, compared to 44 percent who said he was, according to the Fox News Voter Poll.

When asked how they feel about the direction of the country, 38 percent said they were angry, 37 percent said they were dissatisfied, 18 percent said they were satisfied, and just 7 percent said they were enthusiastic.

“Fox News ratings are way down (27%!) because they’re spending too much time covering the Trump Deranged Dumocrats! All of those people who used to watch Fox, and no longer do, get it. It’s them, not me — My numbers are better than they have ever been,” Trump insisted in a follow-up post.

News.title: Democrats get early Election Night taste of a big blue tsunami with two key midterm wins
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Democrats are projected to flip a Senate seat in North Carolina and secure another in Georgia while picking up significant victories in tight House and state-level races in Republican-dominated states, an early glimpse of an expected Democratic sweep in midterm elections this year.

Georgia’s Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff is projected to win re-election, securing a seat that Republicans were hoping to flip to preserve their slim majority in the upper chamber of Congress.

And in North Carolina, former governor Roy Cooper is projected to triumph over Donald Trump’s ally Michael Whatley, former chair of the Republican National Committee. The GOP had largely abandoned the state in recent weeks — retiring Senator Thom Tillis, a Republican, has emerged as an outspoken critic of the president — but Cooper will likely be the first Democrat to win a Senate seat in the state since 2008.

Democrats had anticipated a challenging path to winning control of the Senate — the party needed to win at least two states that Trump won by double digits — but early victories on election night and tides turning in critical state-level races elsewhere suggest the road may be less murky.

After following Trump’s command to redraw congressional districts to give the GOP a legally dubious competitive boost in midterms this year, Republicans could end up losing in newly drawn districts they were expecting to win.

Georgia Senator Jon Ossoff is projected to win re-election, securing a hotly contested seat that Republican had hoped to flip to keep control of the upper chamber ( Getty )

Democratic Rep. Jared Moskowitz is projected to win reelection after running in a Florida district that Republicans redrew to favor his Republican opponents. Trump carried Florida’s redrawn 25th district by nine percentage points in 2024.

In another welcoming sign for Democrats, the party has flipped enough seats in Florida’s state House to break a Republican supermajority.

Over the last several years, Florida Republicans have narrowly held two-thirds of both the Florida state Senate and House, giving them significant power to support Governor Ron DeSantis’s agenda while passing procedural rules without any Democratic input.

“Florida Democrats just delivered a decisive victory and smashed the Republican supermajority in the House. Florida Republicans have abused their power for years to push an unpopular and dangerous agenda, including attacking voting rights and rigging their congressional maps,” Democratic Legislative Campaign Committee President Heather Williams said in a statement on Tuesday night.

“Now that we have broken the supermajority in the House, Democrats are better positioned to fight back against rampant extremism and protect against attacks on our democracy,” she said.

Georgia voters also elected Keisha Lance Bottoms to the governor’s office, making her the state’s first-ever Black governor and first woman headed to the state’s top office — flipping a critical seat of power in the South that has been held by a Republican for more than 20 years.

Meanwhile, in Kentucky, Democratic candidate Zach Dembo won a congressional district that Trump won by 15 points just two years ago, marking a key victory that is putting Democrats on the path of securing a House majority.

Democrats are now looking to Texas and South Carolina, states that have not sent a Democrat to the Senate in decades.

In South Carolina, Democratic nominee Annie Andrews could flip a Senate seat that has been held by a Republican since Strom Thurmond switched parties in 1964.

And in Texas, James Talarico is poised to trounce the state’s Republican attorney general Ken Paxton for an open seat in the Senate. Texas voters haven’t sent a Democrat to the Senate since 1988.

News.title: Emery endures heaviest European defeat at the hands of old foes Barcelona
News.content:
“[Barcelona] have [Lamine] Yamal. He is a special player. You can see in him as a player who could end up being the best. He needs a few things but he could end up being a great player. Rodri gives personality to the team. They have [Anthony] Gordon giving them speed and hard work. They have Pedri or Fermin [Lopez] as offensive midfielders.”

Barcelona started strongly in the Champions League, winning their first two games, but lost 4-2 at defending champions PSG last time out. They warmed up for this match with an emphatic 6-1 win over Alaves in La Liga on Saturday. That victory gives them a two-point lead at the summit of La Liga.

“We know that at this level, anything can happen,” Barcelona boss Hansi Flick said. “Against Real Madrid, the result could have been different. These are special matches, but we are staying confident. It is normal to focus more on our last two defeats, but I have confidence in my team, which showed it again on Saturday. Now, we are focused on the Champions League, with the goal of finishing in the top eight. For me, he [Unai Emery] is one of the best coaches in the world and he has reaped extraordinary successes. His team’s style of play is clear and very well organised. Just look at how they execute set pieces; it is something impressive. Their confidence in themselves is unmatched. It will be a tough match against a great team and a great coach.”

Team news from Nou Camp to follow shortly.

News.title: Man Utd show fight on night of chaos to give Carrick a glimpse of hope
News.content:
So maybe there is some fight left in the old dog yet?

At half-time, Manchester United looked down and out and Michael Carrick’s reign as manager as good as finished.

Roma were 2-0 in front and coasting, gorging on a desperate United’s litany of errors, and there was full-scale mutiny in the stands at Old Trafford. A fifth defeat in six matches and the club’s longest winless run for 48 years beckoned. It was toxic on and off the pitch.

And then something changed. United, from being a dishevelled, disorganised mess, suddenly seemed to remember who they are supposed to be and what they are supposed to represent. Surrender gave way to fight. A team that had been feeling sorry for themselves discovered some pride. A crowd that had been baying for blood turned Old Trafford into a bear pit of a very different kind, and Roma simply did not know what had hit them.

This club has served up some famous comebacks over the decades but it was hard to think of too many occasions when the mood and momentum had shifted this violently from one half to the next.

United fans were in open revolt in that first half, releasing green and gold balloons in protests before kick-off and then throwing tennis balls on to the pitch amid furious chanting against the Glazers and Sir Jim Ratcliffe. The players looked like they would rather have been anywhere else.

News.title: Gabonese TikTokers fight back against toxic skin lightening products
News.content:
There is a buzz among the pupils at Nzeng-Ayong 2 primary school in Libreville, the capital of Gabon. At least among those who use TikTok. Black Choco is here: social media personality, entrepreneur, and a bona fide celebrity. With the fervour of a revivalist preacher, she takes over the lesson. Today’s topic is kwandza, the Gabonese term for skin-lightening.

“Is kwandza good? No! It’s like pouring boiling water on your skin. And we don’t do that, do we?”

Why do people want to become white, she asks the pupils – boys and girls between eight and 12 – before answering the question herself.

“To please other people! Aren’t you proud of your skin? Our skin is our identity!”

She asks a handful of pupils to stand up. “Look at them! Aren’t they beautiful with their dark skin? Let them hear it!”

“Gloire, you are beautiful,” the whole class chants.

News.title: Newcastle fans turn on Jaissle as defeat triggers relegation concerns
News.content:
Newcastle United did not just lose to Everton, they lost the home crowd, whose enthusiasm to back their team has drained from them at alarming speed.

This was a performance that belonged in the pre-takeover era, those bad old days under Steve McClaren, John Carver and Steve Bruce. It was a hugely satisfying evening for Everton manager David Moyes, who insisted there was “a way back” for Jack Grealish, even though he was once again left at home after he missed training last week without permission.

The atmosphere went flat early and gradually turned into anger and frustration. The crowd initially tried to stay with their team but were repeatedly punched in the face by the grim reality of the spectacle in front of them. They do not like the style of play, they do not like the application of the players and they cannot accept the results. They are fed up with pretending otherwise.

This was another miserable performance from Matthias Jaissle’s side, who did not manage a shot on target until the 86th minute. He has only been in the job three months, but nothing seems to be getting better.

News.title: US dairy worker dies from bird flu as outbreak rages in cattle
News.content:
“People at greater risk include dairy workers and others who have close or prolonged contact with infected animals or environments contaminated with the virus. Transmission of avian influenza between humans is extremely rare and has never been documented in the United States. Public health officials are continuing to monitor individuals who had close contact with the patient for symptoms,” the health district said in a statement.

Experts say the US bird flu outbreak is not only costing the dairy industry millions of dollars but also raises the risk that the virus could mutate to spread more easily between mammals. They are also concerned that authorities are doing little to check the spread.

Marc Johnson, a virologist at the University of Missouri, told the Telegraph last week that the outbreak in dairy cattle was “completely preventable”.

“Cattle infections last only a few weeks before the animals recover. If infected herds were simply isolated until the outbreak fizzled out, it would stop.

“But cattle keep being moved around, spreading it into new states,” said Dr Johnson, referring to the way the US dairy industry operates, in which cows are routinely transported across state lines, whether to join new herds, for breeding, or to replace animals at large milk-producing operations.

A bird flu outbreak has also been raging on a mink farm in Utah for the last couple of months, according to news outlet ProPublica.

Jonathan Ball, professor of molecular virology at the Liverpool School of Tropical Medicine, said allowing a virus to rage unchecked raises the risk of it mutating.

“Viruses like influenza are constantly exploring new hosts, and more often than not, it burns out. It’s not quite got the right combination of genetic changes to allow it to efficiently infect, efficiently replicate, and then efficiently transmit to the new host. But the longer these steps - adaptive changes, so genetic changes - are happening in these sporadic outbreaks, the more likelihood you’ve got of it mutating. It’s a bit like a one-armed bandit machine - if you keep pulling that handle, eventually you’re going to get three cherries,” he said.

News.title: First ever trial of long-acting injection against malaria to launch in Africa
News.content:
Dr Cristina Donini, executive vice-president of research and development at MMV, said the compound would be “complementary” to existing tools, rather than replacing them.

“The vaccine is doing a fantastic job in infants but if you could add onto that another tool that can cover a broader population with a longer regimen then we would be in a very good position to eliminate the disease,” she said.

Children in malaria-endemic regions are already given prophylactic drugs during the malaria season and studies have shown that these combined with the vaccine are highly effective. However, resistance has developed to these drugs and they have to be given monthly.

The malaria season in Africa varies by region but usually peaks after periods of rainfall. If the season lasts longer than three to four months it’s likely that people would need two injections. However, Dr Donini and her colleagues are working on a second generation LAI which they hope would provide year-long coverage.

Full costs have not yet been worked out but Dr Donini said affordability was an important factor in assessing the LAI’s suitability.

“It’s too early to say whether it will be cheaper than an injection - hopefully, yes. The beauty of it is that if you simplify it and decrease the number of injections needed you decrease the cost,” she said.

LAIs are gaining traction in the fight against infectious diseases - Lenacapavir, now being rolled out after being approved in 2025, provides almost 100% protection against infection from HIV and many believe it could help end the HIV pandemic. There are also LAI candidates in development for the prevention of tuberculosis, treatment and prevention of which usually relies on daily pills being taken over many months.

Lottie Renwick, global campaign director at Malaria No More UK, welcomed the launch of the trial.

“Thanks to sustained investment in malaria science including here in the UK, we are now on the brink of a number of breakthroughs which could turn the tide on the fight against the disease. And the long-acting injectable, specifically, could be a valuable addition to this toolbox as it has the potential to provide sustained protection from a single shot, avoiding the need for repeat doses.

“This phase of the trial also builds on earlier research conducted in the UK, highlighting the importance of the UK’s ongoing role as a malaria science superpower and the value of continued investment in malaria R&D. We look forward to the trial progressing further and eagerly await the results.”
