Puente's predicament presented him and the prime minister with a dilemma - refusing to resign might look insensitive in the wake of the accident and stepping down could look like acknowledging he and the government were at fault.

In the end, Puente opted for the second option, insisting his decision had been driven by "political dignity".

The prime minister praised his colleague who had "faced up to the situation, provided answers and solutions, and then stepped aside".

"Out of dignity. Of his own accord. Out of respect for the victims," SÃ¡nchez added.

Many Spaniards will now ask whether Puente's successors will manage to restore faith in the country's railway system.

World.title: Seven flights across Europe targeted by suspected bomb threats
World.content:
Seven passenger planes across Europe, two of which departed from the UK, have been inspected following a series of suspected bomb threats.

Two Ryanair flights, one originating from Dublin and the other from Lisbon, were searched after landing in Rome following anonymous tips but no explosives were found, sources at the city's Fiumicino airport told the BBC.

The Dublin flight was escorted by the Italian Air Force until landing. Authorities have also searched planes in Poland, Spain and Bulgaria.

While officially there is no link between them, authorities from various countries will be co-operating to assess whether this was a co-ordinated attack, designed to disrupt airspace.

The UK government described the incidents as "malicious hoax threats".

In a statement it said it had "one of the most robust aviation security systems in the world, with well-tested processes for dealing with any potential threats, as well as malicious hoax threats, like those we've seen today".

Aviation security expert Paul Mason said bomb threats on passenger planes "don't happen that frequently", which made the latest incidents "unusual".

"It sounds like they've been made in a credible manner across a broad range of airlines," Mason told BBC Radio 5 Live. "That would suggest to me that it's been a very deliberate act by a typical actor rather than a load of coincidental, malicious calls."

He said "there are a lot of processes" that the onboard crew and people on the ground must go through "to validate the credibility of the threat".

A flight may be asked to divert if the credibility of a threat "is of a certain level", Mason added, and in some cases the onboard crew may not even be advised on what the ground operators were dealing with.

World.title: Binance says fake job interviews used as part of $6.3bn crypto hack
World.content:
Hackers who stole a record $6.3bn (Â£4.7bn) from Binance used fake job interviews and a compromised internal AI tool, the firm has revealed.

Initial findings published by the company, which operates the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, said hackers gained access to its systems through "sophisticated, multi-stage campaign".

It said they used a range of techniques such as malicious software downloads to compromise the computers of Binance engineers and gain control over tools to drain its wallet of billions of dollars worth of crypto.

Binance called it a "serious and highly sophisticated security incident" and apologised, saying "this should not have happened".

In a post on X, external, Binance said hackers targeted its engineers using social engineering techniques.

These see hackers use approaches such as phishing to trick people into parting with sensitive or personal details, that can then be used to try and access their accounts.

Binance said as part of the hack, one of its engineers was contacted through a legitimate job-hunting platform and invited to bogus job interviews with fake company representatives.

It said the perpetrators used "more advanced and deceptive" methods to build trust with him, such as sharing social media accounts that contained personal images.

The engineer in question was instructed to download malware masquerading as an "assignment" during a second interview, that deployed malicious code with "obfuscation techniques" evading detection.

Binance said hackers then leveraged the engineer's compromised computer and a compromised internal AI tool in October to gain control over two other engineers' laptops, and execute the next steps of the attack.

The incident led Binance to suspend withdrawals for customers globally, meaning users could not get their cryptocurrency out of the platform until the service was restored on Sunday.

Customers withdrew billions of dollars worth of assets after it reopened.

"We apologise for the concern, disruption and uncertainty it caused our users, partners and the wider industry," it said.

The company added it had taken a range of steps following the incident, including working with law enforcement to trace and freeze affected assets.

It said it had also set aside more than 100% of the funds needed to cover the loss, noting 98% of the token assets impacted had been "replenished" as of Saturday.

The record $6.3bn (Â£4.7bn) attack is thought to be the largest crypto hack to date.

World.title: NTSB says crucial plane parts found three miles from Florida crash site
World.content:
"Knowing that it was lost is a very important piece of evidence in terms of pointing us towards other things to investigate," he said.

Chapman said officials were still working out whether losing the left elevator caused the plane to nosedive or whether the part fell off because "forces on the aircraft caused that to separate".

He said the part of the plane that controls upward and downward movement may not have been "effective" at the speed the plane was travelling.

The Learjet 60 was bound for the Bahamas from Austin, Texas, when it nosedived into a multi-lane highway and exploded on impact.

In air traffic control audio recordings, someone in the cockpit can be heard reporting "moderate turbulence" and that the crew was "managing the ice".

They are then heard saying the plane was "picking up precipitation" and "we need to climb". Moments later, the same voice said the plane was descending at a rate of 10,000ft (3,048m) per minute.

An emergency was declared and the pilots can be heard yelling "we are in an overspeed condition descending 20,000ft per minute", before saying, "we are going to crash into the ground".

NTSB plans to investigate the role weather played in the crash. Officials were struggling to access the wreckage due to the huge crater created by the jet on a road in Palm Beach.

Chapman said on Tuesday that the force of the impact severely damaged the wreckage.

Seven passengers died on board, named in a joint statement as tech entrepreneur Adam Robinson, his wife, Helen Sharp, and their two children - Emma, four, and Charlie, two - as well as friends of the family Rachael Reed and Charmi Fehr, and Anita Maria Cetina, a nanny.

The pilot was named in media reports as 55-year-old Jeffrey Gregory. Nathalia Filgueiras, 20, who earned her pilot's licence when she was 17, was reported to be the co-pilot.

World.title: Libya's top religious authority rules against wearing Nike clothes
World.content:
Libya's highest religious authority, the Dar al-Ifta, has issued a ruling banning Muslims from buying, selling or wearing clothing bearing the Nike logo.

The ruling, issued by the Tripoli-based institution, states that the US sportswear giant was named after the Greek goddess of victory and that its famous swoosh logo was inspired by her wings.

It argued that wearing clothing displaying the logo amounted to promoting symbols associated "with polytheism," or the worship of more than one god.

Libya is home to the ancient Greek city of Cyrene, where archaeological remains include a statue of the Greek goddess of the same name.

The religious committee also accused Nike of supporting Israel and called for a boycott of companies that back the country.

It referred to a statement issued by its Council for Research and Sharia Studies on 5 November 2023, urging Muslims to boycott Western companies it considers supportive of Israel during the war in Gaza.

The ruling, known as a fatwa, is a religious opinion on a matter of Islamic law. It was approved by Libya's Grand Mufti, Sadiq al-Gharyani.

The BBC has contacted Nike for comment.

The Dar al-Ifta is an influential religious institution based in Tripoli, in western Libya. The country is politically divided, with rival authorities and institutions operating in the east and west after years of conflict following the toppling of long-time leader Muammar Gaddafi in 2011.

Although its religious rulings can carry considerable social influence, they are not necessarily government orders or legally enforceable.

Last year it ruled against wearing jewellery and watches bearing the logo of French luxury jewellery house Van Cleef & Arpels, arguing that its four-leaf clover design was associated with Christian beliefs and the pursuit of good luck, which it said contradicted Islamic teachings.

The latest fatwa does not announce a state ban on Nike products or specify penalties for people who continue to buy or wear them.

Social media reactions were mixed, with some users welcoming the ruling, while others questioned its significance, describing it as ironic or a distraction from more pressing issues.

The ruling comes amid wider debates over the rise of religious conservatism in public life in Libya.

In 2025, authorities in eastern Libya announced restrictions on rap music, theatre and dance performances, citing concerns that some lyrics and performances violated public morals and Islamic values.

The measures were subsequently extended to western Libya.

The Dar al-Ifta has also previously issued religious rulings against music, although there is no clear evidence that it was directly involved in the restrictions on performances.

Nike does not operate an official store in Libya, however Nike-branded products are available through local sportswear retailers.

Sportswear brands such as Nike and Adidas are popular across North Africa.

In Libya, as in other countries in the region, counterfeit versions of popular sportswear brands are also sold in local markets.

World.title: Europe on alert after supermarket freezers hit by cyber-attacks in 10 countries
World.content:
The European Union has raised concerns about the attacks, which come three weeks after a cyber-attack disrupted as many as 700 French grocery stores, causing food losses estimated at tens of millions of euros.

The security of refrigeration systems as well as other devices that can be monitored remotely has heightened concerns about government-backed hybrid attacks.

The EU's food and agriculture commissioner, Christophe Hansen, said the bloc was taking the incidents very seriously and warned of further disruption in the future.

Commission spokesman Thomas Regnier was careful not to attribute blame, but said: "These incidents of course show once again how cyber-attacks can disrupt essential services and affect citizens' daily lives."

"These are not isolated incidents and of course we have to be collectively resilient and prepared for such cyber incidents."

In Italy, Giorgia Meloni's government called a meeting with intelligence chiefs, but said the impact was "currently very limited" and most of the food distribution chain had up-to-date security systems able to fend off such attacks.

At least four Co-op supermarkets in Sicily and one business in Tuscany were affected, according to the national cybersecurity agency.

Meloni's office said those businesses affected were "mostly still equipped with obsolete security systems, with interfaces directly exposed to the internet and inadequate authentication mechanisms".

Belgian supermarkets were among those hardest-hit, with dozens of stores reporting refrigeration failures. Federal prosecutors have opened an investigation.

World.title: Death toll rises in Ukraine after Russia attacks aid centre, hospice and hospital
World.content:
Russian strikes on Ukraine â including on an aid centre, a hospice and a hospital â have killed at least 38 civilians and injured scores of others over the last 24 hours.

At least 33 people are known to have died in a glide bomb attack in the southern Zaporizhzhia region on Monday night, and President Volodymyr Zelensky said the number of victims was set to rise as more than 50 people could be trapped under the rubble.

He called the strike in Komyshuvakha village "one of the largest mass killings committed by Russia during this war".

Ukraine had proposed to extend and expand last week's ceasefire in the Kherson region which allowed people from the frontline Russian-occupied town of Oleshky to evacuate, Zelensky added.

The attack on a school building being used as an aid distribution centre in Komyshuvakha was Moscow's response, he said.

Elsewhere, a hospice was attacked in the central city of Dnipro and a hospital was hit in the north-eastern city of Kharkiv, where Zelensky said 73 people were wounded, most of them elderly patients.

Nine 3,000kg aerial bombs hit Komyshuvakha as residents were gathering to receive humanitarian aid at a distribution centre, authorities said. Local media reported that when the attack began, people took refuge underground but the roof collapsed, trapping many underneath.

"The scale of the tragedy is difficult to comprehend," regional head Mykhailo Semikin said.

Russia's defense ministry said the attack had targeted Ukrainian military units and killed 25 servicemen.

However, there was no credible evidence that the site was being used by the Ukrainian military and there were no major military or industrial facilities in the settlement of Komyshuvakha, reports BBC News Russian defence correspondent Ilya Abishev.

The village is to the south-east of the city of Zaporizhzhia, which has come under constant Russian bombardment.

According to Abishev, Komyshuvakha is of high military importance as part of Ukraine's defensive and transport network on the approaches to the regional capital.

But the UN's human rights monitoring mission said the distribution of humanitarian aid at the local school had been highly publicised and the attack "seems to have violated the most fundamental principles of international humanitarian law", external.

World.title: US strikes Iranian island ahead of midterm elections
World.content:
The US has carried out strikes on Iran's Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, US officials have told CBS, the BBC's US partner.

The officials described the strikes as limited and defensive, and said they were in response to Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) firing on a US aircraft.

Iranian state news agency Irna reported explosions on Qeshm on Monday. The IRGC did not comment but said its forces had shot down two US MQM-170 drones south of the island and a US MQ-9 drone east of the Strait of Hormuz.

The US military has not commented on the strikes, which came as mediators stepped up their efforts to prevent a return to all-out war after the US midterm elections on Tuesday.

Trump has been facing falling polling numbers and pressure from within his Republican Party to end the war, which began when the US and Israel attacked Iran in February.

Earlier on Monday, the president told reporters that he was in "no rush" to ramp up strikes on Iran.

"One way or the other, we will do something, but there is no rush. We crippled them financially," he told news outlet Axios. "They have no money, no gasoline and their people are getting very tired of it."

He also said the US "might need to go after Pickaxe [Mountain]", an underground site linked to Iran's nuclear programme, in an interview with Fox News on the eve of the midterms.

This was "not a big deal" and could be done in "one hour", Trump added.

There has been mounting speculation in the last few days that the US may resume significant strikes in Iran again after the midterms. But asked by a reporter on Monday if that was the case, Trump said "no".

Meanwhile, the Associated Press cited two regional officials as saying that, during a weekend phone call, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had pushed Trump for another wave of strikes on Iran following the midterms.

World.title: 2027: ‘Tomorrow is Here’ group rallies Nsukka voters for Mbah, Tinubu’s re-election
World.content:
The Tomorrow Is Here Movement (THM), a prominent political support group in Enugu State, has mobilised thousands of voters across Enugu North Senatorial District, popularly known as Nsukka Zone, in support of the re-election of Governor Peter Mbah, President Bola Tinubu and all candidates of the All Progressives Congress (APC) in the 2027 general elections.

The mobilisation, which featured a victory walk across several communities in the district, attracted thousands of residents and supporters, with political leaders declaring that the zone was increasingly aligning with the APC ahead of the elections.

The Executive Chairman of Igbo-Etiti Local Government Area, Hon. Martins Ugwu-Amadieze, reaffirmed the commitment of the zone to the APC, insisting that Nsukka voters would no longer be deceived by politicians without credible development agendas.

The rally, tagged “Victory Walk for All APC Candidates in Enugu North Senatorial Zone,” commenced at Opi, Nsukka, and proceeded through Orba, Obollo-Afor and Obollo-Eke in Udenu Local Government Area, before extending to Ogrute, Enugu-Ezike, in Igboeze North; Ibagwa-Aka in Igboeze South and other communities in Nsukka Local Government Area.

Speaking during the exercise on Monday, the Leader of the movement, Chief Tony Okonkwo, thanked the people for their massive participation, disclosing that the mobilisation, initially planned for about 200 persons, attracted thousands of supporters.

He attributed the turnout to the growing acceptance of the Mbah and Tinubu administrations, citing infrastructure development, educational interventions, healthcare delivery, agricultural empowerment and improved transportation.

“We were not prepared to see this number of people enduring a long walk across different parts of the zone that took several hours. Your presence today shows appreciation for what Governor Peter Mbah and President Bola Tinubu are doing.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“The ongoing dual carriageway from 9th Mile through Igbo-Etiti, Nsukka and Udenu to Benue is a major infrastructure investment that will transform our communities. Nsukka has also produced its first indigenous Vice-Chancellor of the University of Nigeria, Professor Simon Ortuanya, after 50 years. Our people are benefiting from federal appointments, agricultural programmes and the Nigerian Education Loan Fund.

“Under Governor Mbah, we have witnessed improved security, Smart Green Schools in every ward, modern healthcare facilities and ongoing road projects. Over 50 CNG buses are also operating from the Nsukka Central Terminal, providing affordable transportation and security to passengers.

“These are visible interventions. We are glad that our people are embracing the APC. The good work must continue, and this is possible if we support the APC from the Presidency to the House of Assembly,” he said.

In his remarks, Ugwu-Amadieze urged voters to reject attempts by opposition politicians to exploit tribal sentiments and political emotions ahead of the 2027 elections, insisting that the APC had demonstrated greater commitment to the development of the zone.

He said the massive turnout at the victory walk reflected the willingness of residents to identify with Governor Mbah, President Tinubu and other APC candidates.

“What happened today was a victory walk for Governor Peter Mbah, President Bola Tinubu and all APC candidates in the zone. From what we have witnessed across Nsukka, I can boldly tell you that our people are happy to identify with Governor Peter Mbah.

“Our zone has settled for APC. We cannot be deceived again by politicians who have no clear agenda for our people. Our people have embraced the ideology behind the broom and are ready to vote for all APC candidates.

“When we approached Governor Mbah with two requests; to assist in securing the Vice-Chancellorship of the University of Nigeria for an indigene of Nsukka and to consider the dualisation of the Penoks–Nike–Ugwogo–Ekwegbe–Opi–Nsukka road, little did we know that he would exceed our expectations within a short period of time. That has never happened in the history of our zone. The people of Nsukka are prepared to reciprocate his commitment through their votes in 2027,” he declared.

Also speaking, the Chairman of Igboeze North Local Government Area, Dr. Chris Onyekachi, reaffirmed his people’s support for the APC, attributing increased financial capacity of subnational governments to the economic reforms of the Tinubu administration.

He said improved allocations to state and local governments had created opportunities for increased development interventions and infrastructure delivery at the grassroots, urging residents to support the continuity of the ongoing reforms.

Similarly, the Deputy ALGON Chairman and council boss of Igboeze South Local Government Area, Barr. Ferdinand Ukwueze, said the achievements of the Mbah administration and interventions by local government councils had demonstrated the APC’s capacity to deliver development.

He expressed confidence that the party would secure victory across the senatorial district in 2027, assuring that APC candidates would receive massive support from voters in the zone.

Among dignitaries who attended the rally were the APC State Secretary, Chukwudi Nnadozie; APC State Financial Secretary, Hon Ejike Idodo; Deputy Speaker of the Enugu State House of Assembly, Hon Ezenta Ezeani; Dan Shere; William Amuta; Hon Favour Asogwa; and the Deputy Mayors of Udenu and Igboeze South Local Government Areas.

Others included Chief Chukwukwurote Odo, popularly known as Messiah na Nsukka; Mrs. Nkiru Ugwuagu, Deputy Mayor of Ezeagu Local Government Area; Vitalis Okonkwo (Oil Money), Special Personal Assistant on Grassroots Mobilisation; Osita Ajih; Local Government Coordinators of the Tomorrow Is Here Movement; and several other APC and THM faithful.

World.title: 2027: Tinubu’s performance enough for his re-election, says education minister Tunji Alausa
World.content:
The Minister of Education, Tunji Alausa, on Tuesday, called for President Bola Tinubu’s re-election for second term on the strength of his prformance in the last three and a half years in office.

“There are objective programmatic deliveries that President Bola Tinubu has made in transforming this country for good in a way that it’s never been transformed before. Nigerians, President Bola Tinubu has done phenomenally well for this country. He has transformed every single sector of this country, and he deserves to be re-elected come 16 January 2027,” Mr Alausa said.

Speaking as a guest on Channels Television’s Politics Today programme monitored by PREMIUM TIMES on Tuesday, Mr Alausa said Nigeria, under the Tinubu administration, now has over $55 billion in foreign reserves, a stabilised exchange rate, GDP growth of almost 4.43 per cent, quarter over quarter, and infrastructural upgrade. He also noted that states have been able to pay salaries.

While the minister praised the administration’s efforts, many Nigerians continue to struggle with the harsh realities of the administration’s policies.

The macro-economic gains often touted by a officials and supporters of the administration have not trickled down to the ordinary Nigerians. Residents have staged a series of protests to express their displeasure.

In his Independence Day address, the President acknowledged the severe economic strain citizens are facing.

He noted that the reforms that followed were difficult and its side effects were real.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

But he said the medicine must not be confused with the disease, arguing that his administration’s “overriding purpose” in the past three years was to “correct our nation’s course.”

Educational score-card

Mr Alausa said that the renewed hope agenda of the Tinubu administration “delivered 100 per cent” in the education sector.

He listed the educational policies, including the student loan scheme, the Inspired Live initiative reaching remote areas, and the Federal Ministry of Education (FME) Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVET) Initiative.

“We’ve made a significant increase in the salary. We call it CATA: Consolidated Academic Tool Allowances. Over 500 billion has been injected into the economy just based on stable tertiary education.

“We have significant money from the Nigerian Education Loan Fund of almost about N370 billion, with about N192 billion in student stipends..We now have students in school all year, all sessions around,” the minister said.

But the out-of-school children crisis remains persistent in the country.

Mr Alausa rejected UNICEF’s out-of-school children statistics. Nigeria is believed to have between 15 million to 17.5 million out-of-school children, an estimate mR Alausa rejected.

He anchored his objection on lack of an updated census figures in the country.

Mr Alausa projects Nigeria bas only eight million out-of-school children. He added that 1.2 million children have been taken off the streets through multi-layer intervention.

He noted thar the National Bureau of Statistics is carrying out a general household survey to “count the number of out-of-school children across the country,” from January 2026.

“I can tell you at the end of the day we’ll have about 8 million out-of-school children,” the minister said.

Meanwhile, abductions of students during President Tinubu’s administration have caused major disruptions in school calenders in different parts of the country.

In November 2025, terrorists abducted 25 schoolgirls from Maga Comprehensive Girls’ Secondary School in Danko/Wasagu Local Government Area of Kebbi State, North-west Nigeria, and killed two teachers.

Within the same month, terrorists attacked St Mary’s School, a Catholic-owned institution in Papiri community, Agwara Local Government Area of Niger State, north-central Nigeria and abducted 265 students and staff members.

In reaction to the Niger and Kebbi kidnappings, the federal government ordered the closure of all Unity Schools, and the governors of Katsina, Kebbi, Plateau, and Yobe States similarly halted school activities.

In September, students and workers of Federal Unity Schools in Anambra, Ebonyi and Enugu states stayed away from school as education unions’ strike delayed the commencement of the 2026/2027 academic session.

Public schools in the Federal Capital Territory (FCT), Abuja, faced a similar ordeal as FCT workers went on an indefinite strike.

Dozens of students and their teachers who were kidnapped in two separate attacks between May and June in Askira/Uba LGA of Borno State remains in captivity.

The first abduction took place in Mussa, and coincided with the coordinated kidnapping of 39 students and seven teachers from three schools in Oyo State.

While the Oyo students were freed after 57 days in captivity, their Borno counterparts are still held captive, with their parents accusing the federal government of selective response.

PRMIUM TIMES reported in October how more than 2,000 students have been abducted in roughly 30 mass kidnapping incidents, and how school abductions have grimly evolved into a normalised feature of Nigeria’s security landscape.

World.title: NBS: Enugu records lowest ‘tax revenue-to-IGR ratio’
World.content:
Enugu State recorded the lowest tax revenue-to-Internally Generated Revenue (IGR) ratio in 2025, StatiSense has said, quoting figures from the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS).

According to statistics published on StatiSense’s verified X handle, only N51.52 billion, or 12.67 per cent of the N406.7 billion in IGR generated by Enugu State in 2025, came from tax revenues, while the rest came from non-tax revenues.

Recall that the NBS had earlier in the year rated Enugu State as number one in IGR growth among the 36 states and the FCT, coming only behind Lagos and Rivers States, in that order.

However, in terms of the tax component of IGR, the state recorded the lowest tax-to-IGR ratio, while Abia State led with 100 per cent of its N70.41 billion IGR in 2025 coming from taxes.

Abia was followed by the FCT, which had 100 per cent of its N356.34 billion 2025 IGR coming from tax revenues.

Bayelsa (99.39 per cent), Rivers (96.72 per cent) and Sokoto (92.44 per cent) make up the top five tax-dependent states for IGR.

But joining Governor Peter Mbah’s Enugu on the list of states with the least tax dependence for IGR are Kwara (38.42 per cent), Katsina (39.93 per cent), Osun (41.53 per cent) and Ogun (44.10 per cent).

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

At a recent town hall in Enugu, televised live by some national television stations, Governor Peter Mbah had dismissed the narrative that his administration was overtaxing the people, noting that it was being fuelled by the opposition and beneficiaries of the corruption and sharp practices that prevailed in the revenue collection system until his administration came on board and implemented reforms, introducing technology in the process to plug revenue leakages.

Mbah also maintained that, contrary to perception, the surge in the state’s revenue was driven by innovation and economic diversification under his administration, which had expanded revenue sources.

He also reminded the audience that taxation was on the Exclusive Legislative List of the Constitution; hence, no state could legislate to increase or lower any form of tax, be it Personal Income Tax, Company Income Tax, Value Added Tax, Withholding Tax, among others.

He said his administration had widened the tax net to bring in more people who had never paid tax, but had never increased taxes.

“This is one falsehood that has been so peddled that it’s even beginning to take a semblance of a truth. Meanwhile, overtaxation does not exist, and I think those who think we may be taxing more are essentially looking at the sort of growth we have recorded in our IGR.

“Because they couldn’t have imagined such growth happening within the period it happened, they felt perhaps the only justification is that we have burdened the people of Enugu to realise that. But that’s far from the truth.

“So, what did we do to grow our IGR? First of all, we plugged all the leakages. We ensured that nobody makes payments in cash on behalf of the state government.

“But, importantly, we have so far activated a whole lot of our dormant assets. We now earn quite a lot from those assets, and we built new ones,” he stated.

He named the Hotel Presidential, Enugu United Palm Products Limited, Nigergas, Nike Lake, the International Conference Centre, among other moribund assets his administration recovered, completed or resuscitated, then optimised and monetised.

The governor also named new revenue-yielding assets like Enugu Air, saying tax revenues constituted a marginal component of the state’s IGR.

He, however, said that his administration expected the tax component to grow with time as more economic activities occurred in the state.

Mbah added that most people also mistake payments for services that government renders, such as the issue of C-of-O, refuse disposal by the Enugu State Waste Management Authority (ESWAMA) for taxes, noting that his administration had also consolidated most of the services and costs.

“How much did we say they should pay? N36,000 annually for businesses. And that includes business premises and other rates and services. So, it’s N100 per day.

“We also had the complaints about people going to the market, I’m sure maybe from the local governments, to collect money. I made an announcement to stop that; that nobody should collect N100 or N200 from our market women,” he had explained.

World.title: Ogun reconstitutes Awujale Interregnum Council, names Adesanya Chairman, Okunowo Secretary
World.content:
The Ogun State Government has announced the reconstitution of the Awujale Interregnum Administrative Council (AIAC), reaffirming its legal authority to oversee the administrative and traditional affairs of Ijebuland pending the appointment and coronation of a new Awujale.

The decision follows the reported withdrawal of some members of the council, established by the state government in August 2025, amid disagreements over the emergence of a group reportedly known as Adele Oba Awujale.

In a statement issued on Tuesday by the Commissioner for Local Government and Chieftaincy Affairs, Hon. Ganiyu Hamzat, the government said the withdrawal of some members did not invalidate the council, which remained the only legally recognised administrative body empowered to manage the affairs of Ijebuland during the interregnum.

The government clarified that Chief Chris Okunowo and Alhaji Rasheed Adeoye Adesanya, the Olisa of Ijebu-Ode, had publicly dissociated themselves from the reported mass withdrawal.

Addressing the emergence of the Adele Oba Awujale group, the government declared that the body had no legal or customary recognition under the Awujale Chieftaincy Declaration or the existing chieftaincy legislation in Ogun State.

According to the statement, neither the Awujale Chieftaincy Declaration nor the Obas and Chiefs Law of Ogun State 2021 makes provision for an Adele Oba Awujale group or assigns it any recognised responsibility in the management of the Awujale stool.

It further explained that the Chiefs Law of 1957, which some former members reportedly relied upon to justify the emergence of the group, was a pre-independence legislation that no longer applied to Ogun State, which had operated under its own laws since its creation in 1976.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The government also cited a consent judgment delivered by the Ogun State High Court in suit number HCJ/180/2025, involving Rasheed Adeoye Adesanya (the Olisa of Ijebu-Ode) against the Executive Council of Ogun State and 16 others, as judicial affirmation of the legality and authority of the AIAC.

It noted that all members of the council were parties to the suit and had consented to the judgment, which acknowledged the legality, validity and authority of the administrative body established by the state government to oversee the administrative and traditional responsibilities of Ijebu-Ode pending the appointment and coronation of a new Awujale.

The government further recalled that the court affirmed that where there was a conflict between the responsibilities of the administrative body and the traditional functions of the Olisa, the authority of the administrative body would take precedence.

It stressed that the judgment had not been appealed and remained binding on the parties.

While acknowledging the right of individual members to withdraw from the council, the government maintained that such decisions could not confer legal authority on another body to assume the responsibilities of the AIAC.

It consequently warned members of the public against engaging in official transactions or administrative dealings with individuals who had withdrawn from the council in their purported capacity as members of an alternative administrative body.

The government also urged the former members to refrain from actions capable of contravening the law or undermining the peace and stability of Ijebuland.

To ensure continuity in the administration of Ijebuland during the interregnum, the government announced the reconstitution of the council with the following members:

1. Chief Rasheed Adesanya, Olisa of Ijebu-Ode – Chairman.

2. Chief Chris Okunowo, Bobasuwa – Secretary.

3. Professor Jide Ajayi, Jagun Aso – Member.

4. Chief Stephen O Bakare, Babalaje – Member.

5. Chief Alade Shote, Otun Balogun – Member.

The government said the reconstituted council would continue to discharge the legally recognised administrative and traditional responsibilities of the AIAC until a new Awujale was appointed and crowned.

It reaffirmed its commitment to upholding the rule of law, respecting established traditional institutions and ensuring a peaceful and transparent process in the succession to the vacant Awujale stool.

World.title: ADC warns Sokoto govt, vows to hold governor responsible for intimidation, violence against opposition
World.content:
The African Democratic Congress (ADC) has warned Sokoto State Governor Ahmed Aliyu that it will hold him responsible for any violence against opposition members as the party prepares to launch its presidential campaign in the state on Wednesday.

The warning came on Tuesday, a day after the state government sealed an ADC campaign office along Ahmadu Bello Way in Sokoto, citing a property ownership dispute and security concerns.

In a statement signed by its National Publicity Secretary, Bolaji Abdullahi, the ADC accused the state government of political intimidation and demanded an end to interference with its activities.

“The Sokoto State Government must understand that governing a state does not confer ownership,” the statement said. “No governor has the power to decide which party can campaign, which candidate can speak, or which political choices the people of Sokoto are allowed to consider.”

The party warned that public officials who obstruct lawful political activities should be prepared to face legal consequences.

Dispute over campaign activities

Commissioner for Lands and Housing Nasiru Dantsoho said government records showed that the sealed property belonged to Savannah Bank, with no documented transfer of ownership.

He said the government had written to the Nigeria Deposit Insurance Corporation (NDIC) for clarification and would keep the premises sealed pending a response.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Mr Dantsoho also cited a disturbance involving political supporters near the property as a reason for the closure.

Aminu Abdullahi, spokesperson for ADC governorship candidate Manir Dan’iya, alleged that the government demanded ₦30 million for a venue for the campaign launch.

He said the party agreed to the amount but was not provided with payment details. PREMIUM TIMES has not independently confirmed the alleged demand or obtained a government response to it.

The office closure followed an alleged attack on Mr Dan’iya’s convoy near Sokoto airport on 30 October.

The governorship candidate accused personnel linked to state security outfits of obstructing his convoy and damaging his vehicle. The All Progressives Congress (APC) disputed allegations of politically motivated violence, while police said they were investigating the incident.

Separately on Tuesday, Atiku Abubakar accused the State Security Service of recruiting protesters to disrupt Wednesday’s campaign launch.

He alleged that the protesters were being mobilised to create disorder that could justify a curfew and stop the event. This newspaper has not independently established the allegation. The SSS had not responded to earlier enquiries at the time of that report.

The ADC said it would proceed with the launch despite the dispute.

“Let there be no misunderstanding. The ADC will campaign in Sokoto State. We will not be intimidated, obstructed or pushed out of any part of Nigeria,” the party said.

It urged its supporters to remain peaceful and called on security agencies to protect the rights of all political parties.

World.title: Enugu govt empowers 520 vulnerable persons with grinding machines
World.content:
The Enugu State Government has empowered 520 vulnerable persons across the 260 wards of the state with grinding machines to improve their economic well-being and reduce poverty.

The beneficiaries, drawn from the 17 council areas, received the machines during an empowerment programme organised by the state Ministry of Human Development and Poverty Eradication in Enugu on Tuesday.

Distributing the machines on behalf of Governor Peter Mbah, the Secretary to the Enugu State Government (SSG), Chidiebere Onyia, said the intervention was part of the administration’s commitment to human capital development and poverty eradication.

Mr Onyia said the administration had, from inception, set a target of reducing the state’s poverty headcount index from 58 per cent to zero.

He described the distribution as one of several interventions designed to support vulnerable persons and improve their economic independence.

The SSG said the state government did not only build roads, schools and hospitals but also support the poor in the state.

According to him, the beneficiaries were selected based on clearly defined socio-economic indicators to ensure that the intervention reached genuine vulnerable households.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“What you are experiencing today is just one of the interventions put in place to ensure that vulnerable persons develop skills and use the equipment for productive economic activities.

“The aim is to enable them to generate income and have more disposable revenue to improve their quality of life,” said Mr Onyia, a professor.

He said the government had also established a monitoring mechanism through the Ministry of Budget and Planning to track the use of the equipment and ensure that beneficiaries put them to productive purposes.

He cautioned the beneficiaries against selling the machines, stressing that the equipment was provided to promote self-sufficiency and not for resale.

The SSG added that the empowerment programme would be sustained, noting that beneficiaries would also be supported with agricultural inputs, digital skills training and other interventions across relevant sectors.

He said the government would continue to use data to plan, monitor and evaluate its interventions to ensure that they produced measurable results.

How beneficiaries were selected

In her welcome address, the state Commissioner for Human Development and Poverty Eradication, Benedette Okoli, said the distribution was organised to commemorate the 2026 International Day of the Poor.

Ms Okoli said the 520 machines were allocated to two vulnerable persons from each of the 260 political wards across the state’s 17 local government areas.

She said the programme was made possible through the approval of Governor Mbah, whose administration remained committed to improving the welfare of poor and vulnerable citizens.

According to her, the grinding machines are not merely equipment but economic empowerment tools that will enable beneficiaries to engage in productive activities, generate income and support their families.

The commissioner said the beneficiaries were selected from the Enugu State Social Register of the Poor and Vulnerable, prepared by the State Operations Coordinating Unit (SOCU).

She explained that the selection process was transparent and free from political considerations, favouritism or personal connections.

She assured them that the ministry would work with relevant stakeholders to monitor the programme and provide the necessary support to ensure lasting benefits.

Also speaking, the State Coordinator of SOCU, Joy-Blossom Eneh, represented by the Head of Monitoring and Evaluation, Christopher Nnam, expressed appreciation to the governor for supporting the use of the state’s social register to identify vulnerable households.

Mrs Eneh said the social register had provided an evidence-based approach to identifying beneficiaries and ensuring that government interventions reached those who genuinely needed assistance.

She said the unit had captured 586 beneficiaries, including indigent persons and petty traders, for various government interventions.

She described the empowerment programme as evidence that the governor’s commitment to using the social register was yielding tangible results.

One of the beneficiaries, Ndidamaka Ejiri from Igboetiti Local Government Area, while responding on behalf of others, expressed gratitude to the state government.

Mrs Ejiri said the machine would, no doubt, significantly improve their family’s income.

“I thank Governor Peter Mbah for this gesture. Coming 2027, my vote belongs to him, and I promise to put the equipment into productive use to help myself and my family,” she said.

(NAN)

World.title: Police probe teenager’s corpse found in Cross River community
World.content:
The Police Command in Cross River State has begun an investigation following the discovery of the beheaded body of an unidentified teenager in Yahe River, Yala Local Government Area of the state.

The victim, believed to be about 16 years old, was discovered dead in the river on Tuesday, 27 October, with his head severed from his body.

Sunday Eitokpah, the police spokesperson in Cross River, disclosed this in a statement on Monday in Calabar.

Mr Eitokpah, an assistant superintendent of police, said the incident was reported at about 5:30 p.m. by the Officer-in-Charge of Yahe Outstation, Ekurbe Abi, an assistant superintendent of police, which led to the recovery of the body from the river.

He said bloodstains were observed at the scene, raising concerns about the circumstances surrounding the teenager’s death.

According to him, the corpse was subjected to medical examination and subsequently deposited in the mortuary, while efforts are ongoing to establish the identity of the deceased.

The Commissioner of Police in Cross River, Ajo Ordue, has directed a thorough investigation to ensure that anyone found responsible is brought to justice, according to the statement.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Mr Ordue appealed to residents of Yahe and neighbouring communities to report any missing person matching the deceased’s description or provide credible information that could assist the investigation.

He urged members of the public with useful information to contact the nearest police station or the command control room.

He assured residents that further developments would be communicated as the investigation progresses.

(NAN)

World.title: ﻿WSCIJ to host conversation on journalism, civic space in Nigeria
World.content:
The Wole Soyinka Centre for Investigative Journalism (WSCIJ) has announced its November edition of the Journalism and Society Conversations, themed “Policy Brief Presentation and Conversation on Journalism and Civic Space in Nigeria”.

Motunrayo Alaka, WSCIJ’s chief executive officer, said in a press statement on Tuesday that the virtual event would bring together key decision-makers to evaluate the state of journalism and civic freedoms in Nigeria, as well as discuss practical measures for strengthening institutional accountability and protecting journalists and civic space.

The event is scheduled to hold on Tuesday, 10 November, at 11 a.m. on X.

A key highlight of the session will be the presentation of a policy brief drawn from the centre’s 2025 status report, titled “Silenced Voices, Shrinking Space: Civic Freedoms Under Pressure.”

Speakers

The panel features prominent figures, including human rights lawyer Ayo Obe; Peter Maduoma, executive director of the CLEEN Foundation; Edetaen Ojo, executive director of Media Rights Agenda; and Motunrayo Alaka, executive director and CEO of WSCIJ.

The conversation will be moderated by Nabilah Usman, general manager of Radio Now 95.3 FM.

The policy brief

The 2025 Journalism and Civic Space Status Report, “Silenced Voices, Shrinking Space: Civic Freedoms Under Pressure”, presents an analysis of reported civic space violations.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

According to the report, Nigeria recorded 245 incidents of civic space violations in 2025, with state actors involved in 219 of the cases.

The incidents were documented through systematic monitoring of reports published by 54 media organisations between January and December 2025.

“Data was collected through continuous monitoring of reports on civic space violations across physical and digital spaces. Every incident was verified through cross-checking with multiple credible sources before inclusion in the dataset. Where additional context was required, Key Informant Interviews (KIIs) were conducted,” the report stated.

The report said incidents reported by multiple media organisations were counted as a single verified incident to avoid duplication.

It added that the 245 incidents analysed were referenced in reports published by 54 media organisations, comprising 16 newspapers with print and online editors, 26 online-only news platforms, 10 television stations and two radio stations.

The report said the findings showed that Nigeria’s civic space remained under significant pressure despite the country’s democratic system and constitutional guarantees of fundamental rights.

It also identified the Nigeria Police Force as being involved in 118 of the 219 incidents involving state actors.

World.title: Experts seek soil-based fertiliser recommendations to improve yields
World.content:
By Cynthia Alo

Agricultural experts have called for a shift from one-size-fits-all fertiliser recommendations to soil-based application, warning that farmers may be wasting money on nutrients their crops do not need.

They said differences in soil conditions and crop requirements meant that applying the same fertiliser rates across farming locations could result in poor nutrient use, higher production costs and lower productivity.

The experts spoke at the 2026 Nigeria Fertiliser Summit on Phosphorus and Food Security, organised by the Institute of Agricultural Research and Training (IAR&T), Obafemi Awolowo University and the Fertilizer Producers and Suppliers Association of Nigeria (FEPSAN), with the Fertilizer and Inputs Support Services Department of the Federal Ministry of Agriculture and Food Security as co-convener in Abuja.

Findings presented at the summit by the Regional Hub for Fertilizer and Soil Health for West Africa and the Sahel showed that phosphorus requirements for maize and rice in northern Nigeria ranged from zero to more than 60 kilogrammes of phosphorus pentoxide per hectare, depending on soil conditions.

Phosphorus is an essential plant nutrient that supports root development, crop growth and grain formation.

However, its availability to crops varies with soil properties and farming conditions.

A soil scientist and modelling expert at IAR&T, Prof. Vincent Aduramigba-Modupe, said improving agricultural productivity required more than increasing fertiliser application.

“Improving crop productivity is not only about applying fertiliser. It is about ensuring the right nutrient is applied in the right amount, at the right place, and under the right conditions,” he said.

The Minister of Agriculture and Food Security, Aliyu Abdullahi, represented by the Director of Agricultural Land and Climate Change Management Services, Oshadiya Olanipekun, emphasised soil data, testing and crop-specific fertiliser recommendations as important tools for improving farmers’ outcomes.

Also speaking, Prof. Jibrin Mohammed Jibrin, Visiting Scientist with the Regional Hub and Professor of Soil Science at Bayero University, Kano, described soil information as fundamental to food production.

Jibrin also called for better coordination among agricultural stakeholders, warning that fragmented interventions could undermine efforts to improve soil health.

“The basis of food production and food security is the soil. You need healthy soil to produce well and feed the nation with nutritious food. To do that, you need soil intelligence.

“Too many initiatives have been implemented in silos. Real progress will come when stakeholders align, collaborate and follow through on agreed actions,” he said.

Senior Agronomist at the Regional Hub, Dr. Bello Shehu, said improving phosphorus management was not about applying more fertiliser but understanding the nutrient requirements of different soils and crops.

The Vice-Chancellor of Obafemi Awolowo University, Prof. A.S. Bamire also stressed that agricultural productivity depended on responsible nutrient management, research, innovation and stronger partnerships.

World.title: Lagos targets 100 food-processing plants around logistics hub
World.content:
Gov Sanwo-Olu

By Cynthia Alo

Lagos State Government is planning to establish between 50 and 100 small food-processing plants around its proposed food systems and logistics hub as part of efforts to promote local processing, add value to agricultural produce and strengthen the state’s food supply chain.

Governor Babajide Sanwo-Olu disclosed this at the Executive Business Breakfast organised by the Nigerian-British Chamber of Commerce, where he outlined the state’s plans to develop an integrated system for food storage, processing and distribution.

He said the proposed processing plants would be located around the logistics hub and supplied with agricultural produce brought in from different parts of the country.

According to him, the arrangement is designed to create opportunities for value addition by ensuring that food commodities are not only stored and distributed but also processed within the state.

He stated: “The second part of that logistics hub is that it’s also going to feed about 50 to 100 small food processing plants.”

He added that the government had made provision for processing facilities around the hub as part of its master plan.

“We’ve created about 1,000 hectares all around that business, so we’re going to have layouts of small processing mills around it that can often do a lot of value addition,” he said.

The proposed hub is expected to receive food from different parts of Nigeria, with facilities for cold and dry storage, silos and a large trailer park to support the movement of commodities.

Sanwo-Olu said the facility was almost completed, describing it as one of the largest food systems and logistics hubs in Sub-Saharan Africa.

World.title: Osun lawyers urge Adeleke to avert collapse of court buildings
World.content:
By Shina Abubakar, Osogbo

Lawyers in Osun State have raised the alarm over the deteriorating condition of court buildings across the state, urging Governor Ademola Adeleke to urgently intervene to prevent further decline in the administration of justice.

The lawyers, under the aegis of the Nigerian Bar Association (NBA), representing the five branches in Osogbo, Ikirun, Iwo, Ile-Ife and Ilesa, said dilapidated buildings and inadequate facilities were disrupting court proceedings and undermining justice delivery.

In a letter to the governor dated October 29, 2026, and received at the Governor’s Office on November 2, the association called for the comprehensive rehabilitation, renovation and modernisation of court buildings and facilities across the state.

The letter was signed by the chairmen of the five branches: Maruf Adediran (Osogbo), Abdulkareem Azeez (Ikirun), Emmanuel Gbadegesin (Iwo), Olawoye Festus (Ile-Ife) and Adefunso Esan (Ilesa).

According to the lawyers, several court buildings have deteriorated to the extent that they threaten the dignity of the judicial institution and expose judicial officers, legal practitioners, litigants and witnesses to avoidable hardship.

They identified leaking roofs, damaged ceilings, inadequate seating arrangements and other infrastructural deficiencies as major concerns.

The association said rainwater entering some courtrooms had forced proceedings to be interrupted or suspended, resulting in unnecessary adjournments and delays.

“It is unacceptable that court proceedings in a state governed by the rule of law should be dictated by the weather because the buildings in which justice is administered cannot adequately withstand rainfall,” the lawyers stated.

They said the problem extended beyond courtrooms to the office of the Chief Judge and the chambers of other judicial officers, raising concerns about the safety of court records, official documents, furniture and electronic equipment exposed to water leakage.

The association urged the state government to conduct a comprehensive audit of facilities across the High Court, Customary Court of Appeal, Magistrates’ Courts and District Customary Courts.

It said the exercise should cover affected locations, including Osogbo, Ikirun, Ilesa, Ile-Ife, Iwo and Ede.

Beyond structural repairs, the lawyers called for modern judicial equipment, including electronic case management systems, digital recording devices and computers, as well as adequate funding for maintenance and training of judicial and registry personnel.

They also urged the government to prioritise emergency repairs to buildings posing safety risks and involve the judiciary and NBA in identifying needs, setting project priorities and monitoring improvements, while respecting judicial independence.

“Our appeal is not merely about the physical appearance of court buildings; it concerns the ability of a critical institution of government to discharge its constitutional responsibilities effectively and the ability of the people of Osun State to access justice without avoidable hardship,” the letter stated.

The lawyers added that judicial officers should not be left to administer justice in buildings with leaking roofs, inadequate courtroom facilities or offices that expose personnel and court records to preventable risks.

They also stressed the need to equip courts with modern facilities and technology to improve efficiency and strengthen public confidence in the justice system, adding that the welfare of judicial officers was important to effective justice delivery.

World.title: Ogun indigenes reaffirm support for Adebutu ahead of 2027
World.content:
…PDP candidate’s supporters pledge grassroots mobilisation for ‘Ogun for Ogun’ agenda

By James Ogunnaike, Abeokuta

Indigenes of Ogun State have reaffirmed their support for the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) governorship candidate, Oladipupo Adebutu, and his running mate, Yemi Sowunmi-Kolapo, pledging grassroots mobilisation for their ambition ahead of the 2027 governorship election.

The pledge was made during ward-to-ward engagements by the candidates across local government areas of the state, where residents expressed concerns about poor infrastructure, unemployment, inadequate agricultural support and the need for improved access to modern farming equipment.

The campaign tour is also aimed at presenting the candidates’ seven-point development agenda, tagged ITURA DE, to the electorate.

At the ward meetings, community leaders, market women, farmers and youths turned out to receive the candidates and discuss their expectations from the next administration.

Several stakeholders pledged support for the ‘Ogun for Ogun’ initiative, arguing that the state’s leadership should reflect the interests, heritage and aspirations of its indigenes.

At Alagada Ward in Obafemi Owode Local Government Area, a market leader, Mrs Folasade Ogunye, said her support for the movement was informed by the belief that indigenous leadership would better understand the challenges confronting grassroots communities.

She lamented the poor condition of roads leading to markets and the limited employment opportunities available to young people, pledging to mobilise women for door-to-door campaigns.

“We, the women of Obafemi Owode, have suffered neglect. Our roads to the markets are bad, and our children need jobs. We want someone who grew up here, who knows our language and understands our struggles,” she said.

At Alapakooni community, also in Obafemi Owode, some residents said to be former members of the All Progressives Congress (APC) publicly renounced their membership of the party.

The defectors reportedly set bunches of APC brooms ablaze to symbolise their departure, citing dissatisfaction with the party’s political leadership and questions surrounding the identity of its governorship candidate.

A community youth coordinator, Tunde Akinola, said their decision to align with Adebutu was motivated by their desire for leadership they could identify with and hold accountable.

He said the group wanted to support a candidate who understood the state’s challenges and could deliver on his promises.

Similarly, a community stakeholder and farmer at Onidunu Ward, Deji Bamidele, said farmers in the area wanted a government that would prioritise agricultural development through mechanisation and improved access to farming inputs.

He said a farmers’ cooperative with more than 300 members had pledged support for the ‘Ogun for Ogun’ initiative, following Adebutu’s presentation of his agricultural plans under the ITURA DE agenda.

At Owode Ward 3, a retired teacher, Alhaja Sariyu Bankole, described the movement as an opportunity to preserve the state’s political heritage.

She said residents should participate actively in the election to ensure that their voices counted in determining the state’s future.

In Sagamu Local Government Area, a youth leader, Comrade Bayo Oduwole, pledged to mobilise young people through voter education and door-to-door campaigns.

Speaking at Ward 10, Oduwole said the ‘Ogun for Ogun’ campaign should be driven by competence, accountability and an understanding of the state’s needs.

Responding to the expressions of support, Adebutu described the ward-to-ward engagements as an opportunity to understand the needs of communities and build a development agenda around them.

He said the ITURA DE agenda was designed to address the state’s socio-economic challenges, particularly in infrastructure, agriculture, employment generation and improved living standards.

“This tour has shown me that our people are yearning for homegrown leadership that understands their challenges and is prepared to address them.

“The ITURA DE agenda is not just a slogan; it is a social contract to restore dignity, fix our roads, empower our farmers, create jobs for our youths and return Ogun State to its rightful place,” Adebutu said.

He added that the campaign was not only about seeking votes but also about listening to residents and understanding their concerns.

His running mate, Kolapo, assured residents that a PDP administration would prioritise inclusive governance and ensure that grassroots communities were represented in policy decisions.

She highlighted the importance of women, children, education and primary healthcare in the proposed administration’s development plans.

Kolapo said the reception across the wards reflected residents’ desire for a government that would listen to them and address their needs.

The PDP candidates said their grassroots engagements would continue across the state as they seek to consolidate support and present their policy proposals ahead of the 2027 governorship election.

World.title: 2027: I’m on a mission to rescue Abia South — Ikonne
World.content:
By Ugochukwu Alaribe

UMUAHIA — The All Progressives Congress (APC) senatorial candidate for Abia South in the 2027 general election, Prince Paul Ikonne, has pledged to attract federal projects and employment opportunities to the zone if elected.

Ikonne made the pledge while addressing members of the Catholic Women Organisation (CWO) at Christ the King Cathedral, Aba Diocese, where he described his candidacy as a mission to rescue the zone and accelerate its development.

He alleged that Abia South had suffered poor representation over the past 20 years, resulting in inadequate federal presence, infrastructure and empowerment opportunities.

The candidate promised to attract federal projects to the zone, facilitate federal employment for youths and secure agricultural and business grants for artisans, market women and entrepreneurs.

He also pledged to ensure that Aba, which he described as the commercial hub of the South-East, received its share of federal infrastructure.

Ikonne urged residents to support his ambition, saying his proposed representation would be focused on delivering measurable benefits to the constituency.

“Enough is enough. For 20 years, we have had representation without results, or projects, and leadership without impact. It is time to change that narrative.

“My representation will be vocal, visible and valuable. I will not be a Senator in Abuja without impact to my constituency while my people suffer. We will move from excuses to progress, from lamentation to legislation,” he said.

He called on members of the CWO to mobilise voters in support of his candidacy, describing women as an important grassroots political constituency capable of influencing electoral outcomes.

Ikonne also commended the organisation for its contributions to family life, the growth of the Catholic faith and community development.

In separate remarks, the CWO President in Aba Diocese, Lady Nneoma Florita Ngozi Anwuacha, and some parish presidents commended the candidate for what they described as his support for the diocese.

They assured him of the organisation’s support in the 2027 election, citing his association with the church.

World.title: Reductionism and the national question: restructuring or grievance? (I), by Usman Sarki
World.content:
“The co-existence of several nations under the same State is a test, as well as the best security, of its freedom.” — Lord Acton

Nigeria’s convoluted debate on restructuring has endured for decades because it supposedly speaks to questions of power, identity, representation, resource distribution, security, federalism and belonging. Precisely because the debate has been driven largely by sectional advocates and habitual agitators, however, it has also become increasingly burdened and polarised by a tendency towards reductionism, or the habit of explaining the country’s many and complex difficulties through a single grievance, a single historical narrative, a single ethnic experience or a single constitutional remedy. It is here that the discourse on the so-called “national question” becomes difficult, protracted and, at times, almost futile. Nigeria undoubtedly has structural problems, just as other countries do. It also has governance challenges, adversarial politics, elite misconduct, civic indiscipline, institutional weakness, manufactured discontents and problems arising from deep historical memories. To collapse all these into one argument that Nigeria will work better only if one particular restructuring formula is adopted may be emotionally satisfying, but it is intellectually shallow and politically reactionary.

The central question, therefore, is no longer simply whether Nigeria should restructure. It is whether restructuring is being presented as a panacea, pursued as a genuine national project, or increasingly deployed as an instrument of demagoguery, a mockery of democracy and a vocabulary through which competing groups selfishly articulate accumulated grievances. That distinction is essential if an honest national discourse is to be undertaken. A federation is, by its nature, an arrangement for managing diversity. It seeks to reconcile unity with autonomy, common citizenship with regional identity, and national authority with sub-national self-government. Nigeria’s problem is not that diversity exists; that is an enduring fact. The more difficult question is whether the state has developed institutions capable of managing that diversity fairly, equitably, peacefully and productively.

Lord Acton’s dictum is instructive in this regard. The coexistence of several nations within one state is not necessarily evidence of political failure. It is, rather, a test of liberty and constitutional maturity. The challenge is whether institutions can make diversity compatible with freedom, equality and political order.

When those institutions are compromised and rendered incapable of delivering satisfactory governance, every disagreement acquires an ethnic or sectional interpretation. Administrative failures become evidence of domination. Economic inequalities are interpreted as deliberate marginalisation. Political defeat is transformed into collective humiliation. Historical assumptions become territorial claims. Every federal appointment, budgetary allocation, state boundary or constitutional provision is then subjected to ethnic or regional arithmetic. It is at this point that restructuring ceases to be merely a constitutional discussion and becomes part of the broader politics of grievance. There is nothing illegitimate about nursing a grievance or articulating it where it genuinely exists. Nations must allow legitimate grievances to be expressed freely and intelligently. Indeed, suppressing them may constitute a greater threat to national stability than openly debating them. But grievance must ultimately be converted into a constitutional proposition, not transformed into fuel for agitation and disunity. It must answer practical questions. What precisely is wrong with the country? What institution should be rearranged or changed? By what process? To whose benefit? At whose cost? And how will the rights of others be safeguarded?

Without this discipline, restructuring becomes an endlessly expanding concept into which every disappointment may be inserted. For some Nigerians, restructuring means a return to the regional arrangement of the First Republic. For others, it means fiscal federalism and greater resource control. Some understand it as devolution of powers from the Federal Government to the states. Others advocate state police, constitutional recognition of traditional institutions or the creation of additional states. Still others propose the consolidation of the present 36 states into larger regions. At the furthest end of the argument are those for whom restructuring is essentially a transitional language for confederation, self-determination or eventual separation. All these positions are described by the same word; however, they do not necessarily lead to the same destination. That is why the restructuring debate must first be rescued from ambiguity, inconsistency, shallowness and opportunism. Recent arguments surrounding the idea of autonomous regions illustrate the difficulty. One school of thought sees historical regions as natural foundations upon which a new federation may be reconstructed. Another insists that communities cannot simply be reassigned to reconstructed regions on the basis of historical maps, ethnic narratives or claims advanced on their behalf. Contemporary consent, according to this argument, must be central.

This raises one of the most profound questions in any future restructuring of Nigeria: who actually owns territory? Is territory inherited by historical regions? Does it belong to so-called ethnic nations? Is it defined by existing state boundaries? Or does ownership and political legitimacy ultimately rest with the communities presently inhabiting the territory? If so, when did such communities come into possession, and through what means — migration, conquest, displacement, allocation or settlement?

History unquestionably matters. No serious constitutional settlement can disregard it. Present identities, boundaries, conflicts and solidarities are themselves products of history. But history cannot be invoked selectively. Every part of Nigeria possesses multiple historical layers, shaped by the expansion and contraction of kingdoms, the movement of peoples, the emergence of emirates and chiefdoms, colonial boundaries, the rearrangement of older political communities, and the creation, merger and division of provinces.

So too did the establishment of regions, later abolished and succeeded by states in exercises beginning in 1967 and continuing through 1996, alter these historical arrangements. There is therefore no single pristine map to which Nigeria can simply be returned. This is precisely where reductionism becomes dangerous. Once history is reduced to one preferred narrative or period — whether 1914, 1960, 1963 or some earlier moment — that chosen point becomes a political entitlement. One group may point to the map of 1963, while another invokes the nineteenth century, pre-colonial kingdoms, colonial provinces or present administrative boundaries. A nation of more than two hundred million people, composed of hundreds of ethnic groups and subgroups, cannot build its constitutional future by allowing competing historical narratives and imaginary maps to become instruments of possession. Any restructuring that alters territorial relationships must therefore contain a strong element of consent. Communities should not simply be transferred from one political arrangement to another as though they were administrative property. But consent itself requires careful definition and a rational legal basis.

If every village, ward, town, district or local government were independently entitled to choose its preferred region, the federation could become permanently fluid and unstable.

Territorial politics might descend into an endless series of claims, referenda and counterclaims. Economic viability, geographical contiguity and administrative coherence would become increasingly difficult to sustain. The principle of consent must therefore operate within an agreed national constitutional framework. It cannot mean an unlimited right of territorial fragmentation elasticity.

This is the essential balance Nigeria must find: historical identity without historical domination; community choice without permanent atomisation; and regional autonomy without national disintegration. The danger of the current discourse, driven increasingly by ethnic nationalism, is that too many actors approach restructuring from the standpoint of what their own group has lost or stands to gain rather than from the standpoint of what constitutional order all Nigerians can live under.

The language is revealing. One hears of stolen territories, denied access, lost political influence, historical ownership, strangers, domination, marginalisation and restitution. These are the vocabularies of discontent, grievance and, occasionally, unreason. They may describe apparently genuine experiences, but they cannot, by themselves, constitute a national federal constitution.

A constitution is necessarily a compromise and an accommodation among competing claims. The Kanuri, Hausa, Yoruba, Igbo, Fulani, Tiv, Ijaw, Ibibio, Nupe, Gbagyi, Jukun, Edo, Igala, Birom, Angas, Egbira, Idoma, Urhobo, Marghi, Itsekiri and Nigeria’s numerous other communities all possess historical narratives. None can reasonably expect its own narrative to become the overriding and exclusive organising principle of the federation.

The purpose of restructuring should therefore not be to transform historical recollections into territorial entitlement or grievance into constitutional ownership. History should inform the debate, certainly, but it should not imprison it. Any sustainable arrangement must recognise contemporary populations, existing communities, economic viability, constitutional order and, above all, the legitimacy of consent.

The real test is whether Nigerians are discussing restructuring in order to build a more workable and durable federation, or whether they are merely seeking a new constitutional vocabulary through which old disputes can be pursued. That is where the distinction between genuine and rational restructuring, on the one hand, and irrational grievance and reductionism, on the other, begins.

World.title: Igbo youth rebuff of Nigerian Army (III), by Ochereome Nnanna
World.content:
Ochereome Nnanna

The purpose of this series is to explain why the young people of Igbo extraction now reject the offer to join the Nigerian Army. In the first part, we saw how the Army that Igbo senior officers once led with distinction became the instrument for their subjugation, both during and long after the Biafra War, despite promises to the contrary. In the second part, we also saw how the military, as a political force, was used to prevent the Igbo resumption of their pride of place, not only in the political power arena but also in virtually every sector of Nigeria’s affairs. Each time the Igbo are poised to lead the country, the Establishment uses the Nigerian Army to stop them in preference for less-fancied options, which is why the country is dying, not growing. The straw that finally broke the camel’s back was the return of Muhammadu Buhari in 2015 as an elected president. Ndi Igbo had wholeheartedly thrown their support behind Dr Goodluck Jonathan in the 2011 presidential election. Jonathan obtained victory despite withering opposition from the North and South West, and he identified Ndi Igbo as the great, avuncular force behind his victory. He appointed Igbo sons and daughters into commanding positions in his government, giving them posts that had always been denied them by the military and its civilian agents. These included Secretary to the Government of the Federation. Jonathan even mandated Ndi Igbo to nominate a candidate of their choice.

He also brought back Dr Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala to serve as Minister of Finance and Coordinating Minister for the Economy. She commanded the power of a virtual Prime Minister and helped build the Nigerian economy to emerge as the largest in Africa in 2014 after a strategic rebasing, with a GDP value of $509.9bn. By contrast, our economy has currently slid to the third position, behind South Africa and Egypt, with a GDP value of $386.67bn, according to many authoritative sources, including Business Insider Africa. It was also during that era that Nigeria stood on the threshold of defeating Boko Haram, with the Nigerian Army under the supreme command of Igbo-born Chief of Army Staff, Lt-Gen Azubuike Ihejirika. The North and South West plotted the defeat of Jonathan in his re-election bid in 2015. Ndi Igbo felt the pain of Jonathan’s loss as if he were their ethnic kinsman. They were also made to pay for their support of him by the new All Progressives Congress (APC), whose candidate, Muhammadu Buhari, emerged victorious. Glowing in his victory, Buhari went to America, apparently to thank President Barack Obama for his support after three previous failures. At the US Institute of Peace on 25th July 2015 in Washington, DC, Buhari uttered a grossly irresponsible undertaking: that he would give his supporters 97 per cent and only 5 per cent to those who did not support him. To show he meant it, he loaded his cabinet’s juiciest positions and the military’s high commands with mostly Northern Muslims, with generous concessions to his South West partners.

He thus drove the Igbo nation, especially the youth, into the waiting hands of the Mazi Nnamdi Kanu-led Indigenous People of Biafra (IPOB). Before Buhari’s unpatriotic utterance, the incendiary separatist broadcasts of Mazi Kanu, who had established Radio Biafra in London back in 2009, were generally ignored by most Igbo audiences, including this writer. He came strongly into the picture when he capitalised on the move for Brexit referendums to enable Britain to leave the European Union. Kanu argued that Nigeria’s amalgamation had expired in 2014, and that referendums should be staged to enable its indigenous people decide democratically and peacefully whether to stay on in Nigeria. He was very convinced that the people of the East, especially Ndi Igbo, would overwhelmingly vote for Biafra’s actualisation.

After Buhari’s hate declaration and subsequent hate actions to sideline Igbo people, Kanu’s messages started sounding like music, and many flocked to him. The Biafra agitation drew heavy traction, as youths joined the Biafra independence protests, leading to the proscription of IPOB and Kanu’s arrest and trial.
