Buhari used the Army, Police and security agencies to kill, harass, intimidate, arrest, detain and dehumanise Igbo youth and devastate communities suspected to be IPOB bases, especially in Abia, Imo and Anambra States. Worst of all, his regime funded armed Fulani herdsmen to set up ruga in no fewer than 350 forest bases in the South East alone. This was a strategic part of his evil Islamisation and Fulanisation agenda, with the military and security forces used to protect them. This led Kanu, who had escaped into exile, to establish the Eastern Security Network (ESN), specifically to protect Igboland from Fulani expansionism.

Till today, under President Bola Tinubu’s watch, IPOB and ESN remain proscribed, Kanu is in jail in Sokoto, and the Nigerian Army is sinisterly deployed in the South East. The Monday Sit-At-Home is passive resistance to protest Kanu’s unjust imprisonment and the siege of Igboland by the Nigerian Army. Igbo youth see the Nigerian Army as an oppressive, occupying force deployed to grease the wheel for armed Fulani conquest of their land. Secondly, the federal government’s suspicious handling of the war against terrorism (Boko Haram, bandits, ISWAP, Fulani herdsmen militias) and unconcerned attitude to Christian genocides aren’t helpful. Also, the unconfirmed general perception that “repented” Boko Haram terrorists are absorbed into the forces and sent to the East to kill people remains rife. The use of military and police checkpoints to harass and extort people in the South East is at a level not found anywhere else in the country.

Joining the military is the duty of all patriotic youths. But this is impossible when the armed forces are seen as oppressors; weapons fashioned against a particular ethnic group for no reason other than blind hatred and extreme bigotry.

CONCLUDED.

World.title: AI as election bogey, by Okoh Aihe
World.content:
Okoh Aihe

As he walked across the stage to address the gathering, the young MC joked on Monday morning that Prof. Joash Amupitan is one man nobody would really want to envy in Nigeria today. This was beyond a joke, which the INEC Chairman soaked in with some equanimity. In less than three months, his agency, which has struggled with a bout of image concerns, would be organizing some major elections which may give him a redeeming opportunity to change the calculus, to convince Nigerians that he can write a good story from a previously bad plot. It was the reason Amupitan was at the Continental Hotel in Abuja. Offered a platform at the National Summit on Electoral Information Integrity, jointly organized by the International Press Centre (IPC), the Centre for Media and Society (CEMESO) and DAI, with support from the European Union, he delivered a deeply troubling paper which could be summarized as follows: the fear of artificial intelligence (AI) is the beginning of good elections. “Today, elections can be undermined long before the first ballot is cast. The threat is no longer limited to physical interference (such as violent ballot snatching) at the polling unit; it takes shape within digital networks through synthetic media, automated misinformation/disinformation, deepfake fabrications, digital micro-targeting, and Foreign Information Manipulation and Interference (FIMI). The troubling reality is that many democracies are not really prepared for these,” Amupitan said.

Addressing the Summit theme, Beyond the Ballot: AI, FIMI, and the Integrity of Nigeria’s 2027 Elections, Amupitan gave no room for fear but instead displayed a commanding grasp of the electoral ecosystem to rally stakeholders to the realization that the democratization of AI has unleashed more challenges for electoral managers to handle. We can help Amupitan tell his story from there. There was already AI in February 2023. But it was a computer glitch from the backend of the INEC setup that blemished the integrity of a national election which had gone well until that unfortunate intrusion. The exponential growth in AI technology, which even the promoters are beginning to be afraid of as they fear it can imperil life and other human activities, is creating a cluster of concerns globally, with Amupitan now having to call on the concerted efforts of stakeholders to rescue the 2027 elections from a technology which carries so much good and evil. Unfortunately for all of us, there are so many tech mavericks, the troubled cyber denizens who will always want to take advantage of the negative side of technology to create and extend damage just to satisfy their satanic instincts. This explains why the INEC boss alerted that the rapid democratisation of generative AI models has dramatically lowered the barrier to entry for malicious minds.

So, there is so much to watch out for. This is the more reason Amupitan warned that as we prepare for the 2027 elections, the undeniable truth that we must confront is that public awareness alone is no longer an adequate defence against synthetic content and digital manipulation. Informing citizens that deepfakes exist or urging caution when consuming online news is useful, but it is insufficient against well-coordinated, highly funded, and hyper-targeted information operations designed to erode public trust in election administration. “What Nigeria urgently requires,” he suggested, “is a trusted, coordinated, and rights-respecting operational ecosystem – an institutional structure through which public authorities, security bodies, independent fact-checkers, media networks and platform operators can collectively anticipate emerging threats, verify evidence, escalate incidents without delay, communicate authoritatively, and institutionalize post-event lessons.”

Amupitan’s fears and expectations are not misplaced. He gave this illustration. In 2023, just two days before Slovakia went to the polls – during a mandatory 48-hour electoral blackout period when political parties and traditional news outlets were legally restricted from campaigning or broadcasting political responses – an AI audio recording went viral on local media. The cloned audio purported to capture a high-ranking political party leader actively discussing a scheme to buy votes and manipulate election results. It was a deliberate act, perfectly timed to coincide with the blackout period when campaigning was statutorily prohibited. Unfortunately, the sheer speed of digital dissemination, combined with the restricted response window, paralyzed institutional verification efforts. Amupitan observed that there are some vulnerable moments that some devious people would want to exploit, but, without throwing up his hands in the air in wanton helplessness, he declared very boldly that “our commitment to 2027 is rooted in technological resilience and transparency. To this end, Voter Education is moving beyond ‘how to vote’ to ‘how to verify,’ ensuring citizens can distinguish official INEC communication from AI-generated deepfakes. Furthermore, the electoral agency is also strengthening its digital infrastructure to withstand Foreign Information Manipulation and Interference (FIMI), while establishing robust internal mechanisms to debunk viral misinformation within minutes of its emergence.” He informed that INEC was partnering with global social media platforms such as TikTok, Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, YouTube, Facebook Messenger, Telegram and X (formerly Twitter). An MOU has already been signed with TikTok, he informed.

Amupitan is giving the assurance of INEC’s capacity to withstand everything thrown at it by perennially enraged cyber geeks. He appealed, however, that “as we construct this information defence system, we must proceed with strict institutional restraint. The legitimate threat of AI manipulation must never become a pretext for state overreach, digital censorship, or the suppression of political dissent.” It is gladdening that IPC, CEMESO and DAI have provided a platform to thrust the 2027 elections and AI onto the front burner, where they will now attract further interrogations from concerned citizens. While AI may have the good and the bad in equal measure, I want to observe that localizing the problems makes our situation significantly different.

My deduction comes from the fact that Nigeria has a large digital army of very unhappy people, homogenized only by their misery and bitterness against a country that has placed them at the margins. This army, which comes under several names, is readily available to any willing buyer who is ready to pay a little cash. Apart from their desire to make money and take as much of it as possible from the politicians who have confined them to undeserved servitude, there is also the revenge instinct to pay the nation back for letting them down. They don’t need condemnation. The INEC boss is right. We all need to build trust and be educated about the electoral process and specifically know the roles ascribed to each of us as collective stakeholders in the destiny of our nation. The digital army must be made to feel a part of this nation and be assigned roles they can happily execute. You can’t live in a house and burn it over yourself. Putting AI to rogue use during the elections could be worse than burning a house over yourself. The effects could be too extensive to contemplate. Irrespective of how we feel, Nigeria demands from us that we make her a better nation, more able to provide good living conditions for the generations on their way here.

World.title: Visibility, Networking, Key to Achieving Wealth, Influence, Experts Say
World.content:
Visibility and networking have been identified as key ingredients to achieving influence and wealth in a fast-changing global economy.

This was the main talking point at the Future of Wealth and Influence Conference held in Yaba, Lagos, recently.

The conference, hosted by Immigify, a US-based immigration technology company, brought together about 100 business owners, creatives, budding entrepreneurs and students to discuss wealth and influence.

The first keynote speaker, Emma Olorunsheyi, CEO of Immigify, began by reframing the idea of a career. He said a career is not a destination, but a launchpad, stressing that a great career should be seen as an asset rather than a finish line.

Central to his message was the idea of career capital, which he said comes before financial capital. According to him, while a salary pays for what one does, career capital creates opportunities from what one knows.

Drawing on his own journey, Olorunsheyi described having been on both sides of the table. Having worked with large companies, including Microsoft, HPE, Ford, Rackspace and Michaels before building his own ventures, he said he now sees those years not simply as a period of earning paychecks but as an opportunity to accumulate valuable assets.

“Don’t just go to work every day to carry out your assigned responsibilities, earn a salary and go home. Treat your workplace as a business school. Study your customers. Understand why they buy, what makes them stay, and what causes them to leave. Pay attention to how the company makes money, how it attracts and retains customers, and how it turns ideas into profitable products or services.

“Observe what makes a product launch successful or unsuccessful. Study how teams make decisions, solve problems, manage challenges and grow. In other words, don’t just work for the company; learn from the company. Every meeting, every challenge, every customer interaction and every business decision is an opportunity to gain knowledge that could be valuable beyond your current employment,” he said.

He also emphasised the importance of building relationships with customers, mentors, peers and partners, explaining that the right relationships could change the direction of an entrepreneur’s journey. He encouraged participants to offer specific help and add value to others before asking for favours.

Other keynote speakers, including Brain Essien, Tunde Okewale and Oladayo Ogunleye, echoed Olorunsheyi’s views, sharing personal experiences and insights on achieving career goals and financial success through wealth creation strategies and breaking barriers.

For Ogunleye, the relationships people build and the trust they earn are what remain when opportunities disappear. He said: “Relationships should be built before you need them because trust takes time, and many opportunities come through the people you know.

“So, become valuable, associate with the right people, attend the right events, improve your communication skills and build your personal brand. Learn to build relationships without always asking for favours. Also, surround yourself with people who encourage your growth and make an effort to maintain those relationships,” he added.

Co-founder of Immigify, Deji Adesola, who joined the event virtually from the United States, encouraged attendees to participate fully and connect with one another to get the best out of the conference.

An interactive session followed, with participants raising questions about self-discovery, the place of immigration in one’s career journey and how individual talents can attract global attention. Olorunsheyi and the other facilitators provided answers to the questions.

One of the attendees, Damilola Akinwande, a product designer, said: “I have learnt a lot today about people’s journeys to where they are now. It is more like a reflection for me on how to follow that path to help me build. One thing I will be practising after here is networking. I am still struggling in that aspect, but I am fired up now to push for visibility for my role and also go beyond my job scope.”

Another attendee, Toyin Dami of Ire’s Surprises, said: “I learnt today that you don’t have to have money to start whatever you want to start. You have to take steps in order to go far in life. And from today, I have told myself I will stop procrastinating. There is so much to achieve.”

The conference ended with a raffle session, where a participant, Ebunoluwa Soyege, won a N100,000 prize after the digital spin selected her name. An additional N100,000 was presented by the CEO after the participant became emotional while receiving the dummy cheque.

World.title: Ogundipe Harps on Credible Research to Sustain Quality Education
World.content:
Uchechukwu Nnaike

The Chairman, Governing Board, National Universities Commission (NUC), Prof. Oluwatoyin Ogundipe, has called on universities to step up efforts in promoting quality education through research. He said postgraduate education is key in advanced knowledge creation and innovation in Nigeria.

Ogundipe stated this in a plenary paper, ‘Rebuilding Academic Integrity in Nigerian Postgraduate Education; Governance, Innovation and Sustainable Institutional Reforms’, delivered at the 67th meeting of the Committee of Provosts and Deans of Postgraduate Colleges and Schools in Nigerian Universities, at the Redeemer’s University Ede, Osun State.

Ogundipe, the immediate past Vice-Chancellor, University of Lagos, said the value of the postgraduate schools and colleges’ research and degrees, rests on academic integrity, honest research and accurate attribution, adding that postgraduate schools are hubs for responsible data management and fair assessment.

According to him, where integrity is weakened, the credibility of the country’s postgraduate degree declines, international research collaboration also becomes harder and public confidence in the universities erodes.

“Concerns such as plagiarism, contract writing, unacknowledged use of generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) and weak supervision, are often treated as individual moral failures to be detected and punished.

“This paper argues that they are better understood as symptoms of institutional conditions, inadequate research resources and limited ethics training.

“They are also understood as overstretched supervision and uneven governance. Sanctions remain necessary, but on their own they cannot rebuild integrity,” he stated.

The don added that academic integrity remains an institutional responsibility and not individual, calling on Nigerian postgraduate schools to move from a predominantly punitive approach, to a proactive culture of integrity.

This, he argued must be supported by effective governance, responsible use of technology, as well as quality supervision.

He highlighted structural vulnerabilities, rather than isolated instances of individual misconduct as some of the integrity challenges facing the country’s universities.

According to him, inadequate research resource iss another key challenge facing the universities, saying that more than 60 per cent of postgraduate students lack essential research tools. He identified under funding aa a major constraint.

“The implication of this is that there will be pressure to cut corners, in order to meet degree requirements.

“Another challenge is that of limited research ethics training. Findings have shown that fewer than 30 per cent postgraduate students receive formal research ethics (Akpan 2024).

“The implications of this is that there is usually weak understanding of attribution data management and research ethics. There is also the issue of limited access to plagiarism-detection software, which is another major challenge.

“The implication of this too is usually inconsistent screening of thesis, as well as dissertations and publications,” he said.

Ogundipe further cited unguided use of generative AI. This he said can amount to the risk of AI generated texts or data being presented as original work, among others.

The Professor of Botany then urged provosts and deans within their existing authority and largely within existing resources, to make research ethics training mandatory for all postgraduate students.

This, he said should be initiated before proposal defence, drawing on existing faculty expertise and freely available online resources.

He also called for the introduction of supervision agreements with agreed meeting schedules, a feedback service standard and monitor compliance through the postgraduate school.

Ogundipe also stressed the need for the issuance of school guidelines on responsible AI use, including a disclosure requirement for theses, dissertations and seminar papers.

“There should also be fair and consistent similarity checking of all theses and dissertations, with reports reviewed by supervisors and examiners, rather than applied mechanically, among others,” he said.

According to him, integrity cannot be policed into existence, saying that it must be governed into structures, supported by responsible technology and live through quality supervision everyday.

World.title: UNIZIK Wins South-East Campus Debate, as Medical Student Gets N8m Scholarship
World.content:
David-Chyddy Eleke in Awka

Students of Nnamdi Azikiwe University, Awka, emerged as winners of the South-East edition of the campus debate over the weekend.

A final-year medical student at the university, Nnaemeka Victor, also received an N8 million scholarship from the debate sponsor, Chief Ikenna Okafor, a businessman and philanthropist.

The debate’s grand finale was held in Onitsha, with four tertiary institutions competing for first, second, and third place. The institutions were Chukwuemeka Odumegwu Ojukwu University, Igbariam; College of Health Sciences, Nkpor; Paul University, Awka; and Nnamdi Azikiwe University, Awka.

Chukwuemeka Odumegwu Ojukwu University came third, Paul University clinched second place, and UNIZIK emerged as the overall winner, receiving a cash prize of N1 million alongside other prizes.

Meanwhile, a member of the UNIZIK team, Nnaemeka Victor, who was adjudged the best overall debater, was awarded an N8 million scholarship by the sponsor through his charity foundation, Nzekwuabuo Foundation.

Okafor said the programme aimed to teach young people to disagree with others’ points with superior arguments, instead of resorting to violence.

“We want to start a revolution by training children who can learn how to disagree amicably, children who can present superior arguments, canvass responsible ideas through their debates, and not resort to violence.

“You can see the quality of debates we have had today. The task of making Nigeria work must not be left to government or anyone alone. I’m here because I love mentoring young people. We will support these young ones to harness the talent within them for export,” he said.

Earlier, the Managing Director of Macclemm Marketing Communications Limited, the programme’s organiser, Chido Obidiegwu, said the event will expand to secondary schools in subsequent years.

World.title: Lagos Teacher, Busayo Adeyemo, Emerges as 2026 Maltina Teacher of the Year
World.content:
Uchechukwu Nnaike

Busayo Adeyemo of Lanre Awolokun High School, Gbagada, Lagos, has emerged as the winner of the 12th Maltina Teacher of the Year Competition.

Adeyemo, who was declared the winner at the competition’s grand finale in Lagos, received a ₦10 million cash prize, a Honda HR-V, an all-expenses-paid overseas capacity development training, and a year’s supply of Maltina. The Nigerian Breweries-Felix Ohiwerei Education Trust Fund will also build a ₦30 million school infrastructure project in her honour.

In addition, Governor Babajide Sanwo-Olu rewarded her with a 3-bedroom apartment. She also won the Maltina Prize for Best STEM Teacher, worth ₦1.5 million.

The first runner-up, Yusuf Cariyat of Wisdom International School of Excellence (WISE), Sauka, Lugbe, Abuja, received ₦5 million, while the second runner-up, Ephraim Jacob Inyangudo of Comprehensive Secondary School, Ediene Abak LGA, Akwa Ibom State, received ₦3 million.

Also, 17 other teachers who emerged as state champions received ₦1 million each for their outstanding performance and commitment to excellence in teaching.

The host, Sanwo-Olu, commended Nigerian Breweries-Felix Ohiwerei Education Trust Fund (NB-FOETF) for its commitment to honouring teachers by deploying corporate resources to elevate them.

He described the trust fund’s intervention as the best way to deepen partnership between the company and the public sector while also delivering its corporate social responsibilities.

President Bola Tinubu, who was represented by the Minister of Humanitarian Affairs and Poverty Reduction, Dr Bernard Doro, stated that the trust fund, through the competition, not only gave teachers their due recognition, visibility, dignity and reward through its investment in classrooms, libraries and learning facilities but also improved the learning environment.

Tinubu expressed readiness to partner with NB-FOETF for its planned long-term support for out-of-school children, through its new initiative, to commence in 2027. According to him, the initiative will build on the trust fund’s long-standing focus on teachers and learning environments while expanding access for more Nigerian children.

The Chairman, NB-FOETF, and Managing Director, NB Plc, Thibaut Boidin, explained that the competition, since its inception, has celebrated outstanding educators across Nigeria while recognising their contribution to society’s growth.

He said this year’s edition is symbolic, as it coincides with the company’s 80th anniversary, Maltina’s 50th, and the trust fund’s 32 years of investing in education. While commending teachers for their labour and sacrifices for future generations, he noted that teaching should not be seen as a profession, but an act of service to the nation.

“Tonight, we see your commitment, the sacrifices, surprises that may never appear on a report card. We see the extra time you give to a struggling student, the patience, the courage and the optimism required to keep believing in the next generation. We honour you, and we thank you,” Boidin said.

Minister of Education, Dr Tunji Alausa, applauded the NB-FOETF for sustaining a platform that honours educators and professional excellence in teaching by investing in the foundation of Nigeria’s future. He said NB-FOETF’s recognition of outstanding teachers and support for school infrastructure clearly demonstrate how corporate investment can meaningfully contribute to the education system.

“I am particularly pleased that the Trust Fund is extending its intervention to address the challenges of out-of-school children, which aligns perfectly with the pressing national priority,” he added.

The Public Relations Officer, NB-FOETF/Corporate Affairs Director, Nigerian Breweries Plc, Uzodinma Odenigbo, disclosed that the competition has so far honoured 305 outstanding teachers, supported schools with educational infrastructure, and delivered 11 school infrastructure projects.

According to him, this year’s edition recorded a 30 per cent increase in entries, with an unprecedented 2,510 entries from all 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory, of which 2,243 were valid. He thanked the Teachers Registration Council of Nigeria (TRCN) for its partnership, which contributed to the strong participation, as well as other educational stakeholders for their support.

The partners, Union Bank Plc and Honda Manufacturing Nigeria Limited, commended the trust fund and other stakeholders for their dedication in making the initiative a success and for recognising the people who shape Nigeria’s future, one learner at a time.

A Slum2School Africa scholar, Mariam Alade, who delivered the keynote, spoke on the need to support and empower teachers, given their role in moulding the lives of children who hold Nigeria’s future.

The winner thanked NB-FOETF, the Lagos State government, and the partners for the reward, which she described as a big motivation to do more.

“It’s a reminder that I have a responsibility not to relent but to keep giving my best, committing myself to teachers’ development in Lagos and Nigeria, keep advancing STEM education in Nigeria, and believing in the Nigerian children that tomorrow shall be great,” she said.

Previous winners of the competition are: Rose Nkemdilim Obi (2015); Imoh Essien (2016); Felix Ariguzo (2017); Olasunkanmi Opeifa (2018); Ezem Collins (2019); Oluwabunmi Anani (2020); Abanika Taiye (2021); Alaku Ayiwulu (2022); Adeola Adefemi (2023); Esomnofu Ifechukwu (2024); and Serah Yusuf (2025).

World.title: Inside The Ka’Abah: A Rare Honour And The Message From Makkah
World.content:
Tunde Rahman

When President Bola Ahmed Tinubu arrived in Makkah, Saudi Arabia, on Thursday for Umrah, the lesser Hajj, it was a private spiritual journey. By Sunday, it had become a moment of national symbolism.

In a rare gesture reserved only for visiting Heads of State, monarchs and top dignitaries, the Saudi Royal Court ordered the doors of the Holy Ka’abah to be opened for the Nigerian President on Sunday, November 1, 2026. It is a privilege granted only a few times a year.

Accompanied by several state governors, his son Yinka, captains of industry, including BUA Chairman Abdul Samad Rabiu and Oando CEO Wale Tinubu, and other officials, President Tinubu entered Islam’s holiest site, the Ka’abah, offered prayers, and kissed the Black Stone (Hajar al-Aswad).

For those of us who were there, it was an emotional moment. The symbolism was unmistakable. The Kiswah fencing around the Ka’abah was draped in Green-White-Green, the Nigerian national colour.

After arriving late on Thursday, President Tinubu, dressed in white Ihram, performed the Umrah rites early on Friday, October 30, at Masjid al-Haram. He circled the Ka’abah seven times and went further to perform the Safa and Marwa rituals. Afterwards, he prayed for peace, unity, stability, and prosperity for Nigeria.

But his interview after entering the innermost part of the Ka’abah frames the moment in political terms.

In an interview with the Nigerian Television Authority Correspondent Musbau Dan-Wahab, who covered the Umrah, President Tinubu said the pilgrimage had strengthened his commitment to building a prosperous Nigeria. He thanked the Custodian of the Two Holy Mosques, King Salman bin Abdulaziz Al Saud, and Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman for the honour.

“I want to say a big thank you for the faith, for the recognition. I can’t believe the fencing of the Ka’abah is in Green-White-Green, which reminds us of the Nigerian identity,” the President said.

“It is an honour that I enjoyed, and it is gracious of them to have allowed me to enter inside the Ka’abah. This is history,” he added.

When asked what he prayed for inside the Ka’abah, his answer was telling: “Well, I asked for wisdom and resilience to continue to serve the people. And I know that prayer has been granted.”

Alhaji Abdul Samad Rabiu, who entered with the President among others, described it as an “honour beyond measure” and a once-in-a-lifetime blessing. The businessman had performed many Hajj and Umrah, but he had never been allowed inside the Ka’abah. The same was true for virtually everyone in the Nigerian delegation.

Late President Muhammadu Buhari and his delegation enjoyed that honour too, as the Saudi authorities granted them access to enter and pray in the inner chambers of the Ka’abah in February 2016 during an official visit to Saudi Arabia.

For President Tinubu, this is a fulfilled vow. For any Muslim, stepping inside the Ka’abah is a once-in-a-lifetime spiritual fulfilment. Although this just-ended Umrah was not President Tinubu’s first, it was his first inside that sacred Ka’abah. He has performed many Umrahs, including one before the 2023 election and another after the poll. During an official visit to Riyadh in November 2023, he made time to go to Makkah for Umrah, then proceeded to Guinea-Bissau.

During his visit to Makkah before the 2023 elections, he prayed for Allah’s blessings and grace, promising to return to express his gratitude to God if he won. The 2026 return completes that spiritual circle.

However, beyond the spirituality behind Sunday’s entry into the inner chambers of Ka’abah, the Saudi gesture towards President Tinubu bears a few implications. These fall into three categories: a strong diplomatic signal, political resonance, and moral renewal for governance.

On the diplomatic front, the opening of the Ka’abah, outside its traditional ceremonial schedule, is a state honour, not a tourist gesture. It is a clear sign of the high esteem in which Saudi Arabia holds Nigeria. Saudi Arabia’s decision to grant the honour to President Tinubu, at a time Nigeria is seeking more investment, increased oil cooperation, and a larger Hajj quota, signals that the bilateral relationship remains strong. President Tinubu described it as a reflection of the two countries’ longstanding friendship.

At the political level, the images of President Tinubu in Ihram inside the Ka’abah praying for Nigeria will resonate deeply across Northern Nigeria and among Muslim voters nationwide. Coming just days after his campaign flag-off on October 24 in Kaduna, it reinforces his identity as a leader who respects faith and tradition. In a January 2027 contest where faith and Northern votes will be decisive, this spiritual moment will be politically priceless.

The Northern Muslims will see in the race a Muslim honoured at the holiest site in Islam. His expanding Christian base in Southern Kaduna, the Middle Belt, and the South-East will also see a President who prays for all in Makkah. This neutralises the old religious debate where one candidate campaigned solely on ethnic and religious grounds.

There is also the moral renewal of commitment to governance. President Tinubu himself sees it as a recommitment. The President has demonstrated a strong commitment to reforming and improving Nigeria’s governance story.

From the removal of the fuel subsidy, eliminating many foreign exchange windows, stabilising the naira and modernising the taxes, to improving workers’ welfare through a minimum wage increase, credits for civil servants under the Creditcorps scheme, clearing pension backlogs, providing student loans, and ensuring timely graduation for tertiary institution students, the Tinubu administration is keeping the promise and steadily resetting the Nigerian economy.

Now, he says, “My commitment to Nigeria is stronger than ever.” And after praying for wisdom and resilience in Ka’abah, he is returning to Nigeria to face the final stretch of reforms and a campaign that promises to be heated.

On arrival, he would first visit Akwa Ibom to commission some projects. Then he would head to Port Harcourt, Rivers State, for the campaign on Saturday, November 7.

As the 2027 race intensifies, the image of President Tinubu inside the Ka’abah, praying for Nigeria, will be more powerful than any campaign billboard. That image indicates that leadership is not just political. It is spiritual. Indeed, from the Ranchers Bees Stadium in Kaduna, the heartland of Northern Nigeria, to the inner recesses of Ka’abah in Makka, the cradle of Islam, President Tinubu has, in the last two weeks, framed his re-election message in two powerful arenas- the political and the spiritual-. Is there any reason to think that victory in 2027 is not already guaranteed?

•Rahman, Senior Special Assistant to President Tinubu on Media and Special Duties, is a Fellow of the Nigerian Guild of Editors.

World.title: Nigeria’s  Flamingos Set to Make U17 World Cup History against Brazil
World.content:
Nigeria’s Flamingos are one game away from reaching the final of the FIFA U-17 Women’s World Cup in Morocco, but standing in their way is an illustrious juggernaut – Brazil.

It is a semi-final that promises plenty of excitement, with both teams having shown resilience, character and an ability to find their way through difficult moments.

For Nigeria, though, this is another opportunity to show how far they have come since arriving in Morocco and how much belief has grown within the team. The journey has certainly not been straightforward for Hakeem Busari’s side.

The Nigeria cadet ladies began their campaign with a disappointing 2-1 defeat to Poland, a result that left them with little room for error in their remaining group matches. There were questions to answer, and the pressure was already building.

With qualification for the knockout stages hanging in the balance, the Flamingos needed to respond quickly. They did exactly that, grinding out a 2-0 victory over Puerto Rico to get their campaign back on track.

The real turning point, however, came against defending champions, North Korea. Nigeria produced a performance that announced their arrival as serious contenders, with the Flamingos winning 3-1 and showing confidence, discipline and a level of attacking quality.

It was a statement victory, one that not only secured their place in the Round of 16 but also gave the players a huge boost in belief heading into the knockout stages, where they conquered Mexico in a 2-1 win.

Against Venezuela in the Round of 8, patience and persistence were required. Chances came and went, and it looked as though the contest might need extra time before Azeezat Oduntan stepped up in the 89th minute to convert a penalty and send Nigeria into the semi-finals.

One player Nigeria will certainly need to keep an eye on in the Brazilian side is Greise Kelly. She has been one of the standout performers in Morocco, scoring three goals and providing five assists.

At the other end, Nigeria will once again be looking towards goalkeeper Jane Ijirigho. Her performances have been particularly important during the knockout rounds, with some crucial interventions helping the Flamingos stay in games and progress through difficult moments.

Speaking to FIFA.com, Nigeria’s Head Coach Busari described the semi-final berth as a dream come true and an opportunity to make the country proud. “Reaching the semi-finals is a dream come true for me and a great achievement. I’m looking forward to it because I want to make my country proud. We want to give our best in the next match and show everyone what we can do.”

The semi-final tie is scheduled for today, Wednesday, 4 November, at the Mohammed VI Football Complex, Pitch 3, Rabat, Morocco, with kick off set for 6pm Morocco time (7pm in Nigeria).

World.title: Osimhen Fires Blanks as Russian Gives Gala Hope of Reaching Knockout Stage
World.content:
Duro Ikhazuagbe

Victor Osimhen was in action for all 90 minutes yesterday but failed to hit the back of the net as Galatasaray defeated visiting VfB Stuttgart 2-0 to boost their hopes of reaching the UEFA Champions League knockout stage.

Instead of Osimhen, it was Galatasaray’s Russian forward, Aleksey Batrakov, who fired the two goals in the space of three first-half minutes, that gave the Turkish champions their second win in Europe this season.

The defeat was the first for Stuttgart this season having won two and drew one in their three previous games in the Champions League.

Batrakov opened the scoring in the 12th minute when he fired home an effort after a Roland Sallai cross was cleared to him on the edge of the area.

The Russian soon made it two when he was expertly played through by a low pass from deep by former Tottenham defender Davinson Sanchez, before slotting the ball through the legs of visiting keeper Fabian Bredlow.

It was a difficult start for Stuttgart. Jamie Leweling nearly opened the scoring for the German side, but his low finish struck the far post, rebounded on to the near post and bounced to safety.

They struggled to deal with the relentless Galatasaray pressure and relieved the hosts were wasteful in the final third or they would have extended their lead.

Stuttgart thought they had pulled one back when Chris Fuhrich bent an effort into the far corner from the edge of the area, but his goal was chalked off for an offside in the build-up against Deniz Undav, who had hit the bar.

The result gave Galatasaray back-to-back Champions League victories following their 4-2 win at Lille, moving them to six points after four matches, while Stuttgart remained on seven.

Okan Buruk’s men host Aston Villa in their next Champions League game on 24 November (17:45 GMT), while Stuttgart are away to Inter Milan on 25 November (20:00 GMT).

World.title: Adegbuyi, Akekoromowei Make 2026 CAF Young Player Shortlist
World.content:
Flamingos rising star Kemi Adegbuyi and Falconets and Benfica striker Janet ‘Semenya’ Akekoromowei have made the 10-person shortlist for the 2026 CAF Young Player (women).

Adegbuyi, 16, has been among the goals as the Flamingos reached the U17 World Cup semifinal for only the second time.

She has also been outstanding at the WAFU B level as well as in the NWFL.

‘Semenya’, on the other hand, featured for the Falconets at the U20 World Cup in Poland earlier in the year.

World.title: [Watch] Livid Leon Schuster: ‘You’re p*ssing me off!’
World.content:
Leon Schuster has managed to pull off another epic prank, this time on his interviewer, Leanne Manas.

The veteran comedy actor and comedian sat down with the Morning Live presenter to discuss everything from his health to relationships, and even his scariest prank!

WATCH: LEON SCHUSTER PRANKS LEANNE MANAS

In a snippet from the interview, which takes place in Leon Schuster’s house, Leanne Manas asks the veteran star about his response to being accused of using blackface in his candid camera films, which spanned several decades.



The 75-year-old appeared visibly agitated at the question, responding: “That is a sensitive question and I dont want to answer that

“You have affronted me now, and it p*sses me off, I thought we were going to get along.

Now flustered and losing his cool, Schuster added: “Don’t ask me about stuff like that,please! Don’t do that again, beauce I will walk out of this interview



“You don’t do that to me, not in my own house!

The You Must Be Joking star eventually broke from his character, casually announcing: “You’ve been Shucks’d!”

Leanne Manas – almost in tears at the prank – later shared that she had experienced heart palpitations and rush of emotions during Schuster’s pretend confrontation.



She posted: “When I sat down with the legendary Leon Schuster and the conversation took an unexpected turn, my mind started racing. I was trying to work out how to bring things back on track before it all went too far!

She added: “What happened next caught me completely off guard”.

Watch the full interview below…

‘I’LL DIE A PRANKSTER!’

During his interview with Leanne Manas, Leon Schuster added that he had no ill intent behind his candid camera pranks, some of which have courted controversy for its portrayal of “blackface”.



He shared: “I’m a prankster, and I’ll die a prankster. It’s all part of the culture of this land”

“It’s important you know your audience. I try to give the people what they want. I’m so sorry I can’t make one final candid-camera movie. But one more clap and my neck will break”.

He added: “I want to be remembered as that okie from the Free State who stood firmly on the ground, who didnt a swollen head, and who contributed somehow to unify our nation through my movies”.

World.title: ‘Kaizer Chiefs is bigger than Fernando Da Cruz’
World.content:
There are growing concerns that the Chiefs job is too big for Fernando Da Cruz. Photo: Kaizer Chiefs Facebook

Kaizer Chiefs coach Fernando Da Cruz is under serious pressure after a dismal start to the campaign. Is he a good fit?

What are Da Cruz’s strengths as a coach?

Before his appointment, Da Cruz was known for his emphasis on tactical discipline and defensive structure. So far, the new boss has been insistent on a system using three central defenders, two wing-backs and a midfield pivot. The 3421 allows the front three to be more flexible. Injuries to regular central midfielders Lebo Maboe and Siphesihle Ndlovu were not ideal

A Marcelo Bielsa STUDENT

Fernando Da Cruz worked alongside legendary Argentinian Marcelo Bielsa at Lille. Da Cruz had three stints with the French outfit in several roles, namely, as a scout, caretaker manager and head coach of the B side, where he nurtured talents such as Idrissa Gueye, Lucas Digne, Victor Osimhen, and Eden Hazard.



Da Cruz has been good to his word, but it hasn’t been good enough

Mfundo Vilakazi has been handed 746 minutes. Only veterans Brandon Petersen, Inacio Miguel and Lebo Maboe have played more than the youngster. 20-year-old Luke Baartman has played 480 minutes, while 22-year-old Wandile Duba is proving his worth and winning the trust of the boss, playing 476 minutes so far. 22-year-old Mdu Shabalala has 442 minutes of playing time so far, but Langelihle Phili’s debut season with the club has been cruelly interrupted by a serious ankle injury. It’s clear that the youngsters are being trusted.

Chiefs are out of the title race

Kaizer Chiefs are already 12 points adrift of leaders Sundowns, and their season is only nine matches old. What conclusions can we draw here? Are the players at Da Cruz’s disposal simply not good enough, or is he not getting the most out of a talented young group?

World.title: ‘Here we are’: Ayanda Borotho unveils latest venture, YaNala Auras!
World.content:
Actress and entrepreneur Ayanda Borotho has peeled back another layer of her business ventures by launching YaNala Auras.

The former Isibaya actress recently introduced her brand on Instagram, paired with the tagline: “Healing auras by Nomafu.”

The luxurious brand offers an array of aromatic products crafted to bring warmth and healing to both living spaces and the body. Its range includes diffusers, soaps, luxury candles, scented bath salts, and linen mists.



AYANDA BOROTHO UNVEILS LATEST CREATION, YANALA AURAS

Ayanda has been forthcoming with information which is aimed at enhancing the customer experience.

She shared a detailed price list and a WhatsApp number for customers wishing to place orders from YaNala Auras.

She also shared the six signature scents that customers can choose from: Nala Star, Zaidi Eternal, Sala Whisper, Maisha Blossoms, Aliye Flora, and Raha Sun, offering multiple options from the brand’s catalogue.

‘HERE WE ARE IN CHAPTER YANALA’

In a personal Instagram post, Ayanda explained that she has been working tirelessly to bring YaNala Auras to life.

However, fear of failure almost engulfed her, as she had originally intended to launch the brand in August 2026.

She also revealed how the name YaNala Auras came about, adding that her faith was the catalyst behind forging ahead with the venture.



“I’ve been silently, tenaciously working on this baby. I intended to launch in August, but I chickened out. I was absolutely fearful of failure,” she began.

“And that’s the honest truth. But then I remembered I wrote a book because I was God-led. I yielded.

Here too, I yielded. And my soul remembered what it’s like to be carried,” she added.

“To trust not in the process but in the processor. So here we are in chapter YaNala, a combination of Yahweh (Divine God) and Nala (Abundance, also my name),” she wrote.

FLAIR FOR INTERIOR DECOR AND SUPPORT FOR BLACK-OWNED BUSINESSES

Over the years, Ayanda has often shown support for black-owned businesses in South Africa. Now, she finds herself on the receiving end of that support, thanking those who have shown interest in YaNala Auras.

In June 2026, Ayanda praised the impressive service of Dreamy Furniture, a black-owned business in Johannesburg that manufactures in luxury couches and headboards.

She had bought couches for her living room, which elevated the look and feel of her home’s interior.

World.title: ‘Age is just a number’: Sacha and Sarah Langa break silence on romance

World.title: How teacher salaries in Botswana compare with South Africa
World.content:
Teachers in South Africa and Botswana earn different salaries. Image: Pexels

Teachers in South Africa and Botswana earn different salaries, with qualifications, experience and job grades playing an important role in determining their monthly earnings.

The two neighbouring countries have different public-sector salary structures, but advertised salary scales provide an interesting comparison of what educators can earn.

South Africa’s 2026 teacher salary scales show that educators’ earnings vary significantly depending on their qualifications and experience.



According to salary information published by BusinessTech, the lowest salary notch is R169,707 annually, equivalent to approximately R14 142 per month.

However, qualified teachers with a Relative Education Qualification Value (REQV) of 14 to 17 start at R366 051 annually, translating to approximately R30 504 per month.

Experienced teachers in this category can earn up to R794 151 annually, or about R66 179 per month.



How much do teachers earn in Botswana?

In Botswana, advertised temporary teaching positions provide an indication of salaries available to educators entering the public education system.

A recent recruitment notice for temporary primary and secondary school teachers listed salaries between P108 444 and P123 420 annually for the C4 grade.

This translates to monthly earnings of approximately P9 037 to P10 285.



Teachers appointed under the C3 grade can earn between P127 092 and P150 852 annually, equivalent to approximately P10 591 to P12 571 per month.

Using an indicative exchange rate of P1 to R1.163 on 3 November 2026, the C4 salary range translates to approximately R126 114 to R143 540 annually.

The C3 range is equivalent to approximately R147 808 to R175 441 annually.



South Africa vs Botswana: Who pays teachers more?

The available figures suggest that qualified South African teachers earn more than those advertised in Botswana’s temporary teaching recruitment notice.

For instance, a South African teacher starting in the REQV 14–17 category earns approximately R30 504 monthly, compared with about R14 617 for a Botswana C3 teacher at the bottom of the advertised salary range.

However, the comparison is not a direct like-for-like assessment because the two countries use different grading systems, and the Botswana figures relate specifically to temporary appointments.



Teachers’ actual earnings also depend on qualifications, years of service, responsibilities and applicable benefits.

World.title: Mamelodi Sundowns become the first Carling Knockout semi-finalists

Mamelodi Sundowns coach Miguel Cardoso rang the changes ahead of this weekend’s CAF Super Cup final in mind. Only goalkeeper Ricardo Goss and Bathusi Aubaas retained their places following Saturday’s emphatic win over Durban City.

CARLING KNOCKOUT: MAMELODI SUNDOWNS 1-0 GOLDEN ARROWS

Sundowns were forced to bid their time until the closing stages of the first half to threaten. Bafana Bafana star Iqraam Rayners found Antonio van Wyk with a quality delivery, but the winger’s header flew wide with Dumisani Msibi to beat.

IQRAAM RAYNERS BREAKS THE DEADLOCK

The changes soon made an impact. Two minutes later, Rayners finally broke the deadlock, finishing with an unorthodorth header of a Van Wyk cross.

Golden Arrows enjoyed more possession as the half progressed, but their efforts to push forward were repeatedly shut down before they could make meaningful inroads into the final third. Sundowns defenders Mothobi Mvala and Malibongwe Khoza kept Dion under tight control.



That defensive discipline carried the hosts through the closing stages, as Sundowns comfortably managed the game to secure their place in the Carling Knockout semi-finals.

Coming up next in this weekend’s quarter-finals are the likes of Kaizer Chiefs and Orlando Pirates.

World.title: Authorities investigating bird deaths at Johannesburg’s Zoo Lake
World.content:
Carcasses of Egyptian geese and other waterbirds were discovered at Johannesburg's Zoo Lake this past weekend. Images via Canva @Daniel Mminele/@Aayesha-bebe Mayet

An investigation has been launched following the discovery of dead geese and other birds at Zoo Lake in Johannesburg.

As confirmed by the Zoo Lake Users Committee, the carcasses of more than 20 waterbirds – including Egyptian geese – were discovered at Zoo Lake on Sunday, 1 November 2026.

This prompted concerned park visitors and residents to raise the alarm.



JOHANNESBURG DEPARTMENTS INVESTIGATE

As of Monday, 2 November, Johannesburg City Parks and Zoo’s (JCPZ’s) Environmental Conservation team collected and removed the dead birds from the lake.

To establish the cause of death, veterinarians from the Johannesburg Zoo will conduct post-mortem examinations on selected carcasses.

Meanwhile, teams from JCPZ Conservation and Operations, the City’s Environment and Infrastructure Services Department and Johannesburg Water have collected water samples from the site.

POSSIBLE CAUSE OF DEATH

The JCPZ surmise that seasonal avian botulism, a disease fatal to birds, might have caused these birds’ deaths.

“Seasonal avian botulism is among the suspected causes, particularly during the current hot conditions,” said the JCPZ, per a media statement. “Warmer water and decomposing organic matter can create conditions favourable for the production of toxins that affect waterbirds.”

So far, avian botulism has not yet been confirmed, as they await the veterinary findings and water-quality testing results.



“Water-quality testing falls within the environmental oversight function of [the Environment and Infrastructure Services Department],” the JCPZ continued. “While testing provides information about conditions at the time of sampling, it cannot, on its own, predict every wildlife mortality incident. The timing of the deaths, preceding conditions and any available warning signs still need to be established through the investigation.”

JOHANNESBURG RESIDENTS ADVISED TO EXERCISE CAUTION

With the investigation underway, JCPZ reminds residents that the city’s urban dams and lakes are man-made and receive stormwater run-off. This can carry pollutants, litter and organic waste.

Hence, the appearance of clear water shouldn’t be taken as a guarantee that it’s safe to swim in or fish from.

For the sake of precaution, you are strongly encouraged to:

Refrain from swimming in these water bodies or consuming fish caught in them.

Keep children and pets away from dead or visibly distressed wildlife.

Avoid handling dead birds or fish.

Report dead birds, distressed waterbirds and fish kills to emi@jhbcityparks.com. Ensure that you provide the exact location and photographs where possible.

In other news, the SAHRC has raised concerns about corruption linked to water tanker contracts in Gauteng.

World.title: Ekurhuleni power battle: Can the MK Party weaken ANC support?
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - With just a few hours to go before election day, the country's metros are under the spotlight.

In Ekurhuleni, ongoing water challenges and other service delivery concerns are among the issues the community is facing.

The latest eNCA MarkData poll shows both the ANC and DA stand a chance of winning the municipality: 31,2% of respondents said they will vote for the DA, while 29,4% chose the ANC.

In 2021, the ANC won almost 50% of the vote in ward 52, while the IFP came second with 19%.

Sussman cites hostel communities as the driving force behind this IFP performance.

The political landscape shifted in the 2024 general elections when the MK Party emerged, securing 26% of the vote, while the ANC dropped to 38%.

“Tomorrow, we are going to be watching wards like this to see if uMkhonto weSizwe can create history and win wards off the ANC in townships like Katlehong,” he said.

The Brakpan area was also not left behind as Sussman dissected the political landscape in Ekurhuleni.

“There are about five roadhouses there. This is the area where the Freedom Front Plus did the best in Ekurhuleni in 2021. The DA got over 60% of the vote, and the Freedom Front 17%.” “The Freedom Front scored quite well in the eNCA MarkData poll. And we watch in wards like this, because generally, the ANC has to keep parties like uMkhonto weSizwe, EFF and, to some extent, the IFP, at bay. The DA has to deal with parties like the Freedom Front Plus and the PA,” he explained.

World.title: Lottery licence back to square one after court ruling
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - Trade, Industry and Competition Minister, Parks Tau, has to go back to the starting blocks regarding the National Lottery licence.

The licence to run the Lotto was awarded to Sizekhaya Holdings in May last year.

But the High Court in Pretoria has set aside that decision.

The ruling reopens the battle for one of South Africa's most lucrative licences.

READ | High Court sets aside awarding of Lotto licence to Sizekhaya Holdings

The challenge was brought by two unsuccessful bidders, Ithuba Lottery and the Ringeta Consortium.

In his ruling, Judge Norman Davis, found several flaws in the awarding process, including that Tau had taken advice from a new committee which had run a parallel process to that of the evaluation committee.

The judge suspended the declaration of invalidity for 12 months to not disruption lotto operations which are run by Sizekhaya for now.

World.title: SA Explained | Political Branding: Can Campaign Stunts And Slogans Win Voter Trust? | 03 November 2026
World.content:
The Pothole Has Become a Political Message. But Who Is Accountable for Fixing It?

A flooded road, an overflowing sewer or a dry household tap once represented a local service-delivery problem. Increasingly, these failures also provide the raw material for political campaigns. They can be photographed, filmed, shared and transformed into instantly recognisable symbols of municipal government.

The attraction is understandable. A politician standing beside a neglected road does not need a lengthy speech to explain why infrastructure matters. The image does much of the work. It offers a visible problem, identifies a location and invites the public to consider who should be held responsible. In an election campaign crowded with slogans and promises, that kind of simplicity is powerful.

Yet there is an important distinction between drawing attention to a failure and explaining how it will be corrected. The first requires a camera and a compelling moment. The second requires an understanding of municipal budgets, maintenance programmes, procurement, engineering capacity and the institutions responsible for delivery.

South Africa's municipal problems are also too substantial to be reduced to campaign spectacle. In its 2024–25 local government audit outcomes, the Auditor-General reported that only 39 of the country's 257 municipalities obtained clean audits. It also found continuing weaknesses in financial management, compliance and performance reporting, while metropolitan audit outcomes had regressed over the municipal term.

These findings do not establish that every municipality delivers poor services, nor does a clean audit automatically guarantee functioning infrastructure. They do, however, demonstrate why public accountability must extend beyond individual incidents to the systems that determine whether municipalities can deliver consistently.

The distinction becomes especially important when opposition politicians expose failures under an incumbent administration. Such scrutiny can serve a legitimate democratic purpose. Residents benefit when infrastructure problems that have been ignored receive attention, when officials are asked to explain delays and when promises are compared with actual progress.

But the same standard of scrutiny should apply to the politician offering an alternative. Identifying a pothole is not a road-maintenance strategy. Showing a broken water pipe is not a funded infrastructure programme. A credible public explanation should identify the responsible authority, the likely cause, the proposed remedy, the resources required and the timeframe against which progress can be assessed.

Incumbents face a different but equally demanding test. They may inherit neglected infrastructure, deteriorating finances or longstanding administrative weaknesses. These circumstances can help explain why a problem exists, but they do not eliminate responsibility for managing it. A useful response should make the history clear while showing what the current administration has done, what remains unresolved and when residents can expect measurable improvement.

Reputation strategist Tshepo Matseba offered a useful formulation in a conversation with eNCA's Naledi Moleo: "a brand is a promise fulfilled". Applied to municipal government, the phrase raises a practical question. What evidence should residents expect before accepting that a political promise has been honoured?

The answer cannot depend entirely on public relations. A repaired road, a functioning wastewater system or a reliable water supply requires more than a successful media response. It requires capable officials, credible financial information, maintenance planning, oversight and follow-through. Those processes are less visually appealing than a viral video, but they are what allow improvements to continue after the cameras leave.

The most valuable political content may therefore be the kind that creates lasting public scrutiny. A photograph of a flooded street should lead to questions about drainage maintenance, spending and responsibility. A viral clip about broken infrastructure should invite examination of previous repair commitments and current delivery plans. Public attention becomes more useful when it is connected to evidence that residents can revisit.

Campaign advertising can tell a compelling story about what a party intends to do. Municipal performance provides a record of what governing institutions have actually managed to achieve. Neither should be judged solely by a slogan or a single dramatic incident.

When the posters come down, the roads, taps and public services remain. That is where accountability becomes measurable, and where political promises must finally confront the ordinary demands of governing.

References

· Auditor-General of South Africa. Consolidated Report on Local Government Audit Outcomes 2024–25. https://mfma-2025.agsa.co.za/

· Auditor-General of South Africa. Audit Outcomes Overview, 2024–25. https://mfma-2025.agsa.co.za/pages/audit-outcomes-overview

· SA Explained. Naledi Moleo in conversation with Tshepo Matseba, recorded 2 November 2026. Source: SAX_02NOV_Naledi_Tshepo_2026_LGE_transcript.txt.

World.title: Number Of The Day | 1 Cent | 03 Number 2026
World.content:
The Illusion of the Pump: Why Complex Pricing Ecosystems Defy Common Sense

Few economic indicators touch daily routines quite as intimately as the monthly fuel price adjustment. For millions of commuters, logistics operators, and households, the announcement is an anxious ritual. When the adjustment lands on a microscopic one-cent reduction, public reaction oscillates between dark humour and quiet frustration. A single cent offers negligible comfort against the backdrop of broader cost-of-living pressures. Yet focusing purely on the final digit at the pump misses a far more intricate economic narrative happening beneath the surface.

Fuel pricing operates within a tightly regulated ecosystem governed by international petroleum costs, currency volatility, and domestic tax structures. When global crude markets surge due to geopolitical instability, local consumers brace for punishing hikes. In theory, recent state interventions through temporary fuel levy discounts were designed to cushion these systemic blows. However, the final price at the retail level rarely reflects a straightforward subtraction.

The missing link in the equation is the complex adjustment mechanism known as the slate levy. Designed to absorb cumulative under-recoveries in the oil industry over time, the slate levy acts as a financial shock absorber. When international pricing pressures create discrepancies between what fuel costs oil companies and what consumers pay, the slate adjusts. Consequently, substantial state-led relief measures can be entirely neutralized in a single month by a corresponding spike in the slate balance.

This dynamic highlights a broader truth about modern economic management. Systems exposed to multiple external variables rarely yield linear results. A policy designed to provide relief can be swallowed whole by structural pricing mechanisms operating downstream. For consumers and businesses alike, navigating these fluctuations requires looking past the immediate headline figure. True financial resilience relies on understanding the invisible gears turning behind the scenes, long before the fuel ever reaches the nozzle.

World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - “No excuses will be entertained when crime is committed."

This was a stern warning issued by Deputy National Commissioner for Policing Tebello Mosikili during a media briefing on Tuesday evening.

The briefing centred around security readiness for the 2026 local government elections scheduled for Wednesday.

Mosikili vowed that police and other law enforcement agencies will act decisively against criminality during the elections.

READ| Frustration as ballot delays disrupt Cape Town special voting

On Monday and Tuesday, between 8am and 5pm, voters approved for special votes cast their votes, but the two days were not without incidents.

According to Mosikili, the security environment recorded incidents that required the attention of law enforcement agencies and operational teams

One of the incidents she pointed to was the killing of a uMkhonto weSizwe (MK) Party regional leader in KwaZulu-Natal.

Mosikili said investigations into the matter continue.

Equally, she said the Political Killings Task Team (PKTT) has been seized with these matters and will provide necessary investigative support.

“We are confident that the investigating team will pursue available leads to ensure that those responsible are brought to justice.”

Political parties, their leadership, as well as supporters have also been called to exercise political tolerance and restraint during the voting process.

“Political differences must never translate into violence, intimidation or the loss of lives. We further caution anyone who may be contemplating acts of violence, assassination or any other criminal activity during this electoral period that our law enforcement agencies remain vigilant and will act decisively against criminal conduct,” she said.

World.title: Once midnight strikes, no campaigning will be permitted- NatJOINTS
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - Midnight on 3 November 2026 will mark the end of the official election campaigning period, in accordance with the electoral timetable.

This means that political parties will not be permitted to campaign on Wednesday as South Africans ready themselves to head to the polls for the 2026 local government elections.

Deputy National Commissioner for Policing Tebello Mosikili issued this stern reminder to political parties during a media briefing on Tuesday evening.

She reiterated that political persuasion, solicitation or intimidation of voters at or around voting stations will not be prohibited.

“Every eligible voter must be afforded an opportunity to exercise their democratic right freely, without undue influence, intimidation or interference from any political party or individual."

Mosikili also warned against protest actions during the electoral process.

She said anyone found to be contravening Section 76 of the Municipal Electoral Act 27 of 2000, or any other applicable provision of the law, will be dealt with accordingly.

“Our intention as law enforcement agencies is not to prevent people from exercising their constitutional and democratic rights.

“On the contrary, our deployment is intended to create an environment in which every South African can safely access a voting station and cast their vote without fear, intimidation or disruption,” she said.
