World.title: Rethinking Education Investment and Partnership in Africa
World.content:
This photo was taken at the main round table event at the University of Toronto.

At the Liberia–Canada Education Investment and Partnership Roundtable in Toronto organised by the OFFICE-Liberia Trade and Investment Office in Canada, I invited the institutions and individuals gathered in the room to find themselves in Liberiaʼs education story.

Dr. Jarso Maley Jallah, contributing writer

It was a deliberate invitation.



We had come to discuss the future of an education system serving more than 1.3 million learners, the reforms already underway, and the contributions that universities, colleges, foundations, businesses, and members of the diaspora could make.

Yet as I reflected on our engagements in Canada, I found myself returning to a question that extends far beyond Liberia:

When African countries seek international investment and partnerships, how do we ensure that the relationships we build strengthen our capacity to determine and sustain our own development?

The question is important to me because resources, however necessary, do not settle the deeper issues of ownership, institutional capability, and accountability. A country may attract considerable investment without fundamentally changing the conditions that made that investment necessary. Similarly, a partnership may deliver everything it promised while leaving the receiving institution unable to sustain or build upon those achievements.

I believe we must take these possibilities seriously. They reveal three closely connected questions that should guide our engagement with prospective partners:

Who defines the problem or need, Who assumes responsibility for addressing it, and What remains when the partnership has fulfilled its immediate purpose?

This photo was taken at Mohawk College in a session with with Mohawk College President Paul Armstrong, Associate Vice President for International Thea Laidman, and Manager for Global Markets Engagement Ricardo Rivera.

The first question is particularly important in the African context, where the way our challenges are represented often influences the solutions that are proposed.

Chimamanda Ngozi Adichieʼs reflections on The Danger of a Single Story offer a critical way of thinking about this. Her argument shows us that the stories told about people and places are inseparable from questions of power.

A narrative becomes particularly consequential when it is treated as the definitive account of another personʼs reality.

I see a parallel in how African education systems are frequently presented within international development conversations. The statistics are all too familiar: children out of school, inadequate classrooms, teachers without sufficient professional preparation, and low learning outcomes.

These are serious challenges, and governments have a responsibility to acknowledge them. In Liberia, our emphasis on foundational learning and adult literacy reflects our recognition of persistent learning gaps and our commitment to addressing them through deliberate policy choices and targeted investments.

But the statistics do not tell the whole story.

They reveal educational gaps without necessarily explaining the institutional conditions that produced them. They tell us where learners are struggling but may say little about the teachers working under difficult circumstances, the communities sustaining education despite limited resources, or the public investments already being made.

If we present only the deficits, we risk constructing a narrative in which Africa appears primarily as a place of need and the external partner becomes the principal agent of change. If we present only our achievements, however, we risk obscuring the very inequalities and institutional weaknesses that demand our attention.

Neither approach provides a sufficient basis for effective investment. Our responsibility is to present a more complete account: one that is honest about our challenges, clear about our national ambitions, and equally transparent about the capabilities and resources we bring to the partnership.

This is why the investment case we presented in Canada began with Liberiaʼs development agenda, our education priorities, existing commitments, and the evidence guiding our reforms. We wanted prospective partners to understand the direction Liberia has already established and identify where their contributions could strengthen it. But the power to define the problem is only meaningful if it is accompanied by the capacity and responsibility to shape the response.

Here, I find the work of Zambian economist Dambisa Moyo particularly relevant. In Dead Aid, Moyo challenges the assumption that sustained external assistance necessarily produces sustained development. Her critique raises difficult questions about dependency, political accountability, and the incentives created when governments rely heavily on resources controlled by others.

Her conclusions have generated considerable debate, and rightly so. African countries have benefited from development partnerships that have expanded access to education, strengthened health systems, and supported critical infrastructure. Liberiaʼs own experience demonstrates the

importance of international cooperation, particularly given the scale of our educational needs and the constraints on public resources. I would therefore resist treating the debate as a simple choice between accepting external support and rejecting it.

The more consequential question is what our financing relationships enable governments to become.

Do they strengthen our ability to plan, coordinate, finance, and deliver public services? Do they develop professional and institutional capabilities within the country? Do they reinforce accountability to the citizens whose education and futures are at stake? Or do they create arrangements in which essential functions remain dependent on external expertise, parallel systems, and financing that may not be available indefinitely?

In conversation with Canada Black International Women Excellence Founder Rose Cathy Handy

These are uncomfortable questions because they place responsibility on both sides of a partnership. Development partners must examine whether their funding arrangements strengthen the institutions they intend to support. Governments must confront weaknesses in their own planning, coordination, public financing, and implementation.

We cannot meaningfully demand ownership while avoiding the obligations that ownership entails. In Liberia, this means taking responsibility for the education system long after individual projects conclude. It means understanding what is already financed before inviting new investment, ensuring that different programs reinforce one another, and making difficult decisions about the recurrent costs of the reforms we introduce.

It also means accepting that a signed agreement, a completed project, or an impressive financing announcement cannot substitute for institutional progress.

This brings me to a further question:

What kinds of capabilities should education investment and partnership ultimately develop?

More than half a century ago, Julius Nyerere, in Education for Self-Reliance, challenged African societies to examine the purposes their education systems were designed to serve. He was concerned with the relationship between education, national development, social responsibility, and the realities of the societies in which learners would live and work. His thinking emerged in a particular historical and political context, and no countryʼs educational model should be adopted without examining its limitations. But the underlying question remains important for contemporary Africa: are we developing education systems that equip our people to participate meaningfully in transforming their societies?

In conversation with President and CEO of Atlas International Freight Forwarding Inc. (Atlas Cargo) and Canadian Customs Brokers Inc.

For Liberia, this question has immediate relevance. Our national development ambitions include investment in agriculture, infrastructure, energy, health, industry, and economic transformation. These ambitions require engineers, technicians, educators, researchers, entrepreneurs, and skilled workers.

Yet expanding access to education alone will not guarantee that those capabilities emerge. During our visit to Mohawk College College, I was particularly interested in how technical training connects with industry, practical experience, and employment. It demonstrated the importance of relationships between educational institutions and the environments in which their graduates will apply their knowledge.

For Liberia, the lesson is to examine how such relationships can be developed within our own economic and institutional realities.

A technical training center needs qualified instructors, functioning equipment, relevant curricula, and credible pathways into work. A university partnership should strengthen teaching, research, and institutional competence. Teacher development should result in better professional practice and improved learning.

The value of these investments lies in how the different elements reinforce one another. This is especially important because African countries cannot afford to reproduce systems whose operating costs and technical requirements they are unable to sustain.

A technology partnership, for example, should prompt questions about maintenance, connectivity, accessibility, content, and the capacity of local institutions to manage what is introduced. An infrastructure investment should account for staffing, operations, and the conditions required for the facility to serve its intended purpose. These considerations are sometimes treated as implementation details. I regard them as central questions ofdevelopment.

A partnership that increases a countryʼs dependence on external support may meet an immediate need while creating another long-term vulnerability. Conversely, a partnership that develops local expertise, strengthens public institutions, and improves their ability to solve problems can generate value well beyond its original financing period.

There is also a broader purpose to education that must remain visible within these discussions.

We need education systems that prepare people for productive employment and economic opportunity. But education must also expand peopleʼs ability to think critically, participate in public life, challenge inequality, and exercise meaningful choices about their futures.

The value of a girl completing school, an adult acquiring literacy, or a learner with a disability gaining access to education cannot be fully understood through earnings or labor-market participation alone. These outcomes concern the kind of society we are creating. For this reason, I believe the definition of an effective education partnership must be sufficiently broad to recognize both economic and social value, while remaining sufficiently rigorous to demand evidence of actual results.

That balance is important because if everything is described as impact, accountability becomes difficult. If only immediately measurable outputs are valued, some of the most important purposes of education risk being neglected.

We must learn to hold both considerations together.

As I return to the discussions in Canada, these reflections have practical implications. At our Toronto Roundtable, participants requested 90 days to engage additional institutions, mobilize resources, and consider a coordinated response to Liberiaʼs education priorities. I welcomed that expression of interest and the willingness to undertake further work.

But the true significance of that engagement will depend on what follows. We must ask whether proposed contributions respond to demonstrated needs, whether the institutions involved possess the appropriate capabilities, and whether the arrangements we establish will strengthen Liberiaʼs ability to deliver education.

We must also be honest about the responsibilities we are prepared to assume ourselves. Some partnerships may involve financing classrooms or learning materials. Others may focus on institutional development, applied research, teacher education, workforce training, or technical cooperation. Their structures will differ because the problems they address differ.

What should unite them is a clear contribution to national priorities, shared responsibility for implementation, and a credible understanding of what will remain after the initial engagement.

For me, this is where the perspectives of Adichie, Moyo, and Nyerere converge in a useful way. They approach different questions, but each invites us to examine a dimension of African agency: the ability to represent our realities, take responsibility for our development, and shape institutions that serve the needs and aspirations of our societies.

Their perspectives also challenge African governments to look inward.

We must not allow the legitimate criticism of externally driven development to become an excuse for weak governance, inadequate domestic investment, or poor implementation. National ownership carries little meaning unless it is demonstrated through decisions, institutions, and accountability.

The responsibility is ours to exercise.

I left Canada encouraged by the possibilities for collaboration, but also conscious of the standard to which those collaborations must be held. The question I now carry into our next phase of engagement is the same one that shaped my invitation in Toronto, although I would frame it more precisely.

We have asked prospective partners where they fit in Liberiaʼs education story. We must now determine what we can build together, who will be responsible for sustaining it, and whether that collaboration leaves our institutions more capable of serving our people.

If education investment and partnership are to contribute meaningfully to Africaʼs development, they must expand our capacity to shape our own futures.

That is the measure of partnership I believe Liberia should pursue, and the responsibility we must be prepared to uphold.

Dr. Jarso Maley Jallah serves as Minister of Education, Republic of Liberia.

World.title: LCC, EU Dedicate Trade Facilitation Secretariat Office to Boost Private Sector Growth
World.content:
MONROVIA — The Liberia Chamber of Commerce (LCC), with support from the European Union (EU), has dedicated a renovated office for the National Trade Facilitation Secretariat (NTFS), in a move aimed at strengthening public-private sector collaboration, improving trade procedures, and creating a more conducive business environment in Liberia.

By Francis G. Boayue

The dedication ceremony, held on Thursday, October 29, also recognized logistical support provided by the EU Delegation to Liberia through the Private Sector Development Project, implemented by Expertise France.



Speaking at the ceremony, LCC President O. Natty B. Davis said hosting the Secretariat demonstrates the Chamber’s commitment to bringing government institutions and private businesses together to address challenges affecting investment and economic growth.

“Hosting the National Trade Facilitation Secretariat is a demonstration of our commitment to strengthening collaboration between government and the private sector. We believe that bringing these institutions closer to businesses will help address the challenges affecting investment and economic growth,” Davis said.

He expressed appreciation to the Government of Liberia, the EU Delegation, Expertise France, the Ministry of Commerce and Industry, and the Liberia Revenue Authority for their support toward the initiative.

Davis emphasized that businesses require clear regulations, consistent policies, and predictable government services to make sound investment decisions, particularly for projects involving substantial capital and long-term commitments.

“Businesses need certainty. Investors must be able to operate within a system where policies are consistent, regulations are clear, and government services are predictable,” he stated.

Referencing discussions at the recent Liberia International Mining and Energy Conference, Davis identified inadequate coordination among government institutions as a major concern for private-sector operators.

He said the Secretariat’s presence at the Chamber would provide an opportunity to strengthen institutional relationships and ensure that business concerns receive greater attention in national trade policy discussions.

Davis also disclosed that the office would complement the Chamber’s Trade Desk, which is expected to improve businesses’ access to reliable statistics, trade-related information, and other services necessary for investment and expansion.

Meanwhile, Dimitri De-Pues, Regional Hub Investment Officer at the EU Delegation to Liberia, welcomed the completion of the renovated facility, describing it as an important milestone in the partnership between the European Union and the Liberia Chamber of Commerce.

De-Pues said the collaboration between the two institutions had lasted nearly two years and reaffirmed the EU’s commitment to supporting the initiative throughout the remaining three years of the project.

“Our commitment to supporting private-sector development in Liberia remains strong. We recognize the importance of working together with the Chamber, the Ministry of Commerce and Industry, and Expertise France to create opportunities for businesses and improve the country’s trade environment,” De-Pues said.

He stressed the importance of continued cooperation among implementing partners to ensure the project achieves its intended objectives.

Also speaking, Deputy Minister of Commerce and Trade Wilmot A. Reeves, Chairman of the National Trade Facilitation Committee, welcomed the Chamber’s decision to host the Secretariat, describing it as an important contribution to improving Liberia’s business climate.

Reeves explained that the EU-supported Private Sector Development Project promotes business growth through interventions targeting key value chains, including wood processing, fisheries, and cassava.

“Government cannot do it alone. Our responsibility is to create an enabling environment where the private sector can operate, expand, create opportunities, and contribute meaningfully to national development,” Reeves emphasized.

He said the project also prioritizes public-private dialogue and the removal of barriers that prevent businesses from reaching their full potential.

Another speaker, Buku, underscored the importance of private-sector participation in trade modernization, noting that involving businesses early in the reform process helps ensure that policies address practical challenges encountered by operators.

“Trade reforms must reflect the realities of the business community. When the private sector is involved from the beginning, we are better positioned to identify challenges and develop solutions that respond to the actual needs of businesses,” Buku said.

He welcomed the dedicated workspace, noting that it would strengthen the Secretariat’s ability to coordinate activities and communicate business concerns during trade policy discussions.

The National Trade Facilitation Secretariat operates under the National Trade Facilitation Committee, chaired by the Ministry of Commerce and Industry.

Its presence at the Liberia Chamber of Commerce is expected to strengthen engagement with businesses, improve access to trade-related information, and enhance coordination among relevant institutions.

The initiative is expected to contribute to reducing trade barriers, attracting investment, and supporting sustainable private-sector growth.

However, its long-term impact will depend on the ability of the Secretariat and its partners to translate their commitments into practical reforms that improve Liberia’s business and trading environment.

World.title: Liberian Rights Advocates Urge Abolition of Death Penalty
World.content:
PAYNESVILLE — Naymote Partners for Democratic Development has entered into a partnership with the Civil Society Human Rights Advocacy Platform of Liberia (CSOHRAP) to strengthen human rights monitoring, legislative engagement, and evidence-based advocacy aimed at advancing the abolition of the death penalty in Liberia.

By Francis G. Boayue

The partnership is being implemented under the FCDO Support for the Abolition of the Death Penalty Phase III – A Strategic Advocacy Initiative, through a sub-award agreement effective August 3, 2026, and running through January 31, 2027.



Under the agreement, Naymote will contribute to strengthening civil society engagement with the Liberian Legislature by monitoring legislative developments, gathering and analyzing information on lawmakers’ positions on the death penalty, and developing a standardized legislative scorecard methodology to support evidence-based advocacy.

Adama Dempster, Secretary General of CSHRAP, said Liberia’s continued retention of the death penalty undermines its commitment to international human rights standards and called on the government and Legislature to take concrete steps toward its abolition.

Dempster made the remarks on Monday during a one-day capacity-building training for legislative observers and interns on the Abolition of Death Penalty Project (ADP), legislative engagement and advocacy, organized by SHRAP in partnership with Naymote Partners for Democratic Development, with support from the British Embassy.

He said Liberia was among the first ten countries to ratify the Second Optional Protocol to the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, which seeks the abolition of capital punishment.

According to Dempster, Liberia abolished the death penalty in 2005 but subsequently reintroduced it between 2005 and 2008 following concerns over increasing armed robberies, hijackings, and other violent crimes.

He said the decision was intended to deter criminal activities but had failed to produce the desired results.

“The reintroduction of the death penalty had not reduced crimes at all, and it had not changed society in terms of serving as a lesson for those who are committing crimes daily,” Dempster said.

He argued that Liberia’s commitment to human rights should be reflected in its laws and policies, particularly those concerning the protection of human life.

Dempster cited Article 20(a) of the Liberian Constitution and the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights as legal frameworks that underscore the protection of life.

He also raised concerns about the possibility of wrongful convictions, particularly given what he described as Liberia’s limited forensic capacity to conclusively identify individuals involved in criminal activities.

According to him, executing a person who is later found to have been wrongfully convicted would constitute an irreversible miscarriage of justice.

“The actions taken under the death penalty are irreversible. If we later discover that an individual was not the person who committed the crime, what do we say to such a person?” he asked.

Dempster maintained that Liberia could adopt alternative punishments, including life imprisonment, while strengthening its criminal justice system and improving prison facilities.

He cautioned against using existing prison conditions as a justification for retaining capital punishment, arguing that prisons should focus on rehabilitation rather than punishment alone.

Dempster said SHRAP and Naymote are intensifying engagement with lawmakers to build support for the abolition of the death penalty.

He disclosed that legislative observers and interns would be stationed at the Legislature to monitor proceedings, track lawmakers’ positions, and document debates relating to the proposed abolition.

According to him, the observers will monitor lawmakers who support, oppose, or abstain from decisions concerning the death penalty, providing civil society organizations with information to guide targeted advocacy.

“The legislative interns’ work will help us to know how to engage individual lawmakers and how to win them over to support this bill that has to do with abolishing the death penalty,” he said.

He added that the initiative would help civil society organizations better understand lawmakers’ positions and develop strategies to engage those who remain opposed to abolition.

Dempster said there was political willingness within the Legislature to advance the issue, noting that the position of the Senate could provide an opportunity for further engagement with the House of Representatives.

He urged lawmakers to reconsider the existing legal framework, arguing that abolishing the death penalty would strengthen Liberia’s human rights credentials and demonstrate leadership in the region.

Dempster further argued that Liberia’s international standing creates an opportunity for the country to demonstrate leadership on human rights issues.

He cited countries across Africa and the world that have abolished capital punishment, including Sierra Leone, Guinea, Ghana, and Côte d’Ivoire.

He said Liberia should align itself with evolving international human rights standards, particularly as the country seeks to play a greater role in international affairs.

“We need to show leadership by abolishing the death penalty,” Dempster said.

He maintained that the abolition of capital punishment would not weaken Liberia’s justice system but would instead encourage reforms aimed at protecting lives, strengthening accountability, and ensuring justice.

The Abolition of Death Penalty Project 2026 seeks to strengthen legislative engagement and advocacy through the training of observers and interns, equipping them with the skills to monitor legislative proceedings and support efforts to secure the abolition of capital punishment in Liberia.

World.title: Liberia: Unity Party Officials’ ‘Unit 2’ Meetings Stir Questions Over Who Wields Power in Boakai Government
World.content:
MONROVIA – Three senior officials of the Unity Party-led government have set tongues wagging after posting photos on Facebook of what they described as late-night strategy sessions with “Unit 2,” a label widely read in political circles as a reference to Vice President Jeremiah Kpan Koung.

By Rodney D. Sieh

The posts come at a delicate moment for the Boakai administration, which is still facing questions over its request that the European Union withdraw its envoy to Liberia, partly over remarks she allegedly made about the Vice President’s reach into sectors outside his constitutional remit. For many observers, the timing has sharpened a question already circulating in Monrovia: who is really running the country?



The Posts

Youth and Sports Minister Cornelia Wonkerleh Kruah captioned her photos: “To be a politician is not the thing… It’s the late-night meetings… Check-In with Unit 2…” She tagged the post #StrategicPartnership, #UnityParty and #PreparingForTheSecondLeg.

Mohammed “Mo” Ali, Managing Director of the Liberia Water and Sewer Corporation and a former Unity Party Secretary General, posted photos from the same room, writing: “These late-night strategic sessions keep things moving and on course.”

M. Boakai Jaleiba, Vice President for Administration at the National Oil Company of Liberia (NOCAL), followed with: “After a late-night caucus with Unit-2!”

None of the three posts mentions President Joseph Nyuma Boakai.

The EU Backdrop

Earlier this year, the Government of Liberia formally asked the European Union to recall and replace its Head of Delegation, Ambassador Nona Deprez, accusing her of making statements that undermined the country’s leadership, institutions and investment climate.

In a letter signed by Acting Foreign Minister Ethel Davis, the government alleged that the envoy made a series of derogatory and misleading comments during official engagements with Liberian authorities, investors and development stakeholders.

Some of the remarks were reportedly made at the Liberia-European Union Business Forum in Brussels on February 24-25, where the envoy allegedly questioned governance practices within the Liberian government and raised concerns about Vice President Koung’s role in the mining and energy sectors.

Critics of the move argued at the time that calling for the ambassador’s recall did not, by itself, clear the Vice President, and risked leaving the allegation unresolved in the public space.

Loyalty Signals

Against that backdrop, political watchers say the posts read less like routine party business and more like a public declaration of where loyalty lies. The hashtag #PreparingForTheSecondLeg is likely to be read as a nod to 2029, raising the question of whose second leg is being prepared.

The officials’ own histories add a layer of intrigue. FrontPageAfrica previously reported that President Boakai and his immediate circle blamed Mo Ali, Amin Modad, Cllr. Jeror Cole Bangalu and Rep. Clarence Massaquoi for the party’s defeat in Lofa. Massaquoi, now Chairman of the Liberia Telecommunications Authority, is Minister Kruah’s spouse. For some insiders, a visible alignment with the Vice President by figures once at odds with the President’s inner circle is hard to dismiss as coincidence.

‘The Prezzo Approved This Meeting’

A government official, speaking on condition of anonymity, pushed back on that reading.

“It is my understanding that the Prezzo had approved this meeting. It was primarily to discuss growing disenchantment among the young people in the party. Don’t mind the way it is being projected by the posts,” the official told FrontPageAfrica.

The source conceded, however, that the party’s troubles run deeper. “That, yes, is our biggest problem right now. People want to hold onto their jobs and not pay attention to the party. And even in their jobs, how many of the young people have they brought on board?”

Bad Optics

Critics are less forgiving, noting that most of those in the room owe their positions to President Boakai.

“These are people the President gave jobs. Is he supposed to tell them what to do? Should he provide them money? The optics are bad,” said the source.

Whatever the intent, the episode lands on a government already defending itself against claims that power has drifted from the Executive Mansion. If the meeting was sanctioned by the President, the officials chose to tell the public it was with “Unit 2,” not him. In Liberian politics, that kind of messaging is rarely accidental.

World.title: Liberia: McGill Signals CDC Comeback, Says UP Would Not Have Won 2023 Elections Had He Remained in Government
World.content:
Monrovia – Former Minister of State for Presidential Affairs Nathaniel McGill has reignited political conversations about the future leadership of the opposition Congress for Democratic Change (CDC), declaring that the ruling Unity Party (UP) would not have won the 2023 presidential elections had he remained in government.

McGill, who currently represents Margibi County in the Liberian Senate, made the assertion while defending his political influence and electoral support, despite being placed under United States sanctions.

The former minister maintained that his political standing remained intact even after the sanctions, pointing to his election to the Senate as evidence that he continues to enjoy considerable grassroots support.



“If I had remained as Minister of State, the Unity Party would not have won. Despite being sanctioned, the Liberian people still voted for me and elected me as senator. I had the backing of the people,” McGill said.

His remarks come at a politically significant moment for the CDC, which is facing growing internal conversations over whether to retain its current chairman, Janga Kowo, or install a new leader as the party positions itself for a return to power.

McGill further suggested that the Boakai-led administration was already losing its political grip, declaring that the CDC has the political strength and personnel to reclaim the presidency.

“We have men, we have soldiers in the CDC. And we are coming back,” he said.

Political Scorecard and Claims of Unfinished Projects

Beyond his political declaration, McGill sought to challenge the Unity Party government’s development record, arguing that several projects being presented as achievements of the current administration were initiated or negotiated under the former CDC-led government.

He specifically referenced the Roberts International Airport (RIA) Road Project, the agreement for the construction of an overpass bridge, and a diagnostic laboratory at the 14 Military Hospital.

“The RIA Road Project belongs to us. We signed the agreement for the overpass bridge. The diagnostic laboratory at the 14 Military Hospital was also supposed to be dedicated. We completed more roads, yet this government has not commissioned a single one,” McGill claimed.

He argued that, had he remained Minister of State, he would have demanded explanations from the Ministers of Finance and Public Works over the failure to commission completed road projects.

While McGill’s comments reflect the CDC’s attempt to reclaim political credit for projects initiated during its administration, the claims also underscore the continuing political contest between the former ruling party and the government over development achievements.

Kowo’s Leadership Under Scrutiny

But beyond the exchange over political performance, McGill’s comments have drawn renewed attention to the unresolved question of who should lead the CDC as it attempts to reorganize following its defeat in the 2023 elections.

Janga Kowo currently serves as chairman of the party, having assumed the position following the resignation of Mulbah Morlu, who stepped down both as chairman and from the party.

A former Comptroller and Accountant General of Liberia, Kowo inherited the CDC during one of the most challenging periods in its political history.

His leadership has been credited by supporters with helping to keep the party together amid internal disagreements, political uncertainty and the transition from governing party to opposition.

Under his chairmanship, the CDC has remained vocal in its criticism of the Unity Party-led government. However, some partisans have questioned whether his leadership style is sufficiently assertive to reposition the party for a political comeback.

While critics favor a change at the top, others believe removing Kowo could deepen existing divisions and undermine the relative stability he has helped maintain.

The disagreement presents a difficult choice for the former ruling party: whether to prioritize continuity and internal cohesion or embrace a more confrontational leadership capable of energizing its base.

McGill, Koijee Emerge in Succession Speculation

Sources within the party indicate that former President George Weah and some members of the CDC hierarchy are considering possible alternatives to Kowo.

Among the names circulating is McGill, whose close political relationship with Weah and experience in the former administration have fueled speculation that he could be a preferred candidate for the chairmanship.

Although no formal decision has been announced, McGill’s recent remarks, particularly his declaration that the CDC has the political personnel to return to power, have added another dimension to speculation about his possible political ambitions within the party.

Another prominent name is former Monrovia City Mayor and CDC Secretary-General Jefferson T. Koijee, who has built a strong political following, particularly among the party’s youthful supporters.

Koijee rose through the ranks of the CDC Youth League and remains one of the party’s most recognizable and outspoken figures.

His popularity among younger partisans could make him an attractive option for those seeking a more energetic and combative leadership style. However, his inclusion in the succession conversation also raises questions about the political and reputational implications of his continued presence on the United States sanctions list.

McGill, too, remains under U.S. sanctions, creating a potentially complicated leadership choice for a party seeking to rebuild its national and international political standing.

The sanctions do not automatically disqualify either man from holding the party’s chairmanship.

Other Names in the Leadership Conversation

Other names being mentioned include Eugene Lenn Nagbe, a former commissioner of the Liberia Maritime Authority and special aide to Weah.

Nagbe’s experience in public service and association with the former president have placed him among the personalities being discussed as the party considers its leadership options.

Former House Speaker Jonathan Fonati Koffa has also been mentioned as a possible contender.

Koffa, who previously belonged to the Liberty Party before switching allegiance to the CDC, currently chairs the committee overseeing the construction of the party’s headquarters.

However, sources close to the former speaker say he has no intention of contesting for the chairmanship.

His name nevertheless reflects the broader search within the party for a leader who can command political respect, strengthen internal structures and help bridge differences among competing factions.

A Defining Moment for the CDC

The CDC’s leadership question goes beyond choosing a new chairman. It touches on the party’s identity, its relationship with former President Weah, the influence of its political heavyweights and the strategy it intends to pursue ahead of the next electoral cycle.

Kowo’s supporters see continuity as essential to preserving party unity, while those advocating a change believe the CDC needs a more assertive political figure to rebuild its mobilization capacity and challenge the ruling government.

McGill’s latest remarks have added to that debate, particularly because they come from a former senior official of the Weah administration who continues to command an electoral constituency despite the controversy surrounding his U.S. sanctions.

Whether his declaration signals a genuine interest in the chairmanship or is simply an assertion of his political relevance remains unclear.

What is increasingly evident, however, is that the CDC faces a delicate leadership decision. A poorly managed transition could expose existing divisions, while a carefully negotiated succession could provide an opportunity to rebuild the party’s structures and strengthen its opposition politics.

For now, Kowo remains chairman, and no formal succession process or final decision has been announced. But with McGill, Koijee and other prominent figures featuring in the conversation, the question of who will lead the CDC into its next political chapter is becoming increasingly difficult to ignore.

World.title: NGO withdraws 264 children from Labour
World.content:
Support for Poverty Reduction in Zambia (SPRIZ) has withdrawn 264 children from child labour in Kaoma and Nkeyema Districts of Western Province.

The children were found working in tobacco farms, while others were victims of early marriages and other worst forms of child labour.

This came to light today during the quarterly implementation and monitoring review meeting of the District Child Labour Committee (DCLC) held at Mumu Lodge in Kaoma.

SPRIZ Programme Manager Rodah Banda disclosed that with support from Japan Tobacco International (JTI), the organisation in Quarter two and Three identified 578 children engaged in child labour in tobacco-growing communities.

Ms Banda explained that out of the 578 children identified, 264 have been withdrawn while 267 have been prevented from entering child labour.

“So far, 310 children who had dropped out of school have been reintegrated back into school,” Ms Banda said.

She said the affected communities in Kaoma include Chitwa, Mulalila and Kajejeje, while in Nkeyema the organisation is working in Chibuli, Nakuyuwa and Kakanda areas.

To strengthen prevention, SPRIZ had planned to sensitise 5,968 members of Community Child Labour Committees (CCLCs), out of which 1,817 were children, 1,504 JTI tobacco farmers and 219 JTI farm workers.

The organisation also organised a school debate which attracted 20 schools in both Nkeyema and Kaoma to raise awareness on child rights and the dangers of child labour.

Ms Banda has called for a multisectoral approach among DCLC members comprising different government departments and other partners if child labour is to be eliminated in the two tobacco-growing districts.

She further called on the Department of Labour in the districts to prosecute parents who are in the habit of engaging children in labour instead of taking them to school.

And speaking earlier, Kaoma District Assistant Labour Officer Kim Mweemba commended SPRIZ for coming on board to spearhead child protection issues.

Mr Mweemba observed that the fight against child labour is yielding positive results with SPRIZ supporting DCLC activities in the two districts.

He attributed child labour to poverty and early marriages, noting that some households expect children to fend for themselves.

“Some parents would rather let children work in tobacco fields than go to school,” Mr Mweemba said.

He reaffirmed the Labour Office’s commitment to bring perpetrators to book to serve as a warning to would-be offenders.

Meanwhile, DCLC member departments have pledged to each play a vital role in eliminating child labour in the two districts.

SPRITZ is a non-profit organization whose mission is to empower communities to reduce poverty through advocacy, capacity building and service delivery.

It is the main implementing partner for the International Labour Organisation (ILO) and Japan Tobacco International (JTI) programme in Zambia to eliminate the Worst Forms of Child Labour in tobacco farming.

World.title: Orbis, ZOS host women’s eye health workshop
World.content:
Orbis International in collaboration with the Zambia Ophthalmological Society (ZOS) has hosted the Women in Ophthalmology annual workshop to strengthen collaboration, mentorship and inclusive leadership in the eye health sector.

The workshop held in Lusaka today was under the theme “Stronger Together: Creating Collaborative and Inclusive Teams in Ophthalmology.”

The event, which precedes the 10th ZOS Annual Scientific Congress, provides a platform for women in ophthalmology to exchange experiences, build professional networks and explore ways of strengthening teamwork within the sector.

Orbis Country Director, Lucia Mvula, highlighted the importance of wellness, stating that it must begin with women who strive to serve others in order to deliver high quality patient care.

Ms Mvula emphasised on deliberate investment in the wellbeing of female health workers, as their health and motivation directly affect service delivery.

She noted that the meeting aims to promote peer support, mentorship and sponsorship among women professionals in ophthalmology and to foster career progression as well as professional fulfilment for women in the health sector.

Meanwhile, Renaissance Managing Consultant, Mutale Kabumbu, emphasised the importance of work-life balance in enhancing productivity and personal wellbeing.

World.title: Cabinet approves 2027 budget
World.content:
Cabinet has approved the 2027 National Budget and two major trade measures aimed at driving economic growth and protecting local industry.

Minister of Information and Media, Elvis Nkandu said this in a press statement issued to the media after the 3rd Cabinet Meeting of the second term, held at State House on Friday 30th October, 2026 chaired by President Hakainde Hichilema.

Mr Nkandu, who is also Chief Government Spokesperson, said Cabinet approved the 2027 Estimates of Revenue and Expenditure, including revenue mobilisation, public expenditure and structural reform measures for the 2027 fiscal year.

He said Cabinet noted that the country is on a positive economic trajectory and stressed that sustained macroeconomic stability will be critical in advancing the Grow Zambia Agenda, strengthening investor confidence and stimulating private sector involvement.

“Cabinet has called for prudent fiscal management in 2027 as Government translates the Grow Zambia Agenda into concrete programmes and activities,” he said

Meanwhile, the Cabinet has approved the signing of the Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA) between Zambia and the United Arab Emirates (UAE).

Mr Nkandu said Cabinet also approved the establishment of an implementation, import-surveillance and periodic review mechanism for the agreement.

He explained that sustained private-sector growth requires access to larger external markets to support economies of scale, export diversification, technology transfer and integration into regional and global value chains.

“The UAE is an important commercial, logistics, investment and export hub. Therefore, a predictable bilateral framework can greatly improve the conditions under which Zambian exporters access the UAE market and provide a platform for attracting investment into productive sectors in Zambia,” Mr Nkandu said.

He said the CEPA is relevant to the Government’s growth agenda to achieve the eight-point development targets planned for the next five years in agriculture, energy, mining and tourism, and is expected to expand commercial opportunities subject to Zambia increasing its productive capacity and value addition.

The Cabinet has approved in principle the introduction of the Trade Remedies Bill, 2026 in Parliament.

Mr Nkandu said the Bill will provide mechanisms to strengthen the legal framework for trade remedies and will amend the Control of Goods Act and the Customs and Excise Act.

He said to maintain a viable Industrial sector amidst trade liberalisation, Zambia requires adequate legal and institutional frameworks that provide alert systems and defence mechanisms against unfair international trade practices.

“The new legislation seeks to provide for trade remedies under a single legislation, enhance the provisions with more and better administrative details and strengthen the laws by modernising the provisions and adding safeguards for a number of sectors,” he said.

He added that once enacted, the law will strengthen protection of domestic industry from unfair trade practices in line with World Trade Organisation guidelines.

The 2027 Budget will be presented to Parliament on Friday, 6th November 2026.

World.title: Govt responds to EU EOM 2026 general elections report
World.content:
Minister of Information and Media Elvis Nkandu says Zambia welcomes constructive elections observations that contribute to strengthening democratic institutions.

Reacting to the final Report issued by the European Union (EU) Election Observation Mission (EOM) regarding the 13 August 2026 General Elections, Mr Nkandu however highlighted several concerns regarding some of the conclusions reached and recommendations advanced in the report.

Mr Nkandu who is also Chief Government Spokesperson explained that government was not afforded sufficient opportunity to provide historical, institutional and security context regarding a number of issues upon which significant conclusions appear to have been based.

In a statement issued to the media, he noted that certain findings risk presenting an incomplete picture of Zambia’s democratic journey.

He cited the concerns raised regarding legal and electoral reforms undertaken in proximity to elections, saying that the report creates the impression that amendments to electoral laws and constitutional provisions in an election year are exceptional developments under the administration of President Hakainde Hichilema.

“This portrayal is inconsistent with Zambia’s constitutional and political history. Successive administrations have undertaken significant constitutional and electoral reforms during election years. The historical record demonstrates that this has occurred under multiple administrations across different political eras,” he indicated.

He explained that to present the 2026 reforms without a historical context risks creating a misleading impression that the current administration acted in a manner unprecedented in Zambia’s democratic development.

Further, the Minister stated the government’s concern on conclusions relating to the performance and conduct of the Zambia National Broadcasting Corporation (ZNBC) that appear to have been reached without adequately engaging the institution itself.

He noted that the report states that ZNBC was overwhelmingly biased toward the incumbent, a conclusion which would have benefited from direct engagement with the broadcaster regarding its statutory mandate, editorial obligations and operational practices.

And Mr Nkandu underscored that election observation missions can only provide an assessment of what they directly observe and that they do not necessarily possess access to all intelligence, security information, law enforcement investigations or national security assessments available to sovereign state institutions.

“In a number of cases during the electoral period, law enforcement agencies were dealing with conduct that went far beyond normal political activity. Some political actors and their supporters were subjects of investigations involving serious allegations of criminal conduct,” he added.

The Minister stressed that certain matters touched on activities prohibited under the laws of Zambia and posed legitimate concerns for public order and national security.

He noted that without structured engagement with relevant government institutions, it would have been difficult for an observation mission to fully appreciate the circumstances surrounding some of the decisions and actions undertaken by state agencies.

“This does not diminish the value of election observation. However, it highlights the importance of balanced consultation and a comprehensive understanding of local realities before definitive conclusions are reached,” Mr Nkandu said.

On matters relating to freedom of expression and media freedom, Mr Nkandu reiterated Government commitment to the constitutional rights of all citizens, saying that the media environment in Zambia remains vibrant, diverse and highly pluralistic, with public, private, community and online media platforms freely expressing a wide range of views, including criticism of government.

“While we respect the observations and recommendations of the European Union Election Observation Mission, we believe that a fuller appreciation of Zambia’s constitutional history, institutional realities, media landscape and security environment would have yielded a more balanced assessment of the 2026 elections,” Mr Nkandu stated.

He reaffirmed that Zambia’s democratic journey is neither perfect nor complete, but a journey characterised by peaceful political transitions, constitutional evolution, expanding political participation and a sustained commitment to democratic governance.

Meanwhile, the Minister appreciated the Mission’s acknowledgement that the elections provided Zambians with a competitive choice, polling staff administered voting efficiently, the legal framework provided a broadly adequate basis for democratic elections, and that ECZ was well prepared for the electoral process.

World.title: Nakonde Council orders street vendors to relocate to Markets
World.content:
Nakonde Town Council in Muchinga Province has ordered all street vendors operating in non-designated trading zones to immediately cease illegal trading and relocate to designated public markets.

‎

‎Nakonde Town Council Secretary, Donald Mwanza said the local authority has given vendors seven days to voluntarily vacate the streets and relocate to official designated market places.

‎

‎Mr Mwanza made this pronouncement in a notice made available to ZANIS in Nakonde.

‎

‎He said all vendors must vacate the streets by Wednesday, November 4th, 2026 at 17:00 hours.

‎

‎”Notice is hereby given to all street vendors operating in non-designated trading zones, including streets, footpaths and road reserves, to immediately cease illegal trading and relocate to designated public markets,” reads the notice in part.

‎

‎Mr Mwanza stated that unregulated street trading causes severe municipal, health and safety risks.

‎

‎Mr Mwanza said some of the risks include inadequate access to sanitation facilities which creates serious environmental health hazards and risk of disease outbreaks, obstruction of streets and walkways which creates traffic congestion and exposes pedestrians to road hazards.

‎

‎He named other risks as blocked roadways which impede rapid response of emergency services including fire trucks and ambulances.

The Council Secretary adds that illegal vending also undermines compliant traders who are operating legally within designated municipal markets.

‎

‎He pointed out that the action is being taken pursuant to legal powers vested in the local authority under the Local Government (Street Vending and Nuisances) (Amendment) (No.2) Regulations, 2018 read as one with the Local Government (Street Vending and Nuisances) Regulations, 1992.

‎

‎”Under these regulations, trading in undesignated public areas, obstructing pathways, or causing public nuisances is strictly illegal,” he stated.

‎

‎Mr Mwanza warned that failure to comply by the stipulated deadline will result in strict enforcement including immediate eviction, confiscation of mechandise and legal prosecution.

‎

‎The Council Secretary further advised vendors to report to the Market Master for stall allocations and market registration.

‎

‎Meanwhile, a resident of Nakonde, Chiwanza Nakaonga, has welcomed the move by the local authority.

‎

‎Ms Nakaonga said street vending has been causing congestion and making the town dirty.

‎

‎She has also urged vendors to comply with the directive and relocate to designated markets.

‎

‎”I want to thank the Council for this move. Our town was becoming too congested and dirty because of street vending. This will bring order and cleanliness back to Nakonde,” she said.

World.title: Mukankata calls for participation in electoral process
World.content:
Kanchibiya Constituency Returning Officer Poster Mukankata has urged stakeholders to actively participate in electoral engagements to promote a common understanding of the electoral process ahead of the Lubaleshi Ward Councilor by-election scheduled for November 5, 2026.

Mr Mukankata said the Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ) stakeholders’ meeting held at Kanchibiya Town Council New Civic Centre today was aimed at promoting transparency and inclusivity in the electoral process.

He thanked stakeholders for turning up in large numbers, saying their participation demonstrated the importance attached to ensuring a transparent and well-understood electoral process.

Mr Mukankata said the meeting provided an opportunity for stakeholders to discuss various electoral matters and seek clarification to avoid misunderstandings that could arise during the electoral process.

“You as stakeholders are important to this meeting. Feel free to participate and let’s engage each other wherever we may be left behind,” he said.

Meanwhile, United Party for National Development (UPND) member, Remmy Lumpa said the meeting had provided an opportunity for political stakeholders to ask questions and obtain clarity on how the electoral process would be conducted.

Mr Lumpa said such engagements were important in ensuring that all stakeholders understood the procedures governing the by-election.

And Citizens First (CF) member Godfridah Bwalya also commended ECZ for organising the meeting, saying it had provided her party with an opportunity to receive clarification on various electoral matters.

Ms Bwalya said her party was ready for the Lubaleshi Ward by-election scheduled for November 5, 2026.

World.title: Govt. calls for stronger collaboration in one health approach
World.content:
Government has called for stronger collaboration across human, animal and environmental health sectors to prevent disease and protect livelihoods.

Minister of Health, Roma Chilengi, says health protection must be planned and financed alongside economic expansion to protect farmers markets, workers livelihoods and family wellbeing.

Dr Chilengi said this in a speech read on his behalf by the Ministry’s Permanent Secretary for Donor Coordination, George Sinyangwe, during the commemoration of One Health Day in Lusaka today under the theme “Act Together for One Health”.

The Minister said the theme reflects the connection between the health of people, animals, plants and the environment, and brings government institutions, professionals and communities together to prevent disease, detect health threats early and respond jointly.

“Zambia has seen these connections directly. During the 2023 anthrax outbreak in Sinazongwe, health, veterinary and wildlife teams investigated together.

“Veterinary laboratory testing helped confirm infection in people,” he said.

And the Minister further indicated that the El Niño-related drought of 2024 also affected food production, water supplies and electricity generation, with consequences for nutrition, animal health and essential services.

He added that the current El Niño warnings reinforce the need for early coordinated action.

Dr Chilengi also pointed out that under the leadership of President Hakainde Hichilema, the Grow Zambia Agenda seeks increased production, investment and employment, and that One Health helps to protect those gains.

ZNPHI Director Public Health, Policy, Diplomacy and Communication, Doreen Shempela, said communities experience health challenges as one connected reality, giving an example that for a family that depends on a few cattle, losing an animal means losing means to pay school fees, while contaminated water affects the household, the farm and the clinic.

She said Zambia often discovers how much sectors need each other during an emergency, but the harder task is to build dependable relationships before the emergency.

“Coordination is not measured simply by committees established or meetings convened. It is measured by the decisions those arrangements enable and the action that follows,” Dr Shempela said.

Meanwhile, World Health Organization (WHO) Country Representative, Clement Lasuba, in remarks delivered on his behalf by Team Lead Emergency Preparedness and Response, Shikang O- Tipo, said One Health begins with everyday realities of water, food, animals and ecosystems.

Dr Lasuba said health threats cross borders hence preparedness must also connect across borders, citing anthrax events in Muchinga Province this year which required health workers, veterinary officers, wildlife authorities and laboratories to act together, and the Zambia-Namibia preparedness exercise in Sesheke in May which tested joint action.

He commended Zambia’s progress in strengthening One Health coordination and prioritising zoonotic threats.

Dr Lasuba said WHO contributes through the quadripartite partnership with FAO, UNEP and the World Organisation for Animal Health, and through the Quadripartite One Health Joint Plan of Action extended to 2029.

He highlighted three priorities going forward that include making collaboration routine through joint planning and timely information sharing, investing in prevention including surveillance, laboratories, skilled workforce and safe water as well as accelerating action on antimicrobial resistance by preventing infections and promoting appropriate use of antimicrobials.

World.title: Milupi pledges to prioritise funded stalled projects
World.content:
Minister of Transport and Logistics, Charles Milupi, says the Ministry will not commence new projects until already funded but stalled projects are completed, calling for prudent utilisation of public resources.

Mr Milupi says every money allocated to the ministry belongs to the Zambian people and must be accounted for through responsible financial management.

Speaking in Lusaka today when receiving the Ministry’s policy brief from immediate past Minister, Frank Tayali, Mr Milupi said no new project will be launched while funded projects remain stalled.

“Every kwacha appropriated to this Ministry belongs to the Zambian people. It is not ours, it is held in trust, we will therefore, complete before we commence,” Mr Milupi said.

He added that all procurements in the Ministry and its statutory bodies will be assessed against cost, quality and time to ensure value for money and timely delivery of projects.

Mr Milupi has warned procurement and project officers against compromising public resources, stating that he will defend those who uphold procurement standards, adding that those who facilitate irregularities will not be protected.

He said the Ministry will attach measurable outcomes, responsible officers and timelines to every undertaking ensuring that the public is informed about both achievements and delays.

Meanwhile, Mr Tayali said the Ministry has made significant progress towards positioning Zambia as a regional transport and logistics hub during his five-year tenure.

He cited the return of the national flag carrier to the skies in December 2021, the 31-year US$1.4 billion concession for the revitalisation of TAZARA and the signing of the concession for the 801-kilometre Zambia-Lobito Railway among the major milestones.

Mr Tayali further highlighted the ratification of six regional trade corridors, including the construction of Samfya and Nchelenge harbours, upgrading of provincial airports and preparation of the ten-year national road investment plan.

He has urged his successor to maintain consistency in implementing long-term infrastructure projects, adding that investor confidence depends on government honouring commitments beyond changes in office holders.

“My only plea is consistency, corridors are built across years, not across new cycles, and the investor who signs today does so on the faith that Zambia’s word outlives its office-holders,” he said.

Mr Tayali stated that continuity in government programmes is essential to ensuring that previous investments and reforms contribute to the country’s development.

World.title: Africa: All of Africa Today - November 3, 2026
World.content:
press review

US to Cut South Africa and Rwanda from AGOA Trade Deal

U.S. President Donald Trump has notified Congress of plans to remove South Africa and Rwanda from the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA), effective 1 January 2027, after a review found both countries failed to meet the programme's eligibility requirements. The US cited trade and investment barriers, national security and foreign policy concerns, with additional concerns over corruption in South Africa and human rights, political pluralism and workers' rights in Rwanda. The decision comes amid strained relations between Washington and both countries, with Rwanda also facing US sanctions over its alleged support for M23 rebels in eastern DR Congo. South Africa's Trade Minister Parks Tau described the move as unfortunate, saying Washington had raised new concerns not part of ongoing trade negotiations. He said the government would continue diversifying export markets to protect jobs.

Uganda Begins Withdrawal of Troops from Somalia After 20 Years



Uganda has begun withdrawing its troops from Somalia after nearly 20 years of military involvement. The first group of soldiers is already returning home. The phased withdrawal, announced by the country's military leadership, is expected to be completed by the end of 2027 and will include troops serving under the African Union mission. Uganda was the first African country to deploy forces to Somalia in 2007 under the African Union Mission in Somalia (AMISOM), helping government forces push al-Shabaab militants out of Mogadishu and other strategic areas. Uganda's army spokesperson Chris Magezi said the withdrawal would allow Somalia to assume full responsibility for its security. The move follows talks between Somali President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud and Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni, during which Somalia reportedly asked for an extension of Uganda's military presence. The withdrawal comes as the AU's current mission faces uncertainty over future funding and ongoing efforts to build up Somalia's security forces.

UNESCO Warns 86% of Journalist Murders Worldwide Remain Unpunished

UNESCO has warned that 86% of crimes committed against journalists worldwide remain unpunished, highlighting persistent threats to press freedom and the safety of media workers. In a report released on the International Day to End Impunity for Crimes Against Journalists, the UN agency said more than 1,600 journalists had been killed globally over the past 20 years, with local journalists accounting for nine out of every ten victims. Africa continues to face serious challenges, with journalists in countries such as Somalia, Uganda and the Sahel region exposed to killings, intimidation and online harassment. Reporters Without Borders recorded two journalist deaths in Africa this year, in Uganda and Somalia, with neither case resulting in arrests or convictions. UNESCO also raised concerns about the growing use of social media campaigns to discredit journalists and warned that reporters are increasingly being targeted in conflict zones, including through drone attacks. The agency called for greater accountability and protection for journalists, stressing that press identification does not guarantee their safety.

Tensions Flare at Inquiry Into Malawi's Deadly Plane Crash

A parliamentary inquiry into the plane crash that killed former Malawian Vice-President Saulos Chilima and eight others descended into heated exchanges after independent campaigner Christy Lwara clashed with lawmakers over his testimony on the military's handling of the search operation. Lwara told the Ad Hoc Parliamentary Committee that he was dissatisfied with the military's response, questioning why soldiers allegedly stopped people from proceeding to Kasangazi, citing fuel shortages. He said his discussions with officers had led him to believe the aircraft had crashed in the area, prompting him to continue searching there. However, lawmakers challenged his account, accusing him of giving contradictory statements about the search operation. The questioning escalated into personal insults between Lwara and MPs George Jivason Kadzipatike and Joshua Malango, forcing committee leaders to repeatedly intervene to restore order. Committee chairperson Macmillan Water Nyamilandu Manda said he was frustrated by the conduct and warned members that the enquiry could not continue in such an atmosphere. The confrontation comes as lawmakers continue to investigate the circumstances surrounding one of Malawi's deadliest aviation tragedies.

Renewed Tigray Conflict Threatens Ethiopia's Economic Recovery

Ethiopia's strong economic growth prospects are facing renewed uncertainty as escalating tensions in the northern Tigray region threaten to undermine the country's recovery from years of conflict. The International Monetary Fund forecasts economic growth of 9.2% for the 2025–26 fiscal year, driven by agriculture, mining and electricity generation. The conflict caused huge damage to infrastructure and great economic losses. Increased military spending may divert resources away from infrastructure, education and social services, discouraging investment and cutting government revenues, according to financial analyst Abdulmenan Mohammed. If the conflict starts up again, there is a danger of increased military spending. More instability could also exacerbate inflation, shortages of foreign currency and pressure on the national currency. Agriculture and tourism are highly susceptible to insecurity, disruption of transport routes, poor rainfall and climate-related crop challenges that threaten livelihoods and production. Analysts warn that a prolonged conflict could reverse economic gains and place additional pressure on already struggling households.

Close 

Five Arrested Over Attack on South African Farmer

South African police have arrested five suspects in connection with a brutal attack on a 50-year-old cattle farmer, Donovan Marx, at his farm in Ventersdorp, North West. Marx was ambushed by masked attackers during a house robbery last Wednesday, shot, stabbed, and had his ears cut off before the suspects fled with three firearms and his vehicle. Police said the attackers first tied up a farm worker before assaulting Marx when he returned home. The worker later managed to free himself and alert authorities. Marx remains in hospital and may require prosthetic ears after surgeons were unable to save his. His family has welcomed the arrests, saying the legal process must now take its course. The five suspects, aged between 26 and 56, are expected to appear in court facing charges including house robbery, attempted murder and illegal possession of firearms and ammunition. Agriculture Minister Willie Aucamp condemned the attack, while Parliament's police committee chair Ian Cameron called for a thorough investigation and prosecution.

World.title: South Africa: Cape Town Taxi Rivals Agree to Seven-Day Truce - South African News Briefs - November 3, 2026
World.content:
press review

Cape Town Taxi Rivals Agree to Seven-Day Truce

Rival Cape Town taxi associations, the Cape Amalgamated Taxi Association (CATA) and the Cape Organisation for the Democratic Taxi Association (CODETA), have agreed to a seven-day truce, reports EWN. This comes after months of deadly violence that has claimed about a dozen lives and disrupted public transport. The agreement is aimed at restoring calm along the Delft-Langa-Epping corridor, where tensions have been fuelled by disputes over unlawful taxi operations. Both associations have also committed to an independently facilitated process to address the underlying causes of the conflict, with a follow-up meeting with government. The South African National Taxi Council (SANTACO) has welcomed the agreement, saying it is important to protect commuters, drivers and taxi operators.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

IEC Warns Voters Against Photographing Marked Ballots

The Independent Electoral Commission (IEC) has reminded voters of the rules at voting stations ahead of the Local Government Elections, reports SABC News. It warned that taking photographs of marked ballot papers is strictly prohibited. Deputy Chief Electoral Officer Masego Shiburi said voters must mark their ballots in private and follow the instructions of election officials. The commission has also warned against campaigning, canvassing, intimidating or attempting to influence voters inside voting stations. It further urged the public not to intimidate electoral staff or take and share unauthorised photographs of officials on social media. Shiburi said that voting booths are positioned to protect ballot secrecy and prevent voters from being pressured into photographing their choices in exchange for favours or other benefits.

SAHRC Urges Urgent Action to Fix Gauteng Water Crisis

The South African Human Rights Commission (SAHRC) has called on Gauteng municipalities and water service providers to urgently rehabilitate failing wastewater treatment plants and improve access to reliable water and sanitation services, reports EWN. The appeal follows the release of the commission’s report on water and sanitation service delivery in the province, which highlights serious challenges affecting water infrastructure and security. The commission found that approximately 1.5 billion litres of water are lost daily in Gauteng due to leaks. While acknowledging the substantial support provided by the Department of Water and Sanitation to the province's water sector, SAHRC commissioner Henk Boshoff warned that greater attention must be given to protecting and rehabilitating water resources. The commission raised concerns about the deteriorating condition of the resources on which Gauteng's long-term water security depends.
