"Now that there’s no campaign, I can’t afford that level of protection, even though I still deal with death threats and trespassers at my property, routinely," he wrote.

World.title: Dem flips key Senate seat in battleground North Carolina as Cooper defeats Trump ally
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

The Fox News Decision Desk projects former Democratic Gov. Roy Cooper of North Carolina defeating former Republican National Committee (RNC) Chair Michael Whatley, a close ally of President Donald Trump.

The high-profile and expensive ballot box showdown gives Democrats another seat in the Senate as Cooper prepares to succeed retiring GOP Sen. Thom Tillis.

The race was projected as a victory for Cooper with 57.63 votes counted, with 66.40% going to the former Democratic governor and 31.96% going to Whatley.

"North Carolina — I’m grateful for your trust," Cooper posted on X. "We have more in common than divides us. Here’s to building better days ahead!"

Cooper's flipping of a GOP-controlled seat in the crucial southeastern battleground state boosts his party as Democrats aim to recapture the Senate majority in the midterm elections.

DEMOCRACY ’26: STAY UP TO DATE WITH THE FOX NEWS ELECTION HUB

The Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee applauded Cooper's victory.

"In the Senate, he’ll carry on the fight to expand health care access, make stuff cost less, and ensure the American Dream is achievable for every North Carolina," the DSCC posted on X.

Cooper's triumph in the Senate race was his seventh straight statewide victory, after winning four elections for attorney general and two for governor.

His continued solid lead over Whatley in public opinion polling spurred top GOP-aligned outside groups a month ago to pull the plug on spending in the North Carolina race. It was seen as a signal that Republicans no longer saw a path to victory in the southeastern battleground state.

Trump, during a rally two weeks ago in North Carolina to try and rescue Whatley, appeared to acknowledge the dire situation, remarking to the crowd that Cooper is "going to become your senator... It’s crazy, you’re going to send him to Washington to represent you."

SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

Cooper, the first Democrat to win a Senate election in North Carolina in nearly two decades, touted that he would be a "strong, independent senator" who would work with Trump when he could and stand up to him when needed. He focused on cost of living and health care issues as he campaigned for the Senate.

Whatley, a North Carolina native who served as the state's GOP chair for five years before Trump picked him in March 2024 to serve as RNC chair, was a first-time candidate.

He pledged to create jobs, raise wages, lower costs and keep communities safe. Whatley also said he would be a Trump ally in the Senate.

Tillis, a vocal Republican Trump critic, announced in June of last year that he wouldn't seek re-election, which the president called "great news."

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

After Tillis' announcement, Trump's daughter-in-law, Lara Trump, was at the top of the president's list for the open seat in the Tar Heel State.

But Lara Trump, a North Carolina native who served as RNC co-chair alongside Whatley in 2024, announced that "after much consideration and heartfelt discussions with my family, friends, and supporters, I have decided not to pursue the United States Senate seat in North Carolina at this time."

World.title: On the ground in Texas, Michigan and Maine: Voters speak out at polls on key Senate races
World.content:
On the ground in Texas, Michigan and Maine: Voters speak out at polls on key Senate races

NBC News' Gadi Schwartz reports from Texas, Stephanie Gosk checks in from Michigan and Monica Alba has the latest from Maine on Election Day.Nov. 3, 2026

World.title: Exit poll: Voters cast ballots against Trump
World.content:
Many voters say they view the midterm election as an opportunity for a major rebuke of President Donald Trump’s performance, according to early results from the NBC News Exit Poll.

Forty-three percent said one reason for their votes was to express opposition to Trump — higher than the share who said the same in the 2018 midterm election during his first term.

The early results show that Trump’s midterm campaign blitz in support of Republican candidates in recent weeks has done little to lift his job approval rating.

Voters said they were unhappy with Trump’s handling of several key issues — with the economy being a big frustration.

Most voters said inflation is causing hardship for their families, with the affordability of gas, food and utilities being a significant concern. Voters blamed Trump for high prices and said his policies are making the economy worse.

Most voters also disapproved of Trump’s immigration crackdown and the war in Iran, and expressed concern about government corruption and artificial intelligence.

There was one issue that most voters expressed confidence in: that the midterm elections were conducted fairly and accurately.

The exit poll was conducted as voters left polling locations across the U.S. on Election Day. Results also include extensive interviews by phone and mail and online with people who voted early or by mail.

Follow live updates on the midterm elections

Trump’s sagging job approval rating

Trump’s job approval rating among voters is lower than the rating of any sitting president on Election Day in nearly two decades, according to the poll.

Thirty-eight percent of voters said they approve of Trump’s performance. That’s substantially lower than in his first midterm election in 2018 (when 45% of voters approved of his performance).

Trump’s dismal approval ratings have dropped in Senate battleground states, as well.

Majorities of Senate voters in Georgia, Ohio, Michigan and Texas all said they disapprove of Trump’s handling of his job — also up compared with 2018.

Voters have negative opinions of both parties

Voters expressed more unfavorable than favorable views of the Republican and Democratic parties, the poll showed. And almost 1 in 5 voters said they don’t have favorable opinions of either party — at least 5 percentage points more than the share who said so during the past two midterm elections.

Fifty-four percent of voters Tuesday said they have unfavorable views of the Democratic Party, while 46% have favorable views. For the Republican Party, 59% of voters today said they have unfavorable views, and 41% said they have favorable views. Voters expressed more unfavorable views toward both parties than they did in the last two midterms.

Voters were likelier to say the Democratic Party could better handle several big issues than the Republican Party, including the economy, foreign policy, healthcare, government corruption and policies about transgender people. The GOP held an advantage on immigration.

On policies related to AI and taxes, voters were split.

Voters also expressed negative opinions about Congress. Three-quarters said they disapproved of the way Congress is handling its job. Republicans were far more likely than Democrats to approve of Congress, 46% to 9%.

Economic pessimism

The economy — once Trump’s strongest issue — is no longer viewed positively by voters, the poll showed.

An overwhelming majority said the nation’s economy is in rough shape (75%) — and 65% said Trump’s policies have worsened economic conditions in the U.S. About half of voters casting ballots said the cost of living was crucial to their votes. That is the opposite of how voters viewed the economy in 2018 — a wave election for Democrats during Trump’s first term. That year, 68% of voters said the economy was in good shape.

The economy topped voters’ list of key issues, with 39% saying it was the most important issue facing the country today. The state of democracy was next, at 32%.

Voters voiced significant concerns about the prices of gas, groceries and utilities, blaming Trump for affordability problems.

Forty-four percent of voters said their finances are worse today than they were two years ago when Trump returned to office. Just 18% say they’re better off. These numbers are in line with the way voters characterized their finances during the 2022 midterms but much worse than in Trump’s first midterm election in 2018.

Driving voters’ financial concerns: the cost of living. Top issues include the cost of gas and diesel fuel (87% said they were “very” or “somewhat” concerned), food and groceries (88% concerned), utilities (86%) and healthcare (85%). All told, just under 8 in 10 voters said inflation is causing hardship for their families.

More than half (65%) say Trump’s policies have made the economy worse; 62% said he’s responsible for high prices.

Other key issues for voters: immigration, corruption, Iran and artificial intelligence

More than half of voters (57%) said Trump’s immigration enforcement actions have gone too far, according to the poll. Twenty-three percent said the crackdowns have been about right, and 21% said they have not gone far enough. Fifty-nine percent of voters said they disapproved of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), the agency carrying out much of the enforcement actions; while 41% said they approved.

Corruption was also a key issue. Ninety percent of voters said it was a crucial or major factor in their vote, but they were divided on which party was better positioned to fight it. Thirty-six percent said the Democratic Party, while 31% said Republicans. The remaining third of voters said they didn’t believe either party would be better.

The war in Iran was largely unpopular among voters, with 62% saying the U.S. made the wrong decision in taking military action against Iran. Forty-five percent of voters who backed Democratic candidates for the House said the war was crucial to their vote, compared with 21% of voters who supported Republican candidates.

Concerns about AI were also high on voters’ minds: 57% said AI will do more to hurt society than help, the poll showed. A large majority, 76%, said they opposed the construction of a new data center in their community. Voters split almost evenly on which party was better able to handle AI.

Amid their concerns, most voters said they were confident in how Tuesday’s elections were run. Seventy-one percent said they were confident about the fairness and accuracy of the elections in their states, and 59% said they were confident in how elections were conducted across the country. Roughly 8 out of 10 voters expressed confidence that people who were eligible to vote would be allowed to vote, and 64% said they were confident that those who were not eligible to vote would be barred.

Groups we’re watching closely as the night unfolds

We’ll closely watch several groups that helped propel Trump to victory in 2024 — but with particular interest in Latino voters and voters under 30.

After having fallen in every national election since 2018, the share of Latino voters who identify as Democrats ticked up this year to 43% from 39% in 2024, the poll showed.

The share of Latino voters calling themselves independents dropped slightly, to 30% from 32%. The share identifying as Republicans also dropped slightly, to 27% from 29% in 2024.

The results halted a steady erosion of the Democrats’ advantage among Latino voters in party identification, which narrowed from 33 points in 2018 to 10 points in 2024. This year, Democrats hold a 16-point edge.

Young voters also seem to be shifting back to the Democratic Party after Trump shrank the margin among them in the 2024 presidential election.

World.title: Former Gov. Roy Cooper wins North Carolina’s Senate race, flipping the seat for Democrats
World.content:
Democratic former Gov. Roy Cooper has defeated former Republican National Committee Chairman Michael Whatley in the contest for North Carolina’s open Senate seat, NBC News projects.

Cooper’s victory secures a crucial flip for Democrats as they try to take control of the Senate. The party must gain a net of four seats to clinch a majority. The result also marks the first time a Democrat has won a Senate seat in North Carolina since 2008.

Cooper will succeed retiring GOP Sen. Thom Tillis, who grew increasingly critical of President Donald Trump during his second term and chose not to seek re-election.

North Carolina Gov. Roy Cooper speaks onstage during the final day of the Democratic National Convention at the United Center on Aug. 22, 2024 in Chicago. Andrew Harnik / Getty

The race was initially expected to be one of the most hotly contested across the Senate landscape. But in the closing weeks of the campaign, a top Republican super PAC canceled its ad spending in the race to focus more on protecting seats in more conservative territory as Cooper built a solid lead in the polls.

Follow live updates on the midterm elections

The abandonment of North Carolina as a front-line battleground resulted from several factors. First, Cooper, a popular former two-term governor, enjoyed high name recognition, while Republicans had few attacks to lob his way. A prized recruit for national Democrats, Cooper also avoided a contentious primary and focused his campaign almost entirely on the cost of living, a top voter concern.

Whatley, who had previously led the state party and earned national recognition as RNC chairman during the 2024 election, had not run for elected office before. Trump, who urged him to launch a bid for the seat, and Vice President JD Vance rallied on several occasions with Whatley down the final stretch to give him a boost.

But even Trump signaled in the closing weeks that Cooper was likely to win. “He’s going to become your senator,” Trump said at an October rally in the state. “And it’s crazy.”

As voters soured on the economy and the Iran war, Whatley could not escape or distance himself from an increasingly unpopular president in the key battleground state.

It was also the first midterm Senate race to take place in North Carolina with Trump in power, an environment that would be tougher for Republicans given traditional backlashes to the party that controls the White House. The state did not hold a Senate contest in 2018, Trump’s last midterm.

World.title: GOP Sen. Ashley Moody wins special Senate election for Marco Rubio’s old seat in Florida
World.content:
Sen. Ashley Moody. R-Fla., defeated Democrat Angie Nixon in the special election for Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s old Senate seat, NBC News projects.

Moody was considered the overwhelming favorite headed into the general election against Nixon, a Democratic Socialists of America-aligned candidate who scored an upset victory in the Democratic primary but faced a cash disadvantage throughout the general election.

Though Moody secured victory, Nixon’s surprise primary night win did elevate the race nationally as her emergence piqued the interest of progressives across the country. Democrats saw her candidacy as an opportunity to gain a footing in a state where their party has not won a Senate race since 2012.

Follow live updates on the midterm elections

Ultimately, Moody continued the GOP’s run of dominance after she largely ran a careful, traditional Florida Republican campaign. She will serve the final two years of the term Rubio won in 2022; the seat will be on the ballot again in 2028 for a full term.

Rep. Angie Nixon, D-Fla. Joe Raedle / Getty

Moody relied on her significant fundraising advantage to flood the airwaves in a state of 23 million people, where being able to afford the pricey ad rates is seen as key to victory.

Moody did face some criticism for declining to debate and doing fewer public events than Nixon, who blanketed the state with in-person events and became a regular on both traditional state media and the center-left podcast circuit.

“Ashley Moody should take a page out of Angie Nixon’s book,” Florida Democratic Party Chair Nikki Fried said at a news conference last month in Tallahassee. “Stop hiding behind attacks. Show up and talk to the people you work for, because Ashley Moody is asking Floridians for their vote, and if she won’t answer their questions, they’ll give her their answer in November.”

The event included a sign that read “Where is Ashley Moody?”

Those hits, however, were not enough to pull down Moody, who also faced criticism for her ties to the Hope Florida scandal, which involved $10 million for a Medicaid settlement being directed to a charity tied to Florida first lady Casey DeSantis. A political committee ultimately used that money to oppose a 2024 ballot measure that would have legalized recreational marijuana in the state.

Moody, who was the state attorney general at the time, had to sign off on the deal. She has denied any wrongdoing, and no charges were brought after a state prosecutor impaneled a grand jury to review the matter.

Moody’s main line of attack was focused on Nixon’s being too liberal for a state that now has 1.5 million more registered Republicans than Democrats, a massive recent reversal after Democrats held an advantage for decades.

Much of Moody’s messaging and campaign ads focused on policies proposed by the Democratic Socialists of America more broadly, even as Nixon publicly distanced herself from them.

“Angie Nixon is actually a socialist,” a narrator says in one of the spots that focused on Democratic Socialists of America issues like “abolishing the police,” which Nixon said she does not want to do.

Moody had won two statewide elections for attorney general, but it was her first time on the ballot for the Senate. Gov. Ron DeSantis appointed her to the seat after Rubio was tapped to serve in Trump’s Cabinet.

World.title: Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff cruises to re-election in Georgia
World.content:
Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff has won re-election against Republican Rep. Mike Collins, NBC News projects, prevailing in Georgia after a nationally watched race that was defined, at times, by heated personal attacks.

Ossoff’s win is a major hold for Democrats in one of the most closely divided battleground states in the country — and one that both sides saw as critical for control of the Senate earlier this election cycle. Ossoff grabbed an early advantage in the race and held on, with a massive money advantage and a sizable lead in most public polling.

His dominant position in a state where both parties have won in recent years turned heads nationally, and clips of Ossoff’s campaign speeches began to catch on among national Democrats throughout 2026.

Follow live updates on the midterm elections

That prompted some talk of whether Ossoff could run for president in 2028, though he said during a debate that he would serve a full second term.

Rep. Mike Collins, R-Ga. Kevin Dietsch / Getty

Much of the race, including two head-to-head debates, focused on the national political atmosphere, with Ossoff tying Collins to President Donald Trump and his low approval rating. Meanwhile, Collins would often try to pivot to votes Ossoff took under former Democratic President Joe Biden, who left office in January 2025.

The economy and the increasingly high price of consumer goods were also at the center of the race. Ossoff repeatedly tried to get Collins to defend Trump’s tariff regime and the Iran war.

Collins would regularly try to brush off questions about Trump’s economy, including the tariffs, and instead try to blame Biden-era policies for high costs.

“That Bidenomics, that Green New Deal my opponent voted for, that’s where this inflation came from,” Collins said at their first Senate debate.

The race also was replete with attacks of a more personal nature.

Ossoff focused on a series of social media posts in which Collins’ son-in-law promoted white nationalist posts, as well as a former Collins staffer’s messages with avowed white supremacist Nick Fuentes.

“You’ve hired half the Third Reich,” Ossoff said at a debate last month.

Collins said he doesn’t support any form of racism or white nationalism.

“I don’t care where the source is, and I tell him that,” Collins said of his son-in-law.

Collins also noted campaign contributions to a pro-Ossoff super PAC from Reid Hoffman, a billionaire whose name appeared in the Epstein files. Ossoff retorted that Collins had taken votes to block full release of the files.

As Trump’s approval ratings continued to drop, Republicans across the country started to try to distance themselves from him, including rebranding their messaging or finding individual policies to start disagreeing with, most notably tariffs and the war in Iran, both of which are overwhelmingly unpopular.

Collins, however, wasn’t one of them.

He defended the war in Iran, promoting the administration’s rationale that it’s needed because Iran can’t be allowed to have a nuclear weapon.

He said the tariffs were “fair” in the context of the state’s major ports and trade with China.

“Savannah Port and Brunswick Port have been on my mind,” Collins said in a debate last month.

World.title: GOP fights to hang on to Senate majority
World.content:
Control of the Senate is on the line Tuesday following a midterm election cycle with races marked by betrayal, allegations of ballot shenanigans and President Donald Trump’s incessant swooning over the backside of one Republican candidate.

Close races were expected in the traditional battlegrounds of Michigan and North Carolina — but also in states that have become more reliably red since Trump’s rise in politics, such as Ohio and Iowa.

Former North Carolina Gov. Roy Cooper won his state’s Senate battle, giving Democrats their first pickup of the night, NBC News projects. He beat former Republican National Committee Chair Michael Whatley.

NBC News also projects that Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff has won re-election in swing state Georgia, defeating Republican Rep. Mike Collins. And in New Hampshire, Democratic Rep. Chris Pappas will succeed retiring Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen after he beat Republican former Sen. John Sununu, NBC News projects.

In Ohio, the race is leaning toward former Sen. Sherrod Brown, the Democrat who is running to unseat Republican Sen. Jon Husted, according to NBC News’ Decision Desk.

Closer-than-expected races are also brewing in even redder states, such as Alaska, Kansas, South Carolina and Texas.

The contest in South Carolina, a state that hasn’t elected a Democratic senator since 1998, is leaning toward Democrat Annie Andrews, with 81% of ballots counted, according to the Decision Desk. Andrews is challenging Sen. Darline Graham, whom Trump appointed to the seat this year after the death of her brother, Lindsey Graham.

In Kansas, where a Democrat hasn’t won a Senate seat since 1932, the race leans toward Democratic pastor Adam Hamilton over incumbent Republican Sen. Roger Marshall, according to the Decision Desk.

And in Texas, a state that hasn’t elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1988, the race now leans toward Democratic state Rep. James Talarico, according to the Decision Desk. Talarico is running against Trump-endorsed state Attorney General Ken Paxton.

Meanwhile, Republican Sen. Ashley Moody survived a tight race with Democratic state Rep. Angie Nixon in Florida, NBC News projects.

Underscoring the high stakes of this year’s Senate battles: In the most expensive election cycle ever, more than $3.4 billion has been spent on television and digital s in Senate races across the country, according to the tracking firm AdImpact.

Republicans hold a 53-47 majority in the chamber, meaning Democrats would need a net gain of four seats to regain control.

Follow live election coverage here.

A Democratic takeover would require them to flip at least two states that Trump won by double digits in 2024.

The likeliest targets are Texas, Ohio, Iowa, Alaska, Kansas and South Carolina. More than 50% of voters in each of those states disapprove of how Trump is handling his job, according to early results from the NBC News Exit Poll.

In Kansas, for example, where Trump won by 16 percentage points two years ago, 57% of voters disapprove of his job performance, according to the survey.

The consequences for Trump are significant. For the past two years, his Republican Party has controlled both chambers of Congress, allowing him to pursue his agenda largely unchecked. But if the Republicans lose the Senate, he’ll need Democratic cooperation to move forward on legislation and appointments. Democrats will have increased power to pursue investigations of the administration.

The NBC News Exit Poll found midterm voters with decisively negative opinions about how Congress is handling its role as a check and balance on Trump — 71% of voters, including 41% of Republicans, said there is not enough congressional oversight of the presidency.

Alaska has emerged late as a closely watched contest. Democrat Mary Peltola is under scrutiny after The New York Times reported that her campaign and other Democrats recruited a candidate into the race — Dan J. Sullivan — with the same name as Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan. The “ballot-stacking” tactic is seen as a way to sow confusion among voters in a state that uses ranked choice voting and has four Senate candidates on the ballot.

Peltola and her campaign have repeatedly denied allegations that they recruited the lesser-known Sullivan.

Polls close in Alaska at 1 a.m. ET.

Clarity about the fight for the Senate will come much earlier in states such as Ohio, where polls close at 7:30 p.m. ET, and Michigan, where the last polls close at 9 p.m. ET.

In Ohio, Husted faces a tough challenge from Brown in the race to serve the remaining two years of JD Vance’s unexpired Senate term. Husted was appointed to fill the seat temporarily last year after Vance was elected vice president.

Polls have shown a close race in Ohio, and Trump held three rallies in the state in recent weeks — as well as one in the Cincinnati media market, in neighboring Kentucky — in an effort to boost Husted. Trump used the rallies not only to promote Husted’s work as a senator, but also to compliment his physique. Trump, who often gives the impression that he is casting for a movie, repeatedly praised Husted’s “ass” in Ohio and elsewhere down the stretch.

“If Husted wins,” a senior Republican official told NBC News last week, “it’s because Trump literally dragged his ass over the finish line.”

Then there’s the Michigan race, which is ending on an explosive note. The Republican nominee, former Rep. Mike Rogers, scored a surprise last-minute endorsement Sunday from Rep. Haley Stevens, who lost the Democratic nomination to challenge him in August.

Stevens had vowed as late as Saturday, publicly and privately, not to break her promise to vote for Abdul El-Sayed. The Democrats had long clashed over his criticism of Israel, but Stevens’ criticism had intensified in recent days, prompting the El-Sayed campaign to signal that she was no longer welcome at his events. Stevens cited that in her decision to defect to Rogers, sparking outrage and accusations of betrayal from House Democratic colleagues.

Another key race to watch Tuesday include Maine, where Republican Sen. Susan Collins is up against Democratic former state Senate President Troy Jackson.

In Texas, the Senate race took on heightened energy after the Republican incumbent, John Cornyn, lost a primary runoff to state Paxton after a heavy push by Trump in Paxton’s favor.

Democrats have been excited by Talarico, who has maintained steady leads in polls, though within the margin of error. Tech billionaire Elon Musk, a Trump ally, meanwhile, has spent at least $150 million to back Paxton.

World.title: Tuesday’s elections bring historic first for Black governors
World.content:
For the first time in U.S. history, multiple elected Black governors will serve at the same time — and it remains possible that voters will elect more this year than the three who have already won.

That historic first is the result of Democratic Gov. Wes Moore’s winning re-election in Maryland, Republican Rep. Byron Donalds’ prevailing in the Florida governor’s race and Georgia Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms’ winning in her state.

Before or to Bottoms’ and Donalds’ victories Tuesday night, the only elected Black governors in U.S. history had been Moore; Deval Patrick, a Democrat who was elected Massachusetts’ governor in 2006; and Doug Wilder, a Democrat who was elected Virginia’s governor in 1989. None served simultaneously.

In an interview with NBC News last month, Donalds said the history-making aspect of his candidacy was “very special.”

“From a larger perspective, there’s so much that has been talked about in politics over the last couple decades around race. Obviously, the country has had some real negative parts of our history surrounding race,” he said. “I’m humbled to be in this position, but I think it says a lot more about the state [of Florida] than it does about me.”

Bottoms, Donalds and Moore may not stay in such rare company for long: Five other Black major-party candidates for governor are on the ballot Tuesday.

Black Democratic gubernatorial candidates are running in another pair of battleground states: Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley in Wisconsin and state Attorney General Aaron Ford in Nevada.

In South Carolina, another Black Democrat, state Rep. Jermaine Johnson, faces a more difficult path to victory in the traditionally red state’s race for governor.

On the Republican side, Rep. John James is running in a competitive governor’s race against Democrat Jocelyn Benson, while Minnesota state House Speaker Lisa Demuth is seen as an underdog in Minnesota’s gubernatorial contest.

World.title: Gov. Josh Shapiro sails to a second term in battleground Pennsylvania
World.content:
Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro easily defeated Republican state Treasurer Stacy Garrity in his re-election bid, NBC News projects.

Shapiro, a potential 2028 Democratic presidential contender, did not face much competition from Garrity, who trailed by double digits in polls in the run-up to Election Day and was vastly outpaced in fundraising.

“The picture is starting to come into focus,” Shapiro said in a victory speech on Tuesday. “This is a good night for our commonwealth. And, it’s looking like it could be a pretty good night for our country too.”

The substantial victory in a key battleground gives Shapiro a springboard into a potential White House bid. In the closing weeks of the contest, he launched a federal political action committee, New Path PAC, his first official step into national politics, which his campaign said was done so he could help congressional candidates in his state.

Shapiro enjoys solid approval ratings in his state, though voters are more mixed on whether he should seek the presidency. He spent much of the campaign seeking to boost downballot House candidates locked in much closer swing races, which could determine control of the chamber, as well as state legislators who could give Democrats full control in Harrisburg for the first time in more than 30 years.

“With the way things are going tonight, I think I’m going to have plenty of ‘GSD’ [get s--- done] Democrats by my side ready to make more progress,” Shapiro said.

Follow live updates on the midterm elections

Pennsylvania Treasurer Stacy Garrity. Marc Levy / AP

Garrity, meanwhile, struggled to break through in the race, and polling showed a large chunk of voters were unfamiliar with her candidacy. Republicans had cleared the field for her run ahead of the primary, seeking to avoid a messy fight that could distract from taking aim at Shapiro.

In his victory address, Shapiro said Garrity called him and “wished me well and said she wants to work together to serve the people of Pennsylvania.”

“Look, we have plenty of disagreements, that’s part of a healthy democracy,” he said. “And I appreciate her service to our commonwealth and our country.”

In the closing weeks of the general election, Garrity sought to put some space between her and President Donald Trump over tariffs, outlining her differences with him in her only televised debate with Shapiro.

The race was never particularly close, though the candidates did get into notable back-and-forths about data center policy, with Garrity coming out in favor of a moratorium, followed by Shapiro announcing new, tougher mandates for developers in the state.

World.title: Democrat Annie Andrews wins South Carolina Senate race
World.content:
Washington — Democrat Annie Andrews defeated GOP Sen. Darline Graham in the South Carolina Senate race, CBS News projects, in a major upset.

Andrews, 45, is a pediatrician and campaigned on healthcare access and affordability, along with fighting corruption in Washington. She faced off against Graham, the incumbent senator who was appointed to serve out the remainder of her brother Lindsey Graham's term after his sudden death in July.

Darline Graham, 62, most recently served as commissioner of the South Carolina Commission for the Blind, before she was appointed to the Senate. She went on to win a special primary election to take her brother's place on the ballot to represent South Carolina for a full six-year term.

Andrews faced an uphill battle in a state that hasn't elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1998, and which President Trump won by 18 points in 2024. She criticized Darline Graham for lacking experience, pointing to comments she made during the condensed primary, when she said she was "not that informed on national security."

The race, which grew much more competitive than expected, forced Republicans to come to Graham's aid with a $5 million investment in October from the Senate Leadership Fund, the main Republican super PAC. MAGA Inc, a super PAC controlled by Mr. Trump, also gave Graham $827,000 in August, and he personally campaigned heavily for Graham after encouraging her to run for the seat. But the efforts fell short amid a difficult environment for Republicans.

With Andrews' projected victory, Democrats secure an unexpected pickup as they look to flip the Senate.

World.title: GOP Rep. Tom Kean Jr. ousted in New Jersey
World.content:
Washington — Democrat Rebecca Bennett ousted GOP Rep. Tom Kean Jr. in New Jersey's 7th Congressional District, CBS News projected.

The two-term congressman missed months of votes earlier this year as he was secretly being treated for depression. Kean did not disclose the diagnosis or his hospitalization until he returned to Washington in late June — nearly four months after his absence became apparent.

In a speech on the House floor upon his return, Kean said "there is no timeline for recovery" for depression. But the lack of details about his condition during his extended absence renewed the debate about how transparent elected officials should have to be about their health.

Kean was one of the most vulnerable House Republicans this cycle. Weeks before the election, the Congressional Leadership Fund, the super PAC allied with House Speaker Mike Johnson, shifted resources away from Kean's race to other critical contests, foreshadowing the 7th District outcome.

Bennett, a former Navy helicopter pilot, had a fundraising edge over Kean according to their most recent quarterly Federal Election Commission filings. Bennett reported raising about $3.9 million from July through September, while Kean reported less than $1 million over the same period. Through the whole election season, Bennett raised nearly $8.2 million compared to Kean's nearly $5.9 million.

Kean, a former state lawmaker, was elected to Congress in 2022. He defeated the Democratic incumbent, Rep. Tom Malinowski, flipping the district for the second time since the 2018 election.

Since August, both House Speaker Mike Johnson and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries campaigned with their respective candidates in the district, signaling its importance to the parties as they vie for control of the lower chamber.

World.title: Democrats flip North Carolina's 11th District
World.content:
Washington — Democrat Jamie Ager flipped control of North Carolina's 11th Congressional District, CBS News projected, marking the first time a Democrat has won the seat since 2010.

Ager, a fourth-generation farmer, was initially supposed to face GOP Rep. Chuck Edwards, who ended his reelection bid in early August. State Rep. Jennifer Balkcom replaced Edwards on the ballot less than 90 days before the election, putting her at a disadvantage in an already tough political climate for Republicans.

The nonpartisan Cook Political Report shifted the race from lean Republican to toss-up after Edwards suspended his campaign. As Election Day neared, election forecasters shifted the race again to lean Democrat.

The House voted overwhelmingly to censure Edwards in September after the bipartisan House Ethics Committee found the two-term congressman engaged in "persistent unprofessional and inappropriate conduct" toward two young women who worked for him.

Though Edwards argued the committee's findings "completely exonerate" him under House rules, he abandoned his reelection bid days later.

World.content: CBS News projects Florida House races CBS News projects that incumbent Florida Democrats Jared Moskowitz and Kathy Castor will hold on to their House seats, and Democrat Pia Dandiya will win her House race. More

World.title: See CBS News exit poll results for the 2026 midterm elections
World.content:
Note: Results will continue to update throughout the night.

North Carolina Senate: Democrat Roy Cooper wins

North Carolina voters liked the job Democrat Roy Cooper did as governor, so they are sending him to the Senate.

Cooper performed better than former Vice President Kamala Harris did in 2024 among key groups, including independents and White women.

Most North Carolina voters thought Cooper's opponent, Republican Michael Whatley was too supportive of President Trump.

The last time a Democrat was elected to the Senate from North Carolina was in 2008, when Kay Hagan won.

South Carolina Senate: Toss-up

CBS News rates the race between GOP Sen. Darline Graham and Democrat Annie Andrews a toss-up. Most voters don't think Darline Graham has the right experience to be a U.S. senator. But it's not a dealbreaker for all voters — about a quarter who hold this view are still voting for Graham, who was named to fill the seat held by her late brother, Lindsey Graham.

At the same time, about half of voters say of Andrews that her views are too extreme. And most of those voters are voting against Andrews.

Georgia Senate: Democrat Jon Ossoff wins

Within 40 minutes of polls closing in Georgia, CBS News projected Ossoff as the winner. Democrat Jon Ossoff is performing very well with Black voters as he defends his seat against GOP Rep. Mike Collins. Ossoff is on pace to win roughly the same share as when he won his runoff election in 2021.

He is also making some inroads with White voters, early exit polls show.

Most White voters are backing Collins, but this would be a really good performance by a Democrat in Georgia among White voters if this holds.

Also, on balance, more voters view Colllins' views as extreme than Ossoff's views.

Overview of CBS News 2026 exit polls for the midterm elections

President Trump is on track for the lowest approval rating for a president in a midterm election, according to early exit polls. Currently at 38%, it's lower than it was during Mr. Trump's first term, and lower than it was for George W. Bush in 2006 when his party lost both houses of Congress.

Midterm elections have often been a referendum on the sitting president, and this one is no exception. Roughly six in 10 say Mr. Trump is a factor in their vote for the House.

This is being driven largely by voters backing Democrats, who are overwhelmingly motivated by opposition to Mr. Trump.

But for those backing Republicans, it's less about the president. Back in 2018, most Republican voters said their vote was to support Mr. Trump. That figure is lower today.

The president has often told his supporters to pretend he is on the ballot, and for many in the MAGA base, they may be doing just that. Most MAGA Republicans say their vote is to support Mr. Trump, but most non-MAGA Reps say he is not a factor.

The mood of the electorate is a sour one

Voters are just plain not happy.

Current exit polls show roughly three-quarters of voters are at least dissatisfied with the direction of the country. More are angry now about how things are going than they were in 2024, as economic anxiety persists. Those voting for Democrats are particularly likely to be angry.

The issue of the economy and trust in Mr. Trump to fix it helped propel him to victory in 2024, but voters feel no better about the condition of the economy today.

In fact, more voters have negative views of the economy now than they did two years ago, and views of the economy are more in line with what we saw in the 2022 midterms, when the party in power lost seats.

Cost of living: Voters are feeling the pinch

Voters are feeling it in their pocketbooks. They are more than twice as likely to say their finances are worse rather than better, based on early exit polls.

Voters across parties express concern about affording everything from gas to groceries to utilities.

For two consecutive elections, most voters have said inflation caused hardship for their family, including about one in five who describe that hardship as severe.

All this adds up to the cost of living being a major factor for voters across parties, but it's more crucial for those backing Democrats. Immigration enforcement is more crucial for those backing Republicans.

When voters are asked to pick their most important issue from a list, the economy comes out on top, followed by the state of democracy. Those voting for Democrats prioritize the state of democracy — an issue that has long concerned them.

For those backing Republicans, the economy is their most important issue, followed by immigration.

Voters who pick the state of democracy as their top issue are particularly likely to say government corruption is a crucial factor in their vote.

Government corruption: It's a major factor for voters across party lines

Roughly nine in 10 voters nationally say government corruption is a major factor in their vote — about the same as cost of living — and it's crucial to those voting for Democrats.

About six in 10 voters think President Trump puts his own personal interests over the country.

The Iran War

While the war with Iran is less of a factor for voters than the cost of living, the conflict is not popular. Most think the U.S. made the wrong decision to take that military action, including about a quarter of Republicans.

Those most concerned about affording gas are the most likely to disagree with the decision to attack Iran.

Does all this dissatisfaction translate to satisfaction with the party out of power?

Neither political party is viewed favorably by a majority of voters.

About one in five backing Democrats for the House have an unfavorable view of the Democratic Party. Most Democrats are motivated by their opposition to Mr. Trump.

And the Democratic Party isn't overwhelmingly seen as the party better able to handle key issues.

Emerging issues

Data centers arose as an issue in this campaign. In all the Senate battlegrounds, majorities oppose the construction of a data center in their community.

More voters see artificial intelligence as doing more to harm society than to help it.

Voter confidence

Large majorities of voters are at least somewhat confident that their votes will be counted accurately both nationwide and in their own states, and that eligible voters will be allowed to vote. But while they are confident in their votes being counted, those voting Republican are far less confident that people who are not eligible to vote will be prevented from voting.

This national exit poll measures the general preference for voters nationwide in their choice for the House of Representatives. The House of Representatives, of course, is elected seat by seat.

A quick note on the states

Mr. Trump's job approval is currently underwater in nearly all the Senate battleground states, according to early exit polls, including in states that he won by double digits in 2024.

In all the Senate battlegrounds, more say their finances are worse, not better, compared to years ago.

And party control of the Senate was on the minds of voters. Majorities of those voting for Republican candidates and those voting for Democrats say which party controls the Senate was a major factor in their vote.

The CBS News exit poll interviewed thousands of voters across the country at polling locations on Election Day and in the weeks leading up to Election Day. This is how the voter polling was conducted.

World.title: Ashley Moody projected to win Florida Senate election
World.content:
Washington — GOP Sen. Ashley Moody defeated Democrat Angie Nixon in the Florida Senate race, CBS News projects, keeping the seat under Republican control.

Moody, 51, was appointed last year to fill a vacancy left by Secretary of State Marco Rubio. She previously served as Florida's attorney general, after working as a commercial litigator and federal prosecutor.

Moody faced off against Nixon, who's represented portions of the Jacksonville area in the Florida Statehouse since 2020. Nixon, 42, is a democratic socialist candidate who pulled off an upset victory against a more moderate opponent in the primary, setting up the race against Moody.

Nixon's primary victory was among a series of wins by progressive-left candidates this cycle, in a key midterm dynamic as the Democrats grappled with differing visions for the party's future. But the general election contests are another story, especially in a state like Florida.

The formerly purple state has become increasingly red, and President Trump won Florida by 13 points in 2024. And while Democrats sought to make inroads in the Sunshine State, Nixon's opponents seized on the socialist label, which may have alienated some immigrant populations in the state who have fled socialist governments. Nixon repeatedly pushed back on the criticism, saying "it's not about labels," while underscoring her commitment to issues like healthcare and housing affordability.

With the projected victory in the special election, Moody is set to serve out the remainder of Rubio's term, which ends in early 2029.

World.title: Tens of millions cast ballots for midterms despite worries of Trump's interference
World.content:
Tens of millions cast ballots for midterms despite worries of Trump's interference

toggle caption i Salwan Georges/Getty Images

Midterms coverage: Live results | What to know | Stories around the country

Stay connected: NPR Politics Podcast | NPR Politics newsletter | NPR app

Tens of millions of voters cast their ballots Tuesday without widespread disruptions despite concerns of interference by the Trump administration.

Around the country, election administrators responded to relatively common Election Day issues in some communities, from delayed poll openings and long lines to poor signage and voting equipment problems.

Polls remain open in much of the western United States until later Tuesday.

Flooding in parts of Florida and in the Four Corners states of Arizona, Colorado, New Mexico and Utah forced local officials to relocate some polling sites and resort to emergency ballots.

Sponsor Message

The most high-profile technical problem occurred in Westchester County, N.Y., which includes part of the state's competitive 17th Congressional District. A ballot scanner issue took much of the day to get sorted out, meaning voters had to give their ballots to election workers for scanning at a later time. Some right-wing commentators online claimed the issue was a sign of fraud, but both the Republican and Democrat running in the district told voters not to be deterred.

"Every ballot will be counted," Mike Lawler, the Republican incumbent in the district, wrote in an X post after news of the issue arose.

The Trump administration's Justice Department had announced it planned to have around 1,000 monitors at polling places on Election Day, and shortly after the first polls opened on the East Coast Tuesday, the department said it was sending monitors to observe voting in every state.

"Election integrity has been one of the top priorities for this Administration and this Division," Harmeet Dhillon, the head of the Justice Department's Civil Rights Division, said in a statement.

Sending out election observers has been a routine way of documenting any racial discrimination at the polls under past administrations since the passing of the Voting Rights Act of 1965. But ongoing, baseless claims of widespread voter fraud from President Trump and other federal officials had heightened worries among many local officials and election experts that this administration's DOJ election monitors would interfere with voting at the polls.

As of Tuesday evening, however, no such activity has been reported.

But the New Mexico secretary of state's office received reports of DOJ monitors asking unusual questions and questioning voters in Bernalillo County, which is home to Albuquerque. "The New Mexico Department of Justice reached out to the DOJ Team Lead on our office's behalf to address this reported behavior, and we received assurances it would be addressed," spokesperson Lindsey Bachman said in a statement.

Sponsor Message

Concerns about Immigration and Customs Enforcement activity and law enforcement presence near polling sites also did not come to pass, as of 9 p.m. ET.

Instead, voters exercised their rights on what many voting observers considered to be a fairly normal Election Day.

Their ballots on Tuesday joined more than 61 million that were already cast during early voting. Nationally, early in-person and mail-in voters cast 34% more ballots compared to the last midterm general elections in 2022, according to the latest data compiled by the University of Florida's Election Lab. The pre-Election Day surge was driven mainly by in-person voting.

As the counting of ballots continues, voting rights advocates are now looking ahead to any potential controversies over close races and the certification of results. Some election officials have also warned about ballot seizures, especially after the FBI earlier this year seized election 2020 materials from Fulton County, Ga.

"Election Day is the last day that you can cast your ballot. But election season continues after today, and we're going to continue to remain vigilant," said Shaylyn Cochran, deputy executive director of the Lawyers' Committee for Civil Rights Under Law, during a press call on Tuesday.

Edited by Benjamin Swasey

World.title: Melat Kiros becomes the first Gen Z woman elected to Congress
World.content:
Melat Kiros becomes the first Gen Z woman elected to Congress

toggle caption i Timothy Hurst/Denver Post via Getty Images

Midterms coverage: Live results | What to know | Stories around the country

Stay connected: NPR Politics Podcast | NPR Politics newsletter | NPR app

Democratic socialist Melat Kiros has won the race to represent Colorado's 1st Congressional District in the House, according to a race call by The Associated Press, marking the first time a Gen Z woman will serve in Congress.

Kiros, a 29-year-old Ethiopian immigrant and lawyer, cruised to victory Tuesday night in the reliably blue district, which includes most of Denver.

The win comes just months after she handily defeated 15-term incumbent Diana DeGette in the state's Democratic primary, a high-profile party upset where voter frustration with leaders in Washington, D.C., and calls for political change were at the forefront.

Sponsor Message

Loading...

Kiros is one of several winning House candidates on Tuesday who were endorsed by the Democratic Socialists of America or its local chapters.

Many touted a shared core platform: championing issues aimed at expanding the social safety net for working Americans through policies like Medicare for All and universal childcare. They also advocated for more divisive changes, such as abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement and ending U.S. military aid to Israel.

Kiros' fierce criticism of Israel and the war in Gaza became a source of controversy on the campaign trail, sparking blowback from the independent candidate in her race, Shimon Blau, who accused her of espousing antisemitic rhetoric. Kiros has pushed back on that, saying her criticism rests with the state of Israel rather than the Jewish people.

Though the average age of a lawmaker in Congress has gotten younger in recent years, being a Gen Z member of Congress remains a rarity. Kiros will arrive on Capitol Hill at a moment when Democrats continue to confront calls from many of their voters for generational change.

In an interview with NPR in February, she spoke about the role of age in her race, arguing that many of her policy positions appeal to young voters in particular.

Sponsor Message

"Young people understand that we are in the fight of our lives," she said. "We need to have leaders that are going to be fighting for the kind of bold policies that actually get something done, and they're refusing to settle or wait for our turn or ask for permission."

Currently, just one sitting member of Congress is under the age of 30, Florida Democrat Maxwell Frost, who became the first Gen Zer elected to the House in 2022.

World.title: Georgia elects the nation's first Black female governor
World.content:
Georgia elects the nation's first Black female governor

toggle caption i Brynn Anderson/AP Photo

Midterms coverage: Live results | What to know | Stories around the country

Stay connected: NPR Politics Podcast | NPR Politics newsletter | NPR app

Keisha Lance Bottoms will be the first Black female governor elected in the country, after she won the Georgia governor's race, according to a race call by the Associated Press.

Bottoms' win marks the first time Georgia has elected a Democratic governor in more than 20 years, breaking the Republican hold on state government in Georgia. But she will likely be working with a Republican majority in at least one chamber of the legislature.

Bottoms, 56, defeated Republican Rick Jackson, a billionaire healthcare executive endorsed by President Trump. Trump won Georgia in 2024, but lost the state in 2020. Since then, Georgia has evolved from a state that consistently elects Republicans to federal and state office to a swing state with Democratic senators. But the governor's office and the legislature have remained solidly Republican.

Sponsor Message

Throughout her campaign, Bottoms made fully expanding Medicaid in the state, which would require legislative approval, a top campaign promise.

Loading...

Before running for governor, Bottoms served as mayor of Atlanta for a single tumultuous term from 2018-2022, during which the city grappled with the COVID-19 pandemic and the social unrest seen in other major cities at that time. She declined to run for a second term and instead served as an adviser in the Biden administration. Her opponent used her record as mayor against her in attack ads, claiming she abandoned the city after allowing crime to fester — because Atlanta, like many other major cities, saw an increase in crime during the pandemic.

Bottoms harnessed frustration against Trump to propel her campaign. She promised to stand up to the Trump administration while in office, and to find relief for high prices. One of her proposals includes allowing local municipalities to eliminate the sales tax on groceries. She has also said she wants to eliminate the state income tax for public school teachers.

Data centers also emerged as a top campaign issue, as the state leads the nation in new data center construction. Bottoms said she backs a moratorium on new data centers.

Sponsor Message

"We need experts in this field to sit around the table and tell us and give us guidance as to how the state of Georgia should move forward," Bottoms said in October, during her only gubernatorial debate with Jackson.

Bottoms touted Trump's endorsement of Jackson throughout the campaign. Jackson aligned himself with Trump during the primaries, but later distanced himself from the president by removing references to him on his website and leaving Trump's name out of speeches on the campaign trail. Instead, he allied himself with Georgia's current governor, Brian Kemp, who endorsed Jackson after the primary.

Bottoms gained her own endorsements from several high-profile Democrats, including former presidents Joe Biden and Barack Obama. She also regularly campaigned with Sen. Jon Ossoff, one of Georgia's two Democratic U.S. senators.

Sarah Kallis is the politics reporter at Georgia Public Broadcasting.

World.title: Republican Byron Donalds wins governor's race in Florida
World.content:
Republican Byron Donalds wins governor's race in Florida

toggle caption i Jacquelyn Martin/AP

Midterms coverage: Live results | What to know | Stories around the country

Stay connected: NPR Politics Podcast | NPR Politics newsletter | NPR app

Republican Byron Donalds beat Democrat David Jolly in Florida's closely watched governor's race, according to a race call by the Associated Press.

Donalds, who will become Florida's first Black governor, won the race with the backing of President Donald Trump and a sizable campaign finance war chest. He clinched the governor's race against the national backdrop of Republicans growing unhappy with Trump over gas prices and the war with Iran.

Donalds stumped on affordability issues - inflation, housing and insurance - and promised to continue the conservative policies of out-going Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis, who remains popular in Florida and joined Donalds during the campaign.

Sponsor Message

Several polls showed a close race favoring Donalds through much of the campaign in a state that has some 1.5 million more registered Republicans than Democrats, and 3.3 million unaffiliated voters up for grabs.

Loading...

Donalds, 48, who spent most of his career in the finance industry, has served two terms in Congress and two terms in the Florida House. Seen as a rising star in the Republican party, he started as a Democrat and left the party in 2010 . Donalds was an early Trump supporter in the 2024 election, and Trump returned the favor by backing him. Donalds rallied with Trump just days before the election.

Polls taken earlier this year showed Trump was less popular in Florida than DeSantis, and in September, Donalds appeared to distance himself from Trump by taking prominent displays of Trump's name off his campaign website.

Jolly campaigned on a "believe in better" slogan, zeroing in on affordability issues such as housing, inflation and gas prices and the boom in AI data centers. And on the trail, he called Donalds "data center Donalds" for taking campaign contributions from industry players. Donalds introduced legislation this summer that would require data centers to generate their own power and water.

Jolly, 54, served in Congress as a Republican before leaving the party in 2018 during President Donald Trump's first term. He changed his registration to no-party affiliation and then switched to Democrat last year. He has spent most of his career as a lawyer, lobbyist and television political analyst.

Sponsor Message

World.title: Democrat Roy Cooper wins a North Carolina Senate seat
World.content:
Democrat Roy Cooper wins a North Carolina Senate seat

toggle caption i Allison Joyce/Getty Images

Midterms coverage: Live results | What to know | Stories around the country

Stay connected: NPR Politics Podcast | NPR Politics newsletter | NPR app

Democrat Roy Cooper has won North Carolina's open U.S. Senate seat, according to a race call from the Associated Press, providing the party with a key Senate flip.

The former governor becomes the first Democrat elected to the Senate from North Carolina since 2008.

Cooper defeated Michael Whatley, a former Republican National Committee chair who President Trump picked to replace retiring GOP Sen. Thom Tillis.

Cooper and national Democratic Party groups significantly outspent Whatley and Republicans. A few weeks before the election, national GOP organizations pulled TV ads from North Carolina and redirected their money to other battlegrounds like Kansas.

Sponsor Message

Loading...

Cooper, who served as governor from 2017 to 2025, focused his campaign on affordability issues. Each campaign stop he made across the state was promoted as the "Make Stuff Cost Less" tour.

Meanwhile, Whatley's campaign centered around crime and immigration issues. He criticized Cooper over a COVID-era legal settlement that released inmates from state prisons to address overcrowding during the pandemic. But polls indicated that the economy — not crime — was the top concern for North Carolina voters this year.

The race was Whatley's first run for elected office, and Cooper's campaign painted him as a lobbyist for Big Oil who would become a rubber stamp for Trump in the Senate.

Patrick Sebastian, a Republican strategist who did not work on the Whatley campaign, said his party's candidate should have made the economy a bigger focus.

"Really it's the economy is Issue A and then Issue B is probably government corruption, that people are following the most," Sebastian said. "So when we're not talking about those issues, it's going to be hard to connect with people that go to Walmart for their groceries and can only get 80% of what they used to buy because the prices have gone up."

The North Carolina Senate race was initially expected to be one of the most competitive — and most expensive — in the country, but Whatley never led in polling, and Cooper's lead widened over the course of the race.

Even as pro-Whatley TV ads largely disappeared in October, Trump and Vice President Vance came to North Carolina for multiple rallies in the final weeks of the campaign. Sebastian says those visits likely helped improve base turnout for GOP voters, but weren't enough to save Whatley's campaign.

Sponsor Message

Tillis announced in 2025 he wouldn't seek reelection, after Trump threatened him with a primary challenger for failing to support the president's tax cut and spending bill. Rather than campaign for Whatley, he's been promoting his new book criticizing fellow Republicans.

World.title: Jon Ossoff wins reelection in Georgia, easily defeating Republican Mike Collins
World.content:
Jon Ossoff wins reelection in Georgia, easily defeating Republican Mike Collins

toggle caption i Ryan Murphy/AP

Midterms coverage: Live results | What to know | Stories around the country

Stay connected: NPR Politics Podcast | NPR Politics newsletter | NPR app

Jon Ossoff, the only incumbent Senate Democrat defending a seat in a state President Trump carried in 2024, has won the U.S. Senate race in Georgia.

Ossoff defeated Republican Rep. Mike Collins, according to a race call by The Associated Press.

A year ago, Democrats and Republicans envisioned the race in Georgia as one of the cycle's marquee Senate showdowns.

But in Collins, the GOP in Georgia nominated a candidate whose personal baggage alienated independents and some Republican-leaning voters.

Sponsor Message

In Ossoff, Democrats were buoyed by a candidate who won respect at home even from some Republican officials for the strength of his constituent services. And outside Georgia, Ossoff electrified Democrats searching for fresh faces to lead the party out of the political wilderness.

Loading...

On paper, the race should have been closer. In 2021, Democrats flipped both of Georgia's Senate seats blue for the first time in a generation. In the 2022 midterms, Democratic Sen. Raphael Warnock barely held onto his seat in a runoff, even against a deeply flawed opponent.

Otherwise, Republicans have continued to win nearly every other statewide race in Georgia.

In the Republican primary this spring, Trump endorsed Collins over former football coach Derek Dooley, a first-time candidate backed by Georgia's popular Republican Gov. Brian Kemp.

Collins, the owner of a family trucking company, struggled to dispense with scrutiny over his ties to family and former staffers who have espoused white nationalist and antisemitic views. Collins also continued to embrace Trump's false claims about widespread election fraud in 2020.

toggle caption i Mark Schiefelbein/AP

Ossoff, a former congressional aide and documentary filmmaker, first appeared on the national stage when he waged a closer-than-expected attempt to flip a suburban House race in a special election in 2017. After Georgia sent Ossoff to the Senate in a 2021 runoff, he gained attention for his methodical grilling of Trump appointees during hearings on the Hill.

Sponsor Message

As clips from Ossoff excoriating alleged graft in Trump's orbit in rally speeches ricocheted around the internet over the course of the campaign, many Democrats began to mention him as a possible presidential candidate. Ossoff has said he is not running for the White House in 2028.

World.title: Mother and daughter dead in suspected grizzly bear attack near Bella Coola
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Family members have identified the two victims of a suspected fatal grizzly bear attack near Bella Coola, B.C., as Jennifer Balcarras, 48, and her daughter Selah Reed, 20.

Balcarras's remains were discovered Monday in the Snooka West Trail area, the conservation officer service said. In a later update, officers said the second victim in the case was located dead on Tuesday afternoon.

Family reported them missing on Sunday after they didn't return from a walk on the trail — described as a roughly five-minute drive from their home — on Saturday afternoon.

"It's surreal. It doesn't seem real. It feels like a dream," said Josh Balcarras, Jennifer's brother.

"The way it starts is a few hours of not hearing from them. That turns into a day, and then a night … then a second night comes and it becomes a real thing."

Balcarras and Reed were familiar with the trail, according to a family member. (Submitted by Travis Reed)

He said the pair was familiar with the trail, which he said is "not in a remote area."

"Just a casual walk," he said.

WATCH | Conservation officer provides update on presumed attack: 1 dead, 1 missing after suspected grizzly bear attack near Bella Coola, B.C. | Duration 0:58

Balcarras worked as an art therapist in Bella Coola. Her younger brothers remember her as a book lover with a passion for playing guitar, singing, painting and the outdoors. She had four children, Reed her youngest.

"She painted murals in her own kids' home … my home," said her brother Matthew.

"She was very much a central person in our family."

Jennifer Balcarras is seen in this undated handout image. The art therapist was remembered as someone who deeply loved her family. (Submitted by Travis Reed)

Reed was an education assistant who was going to school through Athabasca University’s online learning program.

Family described her as "a gentle, sweet, quiet soul" with a love of ballet, art and hiking.

"She liked a lot of the same things Jenny liked. I think they got along really, really well," said Josh.

"They were two peas in a pod. When Jenny hiked, Selah was right there beside her."

BCCOS searching for bear

In an online statement, the B.C. Conservation Officer Service (BCCOS) says it has a team investigating the suspected attack.

"Our thoughts are with the families of the victims during this tragic time," Insp. Jeff Tyre of the BCCOS said in a video posted online.

Tyre said trapping efforts are underway but no bears have been captured.

The BCCOS said any captured bears would be assessed to determine next steps.

"If the bear is determined to be the bear responsible for the attack, it will be dispatched to ensure public safety, as per provincial human-wildlife conflict response guidelines," it said in a post on social media.

Last year, a group of children and teachers were attacked by a grizzly near Bella Coola, leaving several critically injured on a trail south of Highway 20.

In a statement, the Nuxalk Nation directed community members and media to the conservation officer service for updates.

"While the full circumstances are still unfolding, we understand first-hand the trauma this incident will inflict upon the victims' family members, the victims of last year's attack, and the community at large," elected Chief Samuel Schooner said in the statement.

"Our thoughts are with the victim's family as they learn of this tragic event."

World.title: Carney says U.S. 'asking less and offering more' with 'more intense' trade talks underway
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Prime Minister Mark Carney says Canada and the U.S. have made progress on reaching a trade deal, but stressed more work is needed before any agreement is finalized.

"They're asking less and they're offering more, but we're not quite there," Carney said of the state of negotiations while on the sidelines of meeting with other Commonwealth leaders in Antigua on Tuesday.

After trade talks collapsed dramatically in August, Carney said "more intense negotiations" have since begun.

The prime minister attributed that to the White House's position shifting on some of Canada's "red lines."

WATCH | Carney on the state of U.S. trade talks: 'We've made progress' with U.S. on trade talks, Carney says | Duration closed caption 1:36 Following a conversation with U.S. President Donald Trump over the weekend, Prime Minister Mark Carney said on Tuesday that the U.S. has 'clearly shifted' on Canada's 'red lines' around sovereignty, language and trade deals. 'They're asking less and they're offering more,' Carney said.

When talks fell apart over the summer, the Canadian side said U.S. negotiators took issue with rules that ensure French-language content is easy to find on streaming platforms, such as Netflix, and that the Americans tried to restrict Canada's ability to strike trade deals with other countries.

"Those are now off the table. That's very welcome," said Carney.

The progress, as the prime minister described it, on the trade file comes as Trump's Republican Party faces what could be a tough midterm showing.

Pollsters have been expecting a blue wave as American voters increasingly voice frustrations about the cost of living, driven in part by the war in Iran and tariffs, in the lead up to Tuesday's vote.

In an interview Tuesday morning, Trump told Fox News that his administration was nearing a trade agreement with Canada.

While Carney didn't outline what issues remain, autos are expected to be a key sticking point, as they were in August before talks collapsed — triggering new tariffs on both sides.

Carney said he'll meet Trump in China later this month at the APEC summit.

World.title: Home in Amherstburg, Ont., unlivable after family spent $155K on renovations, police looking for contractor
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Tonya Azevedo says she has lost $155,000 and her family of four can no longer live in their home of 20 years after a contractor who told them he was licensed did work that turned out to be unsafe.

Home in Amherstburg, Ont., unlivable after family spent $155K on renovations, police looking for contractor

Tonya Azevedo says she has lost $155,000 and her family of four can no longer live in their home of 20 years after a contractor who told them he was licensed did work that turned out to be unsafe.

Azevedo said she discovered dirt used to fill concrete blocks in the foundation of the home's addition, live electrical wiring under drywall and a sewer pipe that was ruptured.

The Town of Amherstburg even ordered a stop to construction because the work didn't match approved drawings and "multiple deficiencies" were found, according to documents obtained by CBC News.

"I'm absolutely heartbroken," said Azevedo. "Every time I come here and see what's left of a home that I raised my two children in and all of the happy memories … it's just gone."

She remortgaged her Alma Street home to get $200,000 from the bank for an addition and new garage.

There were plans to build onto the rear of the home, expand the family kitchen and the master bedroom, and add an en suite bathroom and a third bedroom upstairs.

Azevedo said she just finished spending the remainder of the loan undoing and fixing the contractor's work.

In the meantime, the family is living with a relative. Azevedo and her husband are sleeping in that home's laundry room.

"We don't have a home," said Azevedo. "This is just the level of destruction that we're left with."

Police looking to charge contractor

Windsor police said Tuesday that there's now a warrant out for the arrest of contractor Jessie Flaricee after Azevedo filed a report with Windsor police's Amherstburg detachment.

Flaricee is wanted on fraud over $5,000, uttering a forged document and obtaining more than $5,000 under false pretenses.

His company, MBS Home Solutions, was dissolved for non-compliance in November 2024, according to Windsor police.

During a conversation with CBC News on Monday, Flaricee said he offered to fix the issues, has made attempts to reach out to the family and there's been a communication breakdown.

"They pretty much fired me and didn't give me the opportunity to fix any issues."

Jessie Flaricee is the owner of MBS Building Solutions and did work on Azevedo's home from March to August. (Facebook)

Flaricee said he also hired subcontractors, but didn't specify who did the problematic work.

"There is more to the story than portraying it as a contractor trying to take somebody's money. That's not even close to the case," said Flaricee. " There are a lot of layers to this situation that are far more complex than what is being portrayed."

When asked if there's any remaining money that could be returned to Azevedo, Flaricee said "that'll be between me and her."

"There's no intent to take anything from anybody," said Flaricee.

Azevedo said Flaricee told her he was a fully licensed contractor, something she says is not true.

"I guess it expired, so I had to renew it, but I'm insured. My bank account is under my business name and my name," he said.

"People have now touched that project and started working and undoing or doing [work]."

'We trusted this person'

Azevedo said her husband knew Flaricee from the local youth football community and he quickly became a family friend.

"We trusted this person," said Azevedo. "Maybe we shouldn't have listened to him and had just done some more research. I was just too trusting of him."

The Better Business Bureau (BBB) said every contractor should provide the type of licence they have, what agency it's registered with and when it expires.

"So if you want to dig into the broader term of validating licensing, check directly with the issuing authority, which is easy to do online as well," said Jennifer Matthews, CEO of the BBB in southwestern Ontario.

Some tips for consumer protection

Matthews said people should also ask for three references.

The BBB's website allows the public to check the experience and reputation of companies, which Matthews also recommends doing.

"You can look at are their complaints against that business, how have they been resolved."

Demolition and construction first began in March, when she first gave Flaricee $45,000 to get started. That's when the family packed up all of their things and moved out while the work was being done.

They moved back in by June and then the work stopped in August.

Azevedo said Flaricee asked for more money, but she refused.

She remembers telling him that she doesn't "feel comfortable giving you any more money until there is close to $155,000 worth of work here and a home that we can live in safely."

Tonya Azevedo, left, is seen with her husband, Joel Charron, right, her son, Bradley Azevedo and her daughter, Jocelyn Azevedo. (Tonya Azevedo)

In Azevedo's case, there was an attempt to figure out where the money went. She said she asked for invoices and receipts, and never received them.

But Flaricee insisted he was fired and not given the opportunity to fix the problems.

Son's 'safe space and sanctuary' is now gone

Either way, Azevedo said, there's been a lot of "stress and trauma" put on her family throughout this process.

Her 16-year-old son, who has autism, just wants his bedroom back. She calls it his "safe space and sanctuary" and said it's taken a toll on his mental health.

"To have everything stripped away from them and as a mom, not being able to fix that," said Azevedo.

The town's building department noted that the foundation mortar joints didn't comply with the Ontario Building Code and new part of the foundation was not connected to the existing foundation.

After the contractor's demolition, Azevedo said, there's been no heat in the home, the family is without a washroom and there isn't power to much of the house.

"We're not asking for our home to be finished. We're just asking for our home back."

World.title: Correction on our previous reporting on charges faced by Alberta hockey executive
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

On Nov. 3, 2026, CBC News reported that a former Alberta hockey executive facing child luring charges was also wanted on warrants for domestic violence.

That reporting was incorrect.

CBC News received information from the courts that was inaccurate after the Alberta Court of Justice merged the files of two different men so they appeared in court records as one.

Tyler Robb King, 39, was arrested Friday and charged with luring, sexual exploitation and making child sexual abuse material. The offences are alleged to have taken place between 2021 and 2024 when King worked for the Okotoks Oilers of the British Columbia Hockey League as assistant general manager of operations.

According to the Crown’s office, King does not have any history with the courts in Alberta aside from the current charges.

World.title: A part of B.C. now observes the same time as a part of Florida
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The Regional District of East Kootenay, which includes B.C. communities like Cranbrook and Kimberley, now observes the same time as Fort Walton Beach and Crestview in Florida.

With B.C. not rolling back its clocks on Sunday, unlike much of the rest of Canada and the U.S., some far-flung communities now share the same time zones — though they may have different names.

Officials in the East Kootenays in southeast B.C. voted in August to stick with Alberta time year-round, which is mountain daylight time, or a permanent UTC−6 time standard.
