Farmers in Michoacán, Jalisco, Colima and Nayarit were forced to destroy approximately 52 tonnes of avocados over the weekend after detecting the presence of the avocado seed weevil.

The discovery of larvae in fruit destined for export prompted the state authorities and the National Service for Agrifood Health, Safety and Quality (Senasica) to halt shipments.

Tons of avocados were destroyed in Mexico after authorities detected an aggressive pest — known as the avocado seed weevil — in shipments destined for international markets. https://t.co/G1Kt5WAxva https://t.co/HPB14c3p9t — ABC News (@ABC) November 3, 2026

Michoacán Environment Minister Alejandro Méndez confirmed the infestation to reporters, while officials work to determine a timeframe for resuming shipments.

Video shared on social media showed local producers emptying truckloads of avocados and dumping ​crates into pits to be burned and buried, as ​required by pest-elimination protocols.

The avocado seed weevil (Curculionidae) is a snout beetle, or bark beetle, whose larvae develop inside the fruit, boring through the pulp until they reach the seed, where they feed and complete their life cycle.

The adult female pierces the avocado peel with an elongated extension of the mouth called a rostrum and lays one or two eggs per fruit, pushing them close to the seed. The eggs take 12 to 14 days to hatch.

As the entry hole becomes covered with debris and secretions, the peel does not show visible damage, making it difficult to detect the infestation from the outside.

Upon hatching, the larva moves through the pulp toward the pit where it feeds for about two months. It also creates a pupation chamber inside the seed, and remains for another two weeks or more before emerging as an adult.

Applying insecticides to infested fruit is useless; the larva and pupa develop protected inside the seed, out of reach of any chemical product.

Chemical control is only effective against adults during their emergence stage. For larvae and pupae, the options are cultural control — collecting and burying damaged fruit at least 1 meter deep, or burning it — and biological control with entomopathogenic fungi (a specialized group of parasitic microorganisms that infect, disable and kill insects and other arthropods).

The weevil also bores into the branches and trunks of avocado trees, and can ​spread very ⁠aggressively within an orchard and devastate crops if not addressed.

Local authorities have yet to provide an estimate of the economic impact.

With reports from LopezDoriga.com, Reuters and Infobae

World.title: Sheinbaum breaks her US midterm silence for one candidate: Tuesday’s mañanera recapped
World.content:
Listen to this article

Sheinbaum’s mañanera in 60 seconds

👏 Sheinbaum applauds likely election of Xavier Becerra as California governor: Asked about Becerra, the Mexican-American Democratic Party candidate who would become California’s first elected Latino governor if he wins Tuesday’s election, Sheinbaum broke into applause. She noted that around 39 million Mexicans and Mexican-Americans live in the United States and said it is “very good” for them to be politically represented. Polls indicate Becerra is likely to easily beat Republican Steve Hilton.

Asked about Becerra, the Mexican-American Democratic Party candidate who would become California’s first elected Latino governor if he wins Tuesday’s election, Sheinbaum broke into applause. She noted that around 39 million Mexicans and Mexican-Americans live in the United States and said it is “very good” for them to be politically represented. Polls indicate Becerra is likely to easily beat Republican Steve Hilton. 🗳️ Sheinbaum says Mexico will respect US midterm result, declines to comment on races: Asked what a Democratic takeover of both houses of the U.S. Congress would mean for Mexico, especially for the USMCA, Sheinbaum said it’s “not our place to comment.” She said Mexico will wait for the result and respect it, whatever it is.

Asked what a Democratic takeover of both houses of the U.S. Congress would mean for Mexico, especially for the USMCA, Sheinbaum said it’s “not our place to comment.” She said Mexico will wait for the result and respect it, whatever it is. 🏝️ Sheinbaum says IBWC must decide who Rio Grande islands belong to: Responding to Texas’ claim to nine islands along the border, Sheinbaum said it is not up to the Texas government to decide who owns them, but rather a decision for the International Boundary and Water Commission (IBWC). She said she believed Texas’ determination was electorally motivated ahead of the midterms. Mexico’s Foreign Affairs Ministry said in an Oct. 30 statement that the border “cannot be modified by a decision of a state government.”

Why today’s mañanera matters

President Sheinbaum held her Tuesday morning press conference as U.S. citizens were going to the polls in the midterm elections.

A Mexican-American is projected to win one of the most important political offices in the United States — the governorship of California — and Sheinbaum welcomed that prospect.

Thank you, California. When we started, we were underdogs. But you believed in us, made calls, and showed up at every stop. Farm workers and firefighters, teachers and tradesmen, small business owners and service workers: this campaign belongs to you. Tomorrow is Election Day. Let’s finish this together. Vote! — Xavier Becerra (@XavierBecerra) November 3, 2026

However, she declined to express an opinion on the U.S. congressional races and their possible outcomes, in contrast to her willingness to comment on the California gubernatorial election.

According to an opinion article by Duncan Wood and Ivan Zapien that was published by The Hill last month, the midterms “could give Mexico more allies in Washington who value a stable North American partnership,” but “could also give its critics more platforms from which to demand change.”

The elections are taking place at a time when Mexican and U.S. officials continue trade talks aimed at resolving a range of differences that contributed to the Trump administration’s decision to not renew the USMCA free trade pact for an additional 16 years.

Trade differences are one source of tension in the Mexico-U.S. relationship, but they are by no means the only one.

Another source of potential tension arose last week when Texas Land Commissioner Dawn Buckingham announced that the Texas General Land Office (GLO) had identified nine islands along the Texas-Mexico border as property belonging to the State of Texas. Sheinbaum commented on the matter on Tuesday morning, adding another bilateral issue to a press conference that covered current events north of the Rio Grande.

Sheinbaum applauds likely election of Xavier Becerra as governor of California

A reporter noted that Xavier Becerra, the Democratic Party’s candidate in today’s gubernatorial election in California, will become the state’s first elected Latino governor if he wins. She asked the president for her opinion on the matter.

Sheinbaum’s first reaction was to break into applause.

🇺🇸 La presidenta de México, Claudia Sheinbaum, aplaude la candidatura de Xavier Becerra por la gobernatura del estado de California https://t.co/SA55sdBgNG — EL PAÍS México (@elpaismexico) November 3, 2026

She subsequently noted that around 39 million Mexicans and Mexican-Americans live in the United States and declared that it is “very good” for them to be politically represented.

Becerra, a former state and federal lawmaker who served as attorney general of California before becoming secretary of Health and Human Services in the Biden administration, is Mexican-American. He was born in Sacramento in 1958 to Maria Teresa and Manuel Becerra. According to a biography of Becerra on the U.S. House of Representatives website, Manuel was born in Sacramento but grew up in Tijuana, while Maria Teresa was raised in Guadalajara.

Becerra’s Republican Party opponent in today’s election is Steve Hilton, a British-born former Fox News host. Polls indicate that Becerra is likely to beat Hilton easily.

California had a Latino governor for around nine months in 1875, but Romualdo Pacheco wasn’t popularly elected.

Sheinbaum on US midterms: ‘We’re going to respect the result whatever it is’

A reporter raised the possibility of the Democratic Party taking control of both houses of the U.S. Congress. She asked the president what that would mean for Mexico, especially in relation to the USMCA free trade pact.

“We don’t express an opinion,” Sheinbaum responded.

“The election is today. It’s not our place to comment today,” she said.

“… We’re going to wait for the result and we’re going to respect the result whatever it is,” Sheinbaum said.

Asked about “seven or eight Mexicans” accused of voting in the midterms despite not being U.S. citizens, the president said she wasn’t aware of the charges. She said Foreign Affairs Minister Roberto Velasco could provide information about the matter.

Sheinbaum: IBWC must decide who Rio Grande islands belong to

Asked about Texas’ claim to nine islands in the Rio Grande, Sheinbaum said that it was not up to the government of Texas to decide who owns them.

Rather, it’s a decision for the International Boundary and Water Commission (IBWC), she said, referring to the binational body tasked with applying the boundary and water treaties between the United States and Mexico and settling differences that may arise in their application.

The IBWC has to determine whether the islands are on the Mexican or U.S. side of the border, Sheinbaum said.

“If it’s half and half, it’s half and half,” she said.

Sheinbaum said she believed the determination by Texas that the islands belong to that state was electorally motivated ahead of today’s midterms.

In Oct. 26 letters to the Texas Department of Public Safety and the Texas Military Department, Buckingham, the Texas land commissioner, noted that the GLO had determined that nine Rio Grande islands belonged to the state of Texas. She said the GLO had “not been alerted to criminal activity on these … islands,” but added that “previous experience has demonstrated the exploitation of border islands by cartels and smugglers.”

Mexico’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs (SRE) said in an Oct. 30 statement that the border between Mexico and the United States “cannot be modified by a decision of a state government.”

The SRE said that the “limits of the border are defined by criteria established in an international treaty,” adding that the IBWC “is the body both governments have empowered to apply the Treaty and determine on which side of the boundary each island lies.”

World.title: Wheat Fund Falls 1.57% as Corn Slips 0.98% | Grains, Nov 3
World.content:
Farm workers thresh wheat in rural Egypt. The photo is undated and shows wheat, not medicinal plants. Photo: Ahmed Flex777 / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

Key Facts Wheat and corn sank to three-month lows. The wheat-tracking fund WEAT closed at US$21.93 (-1.57%) and the corn-tracking fund CORN at US$17.19 (-0.98%) on Tuesday, 3 November 2026.

The wheat-tracking fund WEAT closed at US$21.93 (-1.57%) and the corn-tracking fund CORN at US$17.19 (-0.98%) on Tuesday, 3 November 2026. Soybeans fell too, more gently. The soybean-tracking fund SOYB has now lost ground for two sessions in a row and is down 7.14% over 20 sessions.

The soybean-tracking fund SOYB has now lost ground for two sessions in a row and is down 7.14% over 20 sessions. Supply is the main culprit. The US harvest is nearly finished, and Conab, Brazil’s national crop-supply agency, expects a record 181.6 million tonnes of soybeans in 2026/27.

The US harvest is nearly finished, and Conab, Brazil’s national crop-supply agency, expects a record 181.6 million tonnes of soybeans in 2026/27. China is shopping in South America. Chinese buyers have already booked 9.04 million tonnes of Brazil’s 2026/27 soybeans, ahead of purchases from the United States.

Chinese buyers have already booked 9.04 million tonnes of Brazil’s 2026/27 soybeans, ahead of purchases from the United States. Wheat has fallen furthest. European wheat futures sit near multi-month lows as peace talks cool fears of disrupted supply.

European wheat futures sit near multi-month lows as peace talks cool fears of disrupted supply. Latin America gets a split verdict. Exporters in Brazil and Argentina earn less per tonne, while grain importers such as Mexico and Peru pay less.

Today’s Focus Grain prices slid again on Tuesday, 3 November 2026, and wheat and corn closed at their lowest levels in at least three months. The wheat-tracking fund now sits 21.7% below its 28 August high, and the corn-tracking fund 15.3% below its 1 September high. The cause is plain: farmers are harvesting a very large crop, and there is more grain than buyers need. The US corn and soybean harvest is close to done, and Brazil, the world’s biggest soybean exporter, is preparing a record planting. China, the largest buyer, is leaning on Brazil and Argentina rather than the United States. That leaves US farmers with heavy stocks and South American growers with the customers. 01 The session in one read

Harvest season is when grain markets feel heaviest, because every field sends its crop to market at once. Tuesday, 3 November 2026 was a textbook example.

In the United States, the corn and soybean harvest is nearly complete, and traders are waiting for the next crop estimates from the US Department of Agriculture, the USDA. Larger supplies were the main reason corn prices slipped.

Brazil, meanwhile, is planting what Conab expects to be a record: 181.6 million tonnes of soybeans from 49.3 million hectares. That area is 1.4% larger than the year before.

Assessment — Harvest glut, not panic MEDIUM The drop has the look of a seasonal supply squeeze rather than a collapse in demand, since the dollar, bond yields and shares barely explain it. Wheat is the weakest link, corn is close behind and soybeans are holding up best, which is what a world awash in cereals would produce. The variable to watch is China’s pace of buying against the November USDA crop estimates.

03 Why it moved

Cause one, and the heaviest, is supply. Corn eased as larger supplies met a harvest nearing completion, and even decent export sales failed to lift it.

Cause two is China’s shift to South America. Chinese buyers have booked 9.04 million tonnes of Brazil’s 2026/27 soybeans in advance, while large domestic stocks and thin crushing margins hold back US purchases. The USDA still projects China’s 2026/27 soybean imports at 115.0 million tonnes, so the demand exists, but it is flowing south. Confidence: high.

Cause three, for wheat, is geopolitics. European wheat futures are near multi-month lows on peace talks, which investors read as easing the risk of disrupted shipments. Confidence: medium, because the link is inferred from price behaviour rather than from any trader’s statement.

The usual drivers only partly agree. The dollar index rose 0.14% to 101.89 and the 10-year US Treasury yield rose 7 basis points to 4.97%, which makes dollar-priced grain a little dearer abroad. Yet the S&P 500 gained 0.36% to 7,569 and the USO oil fund rose 0.83%, so there was no broad risk-off panic. The VIX fear gauge closed at 20.83. The grain slide is therefore its own story.

04 The trend behind it

This is a continuation, not a new phase. Soybeans are 8.5% below their 12-month high of 28.14 on 10 September, yet still 18.6% above the 21.71 low of 13 January.

Corn is down 10.89% over 20 sessions and sits 4.4% above its 12-month low of 16.47 on 29 June. Wheat is down 13.97% over 20 sessions and 8.7% over 60.

Our own history offers a rare calibration. After earlier falls this large, soybeans were higher 20 sessions later in 16 of 29 cases and corn in 11 of 20, with a median gain of 0.6% for both. The worst cases were falls of 7.8% and 7.7% respectively.

Wheat tells a harsher tale. After 13 earlier drops this size, it was higher 20 sessions later in only 4, with a median of -1.6% and a worst case of -16.6%. History is not a forecast.

05 What it means for Latin America

Brazil and Argentina sell grain in dollars, so every drop in price trims export revenue per tonne. Brazil’s record crop partly offsets that through volume, and a weaker real helps farmers whose costs are in reais.

Argentina’s grain exporters bring in the dollars that its economy relies on, so a prolonged slide matters more there than the daily figures suggest. We lack a verified real or peso level today, so treat the currency effect as direction only.

Importers gain. Mexico buys large quantities of US corn for tortillas and animal feed, and Peru relies on imported wheat and corn, so cheaper cereals ease food bills.

For a traveller or saver, the effect shows up slowly in bread, meat and poultry prices rather than overnight.

06 The names to watch

The three trackers, SOYB, CORN and WEAT, are the cleanest gauge for foreign investors. Conab in Brazil and the USDA in Washington set the official crop numbers that move them.

Among companies, Brazilian farmland group SLC Agrícola earns from soybean and corn prices, while grain traders and processors such as Bunge and ADM profit from volume and crushing margins.

07 What would end it

Nearby levels are clear. For soybeans, support is the round 25 mark and then the 21.71 low, with resistance at the 28.14 September peak.

Corn finds support at the 16.47 June low and faces resistance at its 20.29 high of 1 September. Wheat has resistance at its 28.00 high of 28 August and the round 20 mark as the next landmark below.

The dated catalyst is the USDA’s November crop estimate, followed by Brazil’s planting progress and further Chinese purchases. If China keeps buying mainly from South America, the glut persists, and a bad South American growing season is the one thing that would change the picture.

08 What to watch

USDA November estimates: Any cut to US yields or stocks could stop the slide in corn and soybeans.

Any cut to US yields or stocks could stop the slide in corn and soybeans. China’s buying: Further bookings of Brazilian beans beyond 9.04 million tonnes would confirm the shift away from US supply.

Further bookings of Brazilian beans beyond 9.04 million tonnes would confirm the shift away from US supply. Brazil planting and weather: A weather scare in the Brazilian crop belt is the classic way to end a glut.

A weather scare in the Brazilian crop belt is the classic way to end a glut. Peace talks and wheat: Failed talks would revive supply fears for wheat, the weakest of the three.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why are grain prices falling?

A large harvest is arriving, the US crop is nearly gathered and Brazil is expected to produce a record. China is also buying more from South America.

Does the fall mean cheaper food?

Slowly. Lower grain costs reach bread, meat and poultry prices over months, not days.

Who gains and who loses in Latin America?

Exporters in Brazil and Argentina earn less per tonne, while importers such as Mexico and Peru pay less.

Are these prices for actual grain?

No. They are for exchange-traded funds that track soybeans, corn and wheat, so they follow grain but are not the grain price itself.

Oil is expensive because fuel, not crude, is scarce, and that kind of shortage lasts until refineries or shipping routes recover.

01 The session in one read

Think of oil as a bathtub with a blocked drain: crude is arriving, but the refined fuel that people actually buy is not coming out fast enough. That is the market on Tuesday, November 3, 2026.

The fund that tracks US crude (USO) rose 0.83% to US$158.17, its first gain after a short slide. It remains 6.7% below the 23 October high of 169.53.

The fund is a proxy, meaning it follows crude futures rather than showing the price of a barrel itself. Even so, its direction is a reliable guide to the mood of the market.

Assessment — Tight fuel, not tight crude, supports prices MEDIUM The best-supported reading is that the war has broken the link between crude and finished fuel, which keeps prices high even on quiet days. We are medium-confident, because the day’s own move was small and the dollar and bond yields pointed the other way. The variable to watch is the weekly US inventory count, because a third straight large draw would confirm that supply is still tightening.

03 Why it moved

First, and with most weight, is the fuel shortage. Asian crude imports are back to pre-war levels, but imports of diesel and gasoline from the Middle East have collapsed because refineries there are running at reduced capacity.

Second, American stocks have been falling. The American Petroleum Institute, an industry group, estimated a fall of 2.031 million barrels in the week to 23 October, and the next reading was not yet available to us.

The usual drivers disagreed with the rise. The dollar index edged up 0.14% to 101.89 and the ten-year US Treasury yield rose 7 basis points to 4.97%, both of which normally weigh on oil.

The most likely reading is a rebound after a 3.48% five-session dip, helped by the shortage and by the falling stocks. Election Day in the United States is a possible background factor, but we found no reporting tying it to oil. Confidence in this ranking is medium.

Producers are also gaining. Saudi Aramco’s results, released on 3 November, show profits rising even as its physical operations are strained, and executives at an energy conference in Abu Dhabi said the war has tripled logistics costs for oilfield contractors.

04 The trend behind it

This is a continuation, not a new phase. The oil fund has gained 9.15% in 20 sessions and 25.6% in 60, and stands 139.0% above its 16 December 2025 low of 66.17.

The peak of 169.53 on 23 October marked the top so far, and the past week has been a pullback within an uptrend.

Our own price history since 2007 offers a cautionary note. After 89 earlier rises of this size in 20 sessions, the fund was higher 20 sessions later in 46 cases, or 52%, with a median change of +0.5% and a worst case of -24.0%. History is not a forecast, but it shows that a rally this large is close to a coin toss from here.

Wider markets are nervous. The VIX, Wall Street’s fear gauge, closed at 20.83 after rising 18.89% in five sessions, while the S&P 500 rose 0.36% on the day but is down 1.99% over five sessions.

05 What it means for Latin America

Producers gain most. Ecopetrol is still 9.4% below its 15 September high of 18.26, so Colombia’s budget, which leans on oil exports, has room for more recovery.

Argentina is the clearest long-term winner. Its Vaca Muerta shale field is reported to have passed 550,000 barrels a day, and YPF holds six of the ten areas with the largest planned investment there this year.

The risk for everyone is that new supply eventually caps prices. Brazil, Guyana and Argentina together are expected to add roughly 750,000 to 1 million barrels a day of non-OPEC+ output in 2026, which is a counterweight to the war premium.

Importers and travellers feel the other side. Diesel is the scarce product, so freight, farming and bus fares are the first to rise in fuel-importing countries.

06 The names to watch

Petrobras is the oddity, down 11.43% in 20 sessions and 19.4% below its 23 October high of 26.16, though still 15.0% higher over 60 sessions. It has also signed a cooperation agreement with Mexico’s Pemex on a so-called Mexican pre-salt, covering exploration, refining and petrochemicals, though we could not confirm its date.

Venezuela is the wildcard. One Brazilian oil company is reportedly accelerating its push there, betting that looser US sanctions will open the market, but the report does not name it and we have not verified it.

Big Oil is choosing caution. Europe’s six largest majors booked a collective 38 billion dollars of profit in the July-to-September quarter, yet they are putting debt reduction ahead of new spending, which limits how fast new supply can arrive.

07 What would end it

Resistance is the 23 October peak of 169.53, and the next support is the round 150 area, then the 66.17 December low far below. A close above the peak would signal a new leg higher.

The next dated event is the official US weekly inventory report from the Energy Information Administration on Wednesday 4 November at 15:30 Lisbon time, which will show the stocks change for the week to 30 October (previous: a fall of 1.892 million barrels).

The one thing that would change the picture is a lasting end to the Iran war and a restart of Middle East refining. Until then, tight fuel supplies make a sustained collapse in prices unlikely, though pullbacks like the 3.48% dip are normal.

08 What to watch

US inventories: The official weekly report on 4 November will show whether stocks are still falling after the previous fall of 1.892 million barrels.

The official weekly report on 4 November will show whether stocks are still falling after the previous fall of 1.892 million barrels. Iran war: Any ceasefire or restart of Middle East refining would ease the fuel shortage that props up prices.

Any ceasefire or restart of Middle East refining would ease the fuel shortage that props up prices. The 169.53 peak: A close above it would signal a new leg higher; failure would point to a range.

A close above it would signal a new leg higher; failure would point to a range. Petrobras versus Ecopetrol: A gap between a falling Petrobras and a rising Ecopetrol shows markets are pricing politics and payouts, not just crude.

What Prediction Markets Say

Polymarket, a prediction market where users bet real money, shows a 78.0% chance that WTI crude, the US oil benchmark, touches US$100 a barrel at some point in November. It prices 52.0% for US$105, 35.0% for US$110 and 61.5% for a dip to US$90, with US$876,098 traded. Prices were read at 7:55 p.m. ET on 3 November 2026. These are bets, not forecasts.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why did oil rise on Tuesday, November 3, 2026?

The oil-tracking fund rose 0.83%, helped by a global fuel shortage caused by the Iran war and falling US crude stocks. We rate that explanation medium-confidence.

Is the oil price near a record?

The fund is 6.7% below its 23 October high of 169.53 and 139.0% above its December 2025 low of 66.17.

Who gains in Latin America?

Producers such as Colombia’s Ecopetrol and Argentina’s YPF gain most, while fuel importers face higher diesel costs.

Does history say oil will keep rising?

After 89 similar rises, the fund was higher 20 sessions later in 46 cases, or 52%, with a median change of +0.5%. That is history, not a forecast.

Today’s Focus The world’s steel-producer shares have slid to their lowest close in at least three months, and Latin America’s names are feeling it unevenly. The steel-producers ETF (a fund holding steelmakers’ shares) fell -1.35% on Tuesday, 3 November 2026, while the broad US stock market rose. The common thread is a flood of cheap Chinese steel and the trade walls governments are building against it. Those walls help some companies more than others, and that is why the stocks diverged. Steel stocks are falling for industry reasons, not because markets panicked, and the gap between winners and losers depends on who trade protection actually shields.

01 The session in one read

Steel had a poor Tuesday, 3 November 2026, in an otherwise decent market. The steel-producers ETF closed at its lowest in at least three months, and it is 5.57% lower than it was 20 sessions ago.

The fall now stretches back further. Over 60 sessions the fund is down 9.9%, so this is a slow grind lower rather than one bad day.

For a foreign investor the lesson is that steel shares are trading on trade policy and Chinese export prices more than on global growth.

Assessment — Industry stress, not a market panic MEDIUM The weight of evidence says this is a sector problem: imports, tariffs and soft demand, rather than a general sell-off. The S&P 500 rose while steel fell, which rules out a simple risk-off day. CSN’s fall is steeper than the sector’s and probably reflects company-specific worries on top of the industry ones, though we hold that view with low confidence. The variable to watch is whether Brazil’s duties start to cut Chinese volumes.

03 Why it moved

First and heaviest, cheap Chinese steel. Rolled-steel imports into Brazil rose by more than 20% to 5.7 million tons in 2025, and China supplied 64% of them (confidence: high on the direction, medium on the exact figures).

Second, the remedies are slow and unevenly shared. Brazil approved five-year anti-dumping duties (extra charges on goods sold abroad below fair prices) of US$323 to US$670 a ton on Chinese cold-rolled and galvanised steel, which took effect in February 2026.

Usiminas, a Brazilian steelmaker, filed the complaint, and analysts at Safra, a Brazilian bank, rank it the biggest winner, then CSN, then Gerdau. Gerdau has publicly asked Brazil to lift steel import tariffs to 35%, which shows it believes the current wall is not high enough.

Third, in Mexico, Ternium says US Section 232 tariffs (America’s steel import duties) still hurt its manufacturing customers there. It also cites weak Mexican demand and trade-policy uncertainty, and it has shifted sales toward the commercial market.

The usual drivers do not explain the day. The dollar index rose 0.14% to 101.89 and the US 10-year yield rose 7 basis points to 4.97%, which makes building loans dearer, but the S&P 500 still gained 0.36%.

CSN’s collapse, 17.95% lower over five sessions, is bigger than anything in our research explains. Our best reading, at low confidence, is that investors are marking down the group’s heavily indebted, multi-business structure faster than they mark down the sector.

04 The trend behind it

The ETF has fallen for 60 sessions out of a recent peak of 113.57 on 2 June, and it now sits 30.8% above its 20 November 2025 low of 75.82. The pattern is a continuation of a summer-to-autumn decline, not a fresh shock.

Gerdau fell 8.98% in 20 sessions after touching 5.24 on 20 October, yet it remains 42.9% above its 20 March low of 3.26. CSN has done worse, dropping 66.3% from its January peak of 2.12 to a fresh 12-month low.

05 What it means for Latin America

For Brazil, steel is a test of how far protection can go. Duties help domestic mills such as Usiminas, but they raise costs for the carmakers and builders who buy steel, and Gerdau’s 35% request would push that further.

For Mexico, the issue is the border. Ternium sells into a market tied to US factories, and it says progress on removing Section 232 tariffs would help it. Mexico wants those duties lifted, while Washington wants Mexico to do more against unfair trade.

Ternium keeps investing, with capital spending of US$398 million in the third quarter, and its new slab mill in Pesquería is on plan. For Ternium shareholders the guide is steady, not strong: it expects fourth-quarter adjusted EBITDA (operating profit before interest, tax and write-downs) broadly in line with the third.

06 The names to watch

CSN is the stress point: its fall to a 12-month low makes it the name where the next piece of news matters most. Our own history gives a sober guide: after 7 earlier falls this large, it was higher 20 sessions later in only 3, with a median of -2.8% and a worst case of -45.5%.

The wider fund tells a calmer story. After 112 earlier 20-session drops of this size, it was higher 20 sessions later in 59 cases (53%), with a median of +1.0% and a worst case of -44.3%. History is not a forecast, but it says deep falls often pause and sometimes run on.

Gerdau, with 101 earlier cases at 50% higher and a median of +0.2%, is a coin toss on that evidence. Usiminas, the biggest winner of the duties on Safra’s reading, has no verified price here, so we keep it as a name to follow rather than a call.

07 What would end it

The nearest levels are simple. For the ETF, 100 is the round number to regain, and the 2 June peak at 113.57 is far above. For support, there is little until the November 2025 low of 75.82, and for Gerdau the 20 October high of 5.24 is the line to retake.

For CSN, the 12-month low is today’s close, so there is no floor on the chart. A stop in the fall would need a hold above that level over several sessions.

We found no fixed date for the next catalyst. Quarterly results from Gerdau, CSN and Usiminas, and any change to Section 232, are the events that would shift the picture; so would evidence that Chinese imports into Brazil are shrinking.

08 What to watch

Chinese imports into Brazil: Whether the duties from February 2026 cut Chinese volumes below the 5.7 million tons of rolled steel seen in 2025.

Whether the duties from February 2026 cut Chinese volumes below the 5.7 million tons of rolled steel seen in 2025. Gerdau’s tariff request: Any decision on its call for a 35% import tariff, which would lift domestic mills and raise costs for buyers.

Any decision on its call for a 35% import tariff, which would lift domestic mills and raise costs for buyers. US Section 232 tariffs: Ternium says removal would help, and Mexico is pressing for it.

Ternium says removal would help, and Mexico is pressing for it. CSN’s 12-month low: Whether the New York shares can hold above today’s close or break further.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why did steel stocks fall on Tuesday, 3 November 2026?

The steel-producers ETF fell -1.35% mainly on pressure from cheap Chinese steel, tariff uncertainty and soft demand, since the S&P 500 rose that day.

Who benefits from Brazil’s anti-dumping duties?

Safra’s analysis ranks Usiminas first, then CSN, then Gerdau, as Usiminas filed the complaint behind the duties.

What is Ternium’s outlook?

It expects fourth-quarter adjusted EBITDA broadly in line with the third, with lower seasonal shipments offset by a slightly higher margin per ton.

Does history say steel will rebound?

After 112 earlier falls of similar size the fund was higher 20 sessions later in 53% of cases, with a median of +1.0%, but this is history, not a forecast.

Key Facts Zinc’s Latin American miners stalled on Tuesday, November 3, 2026: Nexa Resources closed unchanged and Buenaventura slipped, both still far below their 12-month peaks.

Nexa Resources closed unchanged and Buenaventura slipped, both still far below their 12-month peaks. Nexa sits 31.6% below its 6 May high of 16.72, yet it is still 117.7% above its 12-month low of 5.25, set on 7 November 2025.

yet it is still 117.7% above its 12-month low of 5.25, set on 7 November 2025. Buenaventura is 38.7% below its 27 February high of 43.67, and 26.5% above its low of 21.16 from 4 November 2025.

and 26.5% above its low of 21.16 from 4 November 2025. The zinc market is tight rather than weak: the industry study group forecasts a 2026 shortfall of 88,000 tonnes, flipping to a 25,000-tonne surplus in 2027.

the industry study group forecasts a 2026 shortfall of 88,000 tonnes, flipping to a 25,000-tonne surplus in 2027. Nexa’s third quarter was mixed: adjusted EBITDA, a measure of operating profit, rose 62% year on year to US$301m, yet the company still booked a US$47m net loss.

adjusted EBITDA, a measure of operating profit, rose 62% year on year to US$301m, yet the company still booked a US$47m net loss. Wider markets are jittery: the VIX fear gauge has risen 18.89% in five sessions, while the gold-tracking fund GLD has fallen 3.50%.

Today’s Focus Zinc, the grey metal that coats steel to stop it rusting, is in short supply this year, but the shares of the companies that dig it up are not rewarding that. Nexa Resources, the Peruvian and Brazilian zinc miner, finished Tuesday, November 3, 2026 flat, and Buenaventura, Peru’s big precious-metals producer, edged lower. Both are down sharply over three months, with Nexa off 23.1% over 60 sessions and Buenaventura off 22.6% over the same stretch. The pattern says investors are trading the whole metals complex, not zinc alone. A broad retreat in gold and a nervy stock market pulled miners down together. Against that, zinc’s own fundamentals, a forecast deficit and a recovering Nexa smelter, stayed supportive. Think of the two miners as a thermometer for zinc and its neighbours. On Tuesday, November 3, 2026 the thermometer barely moved: Nexa was unchanged at +0.00% and Buenaventura eased -0.34%.

Quiet days after hard falls often mean sellers are tiring, not that buyers have returned. Nexa has fallen 4.35% over five sessions, and Buenaventura 6.86%, so a flat close is a pause in a decline.

Assessment — Tight zinc, tired miners MEDIUM The best-supported reading is that zinc’s supply shortage is real but already known, while the miners’ shares are following gold and general risk appetite lower, a view we hold with medium confidence because we could not verify zinc’s own close for the session. 03 Why it moved

First cause, and the heaviest: gold and the wider metals complex. The gold-tracking fund GLD fell 0.66% on the session, extending a slide that headlines describe as nearly 30% below gold’s all-time high, and copper has been hovering near a two-and-a-half-month low. Miners trade as a basket, so Buenaventura felt this most.

Second cause: a firmer financial backdrop. The US dollar index edged up 0.14% to 101.89, and the US 10-year Treasury yield rose 7 basis points to 4.97%; a stronger dollar and higher yields make commodities costlier for foreign buyers and make holding metal less attractive. The S&P 500 rose 0.36% to 7,569, and the VIX eased 1.51% to 20.83, yet that fear gauge is still up sharply over five sessions, so caution lingers.

The conflicting signal is zinc itself. The International Lead and Zinc Study Group, the industry’s statistics body, said on 19 October 2026 that the refined zinc market would run a deficit of 88,000 tonnes this year, against 19,000 tonnes forecast in April. A shortage should support prices, yet it is already in expectations, and we rate our reading, that macro selling outweighed zinc strength, at medium confidence.

04 The trend behind it

Nexa’s shares peaked on 6 May at 16.72 and have since lost almost a third of that value, with the last two sessions marginally positive after a longer decline. Buenaventura’s peak came earlier, on 27 February at 43.67, so its slide is older and deeper.

This looks like a continuation, not a new phase. Both stocks remain well above their November 2025 lows, which shows the year’s rally was large and the present drop is a giveback inside it.

05 What it means for Latin America

Peru is the most exposed: both companies are listed with Peruvian operations, and Nexa’s Cajamarquilla smelter, which recovered from a May fire, lifted smelting output 28% on the quarter to 159 kt. Brazil benefits too, as Nexa’s Aripuanã mine raised utilisation to 84% from 71%.

For governments, lower mining shares matter less than metal prices, but Peru, Bolivia and Mexico all lean on mineral exports for tax and foreign-currency earnings. For a traveller or investor, the lesson is that a weaker metals tide can lower local mining stocks without any change in a mine’s output.

06 The names to watch

Nexa is the cleanest zinc proxy. Its third-quarter mined zinc output was 85 kt, up 7% on the quarter, and it lifted 2026 capital spending guidance 10% to US$420m, a sign management expects to keep producing.

History offers a sober note, not a forecast. After earlier falls this large over 20 sessions, Nexa was higher 20 sessions later in 27 of 53 cases, or 51%, with a median gain of 1.5% and a worst result of -54.5%; Buenaventura was higher in 27 of 50 cases, or 54%, median +1.2%, worst -33.3%.

07 What would end it

The nearest floors are the 12-month lows: 5.25 for Nexa and 21.16 for Buenaventura, both far away. The nearest ceilings are their 12-month highs of 16.72 and 43.67, so a stabilisation would first show up as the gold fund holding steady and the dollar index slipping back.

The next dated clue is the study group’s following forecast, which has come in April and October. Does the slide stop? Only when gold stops falling or zinc’s deficit starts moving the shares more than the macro tape does.

What would end or confirm the stall: a rebound in the gold fund GLD, which fell 3.50% over five sessions, or a dip in the dollar index from 101.89 would help miners recover, while a 10-year Treasury yield pushing above 4.97% would extend the pressure.

08 What to watch

Gold fund: GLD fell 3.50% in five sessions; a steady turn would help Buenaventura first.

GLD fell 3.50% in five sessions; a steady turn would help Buenaventura first. US dollar and yields: The dollar index at 101.89 and the 10-year at 4.97% set the tone for all metals.

The dollar index at 101.89 and the 10-year at 4.97% set the tone for all metals. Zinc inventories: Falling warehouse stocks would confirm the deficit the study group forecasts.

Falling warehouse stocks would confirm the deficit the study group forecasts. Nexa smelting: Cajamarquilla’s recovery decides whether smelting profits keep rising.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why did zinc miners stall on Tuesday, November 3, 2026?

Gold and wider metals weakness, plus a firmer dollar and higher bond yields, outweighed support from a tight zinc market.

Is zinc in short supply?

Yes; the industry study group forecasts a 2026 deficit of 88,000 tonnes before a 25,000-tonne surplus in 2027.

Which listed companies track zinc in Latin America?

Nexa Resources, with mines and smelters in Peru and Brazil, is the clearest, while Buenaventura leans more on gold and silver.

Does history say the shares will rebound?

After comparable falls, Nexa rose over the next 20 sessions about half the time, so history is not a forecast.

Key Facts Vale hit a 12-month low: its New York shares closed at US$10.98 on Tuesday, November 3, 2026, after a move of -3.17%, the lowest close in at least 12 months.

its New York shares closed at US$10.98 on Tuesday, November 3, 2026, after a move of -3.17%, the lowest close in at least 12 months. the Anglo-Australian rival closed at US$81.62, a move of -1.34%, its lowest close in at least six months. A smaller Brazilian producer fell harder: CSN Mineração, an iron ore producer, dropped 5.14% to R$4.61 on its first session after the 2 November holiday.

CSN Mineração, an iron ore producer, dropped 5.14% to R$4.61 on its first session after the 2 November holiday. The cause is Chinese steel and weak results: Vale’s third-quarter output fell 6% from a year earlier and its realised price fell 10%, while China’s steel sector keeps struggling.

Today’s Focus Iron ore, the rock that becomes steel, is in a long, grinding decline, and Vale is the clearest way to see it. Its New York shares closed on Tuesday, November 3, 2026 at their lowest level in at least 12 months. The main cause is China, which makes about half the world’s steel and buys most of the world’s seaborne iron ore. Its factories are producing less steel: official data show crude steel output down 2.9% in the first nine months of 2026. Vale’s own third-quarter report added to the gloom. Profit per share came in at US$0.29 against US$0.63 a year earlier, and management said iron ore output would land at the low end of its guidance. 03 Why it moved

First and heaviest is Chinese steel. Official data show crude steel output down 2.9% in the first nine months of the year, and Vale itself called China’s domestic market ‘challenging’ on its results call.

Chinese mills are surviving by exporting about 130 million tonnes of steel, which keeps global output ‘relatively stable’ in Vale’s words but does not add demand for new ore. The MMI daily iron ore report called the price support ‘fragile’, said the earlier recovery ‘did not persist’, and advised a ‘cautious, range bound view’.

Second is Vale’s own report. Production fell 6% from a year earlier, the realised price fell 10%, and core earnings of US$3.5bn were down 20%.

The usual drivers give mixed signals. The US dollar index edged up to 101.89 and the 10-year Treasury yield rose 7 basis points to 4.97%, which is a mild headwind for commodities, yet the S&P 500 rose 0.36% to 7,569, so this was not a general retreat from risk.

Our confidence is medium: the Chinese steel story is well supported, but we found no single trigger for Tuesday itself.

04 The trend behind it

Vale is down 26.3% over 60 sessions and sits 38.4% below its 12-month peak, set on 20 April. The 20-session slide of 22.02% is the sharper leg, so the fall is accelerating.

Rio Tinto is 27.2% below its 12-month high of 112.04, set on 13 May, though it remains 20.2% above its low of November 2025. This looks like a continuation of a downtrend, not a new phase.

Our own history since 2007 offers a sober reference. After 23 earlier falls in Vale of this size in 20 sessions, the shares were higher 20 sessions later in 13 cases (57%), the median change was +0.5% and the worst was a further loss of 43.4%; history is not a forecast.

05 What it means for Latin America

Brazil feels this first. Iron ore is among its largest exports, so a lower price trims export earnings, tax receipts and the flow of dollars that supports the real.

Vale is the country’s most important listed exporter, and a weaker share price hurts Brazilian pension funds and investors who hold it. Peru, Chile and Mexico are less exposed, as they sell copper, silver and manufactured goods, but they share the China demand risk.

Brazilian steelmakers and builders that buy iron ore or steel can gain from cheaper inputs, although weak Chinese exports of steel can also flood their home markets.

06 The names to watch

Vale is the benchmark: its realised price of US$85.1 a tonne in the third quarter shows how much margin a further drop would remove. Rio Tinto, down 4.81% over five sessions, is the global peer to compare against.

CSN Mineração has swung between a 12-month low of 4.08 on 19 May and its September high, and is 19.8% lower over 60 sessions. Tuesday’s fall matters if it breaks toward that low.

07 What would end it

The chart gives no support below Tuesday’s close, because it is the 12-month low, so the next reference is the round number of US$10. The first real resistance is far above, at the 17.82 April peak, which means any rebound would first be tested on its way up.

The one thing that would change the picture is Chinese mills buying again, which the MMI report says depends on orders, margins and mill stocks. Watch China’s next monthly steel output and iron ore import figures, and any new stimulus for property and infrastructure.

Does it stop? Not yet; with sellers in control and no confirmed turn in Chinese demand, a pause is more likely than a rebound.

08 What to watch

China steel output: Monthly output has fallen 2.9% this year; a turn higher would be the first real support for ore.

Monthly output has fallen 2.9% this year; a turn higher would be the first real support for ore. Chinese mill restocking: Orders, margins and mill stocks decide whether buyers return to the market.

Orders, margins and mill stocks decide whether buyers return to the market. Vale’s production: Management guided to the low end of its range, so any further cut would deepen the gloom.

Management guided to the low end of its range, so any further cut would deepen the gloom. The US$10 level: A close below this round number on Vale’s New York shares would extend the slide to new territory.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why does Vale matter for iron ore?

Vale is the world’s number two iron ore exporter, so its share price is a quick read on the iron ore market.

Why is iron ore falling?

Chinese steel output is down 2.9% this year, and mills are not buying enough ore to lift prices.

How does this affect Brazil?

Lower prices cut export earnings and tax revenue, and weigh on the real and on Vale’s shareholders.

Is this the bottom?

Not confirmed: Vale just closed at a 12-month low, and earlier falls this large led to higher prices 20 sessions later 57% of the time.

Albemarle ended at US$90.19 (-0.41%) and SQM at US$53.71 (-1.76%) on Tuesday, November 3, 2026. Albemarle is down 58.2% from its 16 April peak. That peak was 215.62, so the US producer has lost well over half its value in under seven months.

That peak was 215.62, so the US producer has lost well over half its value in under seven months. SQM, Chile’s lithium giant, is 43.6% below its 12-month high of 95.31. It is still 16.5% above its 12-month low of 46.10, so it has more cushion than its American rival.

It is still 16.5% above its 12-month low of 46.10, so it has more cushion than its American rival. The lithium miners fund held steady while the two big names fell. The fund closed at US$60.10, up 0.08%, but it is down 19.6% over 60 sessions.

The fund closed at US$60.10, up 0.08%, but it is down 19.6% over 60 sessions. Albemarle has now fallen five sessions in a row. It is only 2.0% above its 12-month low of 88.45, set on 4 November 2025.

It is only 2.0% above its 12-month low of 88.45, set on 4 November 2025. Albemarle reports third-quarter results on Wednesday 4 November, with its call on Thursday 5 November. The company has already warned of lower sales, profit and margins than in the second quarter.

Today’s Focus Lithium shares are sliding towards the bottom of their year-long range. On Tuesday, November 3, 2026, Albemarle of the United States and SQM of Chile both closed at their lowest in at least six months. The main reason is price. Albemarle has told investors that lower lithium prices and lower volumes will drag on its third-quarter results, and the market is marking the shares down before the numbers arrive. A second cause is a nervous market. The VIX, Wall Street’s fear gauge, has climbed 18.89% in five sessions, and investors tend to sell the riskiest, most price-sensitive stocks first. 03 Why it moved

First and heaviest: weaker lithium prices feeding into earnings. In August Albemarle said it expects lower volumes and lower prices in the third quarter, with higher-cost ore working through its results after a lag of about four months.

The evidence is in the shares. Albemarle is down 31.3% over 60 sessions and SQM is down 26.3% over the same period.

Second: a jittery market. The S&P 500 rose 0.36% on the day, yet it is down 1.99% over five sessions, and the VIX is at 20.83. Lithium miners usually fall further than the broad market in such weeks.

The usual drivers did not push hard. The dollar index edged up 0.14% to 101.89, and the 10-year US Treasury yield rose seven basis points to 4.97%, so they explain little of the fall.

Third: positioning before the results. Albemarle reports on Wednesday 4 November, and investors often trim shares before a quarter they expect to be weak. We rate this explanation as medium confidence, because we found no company or government news dated November 3 itself.

04 The trend behind it

This is a continuation, not a new phase. Both shares peaked on 16 April and have lost ground in a steady grind since, with the lithium miners fund down 34.4% from its 12-month high of 91.62 on 11 May.

Over 20 sessions the fund is down 15.44%, Albemarle 15.20% and SQM 18.83%. Albemarle’s five straight down days show sellers are still in charge.

Our own price history offers a counterweight. Since 2010, in 13 earlier cases where the lithium fund fell this far in 20 sessions, it was higher 20 sessions later in 11 of them (85%), with a median gain of 9.6% and a worst case of a further 9.4% fall.

Albemarle’s record is weaker: higher in 24 of 43 cases (56%), median 1.2%, worst 29.7% lower. SQM was higher in 25 of 35 (71%), median 8.8%, worst 27.5% lower. History is not a forecast.

05 What it means for Latin America

Chile feels this most. SQM is its flagship lithium company, and a share price 43.6% below its April high reflects lower expected profits from the Atacama salt flat, one of the richest lithium deposits in the world.

Argentina and Bolivia sit alongside Chile in the Lithium Triangle, the region that holds much of the world’s known lithium. Argentina’s newer projects and Bolivia’s untested deposits depend on prices staying high enough to justify the capital, and a long slump slows investment.

For Chilean state revenue and the peso, lithium is a smaller story than copper. Still, an SQM executive had expected carbonate prices of US$15 to US$18 a kilogram in 2026, and a market below that range would trim royalties and export income.

06 The names to watch

Albemarle is the bellwether. It sold 65,000 tonnes of lithium carbonate equivalent (the industry’s standard unit) in the second quarter at about US$20 a kilogram, so the third-quarter price it reports is the number to check.

SQM is the stronger operator on paper. It has raised its 2026 sales-volume growth guidance from 10% to 15%, and its 29.6% margin compares with 13.1% at Albemarle, yet its shares still fell harder than Albemarle’s on the day.

07 What would end it

The nearest floors are the 12-month lows: 88.45 for Albemarle, 46.10 for SQM and 59.25 for the fund. A close below those would open fresh lows and confirm sellers still control the trend.

The nearest ceiling is far away, at 91.62 for the fund, so the early test is simply holding the floor. The one date that matters is Albemarle’s third-quarter report on Wednesday 4 November, with its call the next day.

A realised price above its own forecast, or a stronger outlook for electric-vehicle battery orders, would end the slide. Until then, the honest answer is that the slide has not yet shown it is stopping.

What would end or confirm the slide: Albemarle reports on Wednesday 4 November, and a close below its 12-month low of 88.45 would extend the fall, while a close back above that level after the results would suggest the worst is priced in.

08 What to watch

Albemarle results: Due on Wednesday 4 November, call on 5 November: the realised lithium price, volumes and fourth-quarter guidance.

Due on Wednesday 4 November, call on 5 November: the realised lithium price, volumes and fourth-quarter guidance. The 12-month lows: Albemarle at 88.45, SQM at 46.10 and the fund at 59.25; a close below any of them would extend the slide.

Albemarle at 88.45, SQM at 46.10 and the fund at 59.25; a close below any of them would extend the slide. Market fear: The VIX at 20.83 and the S&P 500 after its 1.99% five-session fall, since miners fall hardest in risk-off weeks.

The VIX at 20.83 and the S&P 500 after its 1.99% five-session fall, since miners fall hardest in risk-off weeks. SQM guidance: Whether its 15% sales-volume growth target holds if prices stay soft.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why did lithium stocks fall on Tuesday, November 3, 2026?

Albemarle fell -0.41% and SQM -1.76%, mainly on fears of lower lithium prices and weaker profits. A risk-averse market added to the pressure.

Is the LIT fund the price of lithium?

No. LIT is an exchange-traded fund holding lithium-mining shares, so it tracks company stocks, not the metal itself.

Is this good or bad for Chile?

It is bad for sentiment and for SQM’s value, because lithium is one of Chile’s key exports. Copper still matters more to the national budget.

Could the shares bounce?

Our history shows the lithium fund was higher 20 sessions later in 11 of 13 comparable cases, but this is not a forecast. Albemarle’s results on 4 November are the nearest test.

Key Facts Miners at three-month lows: Southern Copper and Freeport-McMoRan both posted their lowest close in at least three months on Tuesday, 3 November 2026, after falling 3.27% and 1.91% respectively.

Southern Copper and Freeport-McMoRan both posted their lowest close in at least three months on Tuesday, 3 November 2026, after falling 3.27% and 1.91% respectively. Copper slipped again: the CPER fund, which tracks copper futures rather than the physical metal, fell 2.18% to US$38.51.

the CPER fund, which tracks copper futures rather than the physical metal, fell 2.18% to US$38.51. Shares fell harder than the metal: Southern Copper is 20.2% below its 25 August peak, and Freeport is 22.7% below the same peak.

Southern Copper is 20.2% below its 25 August peak, and Freeport is 22.7% below the same peak. Markets turned nervous: the VIX fear gauge is up 18.89% in five sessions, while gold also fell 0.66%, so investors sold both metals.

the VIX fear gauge is up 18.89% in five sessions, while gold also fell 0.66%, so investors sold both metals. Supply is not the problem: Chile’s state copper commission sees refined copper supply growing only 0.2% in 2026 against demand growth of 1.9%.

Chile’s state copper commission sees refined copper supply growing only 0.2% in 2026 against demand growth of 1.9%. History is mildly reassuring: after earlier falls this large, Southern Copper was higher 20 sessions later in 66% of cases, though the worst outcome was a further 43.4% drop.

Today’s Focus Copper miners sold off on Tuesday, 3 November 2026, and two of the biggest listed names ended at their lowest close in at least three months. Southern Copper closed at US$173.49, down 3.27%. Freeport-McMoRan finished at US$61.77, down 1.91%. The metal itself was weaker too. The CPER fund, which holds copper futures (contracts to buy or sell the metal at a set future date), fell 2.18% to US$38.51, and is 7.0% below its 22 September high. The best-supported reading is a broad retreat from risk, not a collapse in copper demand. Investors are demanding high returns from safe bonds, stocks are wobbling and the fear gauge has jumped, so they sell cyclical assets (those that rise and fall with the economy) first. 03 Why it moved

First, and heaviest, was a retreat from risk. The VIX, Wall Street’s fear gauge, is up 18.89% in five sessions, and the S&P 500 is down 1.99% over the same stretch. Gold, usually a refuge, also fell 0.66% on the day, which suggests investors were selling whatever could be sold, not hiding in metals.

Second, borrowing costs stayed high. The US 10-year Treasury yield rose 7 basis points (hundredths of a percentage point) to 4.97%, and the dollar index edged up 0.14% to 101.89. A stronger dollar makes copper dearer for buyers in other currencies, and high yields make it costlier to finance mines and factories.

Third, China, which buys 57.6% of the world’s copper according to Chile’s state copper commission, Cochilco, still has a weak property sector. Cochilco expects Chinese demand to grow just 2.7% this year, so there is little room for disappointment.

The usual drivers did not fully explain the day, since the dollar and yields moved only slightly. We put MEDIUM confidence on risk aversion as the main cause, because the five-day swings in fear and equities are large, and LOW-to-MEDIUM on any China-specific trigger, which we could not confirm.

04 The trend behind it

Copper has been drifting down since its 12-month high of 41.43 on 22 September, and is down 3.80% over 20 sessions. It remains 26.1% above its 12-month low of 30.53, set a year ago on 4 November 2025.

The miners peaked later and have fallen further. Southern Copper is 15.06% lower over 20 sessions and Freeport 14.87% lower. This looks like a continuation of an autumn correction, not a new phase, though three-month lows raise the stakes.

Our own history gives a rare comparison. After earlier falls this large, Southern Copper was higher 20 sessions later in 23 of 35 cases, or 66%, with a median gain of 4.4% and a worst case of minus 43.4%. Freeport was higher in 30 of 57 cases, or 53%, with a median gain of 1.5% and a worst case of minus 41.7%. History is not a forecast.

05 What it means for Latin America

Chile and Peru together mine more copper than anyone else, and mining taxes and royalties feed their budgets directly. Cochilco expects Chile’s output to fall 2.6% to 5.27 million tonnes in 2026, because of lower ore grades (less metal in each tonne of rock), maintenance and slow project start-ups. Lower output at a lower price is a double squeeze on Chilean revenue.

Southern Copper’s mines are in Peru and Mexico, so its fall is felt in Lima and Mexico City, where the company is a major taxpayer and employer. Freeport also operates in Chile and Peru, though much of its output is elsewhere.

For a traveller or saver in the region, the effect is indirect. Weaker copper tends to soften the Chilean peso and Peruvian sol, which makes imports pricier and holidays abroad dearer.

06 The names to watch

Southern Copper has the purest exposure, with Peru and Mexico as its home bases. Its 12-month low of 115.21 and high of 217.40 show how wide the swings can be, and the shares are now 50.6% above that low.

Freeport trades at 59.8% above its 12-month low of 38.65, but 22.7% below its high of 79.91. Both stocks should react to any change in the dollar, yields or Chinese data before the metal does.

07 What would end it

The fund’s nearest support is the recent run of closes near 38.51, then the 12-month low of 30.53 far below. Resistance is the 22 September peak of 41.43, which the fund would need to retake to show that the decline is over.

The next catalysts are China’s monthly trade and industrial output data, due in the coming days, and Cochilco’s next quarterly copper update, after its August report. The thing that would change the picture is a retreat in the 10-year yield from 4.97% together with calmer stock markets.

The honest answer is that the decline can pause quickly because supply is tight, with Cochilco expecting refined copper supply to grow only 0.2% against demand growth of 1.9%. It will not reverse while fear is rising.

08 What to watch

US yields: The 10-year Treasury yield at 4.97% is the main weight on miners. A clear drop would ease pressure on the shares.

The 10-year Treasury yield at 4.97% is the main weight on miners. A clear drop would ease pressure on the shares. China demand: China buys 57.6% of the world’s copper, so its trade and factory data matter more than anything else.

China buys 57.6% of the world’s copper, so its trade and factory data matter more than anything else. Chile and Peru output: Cochilco expects Chile’s 2026 output to fall 2.6%, so mine news from either country can move prices.

Cochilco expects Chile’s 2026 output to fall 2.6%, so mine news from either country can move prices. Fear gauge: The VIX at 20.83 is up 18.89% in five sessions. A calmer reading would help the miners recover.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why did copper fall on Tuesday, 3 November 2026?

The best-supported reading is a broad retreat from risk. The fear gauge is up sharply, stocks are lower over five sessions, and US borrowing costs and the dollar edged up. Our confidence is medium.

Is CPER the price of copper?

No. CPER is a fund that holds copper futures, which are contracts for future delivery, so it can differ from the price of the physical metal.

Why are copper miners falling faster than copper?

Miners carry fixed costs and debt, so small price changes swing profits sharply. Investors also sell shares first when they fear a slowdown.

Does this hurt Chile and Peru?

Yes, through lower mining tax revenue and weaker currencies, although the effect depends on how long prices stay down. Chile’s output is also forecast to fall 2.6% this year.

Think of gold as a very expensive savings account that pays no interest. When government bonds yield 4.97%, the case for holding it weakens, and that is the pressure it met on Tuesday, November 3, 2026.

Gold slipped -0.65% and closed under US$4,000 for the second day running. The largest gold-backed fund, GLD, closed at 359.26, down 0.66%, so ordinary investors moved with the metal.

Silver’s last verified spot close, on Monday, was US$50.63, up 3.18% from Friday’s low. On Tuesday the SLV silver fund lost 1.60%, so the bounce did not last. Silver is a smaller, jumpier market, and it often swings sharply after a heavy fall.

Assessment — Bruised bull market, not a broken one MEDIUM Gold is behaving like a market that is still digesting a huge January surge, with high bond yields and a slightly firmer dollar blocking any sustained rebound. Silver’s earlier bounce faded on Tuesday, when the SLV fund fell 1.60%, and the metal is still down 23.1% over 60 sessions. The variable to watch is the 10-year Treasury yield: a clear move back below 4.97% would ease the pressure on both metals.

03 Why it moved

First and heaviest is the cost of holding metal. The 10-year Treasury yield rose 7 basis points to 4.97%, and the dollar index rose 0.14% to 101.89, so gold lost on both counts.

Second is demand fatigue at these prices. Specialist reporting this week points to India, a giant buyer of gold jewellery, heading for a six-year low in demand because of the price rise, and the World Gold Council’s third-quarter demand review is on readers’ desks.

The conflicting signal is silver’s earlier bounce. Spot silver rose 3.18% from 30 October to 2 November, but the SLV fund’s 1.60% fall on Tuesday suggests the bargain-hunting after a 16.90% fall in 20 sessions faded.

Safe-haven demand did not rescue gold either. The VIX fear gauge fell 1.51% to 20.83 on the day, even though it is up 18.89% over five sessions, and the S&P 500 rose 0.36% to 7,569.

Our confidence is medium: yields and the dollar explain gold well, while the silver bounce is our best reading of the evidence.

04 The trend behind it

Gold peaked at 5,513 on 28 January and has since lost 28.9%. Its 12-month low is 3,875, set on 30 October, and Tuesday’s close is 1.2% above that.

This is a continuation, not a new phase: the metal is down 10.3% over 60 sessions and has fallen 5.85% over the last 20. Silver is the more dramatic case, down 55.8% from its 114.59 peak on the same January day.

RT’s own price history since 2007 gives some perspective. Gold has fallen at least this much in 20 sessions on 49 earlier occasions and was higher 20 sessions later in 28 of them, or 57%, with a median gain of 1.6% and a worst case of a 12.9% further fall.

Silver’s record is stronger: of 15 earlier falls this big, 11 were followed by a higher price 20 sessions later, or 73%, with a median gain of 5.1% and a worst case of 19.9% lower. History is not a forecast.

05 What it means for Latin America

Mexico was the world’s top silver producer in 2025 with 172.9 million ounces, about a fifth of global supply. Peru was second with 130 million ounces and China third with 113 million, according to the Silver Institute’s World Silver Survey 2026.

Mexican output fell 5%, its third annual decline in a row, blamed on operational disruption, government policy and falling ore grades. A weak price makes those problems harder to fix.

Peru’s output rose 7%, mostly silver mined as a by-product of copper. With copper holding above US$14,000, Peruvian miners are cushioned in a way that pure silver producers are not.

The Silver Institute also sees a market deficit of 40.3 million ounces in 2025, widening to 46.3 million in 2026, meaning demand exceeds supply. That is the long-term argument for a recovery, though we have not checked the report itself.

06 The names to watch

In Mexico, the silver producers Fresnillo and Peñoles are the most direct way the market reads this price move. In Peru, Buenaventura and Southern Copper show the mix of silver and copper.

For ordinary savers, gold funds such as GLD track the metal’s fall almost exactly, as the 0.66% drop in GLD shows. Travellers and jewellery buyers in Latin America should note that the metal’s price in local currency also depends on the dollar, which edged up on the day.

07 What would end it

The first line to watch for gold is 3,875, the 30 October low; a close below it would open the way to fresh lows. Resistance is the round US$4,000 mark that gold failed to hold for a second day.

For silver, the recent floor is 49.07, set on 30 October, and the ceiling is far away at 114.59. The one thing that would change the picture is a sustained fall in the 10-year yield from 4.97%.

Watch the next US jobs and inflation reports and the next Federal Reserve meeting, which set the path for yields. Does the slide stop? History says rebounds are more likely than not, but nothing yet shows the turn.

World.title: Djokovic Rallies in Paris to Keep ATP Finals Hopes Alive
World.content:
Novak Djokovic came from a set down to beat Valentin Vacherot 6-7 (5), 7-5, 6-1 in the first round of the Paris Masters on Tuesday. At 39, the Serbian became the oldest player to win a match in the tournament’s history. The win keeps alive his bid to reach the ATP Finals in Turin, Italy. He now faces Australia’s Rinky Hijikata in the second round.

It was no routine opener for a seven-time Paris champion. Djokovic, seeded 10th and without a first-round bye, drew the hottest player on the indoor swing. Vacherot of Monaco won the Swiss Indoors title in Basel on Sunday, and he beat Djokovic in the Shanghai Masters semifinals last year on the way to his first Masters 1000 title.

Vacherot hit 22 aces to Djokovic’s six and took the first set in a tiebreak. He broke in the opening game of the second set to lead 2-0, putting Djokovic a set and a break down. Djokovic broke back for 2-2. Serving at 4-4, he saved three break points that would have let Vacherot serve for the match, then broke again to level at one set apiece.

Both players took medical timeouts during the second set. Djokovic received treatment on his right shoulder, and Vacherot had his left ankle strapped. The deciding set was one-sided. Djokovic broke at the start, built a 3-0 lead and closed it out 6-1 on his second match point with a two-handed backhand winner down the line. The match lasted more than two and a half hours.

Djokovic said the speed of the court made Vacherot’s serve especially hard to handle. “His second serves are faster than my first serves, so it’s very tough to play a guy in these conditions, which are really, really fast,” he said. “For a set and a half, I had difficulty reading his serve,” Djokovic added. “Even if I guessed right, it was coming with some speed.”

The stakes in Paris go beyond one match. Djokovic arrived 11th in the race to Turin after a loss in Basel last week, and the Paris Masters is the last Masters 1000 event of the season. With Jannik Sinner injured and out for the rest of the year, ninth place in the race is the final qualifying spot for the eight-player ATP Finals, which run Nov. 15-22.

By the race math, Djokovic needs to reach at least the semifinals in Paris to stay in contention, and only the title would guarantee his place. Spain’s Rafael Jódar, who opened his Paris campaign with a win over Alejandro Tabilo, holds ninth place. Djokovic played down the Turin chase after the win. Asked whether qualifying was his main motivation in Paris, he said no, and that he is taking the tournament one match at a time.

That is a shift from last month, when he called Turin his goal after winning the title in Beijing and took a wildcard into Basel to chase points. His season has swung between those highs and setbacks such as his early US Open exit against Argentina’s Mariano Navone. His path in Paris does not get easier. Australia’s Alex de Minaur, seeded eighth, could wait in the third round, and top seed Alexander Zverev, who clinched the year-end No. 1 ranking in Shanghai, is the projected quarterfinal opponent.

Hijikata reached the second round by beating Italy’s Luciano Darderi. Whether or not Djokovic reaches Turin, the Australian Open in January looms as his next major test, at the Grand Slam he has won a record 10 times.

World.title: What JetBlue’s Multi-Billion Dollar Debt Means for Costa Rica Flights
World.content:
JetBlue Airways, one of the main carriers linking Costa Rica with the United States, is under mounting financial pressure, and how that resolves could reshape low-fare service to San José and Liberia. The New York-based airline has posted operating losses for six consecutive years and reported about $8.4 billion in debt as of Sept. 30.

In late October, a group of senior creditors, including holders of about $2 billion in notes due 2031, hired investment bank PJT Partners and law firm Akin, The Wall Street Journal reported. Those notes had fallen to about 42 cents on the dollar, down from near 80 cents earlier in the month.

JetBlue shares hit an all-time low on Oct. 26, hours before the company released its third-quarter results. S&P Global Ratings cut the airline’s credit rating to CCC+ in June, deeper into junk territory, citing the surge in jet fuel prices tied to the conflict in the Middle East. Fitch made the same downgrade in April.

The quarterly report showed revenue up 21% to $2.8 billion on steady demand and higher fares. The net loss, however, widened to $257 million from $143 million a year earlier, as fuel averaged $3.91 a gallon, up 57%.

JetBlue ended September with $2.2 billion in liquidity, including an undrawn $600 million credit facility, and expects operating margins to improve year over year in the fourth quarter. It still forecasts a full-year adjusted operating margin of between negative 4.5% and negative 6.5%.

Chief Executive Joanna Geraghty said the airline remains on track to reach sustained operating profitability in 2027. She told Reuters on Oct. 27 that JetBlue is not in talks with its creditors and is not considering a debt restructuring. In an April memo to employees, she said the company was not considering bankruptcy in 2026.

Merger speculation predates the latest turmoil. In March, Semafor reported that JetBlue had hired advisers to explore a sale, with United, Alaska and Southwest among the possible partners. JetBlue said at the time that it was focused on its JetForward turnaround plan.

United is the carrier most often named as a buyer. The two airlines already cooperate through their Blue Sky partnership, which lets travelers earn and redeem points across both carriers and is set to give United slots for up to seven daily round trips at New York’s John F. Kennedy International Airport as early as 2027. JetBlue’s Fort Lauderdale base would also give a buyer a South Florida gateway to the Caribbean and Latin America.

United Chief Executive Scott Kirby has rejected the idea. At an investor conference in May, he said, “The last thing I’m going to do is buy a route network that loses money.” Asked about JetBlue on United’s Oct. 21 earnings call, he said he had nothing new to add. Any deal involving a major U.S. airline would also face antitrust review.

JetBlue has served Costa Rica since March 2009, when it launched a daily Orlando to San José flight, and added New York to Liberia service in 2012. It now connects Fort Lauderdale and New York with both San José and Liberia, and runs seasonal flights between Boston and Liberia.

The airline ended its Orlando to San José route on July 8, citing higher fuel costs and a focus on its Fort Lauderdale hub. The Costa Rica Tourism Board (ICT) confirmed that cut on May 20, less than three weeks after Spirit Airlines ceased all operations, which removed another low-fare option between the two countries.

The outcome for those routes depends on how JetBlue’s situation is resolved. A United acquisition could bring consolidation on overlapping routes, since United already flies to San José and Liberia from hubs including Newark and Houston. A larger United presence in Fort Lauderdale, however, could help preserve or expand South Florida service.

A restructuring that kept JetBlue independent would likely produce a smaller network, and seasonal leisure routes are often among the first to be cut in such cases. A combination with Alaska or Southwest would involve less overlap on the New York routes that feed Liberia. Guanacaste has the most at stake.

Hotels and tour operators in the province rely heavily on direct flights into Liberia from the U.S. Northeast, and the December-to-April high season is about to begin. For now, JetBlue continues to operate normally and has not announced further changes to its Costa Rica service. Airlines that file for Chapter 11 protection typically keep flying and honor tickets and loyalty points during the process, though that is not guaranteed.

World.title: Your 2027 Marchamo Is Lower if You Drive a Private Car
World.content:
If you drive a private car, your 2027 marchamo is probably a little cheaper than last year’s. The National Insurance Institute (INS) puts the average for a private car at ₡208,359 (about $459), down ₡9,347 (about $21), or 4.3%. INS based that average on a 2018 model. Almost all of the saving comes from vehicle property tax, which drops from ₡167,100 to ₡156,054 for that car. Property tax makes up about 59% of the marchamo, so it is the first number worth checking.

Other vehicles pay more as taxis see the steepest rise, 19.87%, to ₡341,355 (about $752). Most of that, 89%, comes from a higher fee that taxi owners pay to Aresep, the public services regulator. Buses go up 16.32%, to ₡387,185 (about $853), and motorcycles rise 3.9%, to ₡130,556 (about $288). In both cases the main driver is mandatory insurance, which rose because those vehicles are involved in so many serious crashes.

Your property tax usually falls a little each year because the Finance Ministry lowers your vehicle’s taxable value as it ages. For cars, it spreads that loss over a 15-year useful life, counted from the model year. Sometimes the ministry’s value is still higher than what your car would actually sell for. If so, you can ask for a review. Start by looking up the fiscal value on the ministry’s AutoGestión page with your plate number.

To file online, sign in to the Oficina Virtual (OVi) in TRIBU-CR, the ministry’s tax platform. Open the Expediente section and choose the review of the fiscal value for Marchamo 2027. Explain why the value is too high and attach evidence such as listings for comparable vehicles and photos of your own. Add a signed request and submit it. The ministry reviews the case and issues a decision.

Setting up an OVi account online requires a current, new-format identity card. If yours won’t register, or you prefer to do it in person, you can file at the tax office closest to your fiscal address. The ministry has not published a deadline for reviews or said how long a decision takes. The Dec. 31 payment deadline doesn’t move, so file early. Ask the tax office whether to pay the current amount while your review is pending.

Paying after Dec. 31 costs more, and each part of the marchamo carries its own charge. Unpaid property tax builds interest at 10.67% a year from the deadline. On the average private car, that is roughly ₡1,390 (about $3) for every month you are late. Mandatory insurance is charged at the Central Bank’s basic passive rate, a benchmark deposit rate, plus five percentage points, prorated by the day. Unpaid municipal parking-meter charges add 2% a month, for up to 12 months. Traffic fines included in your total carry a surcharge of 36% a year.

The bigger risk is on the road. Driving without a current marchamo after Dec. 31 can bring fines under the Traffic Law, and your vehicle can be taken off the road. You can check your total at marchamo.grupoins.com or in the INS Móvil app before you pay. For the new 10-year windshield sticker, the emailed proof of payment and the optional insurance box to watch for, see our guide to paying your 2027 marchamo.

World.title: Forbes Picks Costa Rica’s Rancho Pacifico to Beat the Crowds
World.content:
A Forbes travel feature published Oct. 26 names Rancho Pacifico, an adults-only resort in the rainforest above Uvita on Costa Rica’s southern Pacific coast, as one of its picks for travelers who want to avoid the crowds by going in the shoulder season.
