David Jones’ private equity owners are on the precipice of appointing voluntary administrators as soon as Thursday morning after talks with major landlord Scentre fell over when the department store failed to pay rent for October. Westfield owner Scentre Group, which operates 17 shopping centres in which the prestige department store is located, rejected a restructuring proposal put forward by David Jones. A counter-proposal by Scentre was subsequently rejected by David Jones’ board of directors, according to a source close to negotiations but not authorised to speak publicly. A deal to save the 188-year-old retailer David Jones may be unwinding. Louise Kennerley David Jones’ board directors are now assessing how long the 188-year-old retailer can continue trading before it appoints a voluntary administrator, which is expected to be McGrathNichol, the source said. Chief executive Erica Berchtold and board directors Phillip Cave and Simon Woodhouse, who are executive chair and managing partner at private equity firm Anchorage Capital respectively, are convening a board meeting on Wednesday evening, with a decision on voluntary administration expected to be made by Thursday morning.



Scentre Group chief executive Elliott Rusanow said David Jones had not paid rent since October and “therefore are in breach”. Related Article Fashion retail David Jones hosted Queen Elizabeth II and Dior – but nostalgia won’t save it “We have made a generous offer to Anchorage Capital Partners that would have facilitated the continuation of David Jones trading,” Rusanow said in a statement. “That offer has disappointingly been rejected by them.” David Jones’ initial restructuring deal to Scentre Group initially proposed handing over nine stores from February, three stores kept at rents of 8 per cent of sales, five stores to continue on current terms, and for $45 million in bank guarantees unlocked in exchange for equity in David Jones. “It’s a straight financial calculation as to how they can continue trading,” the source said. “Do they meet the solvency test? They need to sit down and discuss the finances.”



David Jones’ failure to pay rent for October was a key flashpoint in why talks with Scentre Group fell over, a source said. On Wednesday, David Jones’ lender Hilco said in a statement: “Hilco Capital has had no formal update on the status of negotiations.” Hilco Capital confirmed last week that it had provided additional funding to see it through December, traditionally the most crucial time of the year for department stores. “Hilco Capital has funded above the agreed facility to allow David Jones to increase stock holdings ahead of the busy Christmas trade and sales period,” a Hilco spokesperson said. But the group was also negotiating with multiple landlords to slash its rent bill and close some loss-making stores.



Related Article Retail ‘Alarming’: David Jones workers brace for job losses as store closures loom Lease and rent costs totalled $125 million for the 2025 financial year, but its debt burden also weighed heavily on the group with finance costs totalling $153 million, financial accounts released earlier this year show. Suppliers have told this publication they are already restricting the financial terms of sales to David Jones due to lengthening payment terms. They will become unsecured creditors and potentially lose significantly on any outstanding bills if the retailer goes into administration. A spokesman for David Jones confirmed that talks between the group and Scentre failed to resolve the impasse and talks had now stopped. The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. World.title: 100,000 documents stolen from ‘isolated’ NSW Health server
World.content:
Updated NationalNSWCybersecurity 100,000 documents stolen from ‘isolated’ NSW Health server Jack Gramenz Updated November 4, 2026 — 1:23pm ,first published November 4, 2026 — 9:24am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Cybercrime detectives are probing an alleged data breach as a hacker claims they accessed about 100,000 sensitive documents from a NSW Health site used to access dental vouchers before crashing its server. Cyber Security NSW said no patient data had been impacted by the “limited” breach. A spokesperson said it affected an “isolated server” within NSW Health. NSW Police Detective Superintendent Matt Craft addresses the investigations. Nine News “No patient data has been impacted at this time nor is any patient data currently at risk,” they said. NSW Police cybercrime detectives were notified about the alleged breach about 1pm on Friday after it was discovered by NSW Health on Thursday.



Health Minister Ryan Park said authorities were made aware of the issue in “the last couple of days”, but it was not made public due to the police investigation. “They wanted to determine when that goes public,” Park said. Premier Chris Minns similarly said he was informed of the breach at the weekend. “We take advice from the experts, particularly cybersecurity intelligence experts, and they tell us when to release the information. It’s always as soon as possible, but not if it’s going to compromise a successful investigation.” Minns also has “information about the motive but not to be released yet”, and he preferred not to comment on whether any demands had been made of the government.



In a screenshot of a dark web forum post – shared by Dubai-based cyber threat intelligence platform Hackmanac early on Wednesday – a user calling themselves “bytetobreach” said they had accessed “around 100,000 sensitive documents from Australia’s NSW public health systems”. “Threat actor bytetobreach claims to have compromised NSW Health systems by exploiting a misconfigured subdomain, allegedly exfiltrating approximately 70GB of data comprising 100,000 sensitive documents dating from 2020 onwards,” Hackmanac said on social media. View post on X The documents were “snatched from a misconfigured subdomain” according to the forum post. “A full intrusion into the rest of the network was prevented when I accidentally crashed the server,” bytetobreach wrote.



“No ransom is asked from anyone affiliated with the government of Australia, and I have already sent a quick notification to the [Computer Emergency Response Team].” Hackmanac noted the claim was “pending verification”. NSW Police Cyber Crime Squad Commander Detective Superintendent Matt Craft said investigators were working to “test the veracity of that information” as they sought to identify those behind the breach. “There is an international element to this investigation, though,” Craft said. “It’s obvious to us at this stage there’s people that are outside Australia. “With cybercrime, there is no borders.”



Craft said it did not appear artificial intelligence agents played any role in the breach and defended the delay in it being publicly revealed. “There was no threat or risk to public safety, and it was about making sure that we could conduct our investigation and not be hampered or tip people off to what we may be doing,” Craft said. Park said he had been advised no patient data or information had been compromised and no risk to clinical services had been identified, but noted it remained a “live investigation”. “Things can and may, and often do in this type of incident, change,” Park said. He said the government had “very robust cybersecurity systems in place” but would continue to be challenged by hackers.



“This is an evolving criminal activity that changes all the time,” Park said. “We will need to constantly look at what we’re doing in this space, how to strengthen and harden up our systems and controls.” Get alerts on breaking news as it happens.

The alleged rapist of a 14-year-old boy can be revealed as a former Sydney private school principal and a celebrated organist who mentored young musicians at churches across the state. Alan James Caradus, 70, is accused of raping the boy at Echo Point Park by the Roseville Bridge in 2023, and inciting the boy to perform a sex act on him, in what detectives believe was their first in-person meeting after first making contact on a dating app. Loading He has been behind bars since heavily armed tactical police raided his Killara home on October 22. Several electronic devices inside the property were seized in the raid, which occurred almost 12 months after detectives began their investigation. Caradus appeared via video at Hornsby Local Court on Wednesday morning speaking only to confirm his identity to the court, sitting through much of the hearing with his head in his hands.



The court heard that Caradus, who suffers from a string of health conditions including Type 2 Diabetes and ADHD, was taken to Auburn Hospital four days after his arrest following a “chest pain episode”. Caradus, through his lawyers, proposed to live under house arrest at his Killara property with his wife, who volunteered to accompany him on his regular medical appointments and to court. He also nominated to live with his brother, who also resides in Killara. Alan Caradus is accused of raping a 14-year-old boy under the Roseville Bridge. However, bail was rejected after the judge found his medical conditions could be appropriately managed while in custody. Caradus is expected to be transferred to a maximum security facility, ahead of appearing at the Downing Centre Local Court on December 16. Caradus began his career at The King’s School, Tudor House in 1979 and taught English, music and history for 12 years in the Southern Highlands, where he bought property with his wife.



He joined Sydney Grammar as deputy principal of its St Ives Prep School in 1992, spending more than 10 years at the selective private school before starting as head of Pittwater House’s junior school in 2003. Loading Caradus was at the Collaroy co-ed school for three years before moving to Balmain’s Inner City Montessori School, where he served as principal from January 2007 to April 2009. He ended his career at Cranbrook, working on a contract as junior school deputy headmaster that lasted until December 2009. No formal complaints by students, parents or staff against Caradus were made to The King’s School, Sydney Grammar, Montessori or Cranbrook, the schools confirmed to this masthead. Pittwater House didn’t address questions about Caradus’ employment. “We are mindful that there is an ongoing police investigation and the matter is before the court, therefore do not propose to comment further on the matter.”



Caradus gave greater time to the church after he retired from teaching in 2010. As a celebrated organist and former student of the NSW State Conservatorium of Music, he regularly tuned organs at churches across Sydney and mentored school-aged organists. He regularly attended music recitals at churches across Sydney, including at St Andrew’s Cathedral and St Paul’s College at Sydney University, at which he would support school-aged organists under his tutelage. Caradus worked as the organist at St Alban’s Church Lindfield before his arrest, and also supported musical performances at other Anglican churches in Sydney’s northern suburbs. He played a senior role at St Alban’s, including the selection of hymns for services and the music for weddings. St Alban’s didn’t respond to this masthead’s multiple requests for comment before publication. Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) or the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491. Control of the US senate will come down to a handful of tight races.

From Abdul El-Sayed’s headline showdown in Michigan to unexpectedly tight races in red states like Texas and Kansas, we track all the key races live as polls begin to close. Follow them live below and follow along to our full live coverage of the 2026 US midterms here. SENATE Most of the action is in the Senate races, where the Democrats need 51 seats and the Republicans need 50 (because of the tie-breaking vote owned by vice president JD Vance.) Georgia – Ossoff wins for Democrats This race is projected to be a pretty comfortable, possibly double-digit win for the Democrats. But we’re keeping our eye on it anyway because it features rising star incumbent Jon Ossoff, who’s already been linked with a run at the White House. He’s up against Republican Mike Collins.



South Carolina – polls closed This race has found the spotlight for two reasons – it’s a toss-up, and the Republican candidate Darline Graham is the sister of the late senator Lindsey Graham. She’s up against Annie Andrews in a very tight race in what’s typically a safe red state. Ohio – polls closed Ohio Democratic candidate Sherrod Brown is a former senator who chaired the Senate banking committee from 2021 to 2024, when he was a vocal critic of crypto. Ad-tracking business AdImpact says the crypto sector has spent $US68 million on defeating Brown, who is up against Republican incumbent Jon Husted in a high-stakes Senate race. Maine – polls closed



One of the last remaining moderate strongholds for Republicans, incumbent Susan Collins has historically outperformed bad polling numbers to win time and time again. But with a poor net approval rating, she faces a stiff test this time around from Troy Jackson. Texas – polls closed Democrat James Talarico, who is trying to become the first Democrat elected to the US Senate from the conservative state of Texas since 1988, has used concerns about political corruption in his campaign. He’s up against Republican candidate Ken Paxton. Kansas – polls closed A Democrat hasn’t been elected to the Senate in Kansas for 94 years – that’s something the popular pastor Adam Hamilton is hoping change. He’s looking to take down Republican Roger Marshall.



Michigan – polls closed In the swing state of Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed – a doctor, unionist and Muslim – and Republican Mike Rogers are locked in a tight race for the Senate seat being vacated by Democrat Gary Peters. Iowa – polls closed The Senate race between Republican congresswoman Ashley Hinson and Democratic state legislator Josh Turek in Iowa is something of a case study on the popularity of Trump. (Trump has, of course, asked voters to pretend he’s on the ballot these midterms, despite his weakened approval rating.)



Alaska (polls close 5pm AEDT) Surging heating fuel, electricity and grocery prices are disproportionately whacking residents of this remote, traditionally red state. Democrat Mary Peltola, who says Alaskans endure the highest healthcare costs in the country, is facing off against Republican senator Dan Sullivan, and an unaffiliated retired teacher who goes by the same name – Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. GOVERNOR Ohio This race is perhaps most notable for the bitter tone between its candidates. Republican Vivek Ramaswamy was forced to pull an attack ad, where his camp tracked down Democratic rival Amy Acton’s estranged mother Donna, who claimed her daughter to be a serial liar who couldn’t be trusted.

World.title: Old faces, new ideas: Cheika’s plan to revive the Waratahs
World.content:
SportRugby UnionWaratahs Old faces, new ideas: Cheika’s plan to revive the Waratahs Jonathan Drennan November 4, 2026 — 2:11pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Incoming Waratahs coach Michael Cheika is promising a bold new approach in his second stint in charge of NSW, adamant he will not be using the platform to audition for another crack at the Wallabies job. Flanked by assistant coaches Wycliff Palu and Stephen Hoiles at Allianz Stadium on Wednesday, Cheika also revealed a direct pitch from Rugby Australia boss Phil Waugh convinced him to take on the job he walked away from in 2015. Michael Cheika is back with the NSW Waratahs as head coach. James Brickwood Cheika – who guided NSW to the Super Rugby title in 2014 – joins the Waratahs on a one-year deal, fresh from winning the NRL premiership as an assistant coach with the Sydney Roosters. He also oversaw Lebanon’s Rugby League World Cup campaign which ended with a dramatic win over France on Sunday. “It’s more than 10 years later [since the Waratahs’ Super Rugby title] ... so I want to show them something new, right? I want to show them another way to do things that I think – I’m not guessing, I suppose, but I’m imagining that they haven’t experienced before,” Cheika said.



“There’ll be some things I’m going to do this year that I haven’t even done before. “So, yeah, I want to do things differently because I want to get a different outcome. So I think that this is a very new adventure. I’m not going back to the 2014 or 2015 playbook and trying to reinvent that at all ... as far as footy’s concerned, I want to create a new picture, a completely new picture.” Michael Cheika, with Michael Hooper, after the Waratahs won the 2014 Super Rugby Grand Final. Getty Images Since leaving the Waratahs job in 2015, Cheika coached the Wallabies and had stints in Argentina, Japan and English rugby. He is adamant he has no designs on using his time at NSW to get back into coaching Australia.



“There are no springboards [to a Wallabies coaching job], I’m coming here to get this team to try and win the comp. Isn’t that what we want to do at the end of the day? That’s it,” Cheika said. “I’ve always been like this, it’s what you do now and where you are now, how you perform, even when I was a player overseas, I’d have a one-year contract. If I play good, well, then I’m in charge. If I play rubbish, you can get rid of me. That’s fair. Michael Cheika’s 2016 Wallabies side was the last to emerge from a European tour with more wins than losses. Getty “And I’ve got to be judging my own performance here now, not on what’s happened in the past, not on what could happen in the future ... I just think I really want it to be clear that this is where I am, where my feet are, and that’s it.” Before deciding to return to the Waratahs, Cheika was not short of admirers in both rugby codes. The former Randwick player had taken Argentina to the semi-finals of the last World Cup and then steered a struggling Leicester team to a premiership final in his one season there.



Cheika revealed Waugh’s pitch on the Waratahs ultimately proved successful and said he was eager to steer them back to the finals for the first time since 2023. “I had to decide in my own head that I could do what was necessary to make the team go well. It’s not about me, it’s about the team,” Cheika said. Michael Cheika faces the media for the first time as Waratahs coach. James Brickwood. “So teams need a certain type of coach at a certain time, and that fluctuates. You may not be the right guy for that team at that time, and I had to feel like I would be the right guy for this team at this time. “And then I answered in my own head, ‘OK, this is what I think would need to get done. Can I do that? Can I, in the timeframes that I’ve got and all of that type of thing?’ And I answered to myself, ‘yes,’ obviously ...



“So I didn’t really need to be persuaded. I had to answer my own questions about, can I get the team to where we want it to be?” Another familiar face for Cheika from the Roosters is NRL star Angus Crichton, who is recovering from a foot injury and has been travelling in Europe. It is expected that Crichton will primarily play for the Waratahs at inside centre, allowing Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii to gain more experience as a winger. Angus Crichton is expected to slot into inside centre afte recovering from a foot injury. Sitthixay Ditthavong Cheika has enjoyed success with former NRL players including Israel Folau and is confident Crichton can make an impact with the Waratahs, but is putting no pressure on him. “I’m not a real big expectations man, you know, I think that because they usually only lead to regrets,” Cheika said.



Related Article Australian rugby ‘I just kept believing’: Why Kurtley Beale never gave up on a return to the Wallabies “For Angus, he’ll have his own personal ideas and goals of what he wants to achieve, and then he’ll be part of the team’s goals as well. I didn’t talk to him at all about it while we were at Roosters together ... “Angus has been playing league for a long time now, but he played rugby for a while, and I’ve got no doubts in what he’ll bring and how he’ll fit into the team, and what he’ll bring to the team off the field as well.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Friday.

World.title: It took 166 years for a trainer to nail the Cup trifecta. And Ciaron Maher’s not stopping there
World.content:
SportRacingMelbourne Cup It took 166 years for a trainer to nail the Cup trifecta. And Ciaron Maher’s not stopping there Peter Ryan November 4, 2026 — 2:06pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Ciaron Maher is daring to dream with Point Of Law, saying the Melbourne Cup winner could represent his stable overseas against the world’s best once he matures after his stunning victory on Tuesday. After a night of celebrations, Maher was not ruling anything in or out for the northern hemisphere three-year-old who exploded at the end of the two miles with a sensational turn of foot to run the quickest final 200 metres of Tuesday’s meeting. Melbourne Cup winning trainer Ciaron Maher poses with Point of Law at Werribee the morning after their win. The Age Maher, who became the first trainer to prepare a Melbourne Cup trifecta when Zahraan and Juja Kibo filled the placings, said the horse’s connections would map out a sensible plan for Point Of Law but, right now, anything was on the cards. “I always thought, if I had horse good enough, the Gold Cup [Britain’s premier staying race, run at Royal Ascot in June} would be a nice race to have a horse run in. But whether he’s up for that this year or next year or whether at all, he certainly has a few of the necessary ingredients,” Maher said.



Point of Law pokes at the Melbourne Cup which is valued at $1million. The Age He raised the prospect of Point Of Law backing up for next year’s Melbourne Cup, racing in a big Japanese race – given his bloodlines include legendary Japanese stayer Deep Impact – or taking him to Dubai as options connections would discuss over drinks when the time was right. “But we are mindful that he is still raw and has a bit of furnishing left,” Maher said. Despite having achieved almost everything there is to achieve in Australian racing, including winning the 2022 Melbourne Cup with Gold Trip, Maher shows about as much signs of slowing down as any of his stayers. He said his passion remained alive because he loved the sport and the animals.



“I love it. I am a very competitive person naturally, and I love the passion and the culture of the team, and building a team of horses. Getting them to compete on a day like that is a very rewarding feeling,” Maher said. “And [I love] that euphoria of winning.” His stable, which had a record seven runners in the Cup, along with Sydney’s Chris Waller, has led the way with their investment in sport science, horse welfare and data-driven decision-making. Loading Maher said his horses were strategically prepared and placed, taking into account all the information available. “That is the way of any business in this day and age. Everyone uses data and systems [to find] better efficiencies,” Maher said.



“I always look at the way humans are trained, like footy players, compared to the way they are trained 10 years ago. The change is huge compared to the way they used to train, and I think horse racing is no different. The only difference is obviously [a horse] can’t talk. “I am always interested in the why and the how and the science of it all both in the business and also in the horse whether it is nutrition, aerobic or anaerobic.” Point Of Law feasts from the Melbourne Cup the day after delivering the trophy for trainer Ciaron Maher. Eddie Jim That work continues for the remaining two days of the carnival, with Maher teaming up with Ethan Brown in the VRC Oaks on the tough stayer Ice Lady and then running The Everest winner Tempted up the straight in the VRC Champions Sprint. He’ll also saddle up Another Wil in the mile and front-running Cox Plate starters Land Legend and Light Infantry Man in the Champion Stakes. Maher said Ice Lady was “a super chance” in the Oaks after a less-than-ideal run in the Wakeful Stakes when she finished third.



“We went a bit solid so backing up when you go a strong tempo is not ideal, but the horse has had a great prep and I think she’ll run the trip,” Maher said. Related Article Melbourne Cup He used to ride bulls. Now he takes calls from the King and has seven Cup runners He described Tempted as exceptional, now that she has matured into a fully furnished mare. But Wednesday was about Point Of Law as he picked at grass loaded into th Melbourne Cup for the cameras. “He seems pretty good. He knows he has had a run,” Maher said.

World.title: Orbit caps off NSW polymetallic drilling with thick sulphide hit
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Orbit caps off NSW polymetallic drilling with thick sulphide hit Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Andrew Todd November 4, 2026 — 2:03pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Orbit Resources has capped off the latest drilling campaign at its Lewis Ponds gold-silver-zinc project in New South Wales with a bang, intersecting a thick 28.1-metre zone of visual sulphide mineralisation in the program’s final hole. The company says the hole drilled into its Spicer’s Lode hit the zone from 199.5m downhole, with sections containing visual estimates of up to 34 per cent semi-massive sulphides. An old shaft entrance at Orbit Resources’ Lewis Ponds precious and base metals project, in the prolific Lachlan Fold Belt of New South Wales. The intersection marks the successful completion of a four-hole resource development program, with assays for all holes, including a 3.55-metre hit at a whopping 50 per cent estimated massive sulphides, due shortly. Those sulphide minerals can host substantial concentrations of zinc, lead and copper - with some carrying up to 86 per cent of their respective base metal by weight - alongside the potential for valuable gold and silver credits.



‘Assays are needed to confirm grades and widths, but the program has delivered what it was designed to do.’ Orbit Resources managing director Jeneta Owens The drilling program was designed to lift confidence in Lewis Ponds’ existing mineral resource by upgrading sections to the higher indicated category, while also supplying fresh core for metallurgical testwork. That resource already hosts a formidable polymetallic base, sitting at 17.52 million tonnes grading 1.12 grams per tonne (g/t) gold, 53.34g/t silver, 2.06 per cent zinc and 1.1 per cent lead with copper credits. In contained terms, that works out at roughly 630,000 ounces of gold and 30.1 million ounces of silver. The company says its visual logging of the final hole identified a polymetallic sulphide assemblage of pyrite, sphalerite, galena, chalcopyrite and pyrrhotite, noting that three of the four holes drilled at its Tom’s and Spicer’s Lodes intersected visual sulphides. Orbit Resources managing director Jeneta Owens said: “Assays are needed to confirm grades and widths, but the program has delivered what it was designed to do, which was to test the continuity of the lodes within the existing resource and provide fresh core for our next round of metallurgical testwork.”



While drilling is aimed at growing the resource, a scoping study released in February has already put some impressive numbers around Lewis Ponds, outlining a base-case pre-tax net present value of $481 million and an internal rate of return of 24 per cent. However, an upside case using spot commodity prices at the time sent the potential project economics into the stratosphere, delivering a pre-tax net present value of a whopping $1.088 billion and an internal rate of return of 40 per cent. Although Lewis Ponds remains the main game, Orbit’s Narraburra ionic-clay project offers another potentially valuable card up its sleeve, despite currently being on the backburner. The renewed scramble for secure rare earth supply chains and the sharp repricing of Chinese-controlled elements have given the project’s yttrium-rich endowment a serious lift, putting its proven metallurgy back in the spotlight. With low-cost, hybrid ionic-clay characteristics and a much larger prospective footprint beyond the current resource, Narraburra has plenty of room to grow. Management believes further drilling could quickly build on the existing resource, paving the way for a scoping study to test the project’s development potential and put some hard numbers around an increasingly attractive rare earths proposition.



Stage two drilling is now complete at Lewis Ponds, leaving Orbit awaiting a fresh batch of assays before turning its attention back to the project’s latest exploration eye-catcher, the Cousin Jack base metals discovery, 350 metres southeast of the existing mineral resource. Discovery drilling in June delivered some encouraging hits, including 15m at 2.8 per cent zinc equivalent from 314m and 11m at 4.4 per cent from 584m, with a high-grade slice of 1.7m at 13.1 per cent zinc equivalent from 585.3m. The company says the pending results will feed into an updated geological model and help guide the next steps at Cousin Jack to the south, a find that could prove a company maker for Lewis Ponds. On paper at least, Lewis Ponds already has the makings of a feasible Lachlan Fold operation and with a potential billion-dollar price tag in its sights, the wait to get the rods spinning again will feel like a long one. David Jones’ private equity owners are on the precipice of appointing voluntary administrators as soon as Thursday morning after talks with major landlord Scentre fell over when the department store failed to pay rent for October. Westfield owner Scentre Group, which operates 17 shopping centres in which the prestige department store is located, rejected a restructuring proposal put forward by David Jones. A counter-proposal by Scentre was subsequently rejected by David Jones’ board of directors, according to a source close to negotiations but not authorised to speak publicly. A deal to save the 188-year-old retailer David Jones may be unwinding. Louise Kennerley David Jones’ board directors are now assessing how long the 188-year-old retailer can continue trading before it appoints a voluntary administrator, which is expected to be McGrathNichol, the source said. Chief executive Erica Berchtold and board directors Phillip Cave and Simon Woodhouse, who are executive chair and managing partner at private equity firm Anchorage Capital respectively, are convening a board meeting on Wednesday evening, with a decision on voluntary administration expected to be made by Thursday morning.



Scentre Group chief executive Elliott Rusanow said David Jones had not paid rent since October and “therefore are in breach”. Related Article Fashion retail David Jones hosted Queen Elizabeth II and Dior – but nostalgia won’t save it “We have made a generous offer to Anchorage Capital Partners that would have facilitated the continuation of David Jones trading,” Rusanow said in a statement. “That offer has disappointingly been rejected by them.” David Jones’ initial restructuring deal to Scentre Group initially proposed handing over nine stores from February, three stores kept at rents of 8 per cent of sales, five stores to continue on current terms, and for $45 million in bank guarantees unlocked in exchange for equity in David Jones. “It’s a straight financial calculation as to how they can continue trading,” the source said. “Do they meet the solvency test? They need to sit down and discuss the finances.”



David Jones’ failure to pay rent for October was a key flashpoint in why talks with Scentre Group fell over, a source said. On Wednesday, David Jones’ lender Hilco said in a statement: “Hilco Capital has had no formal update on the status of negotiations.” Hilco Capital confirmed last week that it had provided additional funding to see it through December, traditionally the most crucial time of the year for department stores. “Hilco Capital has funded above the agreed facility to allow David Jones to increase stock holdings ahead of the busy Christmas trade and sales period,” a Hilco spokesperson said. But the group was also negotiating with multiple landlords to slash its rent bill and close some loss-making stores.



Related Article Retail ‘Alarming’: David Jones workers brace for job losses as store closures loom Lease and rent costs totalled $125 million for the 2025 financial year, but its debt burden also weighed heavily on the group with finance costs totalling $153 million, financial accounts released earlier this year show. Suppliers have told this publication they are already restricting the financial terms of sales to David Jones due to lengthening payment terms. They will become unsecured creditors and potentially lose significantly on any outstanding bills if the retailer goes into administration. A spokesman for David Jones confirmed that talks between the group and Scentre failed to resolve the impasse and talks had now stopped. The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. World.title: 100,000 documents stolen from ‘isolated’ NSW Health server
World.content:
Updated NationalNSWCybersecurity 100,000 documents stolen from ‘isolated’ NSW Health server Jack Gramenz Updated November 4, 2026 — 1:23pm ,first published November 4, 2026 — 9:24am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Cybercrime detectives are probing an alleged data breach as a hacker claims they accessed about 100,000 sensitive documents from a NSW Health site used to access dental vouchers before crashing its server. Cyber Security NSW said no patient data had been impacted by the “limited” breach. A spokesperson said it affected an “isolated server” within NSW Health. NSW Police Detective Superintendent Matt Craft addresses the investigations. Nine News “No patient data has been impacted at this time nor is any patient data currently at risk,” they said. NSW Police cybercrime detectives were notified about the alleged breach about 1pm on Friday after it was discovered by NSW Health on Thursday.



Health Minister Ryan Park said authorities were made aware of the issue in “the last couple of days”, but it was not made public due to the police investigation. “They wanted to determine when that goes public,” Park said. Premier Chris Minns similarly said he was informed of the breach at the weekend. “We take advice from the experts, particularly cybersecurity intelligence experts, and they tell us when to release the information. It’s always as soon as possible, but not if it’s going to compromise a successful investigation.” Minns also has “information about the motive but not to be released yet”, and he preferred not to comment on whether any demands had been made of the government.



In a screenshot of a dark web forum post – shared by Dubai-based cyber threat intelligence platform Hackmanac early on Wednesday – a user calling themselves “bytetobreach” said they had accessed “around 100,000 sensitive documents from Australia’s NSW public health systems”. “Threat actor bytetobreach claims to have compromised NSW Health systems by exploiting a misconfigured subdomain, allegedly exfiltrating approximately 70GB of data comprising 100,000 sensitive documents dating from 2020 onwards,” Hackmanac said on social media. View post on X The documents were “snatched from a misconfigured subdomain” according to the forum post. “A full intrusion into the rest of the network was prevented when I accidentally crashed the server,” bytetobreach wrote.



“No ransom is asked from anyone affiliated with the government of Australia, and I have already sent a quick notification to the [Computer Emergency Response Team].” Hackmanac noted the claim was “pending verification”. NSW Police Cyber Crime Squad Commander Detective Superintendent Matt Craft said investigators were working to “test the veracity of that information” as they sought to identify those behind the breach. “There is an international element to this investigation, though,” Craft said. “It’s obvious to us at this stage there’s people that are outside Australia. “With cybercrime, there is no borders.”



Craft said it did not appear artificial intelligence agents played any role in the breach and defended the delay in it being publicly revealed. “There was no threat or risk to public safety, and it was about making sure that we could conduct our investigation and not be hampered or tip people off to what we may be doing,” Craft said. Park said he had been advised no patient data or information had been compromised and no risk to clinical services had been identified, but noted it remained a “live investigation”. “Things can and may, and often do in this type of incident, change,” Park said. He said the government had “very robust cybersecurity systems in place” but would continue to be challenged by hackers.



“This is an evolving criminal activity that changes all the time,” Park said. “We will need to constantly look at what we’re doing in this space, how to strengthen and harden up our systems and controls.” Get alerts on breaking news as it happens.

Caradus appeared via video at Hornsby Local Court on Wednesday morning speaking only to confirm his identity to the court, sitting through much of the hearing with his head in his hands.



The court heard that Caradus, who suffers from a string of health conditions including Type 2 Diabetes and ADHD, was taken to Auburn Hospital four days after his arrest following a “chest pain episode”. Caradus, through his lawyers, proposed to live under house arrest at his Killara property with his wife, who volunteered to accompany him on his regular medical appointments and to court. He also nominated to live with his brother, who also resides in Killara. Alan Caradus is accused of raping a 14-year-old boy under the Roseville Bridge. However, bail was rejected after the judge found his medical conditions could be appropriately managed while in custody. Caradus is expected to be transferred to a maximum security facility, ahead of appearing at the Downing Centre Local Court on December 16. Caradus began his career at The King’s School, Tudor House in 1979 and taught English, music and history for 12 years in the Southern Highlands, where he bought property with his wife.



He joined Sydney Grammar as deputy principal of its St Ives Prep School in 1992, spending more than 10 years at the selective private school before starting as head of Pittwater House’s junior school in 2003. Loading Caradus was at the Collaroy co-ed school for three years before moving to Balmain’s Inner City Montessori School, where he served as principal from January 2007 to April 2009. He ended his career at Cranbrook, working on a contract as junior school deputy headmaster that lasted until December 2009. No formal complaints by students, parents or staff against Caradus were made to The King’s School, Sydney Grammar, Montessori or Cranbrook, the schools confirmed to this masthead. Pittwater House didn’t address questions about Caradus’ employment. “We are mindful that there is an ongoing police investigation and the matter is before the court, therefore do not propose to comment further on the matter.”



Caradus gave greater time to the church after he retired from teaching in 2010. As a celebrated organist and former student of the NSW State Conservatorium of Music, he regularly tuned organs at churches across Sydney and mentored school-aged organists. He regularly attended music recitals at churches across Sydney, including at St Andrew’s Cathedral and St Paul’s College at Sydney University, at which he would support school-aged organists under his tutelage. Caradus worked as the organist at St Alban’s Church Lindfield before his arrest, and also supported musical performances at other Anglican churches in Sydney’s northern suburbs. He played a senior role at St Alban’s, including the selection of hymns for services and the music for weddings. St Alban’s didn’t respond to this masthead’s multiple requests for comment before publication. Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) or the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491. World.title: Live battleground tracker: Here’s where 11 key races stand – from Michigan to Texas
World.content:
Control of the US senate will come down to a handful of tight races.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

From Abdul El-Sayed’s headline showdown in Michigan to unexpectedly tight races in red states like Texas and Kansas, we track all the key races live as polls begin to close. Follow them live below and follow along to our full live coverage of the 2026 US midterms here. SENATE Most of the action is in the Senate races, where the Democrats need 51 seats and the Republicans need 50 (because of the tie-breaking vote owned by vice president JD Vance.) Georgia – Ossoff wins for Democrats This race is projected to be a pretty comfortable, possibly double-digit win for the Democrats. But we’re keeping our eye on it anyway because it features rising star incumbent Jon Ossoff, who’s already been linked with a run at the White House. He’s up against Republican Mike Collins.



South Carolina – polls closed This race has found the spotlight for two reasons – it’s a toss-up, and the Republican candidate Darline Graham is the sister of the late senator Lindsey Graham. She’s up against Annie Andrews in a very tight race in what’s typically a safe red state. Ohio – polls closed Ohio Democratic candidate Sherrod Brown is a former senator who chaired the Senate banking committee from 2021 to 2024, when he was a vocal critic of crypto. Ad-tracking business AdImpact says the crypto sector has spent $US68 million on defeating Brown, who is up against Republican incumbent Jon Husted in a high-stakes Senate race. Maine – polls closed



One of the last remaining moderate strongholds for Republicans, incumbent Susan Collins has historically outperformed bad polling numbers to win time and time again. But with a poor net approval rating, she faces a stiff test this time around from Troy Jackson. Texas – polls closed Democrat James Talarico, who is trying to become the first Democrat elected to the US Senate from the conservative state of Texas since 1988, has used concerns about political corruption in his campaign. He’s up against Republican candidate Ken Paxton. Kansas – polls closed A Democrat hasn’t been elected to the Senate in Kansas for 94 years – that’s something the popular pastor Adam Hamilton is hoping change. He’s looking to take down Republican Roger Marshall.



Michigan – polls closed In the swing state of Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed – a doctor, unionist and Muslim – and Republican Mike Rogers are locked in a tight race for the Senate seat being vacated by Democrat Gary Peters. Iowa – polls closed The Senate race between Republican congresswoman Ashley Hinson and Democratic state legislator Josh Turek in Iowa is something of a case study on the popularity of Trump. (Trump has, of course, asked voters to pretend he’s on the ballot these midterms, despite his weakened approval rating.)



Alaska (polls close 5pm AEDT) Surging heating fuel, electricity and grocery prices are disproportionately whacking residents of this remote, traditionally red state. Democrat Mary Peltola, who says Alaskans endure the highest healthcare costs in the country, is facing off against Republican senator Dan Sullivan, and an unaffiliated retired teacher who goes by the same name – Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. GOVERNOR Ohio This race is perhaps most notable for the bitter tone between its candidates. Republican Vivek Ramaswamy was forced to pull an attack ad, where his camp tracked down Democratic rival Amy Acton’s estranged mother Donna, who claimed her daughter to be a serial liar who couldn’t be trusted.

World.title: Vanushi Walters sees India free trade deal success hinging on first three years
World.content:
Labour foreign affairs spokesperson Vanushi Walters believes the success of New Zealand's free trade deal with India will come down to efforts made at home and abroad over the next three years.

Walters, a Sri Lankan New Zealander and former human rights lawyer, was part of discussions on the India trade deal from the opposition benches.

"My strong view is that the success of that agreement depends on the first three years ... to make sure we have an appropriately set up MFAT team on the ground [in India] and that we are engaging the Indian diaspora here to help us leverage what can be an absolutely fantastic agreement," Walters said.

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6407874875112

Walters said the deal offered substantial gains for New Zealand exporters, but it also created legal and commercial risk.

"I did look at the promotion clause of the FTA ... with a fine-tooth comb to understand what our obligations are there," she said, referring to a provision in the deal that commits New Zealand to increasing private sector investment into India by $34 billion over the next 15 years.

"I'm happy that it's a promotion clause but ... the scale of it is considerable.

"There is risk to our exporters who want to establish themselves within the Indian market that, at 15 years, it is very much a unilateral decision as to whether India believes we've achieved that promotion clause or not."

Walters has been a Labour list MP since May 2025, having previously served as the electorate MP for Upper Harbour from 2020 to 2023.

She is Labour's candidate for the newly formed Waitākere electorate this year.

As Labour's foreign affairs spokesperson and shadow attorney general, Walters is a leading candidate to become New Zealand's next foreign minister should the election bring a change of government.

Holding the foreign affairs portfolio would be incredibly symbolic in terms of senior Asian representation in office, but it's not a given even if Labour is able to form a government, as coalition agreements could ultimately determine who gets what seat in Cabinet.

Two Asian New Zealanders - Pansy Wong and Priyanca Radhakrishnan - have previously held Cabinet roles.

Wong held ethnic and women's affairs portfolios, while Radhakrishnan held portfolios relating to ethnic communities and disability issues.

Walters says she is aware of the responsibilities associated with holding the foreign affairs portfolio as someone of Sri Lankan heritage.

"It's a huge privilege and responsibility to hold the [foreign affairs] portfolio, something I take very seriously," Walters said.

"While it's up to the leader to decide where the role sits [after the election], it's certainly one I would like to hold," she said.

"I do see and hear from community members that it means a lot to have me in the role," she said.

"There is a desire in our communities to see political leadership across different portfolios … [and be given] a seat around the table … not only in portfolios that directly affect the ethnic communities but some broader ones as well."

Vanushi Walters is Labour's candidate for the newly formed Waitākere electorate. RNZ / Blessen Tom

Early years

Walters was 6 years old when her family moved to New Zealand in 1987, having left Sri Lanka and spending some time in Zambia.

While she always felt like a typical Kiwi kid, Walters recounted a "jarring" experience with racism she had as a child, noting how it shaped her approach to life based on context and empathy.

"I was walking to my mother's office after school one day," she said.

"I would have been very young, 6 or 7 ... somewhere in that range. I remember being followed by a Pākehā man in a suit who said, 'Go back to your country, you don't belong here'.

"He repeatedly followed me for a while. It was quite jarring.

"I told my mother [later that day] and what she said always stuck with me.

"She took a breath and said, 'That poor man, just think about the life that he's had, that he would speak to a small child that way'."

Walters described a previous Labour-led government's decision to elevate the Office of Ethnic Communities from an office to a ministry as a "significant achievement".

She was an advocate for the Ethnic Diversity Fund, which she said helped communities celebrate and express their cultures while building stronger connections with mainstream New Zealand.

Walters believed social cohesion and racism should be addressed through lived experience, community participation and attention to issues such as bullying in schools instead of relying on legislative change.

Vanushi Walters believes the prime minister is jointly responsible for foreign policy alongside the minister holding the portfolio. RNZ / Blessen Tom

Foreign perspective

Walters highlighted the broad historical consensus among political parties on both sides of the aisle on trade, security and defence.

However, she also noted times when parties butted heads on certain issues, referencing historical moments such as the contentious Springbok tours of the 1970s, the nuclear-free movement of the '80s and the decision to refuse sending troops to Iraq.

Walters said she had a lot of respect for Winston Peters in his role as foreign minister in the most recent parliamentary term.

"I have respect for him in terms of some of the work he has done … including, I would say, in the first half of this term, where he has done a lot in the Pacific and he has developed relationships.

"He has travelled extensively and ensured that we're maintaining our relationships.

"And he's done a lot of good work in terms of protecting the overall budget of Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade at a very critical time, including the aid budget.

"So, there is a lot of good he has done."

However, she also pointed to times when Peters appeared to clash with Prime Minister Christopher Luxon on some international issues.

"At the start of the term, there have been times when [Peters] has called out human rights issues, including in relation to Gaza.

"But that hasn't been consistent. We've seen this very messy foreign policy where we clearly have disagreement between the prime minister and the minister of foreign affairs on some issues and silence from New Zealand on critical issues."

(A spokesperson for Peters said the minister had conducted his portfolio in accordance with the New Zealand government's foreign policy.)

Walters claimed the coalition government had appeared to move New Zealand closer to alignment with the United States and away from an independent position on foreign policy.

She pointed to New Zealand's failure to take stronger positions on Palestinian statehood and sanctions against Israel as examples of this.

(Peters' spokesperson rejected such characterisations on Palestinian statehood, adding that New Zealand had a clear and consistent track record of taking strong sanctions against Israel.)

Broadly speaking, Walters believes the prime minister is jointly responsible for foreign policy alongside the minister holding the portfolio.

"These are decisions about New Zealand's reputation," she said.

World.title: Fire engulfs large building in Christchurch
World.content:
Firefighters have controlled a blaze that engulfed a large building and sent out plumes of smoke near central Christchurch.

Emergency services were called to the fire at a single-storey building on Brisbane Street in Sydenham about 11.30am on Wednesday.

The fire was contained to a 60 by 60 metre building and was not expected to spread.

Fire and Emergency said the cause of the fire was being investigated as crews work to fully extinguish any remaining fire.

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6407872084112

Earlier in the day, a spokesperson said the building was "fully involved in fire" but all people were accounted for.

Health New Zealand advised people affected by smoke to contact their GP or call Healthline for free.

RNZ / Tim Brown

The fire caused traffic to back up for several blocks in some parts of central Christchurch.

World.title: Visionary or conman? The legacy of Bougainville's self-proclaimed King Musingku
World.content:
The recent death of the self-proclaimed King of Papaala, Noah Musingku, has prompted discussion over whether this famous, reclusive Bougainvillean was a visionary or a conman.

Musingku, who died last month in the autonomous Papua New Guinea region of Bougainville, was the mastermind behind the infamous U-Vistract finance scheme, in which many investors from the Pacific lost money.

The prevailing, somewhat comic image of a tiny King in a makeshift crown and British army regalia enhances the impression of a crackpot fraud, but people who knew Musingku from an early age claim he was someone with vision who tried to help others.

Noah Musingku OCCRP / Aubrey Belford

Dennis Lokonai, an administrator with Bougainville's Four Square Church and a former minister in the Autonomous Bougainville Government (ABG) until last year, studied alongside Noah Musingku through school and university and described him as creative and intelligent.

"He was a person who tried to invent new ways or new things. For example, I remember when we were in high school, he had a special handwriting which he developed by himself, kind of a sign writing like the Asian type of handwriting, like Chinese."

At Unitech in the PNG city of Lae, Musingku became president of the Student Representative Council, showing his leadership qualities at an early stage. Lokonai said he saw how his friend was a generous Christian.

"In our university days, we used to receive a 13 kina allowance every fortnight. So while we, the other students, struggled to save money, Noah was able to set aside some tithe or offering, which he used to assist people in need or even contribute to the church."

A former president of Bougainville, James Tanis, also studied with Musingku and echoed Lokonai's points about him, his unique talents and deep faith, saying they remained friends.

"That's why years later when I became [ABG] President, I was able to visit him to encourage him to respect the [Bougainville] Peace Process. Which he did," Tanis explained.

U-turn

In Port Moresby in the 1990s, Musingku developed the U-Vistract scheme, which promised large returns for investors and created his own currency, the Bougainville Kina.

U-Vistract is described as having started out as a Ponzi scheme that ended up more of a "millenarian religious cult" by Aubrey Belford, the Asia Pacific editor of the Organised Crime and Corruption Reporting Project (OCCRP).

"Right from the beginning, this scheme used a lot of the language and symbolism of evangelical Christianity, but that was secondary to the get-rich-quick promise," Belford, who visited Musingku in his remote haven last year to interview him, told RNZ Pacific.

"I think Musingku's main legacy is the thousands of people whose money he took who he left with nothing. Most people who got caught up in U-Vistract worked out sooner or later that they had been conned."

Dennis Lokonai told RNZ Pacific that Musingku didn't set out trying to scam people.

"Noah was a good person, he had a good initiative to start, but later things got complicated because of legal implications in regard to banking and all financial systems couldn't allow him to operate something outside of the law.

"So that was why he was later termed as a conman, and all those things were said to him - but I think Noah had a good intention to start something good to help the people.

Noah Musingku Anthony Kaybing / ABG

Crypto parallels

Musingku was quoted over the years denouncing the global financial system - much like the pioneers of cryptocurrency, he was trying to build a new system and an alternative currency.

Belford noted that Musingku's scheme had some parallels with cryptocurrency, including that his currency was intended to replace the idea of government 'fiat' money.

"In fact, when he first started really pushing the currency and his International Bank of Me'ekamui he actually advertised that he accepted deposits in a whole number of digital currencies -- which weren't based on cryptography -- that existed before Bitcoin.

"But whereas crypto is all about saying that a public bit of mathematics is the basis of a currency, Musingku went with an older idea that also has a fair bit of power among modern right-wing libertarians, that money should be based on gold."

Lokonai said while he himself lost money invested in Musingku's scheme, some early investors did well out of U-Vistract

"We witnessed a lot of people who were helped through that system when they actually withdrew their funds, which they they used to support themselves, build houses, ome built churches, some even bought cars through that money they got from that that system."

The U-Vistract scheme was shut down by PNG authorities in 2000, after which, Musingku fled to Solomon Islands and then back to Bougainville.

Noah Musingku died last month in the autonomous Papua New Guinea region of Bougainville. OCCRP / Aubrey Belford

Becoming King

Forced to retreat to the interior of Bougainville to avoid the arm of the law, Musingku pivoted.

He proclaimed himself King David Pei II of the Kingdom of Papaala in 2004, and later returned to his home village of Tonu in South Bougainville to reign as a king with a group of armed loyalists protecting him.

"As Musingku's scheme fell apart ... the whole thing became more overtly about almost apocalyptic religiosity and grand promises about Bougainvillean independence," Belford explained.

As Bougainville navigated the peace process with PNG, Musingku was not aloof to the process in the way that the Bougainville independence leader Francis Ona was.

Ona's breakaway Me'ekamui-controlled territory in Bougainville had provided Musingku with refuge immediately after he fled PNG authorities, and before he set up his stronghold in Tonu.

Tanis said that Musingku displayed an openness to support Bougainville's pursuit of independence, as it approached the 2019 referendum in which 97.7 percent of Bougainvilleans voted for independence from PNG

"I made a second visit to him during the referendum preparations, to encourage him to allow his supporters to enrol and vote," Tanis told RNZ Pacific.

"He listened to me again. I was able to talk to him because I had no issues against him personally. Most that hated him are his own investors of U-Vistract."

Former Bougainville president and External Relations Directorate international legate James Tanis speaks with delegates at ANU State of the Pacific conference in Canberra, pictured on 5 September 2024. BenarNews / Stefan Armbruster

Musingku's long-term followers and the few remaining U-Vistract investors still holding out hope for a return overlapped as his core base.

"So they were continuing to follow him up until his passing, because they were told that their money was still there and they would receive their money," Lokonai explained.

He said that it's not clear whether Musingku's movement will continue now that he is dead, or if there is a successor.

Belford said although Musingku never got held to account for his investment misdeeds, he ended up as a prisoner of sorts anyway.

"He spent the rest of his life basically hemmed in, in his own dingy complex, giving sermons every week and sending out emails with the same promise that the big payout was going to come next week.

World.title: 'Disappointing': Electoral Commission fixes issues with voter enrolments
World.content:
The Electoral Commission has added around 6,300 people to the electoral roll, after it revealed an issue last week with how enrolment eligibility was processed for thousands of people on residence class visas.

"We are sorry that this breakdown in our processes was a barrier to enrolling for this group," says the Chief Electoral Officer Karl Le Quesne, adding it was "disappointing" it had occurred.

Le Quesne said the EC had established last week that some people with residence class visas who had applied to enrol had been asked to provide information on their immigration status when they didn't need to.

"Our system should have flagged that they were eligible to enrol."

He said their team worked to identify who had submitted valid applications to enrol. Those people have now been notified they are enrolled and can vote.

The investigations also identified approximately 1,200 people who were added to the electoral roll when they "should not have been."

"They are people who were on a temporary entry class visa, such as a work visa, or their visa had expired.

"Their applications should have been flagged as ineligible due to their visa status."

They will be removed from the roll before the official count, he confirmed, and notified in writing.

"If they have already voted in the election, their vote will be disallowed."

The EC will continue to work on the matter, and there could be a small change in the numbers reported of those affected.

"Our priority is to communicate with those affected and fix this problem so that it does not happen again," said Le Quesne.

Audio player for " Overhangs, gangs, rogue-ish polls, & the most unpredictable electorate " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/politics_election-2026/2333956%2Fdisappointing-electoral-commission-fixes-issues-with-voter-enrolments

"We have strengthened our integrity checks since the last election and it is disappointing that this has occurred, but people can still have confidence in the overall quality of the electoral roll for this election."

World.title: Patient breached leave twice before murder, inquest hears
World.content:
A mental health patient twice breached the conditions of his unescorted leave in the weeks before he murdered a woman in 2022, an inquest has heard.

Laisa Waka Tunidau was stabbed to death by Zakariye Mohamed Hussein outside her Sockburn home on 25 June 2022, while Hussein was on unescorted leave from Hillmorton Hospital. Hussein was jailed for life, with a 13-year non-parole period, in November that year, and had previously been jailed for more than six years for kidnapping, stabbing and intimidating people across Christchurch in March 2012.

The second phase of an inquest into Waka Tunidau's death resumed in Christchurch on Wednesday before coroner Alexandra Cunninghame. A psychiatrist who treated Hussein between 2015 and 2022 continued giving evidence on Wednesday. The clinician's identity is suppressed.

Counsel assisting the coroner Stephanie Grieve KC questioned the clinician about how decisions were made to allow Hussein unescorted leave. The court heard Hussein went to locations without permission while on unescorted community leave on 6 June and 10 June 2022.

"[After] the second incident on the 10th of June there wasn't any consequence of that, was there, imposed in terms of a step back of his leave?" Grieve asked.

"No there wasn't," the clinician said.

"There was a discussion with the team in consideration of what it meant and where the risks were at, but there wasn't a consequence."

The clinician said mental health services did not operate on the basis that a patient should be punished for doing something wrong.

"If you're saying to me should a mental health patient who breaches leave two times in four days should there always be a consequence, my answer is no. There should be a considered assessment."

The court heard clinicians were also considering increasing Hussein's leave.

"At that time that was the decision we'd come to that these weren't indicators of increased risk and that things were going generally well for him," the clinician said.

"If you asked me with hindsight then it would've been great to have stopped all his leave and changed everything radically. We weren't to know what was going to happen."

Counsel assisting the coroner Stephanie Grieve KC. RNZ / Nate McKinnon

The court heard Hussein had also been involved in several incidents in the month before the killing in which he became angry, including throwing water at another patient and swearing at staff. The clinician accepted the incidents were relevant to assessing risk, but said they needed to be considered alongside Hussein's overall progress.

"The key thing is you're looking at the wider picture and the knowledge that you've built of someone over seven years," they said.

The clinician said there had been "a lot of really positive things" about how Hussein was doing from late April through May and June, including his ability to talk to staff and work through difficult situations.

"In of itself incidents of irritation or those things that are documented, that's the thoroughness of the staff doing a great job of documenting things, but many of those were small things."

The clinician said the team's view at the time was that Hussein was making good progress.

"Right now we sit here with this tragic event having happened, so of course we want to go back and do things differently, but the team sitting in that moment, with all the structures that we had, our weekly MDT [multidisciplinary team meetings], our case conference in February, our risk management care plan that considered his risks, that's where we were at that time."

World.title: TAIC investigating fatal plane crash near Nelson
World.content:
The Transport Accident Investigation Commission says it is opening an inquiry into a fatal plane crash near Nelson.

Two people died in the crash.

The Cessna plane left the city at about 9.10am on Tuesday and was reported overdue just before midday.

Nelson area commander Steven Collins said the wreckage was found in a remote area, south of Castor Peak.

Police were working with the Civil Aviation Authority to recover the bodies and examine the crash scene.

Cloud on Wednesday morning had hampered efforts to retrieve the two bodies.

A Defence Force spokesperson said a Royal New Zealand Air Force NH90 and crew flew police and Fire and Emergency staff to the crash site on Wednesday morning, and the NH90 had been tasked to assist with recovering the bodies.

Flight tracking data on the website FlightRadar24 showed a Cessna Skyhawk taking off from Nelson Airport at 9.10am and flying into the hills near Whangamoa before its tracking data stopped.

Nelson mayor Nick Smith said the plane got to an altitude of 3100ft but suddenly dropped to 1800ft when it was lost off radar near the Bryant Range, 35 km north east of Nelson.

Nelson Aero Club confirmed it was not one of its planes.

World.title: Nine children sent to Wellington Hospital after head gasket blew on school bus
World.content:
Nine Wainuiomata Primary School students were taken to hospital after smoke and fumes filled a bus on the way to a Kapa Haka event at Te Papa Museum on Wednesday.

Emergency services were called to Cable Street following reports of a bus fire at about 10am.

Fire and Emergency assistant district commander Matt Franklin said 44 people were on the bus headed for the city when the bus appeared to blow a head gasket on the Wellington motorway.

"There's been fumes inside the cabin of the bus. [The students] were transferred to another bus and some have presented with respiratory problems on arrival at Te Papa.

"Steam based, oil has been aspirated…respiratory and abdominal complaints," Franklin said.

Wainuiomata Primary School principal Allison Burdon was on her way to Wellington when she was contacted about the breakdown.

RNZ understands school children were gathered near a cordon at the scene of an incident unfolding near Te Papa Museum in Wellington. RNZ/Samuel Rillstone

"There was fumes and smoke and they evacuated the bus. I arrived just as they arrived and I called 111 just as a precaution," Burdon said.

Emergency services sprang into action and four fire trucks, a Hazardous Materials unit as well as police and several ambulances rushed to the scene on the promenade outside Te Papa.

Health New Zealand said the nine children were receiving treatment and close monitoring following the incident.

Supplied / Jess Gessner

Speaking from Wellington Hospital, Burdon said she hoped all would be discharged without having to spend the night.

She said some were still complaining of "sore tummies" and skin irritations where they had been splashed by what RNZ understood to be engine coolant.

But Burdon said, overall, the student's spirits were high.

"They're excited that they've made the news. They're all in a ward area of ED and they're talking to each other. They're bright as buttons."

Burdon said the remainder of the group would still take the stage at Wednesday's Kapa Haka event with their fellow students at the front of their minds.

"They're going to perform and do it for their mates that can't perform with them," she said.

Fire and Emergency crews left the scene at about 11.45am.

World.title: Investigation launched after train derails near Ōtira Tunnel
World.content:
A loaded KiwiRail coal train derailed as it was approaching the Ōtira Tunnel yesterday, leaving the Midland Line - which runs between Rolleston and Greymouth - closed with extensive damage.

The Transport Accident Investigation Commission have launched an inquiry into the derailment, which happened at about 10pm Tuesday.

The coal train was heading towards Christchurch when the last wagon derailed.

The train stopped inside the Ōtira Tunnel, with extensive damage to the train and rail infrastructure. There were no injuries to the crew reported.

KiwiRail manager engineering Lynne Morton said it was assessing the extent of the damage and repairs needed.

"We are working to restore the line as quickly and safely as possible."

She said today's TranzAlpine service would only operate as far as Arthur's Pass, and services were likely to be affected for the next few days.

"Affected passengers will be contacted directly and offered rebooking or refund options. Replacement buses will be arranged where possible."

"KiwiRail is also working closely with affected freight customers to manage the disruption."

TAIC chief investigator of accidents Louise Cook said a team of investigators had been appointed to gather evidence.

"Our investigators would typically spend two to three days on site. Their first priority is to gather evidence while it is available. That includes examining and mapping the train and the scene, and speaking with people who witnessed the accident or were involved."

She said the commission's investigators will examine the locomotive, rolling stock and rail infrastructure, secure data and maintenance records, and interview the train crew and other staff of the operator.

World.title: Gold Coast triple header as Tszyu goes for two-weight glory
World.content:
Tim Tszyu will headline a stacked triple-header boxing card at Robina Stadium on the Gold Coast.

The 32-year-old will look to become a two-weight world champion when he takes on Cuban-American fighter Erislandy Lara for the WBA middleweight world title on December 13.

That is one of three all-star fights to take place on the night though, with former undisputed super welterweight world champion Jermell Charlo (35-2-1) stepping into the ring for the first time in three years when he takes on Australian power puncher Brock Jarvis (23-1).

Liam Wilson (18-3) will also meet Elnur Samedov (22-1) for the WBA super featherweight world title.

"This is the biggest and best fight card in Australia, full stop," No Limit Boxing chief executive George Rose said.

"A reigning world champion, a former undisputed world champion and two world titles, in a stadium on the Gold Coast. Nothing else comes close."

Tszyu (28-3) has enjoyed a career resurgence since stepping up to middleweight, winning his last three fights at the weight following a run of three defeats in four at light middleweight.

The Australian was crowned WBO light middleweight champion on the Gold Coast in 2023, defeating Brian Mendoza after being elevated from interim champion in the lead up.

His last stadium fight took place in Townsville against Jeff Horn in 2020.

Tim Tszyu is the WBO International Super Middleweight Title holder. (Getty Images: Jeremy Ng)

"This is what I live for," Tszyu said in a statement.

"Lara is a great champion and one of the most avoided fighters in the world. That is exactly why I wanted him. Spence was the first step. This is the one that matters.

"Queensland and the Gold Coast have always backed me.

"I'm ready to take that belt off Lara on the Gold Coast."

Lara (32-3-3), the 43-year-old veteran southpaw, is a two-division world champion and has been the WBA middleweight world champion since 2021.

The former amateur world champion has made four successful defences of the belt, including knocking out Michael Zerafa in two rounds in Las Vegas in 2024.

"Tim Tszyu wanted the best middleweight in the world," Rose said.

"And we got him."

Lara, like Tszyu, has three career defeats, all via the scorecards, losing by majority decision to Paul Williams and split decision defeats to Canelo Álvarez and Jarrett Hurd.

"I'm going to Australia with one goal … to defend my title, put on a great performance and give the fans a fight they'll remember for a long time," Lara said.

Charlo was supposed to fight Tszyu in 2023 before a broken hand scuppered those plans.

Jermell Charlo (right) has not fought in three years. (Getty Images: Sarah Stier)

The then WBA, WBC, IBF and WBO light middleweight champion had been set to fight Tszyu despite the hand injury, only for him to repeatedly delay and ultimately pull out to face Álvarez at super middleweight instead.

Charlo famously said fighting Tszyu "does nothing for my career" by way of explanation, however fighting and losing to Álvarez ultimately cost the American all four of his belts, with the 36-year-old looking to restart his career in Australia.

"I've heard all the talk, and now it's time to remind everybody why Jermell Charlo is still him," Charlo said.

"I'm willing to fight on a co-main event all the way in Australia because that's how hungry I am. I've got so much in me and I wasn't going to let this year end without giving my fans what they've been waiting for."

Jarvis, who has 21 knock out wins in his 24 fights, said his aim was to "ruin" Charlo's comeback.

In the other world title fight, Liam Wilson (18-3), who fought at the Commonwealth Games on the Gold Coast in 2018, will meet Azerbaijani fighter Samedov.

Liam Wilson has twice challenged for the world title. (Getty Images: Chris Hyde)

Wilson is a two-time world title challenger who came agonisingly close to winning the world title in 2023 and 2024 against Emanuel Navarrete and Oscar Valdez respectively.

"I have chased this shot around the world," Wilson said.

"My career hasn't been easy but I've felt the love from fans every step of the way. I have never backed down from anyone and I am not starting now.

"Samedov is the champion. Good. Taking it off the champion means more.

"I boxed for Australia on the Gold Coast at the Commonwealth Games almost a decade ago. Now, I get the chance to win a world title in the same city. You can't not love that."

World.title: NZ teammates stunned as Ponga eyes return 22 days after breaking arm
World.content:
Teammates are marvelling at Kalyn Ponga's resilience as the New Zealand game changer eyes a miracle World Cup return 22 days after breaking an arm.

After being named on an extended bench, Ponga and fellow Newcastle fan favourite Phoenix Crossland could spell double trouble for Tonga in Saturday night's semifinal at Newcastle's McDonald Jones Stadium.

Ponga played with his injury for more than 20 minutes during New Zealand's epic tournament-opening 24-22 loss to Australia before undergoing surgery in the hope of returning for the finals.

A month after playing together in Newcastle's 19-18 NRL grand final loss to the Sydney Roosters, centre Dane Gagai is backing the former Dally M Medallist to terrorise Tonga in what would be a huge boost for the Kiwis.

Ponga (left) played over 20 minutes with a broken arm against Australia earlier in the World Cup. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

"That'll just come down to the boxes he'll have to tick with the physios and stuff, but one thing that's never in question is Kalyn's toughness, and I don't think he gets enough credit or praise for it," Gagai said.

"Some of the games, he's played with injury. It was only maybe a year or two ago with his AC and getting that injected, but he'll put his head in most places that people won't put their hands.

"So I've got no doubt he'll do everything he can to make sure he can take that field. It's just a case of whether he can tick those boxes, and he'll know whether he's capable of playing or not.

"He won't put himself before the team, but we'd obviously love to have him out there."

Phoenix Crossland could potentially return for his first game since being suspended after the preliminary final. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

Crossland could also be a late inclusion after completing a four-game suspension for a hip-drop tackle that broke Nathan Cleary's ankle in Newcastle's preliminary final victory over Penrith.

Knowing New Zealand will need their strongest possible line-up to keep Tonga at bay, Gagai has also welcomed the prospect of the classy hooker featuring in the do-or-die showdown.

"He's come in a bit later into camp, but even though he wasn't playing, he's he's always himself and brings a lot of energy," Gagai said.

"He's awesome to have around the place. It's going to be good to be able to chuck this jersey on with him and nice to know that the game against Penrith wasn't our last together.

"So I'm definitely looking forward to that and I'm super happy for him."

AAP

World.title: Man United claims comeback win after fans launch tennis balls in protest
World.content:
Manchester United has staged a stunning comeback to recover from its worst start to a European home game by beating Roma 3-2 in the UEFA Champions League.
